Carbon shows the property of catenation (forming long chains with itself) to the maximum extent, and this power decreases down the group. The group shows a gradual change from non-metals at the top to metals at the bottom.

Key Points

  • Group 14 (IVA) is the carbon family: C, Si, Ge, Sn and Pb.
  • All have four valence electrons, ns2 np2, and are tetravalent.
  • Their compounds are mainly covalent.
  • Catenation is strongest in carbon and decreases down the group.
  • Metallic character increases down the group.

mcqs.q: Which elements form Group 14, the carbon family?
options: C, Si, Ge, Sn and Pb
Na, Mg, Al, Si and P
F, Cl, Br, I and At
Be, Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba
mcqs.why: Group 14 (IVA) is the carbon family: carbon, silicon, germanium, tin and lead, in that order down the group.

mcqs.q: What is the general valence configuration of Group 14?
mcqs.why: All Group 14 elements have four valence electrons with general configuration ns2 np2, so they are tetravalent.

mcqs.q: How many valence electrons does each Group 14 element have?
mcqs.why: Each has four electrons in its valence shell, for example carbon is 2s2 2p2 and lead is 6s2 6p2 in the table.

mcqs.q: What type of compounds do Group 14 elements mainly form?
mcqs.why: Because they are tetravalent with ns2 np2 configuration, Group 14 elements form mainly covalent compounds, as the notes state.

mcqs.q: What is catenation and which element shows it most?
options: Forming long chains with itself; carbon shows it to the maximum extent
Forming ions; lead shows it most
Reacting with water; tin shows it most
Losing electrons; silicon shows it most
mcqs.why: Catenation is forming long chains with itself; carbon shows it to the maximum extent and this power decreases down the group.

mcqs.q: How does character change down Group 14?
options: Metal to non-metal up the group only
Gradual change from non-metals at the top to metals at the bottom
mcqs.why: The group shows a gradual change from non-metals at the top to metals at the bottom as you go down Group 14.

mcqs.q: What are the electrons in shells for silicon (atomic number 14)?
mcqs.why: Silicon, atomic number 14, has electrons in shells 2, 8, 4 and valence configuration 3s2 3p2, as listed in the table.

mcqs.q: What is the atomic number of lead?
mcqs.why: Lead has atomic number 82, with shells 2, 8, 18, 32, 18, 4 and valence configuration 6s2 6p2 in the Group 14 table.

mcqs.q: What term describes Group 14 elements having four bonds/valency?
mcqs.why: They are tetravalent because they have four valence electrons, ns2 np2, and typically use all four in covalent bonding.

mcqs.q: How does catenation change down Group 14?
mcqs.why: Carbon shows catenation to the maximum extent and this power decreases down the group towards tin and lead.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Group 14 Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in Melting and Boiling Points

The melting and boiling points of Group 14 elements decrease down the group. This is due to the increase in atomic size and the decrease in inter-atomic forces.

ElementCSiGeSnPb
Melting Point (°C)35501420945232327
Boiling Point (°C)48302480285026231751

The melting and boiling points of carbon and silicon are very high because they have tendencies to form macromolecules (giant structures). Tin has the lowest melting point of the group (232°C); the melting point rises slightly again at lead (327°C).

Trends from Non-metal to Metal

Metallic character increases down the group. Carbon and silicon are non-metals, germanium is a semimetal (metalloid), and tin and lead are metals. The electrical properties of silicon are similar to those of a semimetal, which is why silicon is used as a semiconductor.

Key Points

  • Melting and boiling points generally decrease down Group 14 as atomic size increases and inter-atomic forces weaken.
  • Carbon (3550°C) and silicon (1420°C) melt very high because of their giant structures.
  • Tin has the lowest melting point of the group, 232°C.
  • Carbon and silicon are non-metals, germanium is a semimetal, and tin and lead are metals.

mcqs.q: How do melting and boiling points generally change down Group 14?
options: Decrease down the group due to larger size and weaker inter-atomic forces
mcqs.why: Melting and boiling points decrease down the group due to increase in atomic size and decrease in inter-atomic forces.

mcqs.q: Why do carbon and silicon have very high melting points?
options: They are metals with free electrons only
They tend to form macromolecules (giant structures)
mcqs.why: Carbon (3550 °C) and silicon (1420 °C) melt very high because they have tendencies to form macromolecules, i.e. giant structures.

mcqs.q: Which Group 14 element has the lowest melting point and what is it?
mcqs.why: Tin has the lowest melting point of the group at 232 °C; the melting point rises slightly again at lead to 327 °C.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between carbon's melting point (3550 °C) and tin's (232 °C)?
mcqs.why: Difference = 3550 °C - 232 °C = 3318 °C. Carbon's giant structure gives it a far higher melting point than tin.

mcqs.q: How does metallic character change down Group 14?
mcqs.why: Metallic character increases down the group: carbon and silicon are non-metals, germanium is a semimetal, and tin and lead are metals.

mcqs.q: Which Group 14 element is a semimetal (metalloid)?
options: Silicon as the named semimetal in the trend list
mcqs.why: In the trend list, germanium is the semimetal (metalloid), between non-metals carbon and silicon above and metals tin and lead below.

mcqs.q: Why is silicon used as a semiconductor?
options: Its electrical properties are similar to those of a semimetal
mcqs.why: The notes say the electrical properties of silicon are similar to those of a semimetal, which is why silicon is used as a semiconductor.

mcqs.q: What is lead's melting point compared with tin's?
mcqs.why: Lead melts at 327 °C, slightly higher than tin's 232 °C, even though the general trend down the group is decreasing.

mcqs.q: What is carbon's boiling point in the table?
mcqs.why: Carbon's boiling point is listed as 4830 °C, with a melting point of 3550 °C, the highest values in Group 14.

mcqs.q: Which pair are the Group 14 metals?
mcqs.why: Tin and lead are the metals of Group 14, while carbon and silicon are non-metals and germanium is a semimetal.

lessons.title: Oxidation States of Group 14 Elements and the Inert Pair Effect
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group IVA have four electrons in their valence shells and they have an oxidation state of +4. The first three elements may also have an oxidation state of -4 when they are bonded to more electropositive elements. Tin (Sn) and lead (Pb) also show an oxidation state of +2, which is the only oxidation state in which they produce ionic compounds.

The stability of the +4 oxidation state decreases and that of the +2 oxidation state increases on moving down the group. For example, the compounds of Ge2+ are less stable than Ge4+. The compounds of Ge2+ act as strong reducing agents, while those of Ge4+ act as oxidizing agents. On the other hand, the compounds of Pb2+ (for example PbCl2) are more stable than those of Pb4+ (for example PbCl4). The compounds of Pb2+ are ionic and more common than those of Pb4+, and the compounds of Pb4+ act as oxidizing agents.

Inert Pair Effect and the Nature of Bond

The tendency of the ns2 electrons of the valence shell of metallic elements to remain unshared or unionized is called the inert pair effect. The ability of an electron to get closer to the nucleus is called penetration. The penetration power of the s-orbital is the maximum, and it experiences stronger attraction to the nucleus. As a result, the s-electrons fail to participate in bond formation, so the ns2 electrons need more energy to remove. Hence, the oxidation states of the heavier elements (especially the last two elements of Groups IIIA, IVA, VA and VIA) are two less than what would be expected.

Key Points

  • Group 14 elements show the +4 oxidation state; C, Si and Ge can also show -4 with electropositive elements.
  • Sn and Pb also show +2, the state in which they form ionic compounds.
  • Down the group, +4 becomes less stable and +2 becomes more stable.
  • Ge(II) compounds are reducing agents; Pb(II) compounds (like PbCl2) are the stable, common ones and Pb(IV) compounds are oxidizing agents.
  • The inert pair effect is the reluctance of the ns2 pair to take part in bonding, caused by the strong penetration of s-electrons.

mcqs.q: What is the main oxidation state of Group 14 elements?
mcqs.why: Group IVA elements have four valence electrons and have an oxidation state of +4, using all four electrons in bonding.

mcqs.q: Which Group 14 elements can also show -4, and with what partners?
options: The first three, when bonded to more electropositive elements
mcqs.why: The first three elements may also have an oxidation state of -4 when bonded to more electropositive elements, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which elements also show +2, and what is special about that state for them?
options: C and Si; their only gaseous state
Sn and Pb; the only state in which they produce ionic compounds
mcqs.why: Tin and lead also show +2, which is the only oxidation state in which they produce ionic compounds, according to the lesson.

mcqs.q: How do stabilities of +4 and +2 change down Group 14?
options: +4 stability decreases and +2 stability increases down the group
mcqs.why: Down the group the stability of +4 decreases and that of +2 increases, an effect explained by the inert pair effect.

mcqs.q: How do Ge(II) and Ge(IV) compounds behave?
options: Ge2+ compounds are less stable and act as strong reducing agents; Ge4+ act as oxidizing agents
mcqs.why: Ge2+ compounds are less stable than Ge4+, act as strong reducing agents, while Ge4+ compounds act as oxidizing agents.

mcqs.q: Which lead compounds are more stable and common?
options: Pb2+ compounds like PbCl2, which are ionic and more common
mcqs.why: Pb2+ compounds such as PbCl2 are more stable, ionic and more common than Pb4+ compounds; Pb4+ compounds act as oxidizing agents.

mcqs.q: What is the inert pair effect?
options: Loss of all s electrons easily
Tendency of ns2 electrons to remain unshared or unionized
Attraction of bond pairs by fluorine
mcqs.why: The inert pair effect is the tendency of the ns2 electrons of metallic elements to remain unshared or unionized and not take part in bonding.

mcqs.q: Why does the inert pair effect occur, in terms of penetration?
options: s-orbital penetration is maximum, so s electrons are strongly attracted and need more energy to remove
mcqs.why: s-orbital penetration is maximum and experiences stronger attraction to the nucleus, so ns2 electrons need more energy to remove and fail to participate.

mcqs.q: By how much are oxidation states of heavier elements reduced by the inert pair effect?
options: Two less than what would be expected
mcqs.why: Hence oxidation states of heavier elements are two less than expected, e.g. Pb shows +2 instead of only the group state +4.

mcqs.q: For which groups/elements is the inert pair effect especially noted?
options: The last two elements of Groups IIIA, IVA, VA and VIA
mcqs.why: The notes say it applies especially to the last two elements of Groups IIIA, IVA, VA and VIA, explaining their lower oxidation states.

lessons.title: Chlorides of Carbon, Silicon and Lead
lessons.notes_html:
Preparation of Tetrachlorides

Carbon tetrachloride (CCl4) is prepared by the chlorination of methane (or of carbon disulphide):

CH4 + 4Cl2 → CCl4 + 4HCl

Silicon tetrachloride (SiCl4) is prepared by heating silicon with chlorine, or by passing chlorine over a heated mixture of silica and carbon:

Si + 2Cl2 → SiCl4

Lead chlorides: lead (II) chloride is prepared by precipitation, for example:

Pb(NO3)2 + 2HCl → PbCl2 + 2HNO3

Thermal Stability

CCl4 is stable to heat. PbCl4 is unstable and decomposes on heating to the more stable PbCl2, because of the inert pair effect, which favours the +2 state of lead:

PbCl4 → PbCl2 + Cl2 (on heating)

Reactions with Water (Hydrolysis)

CCl4 does not hydrolyse in water: it is stable and does not react. SiCl4, in contrast, hydrolyses readily and vigorously in water:

SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl

This difference exists because silicon is a larger atom and can accept a lone pair from water into its vacant d-orbitals, while the small carbon atom in CCl4 is fully shielded by the four chlorine atoms and has no vacant d-orbital available.

Key Points

  • CCl4 is made by chlorinating methane; SiCl4 by heating silicon (or silica with carbon) in chlorine.
  • PbCl2 is made by precipitation; PbCl4 is unstable and decomposes to PbCl2 and Cl2 on heating (inert pair effect).
  • CCl4 does not hydrolyse; SiCl4 hydrolyses readily to SiO2 and HCl.
  • The +2 state becomes more stable down the group, so SnCl2 is more stable than SnCl4.

mcqs.q: How is carbon tetrachloride prepared?
options: By chlorination of methane: CH4 + 4Cl2 → CCl4 + 4HCl
mcqs.why: CCl4 is prepared by chlorination of methane (or carbon disulphide): CH4 + 4Cl2 → CCl4 + 4HCl, as given in the preparation section.

mcqs.q: How is silicon tetrachloride prepared from silicon?
options: Si + 2Cl2 → SiCl4 on heating silicon with chlorine
mcqs.why: SiCl4 is prepared by heating silicon with chlorine: Si + 2Cl2 → SiCl4, or by passing chlorine over a heated mixture of silica and carbon.

mcqs.q: How is lead(II) chloride prepared in the example?
mcqs.why: PbCl2 is prepared by precipitation, for example Pb(NO3)2 + 2HCl → PbCl2 + 2HNO3, as shown in the notes.

mcqs.q: What happens to PbCl4 on heating and why?
options: It becomes more stable PbCl4 gas
It decomposes to PbCl2 + Cl2 because the inert pair effect favours +2
mcqs.why: PbCl4 is unstable and decomposes on heating to the more stable PbCl2 and Cl2, because the inert pair effect favours lead's +2 state.

mcqs.q: How do CCl4 and SiCl4 differ with water?
options: CCl4 does not hydrolyse; SiCl4 hydrolyses readily and vigorously
mcqs.why: CCl4 is stable and does not hydrolyse, while SiCl4 hydrolyses readily: SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: Why can SiCl4 hydrolyse but CCl4 cannot?
options: Carbon is larger and has d-orbitals
Silicon is larger and can accept a lone pair from water into vacant d-orbitals; carbon is shielded by four Cl and has no vacant d-orbital
mcqs.why: Silicon can accept a lone pair from water into vacant d-orbitals, while small carbon in CCl4 is fully shielded by four chlorines and has no vacant d-orbital.

mcqs.q: What are the products of SiCl4 hydrolysis?
mcqs.why: SiCl4 hydrolyses to silicon dioxide and hydrochloric acid: SiCl4 + 2H2O → SiO2 + 4HCl, as written in the lesson.

mcqs.q: How stable is CCl4 to heat?
mcqs.why: CCl4 is stable to heat, in contrast to PbCl4 which is unstable and decomposes on heating to PbCl2 and chlorine.

mcqs.q: Which tin chloride is more stable according to the key points?
options: SnCl4 is more stable than SnCl2
SnCl2 is more stable than SnCl4
mcqs.why: The key points state SnCl2 is more stable than SnCl4, consistent with the +2 state becoming more stable down Group 14.

mcqs.q: What alternative preparation of SiCl4 is given besides heating Si with Cl2?
options: Passing chlorine over a heated mixture of silica and carbon
mcqs.why: SiCl4 can also be made by passing chlorine over a heated mixture of silica and carbon, as an alternative to heating silicon with chlorine.

lessons.title: Oxides of Group 14 Elements: Structure of Carbon Dioxide and Silicon Dioxide
lessons.notes_html:
The important oxides of Group 14 elements are the monoxides, of general formula MO (examples: CO, SnO and PbO), and the dioxides, of general formula MO2 (examples: CO2, SiO2, SnO2 and PbO2). Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous gas and a strong reducing agent; carbon dioxide (CO2) is the acidic gas used by plants in photosynthesis.

Structure of Carbon Dioxide

Carbon dioxide consists of small, discrete molecules, O=C=O. The molecules are held together only by weak van der Waals forces, so CO2 is a gas at room temperature.

Structure of Silicon Dioxide

Silicon dioxide (SiO2) has a giant covalent structure: each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen atom is shared between two silicon atoms, forming a continuous three-dimensional network. A very large amount of energy is needed to break this network, so SiO2 is a hard solid with a very high melting point. SiO2 occurs as quartz and sand and is used in making glass.

PropertyCO2SiO2
StructureSimple molecules, O=C=OGiant covalent network
Forces to breakWeak van der Waals forcesStrong covalent bonds throughout the network
State at room temperatureGasSolid (very high melting point)

Other important oxides: GeO2 is amphoteric; SnO is a basic, blue-black solid; SnO2 is a white amphoteric oxide; PbO (litharge) is a yellow basic oxide; and PbO2 is a brown, strong oxidizing agent used in lead accumulators (car batteries).

Key Points

  • Group 14 oxides are monoxides (MO) and dioxides (MO2).
  • CO2 is a gas of simple molecules held by weak van der Waals forces.
  • SiO2 is a giant covalent network, so it is a hard solid with a very high melting point.
  • This is why SiO2 is a solid while CO2 is a gas.
  • PbO2 is a strong oxidizing agent used in lead accumulators.

mcqs.q: What are the two families of Group 14 oxides with examples?
options: Monoxides MO (CO, SnO, PbO) and dioxides MO2 (CO2, SiO2, SnO2, PbO2)
mcqs.why: Important Group 14 oxides are monoxides of formula MO and dioxides of formula MO2, with the examples listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is carbon monoxide described as?
options: A poisonous gas and a strong reducing agent
mcqs.why: Carbon monoxide (CO) is a poisonous gas and a strong reducing agent, while CO2 is the acidic gas used by plants in photosynthesis.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of carbon dioxide?
options: Ionic lattice of C4+ and O2-
Small discrete molecules O=C=O held by weak van der Waals forces
mcqs.why: CO2 consists of small, discrete molecules O=C=O held together only by weak van der Waals forces, so it is a gas at room temperature.

mcqs.q: What is the structure of silicon dioxide?
options: Giant covalent structure: each Si bonded to four O, each O shared between two Si
Discrete SiO2 molecules with van der Waals forces
mcqs.why: SiO2 has a giant covalent network where each silicon is bonded to four oxygens and each oxygen is shared between two silicons, forming a 3D network.

mcqs.q: Why is SiO2 a hard solid with a very high melting point while CO2 is a gas?
options: A very large amount of energy is needed to break SiO2's covalent network; CO2 molecules are held by weak forces
SiO2 has weak forces, CO2 has strong bonds
CO2 is ionic and SiO2 is molecular
mcqs.why: Breaking SiO2's continuous covalent network needs a very large amount of energy, while CO2's weak van der Waals forces are easily overcome, so CO2 is a gas.

mcqs.q: Where does SiO2 occur and what is it used for?
options: As a poisonous gas; in car batteries
As a liquid; as a reducing agent
As quartz and sand; used in making glass
mcqs.why: SiO2 occurs as quartz and sand and is used in making glass, as stated in the structure section of the lesson.

mcqs.q: What character is given for GeO2 in the 'other oxides' list?
mcqs.why: GeO2 is listed as amphoteric in the other important oxides, meaning it can show both acidic and basic behaviour.

mcqs.q: What is PbO (litharge) described as?
mcqs.why: PbO, called litharge, is a yellow basic oxide, whereas PbO2 is brown and SnO is a blue-black basic solid in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is PbO2 used for and what is its character?
options: Lead accumulators (car batteries); brown strong oxidizing agent
mcqs.why: PbO2 is a brown, strong oxidizing agent used in lead accumulators (car batteries), as stated in the other important oxides list.

mcqs.q: What is SnO described as?
mcqs.why: SnO is a basic, blue-black solid, while SnO2 is a white amphoteric oxide in the list of other important Group 14 oxides.

lessons.title: Acid-Base Behaviour of Group 14 Oxides
lessons.notes_html:
The acid-base character of the Group 14 oxides changes down the group as the metallic character increases: the oxides pass from acidic at the top to basic and amphoteric at the bottom.

  • CO2 is acidic: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic acid).
  • SiO2 is weakly acidic: it reacts with strong bases: SiO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O.
  • GeO2 is amphoteric.
  • SnO and PbO are basic: they react with acids to form salts.
  • SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric: they react with both acids and bases.

Reactions of Group 14 Elements with Water

Carbon does not react with water at ordinary temperature; with steam at high temperature it gives water gas: C + H2O → CO + H2. Silicon does not react with cold water but reacts with steam and with alkalis. Germanium is unaffected by water. Tin reacts slowly with steam: Sn + 2H2O → SnO2 + 2H2. Lead is unaffected by pure water, but water containing dissolved oxygen slowly attacks it, forming slightly soluble lead hydroxide; this is called plumbosolvency.

Key Points

  • CO2 is acidic and SiO2 is weakly acidic.
  • GeO2 is amphoteric; SnO and PbO are basic; SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric.
  • The oxides become more basic down the group as metallic character increases.
  • Carbon gives water gas with steam at high temperature; tin reacts slowly with steam.
  • Lead is attacked only by water containing dissolved oxygen (plumbosolvency).

mcqs.q: What does CO2 form with water and what is its character?
options: CO and H2; CO2 is neutral
mcqs.why: CO2 is acidic: CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 (carbonic acid), at the top of the Group 14 oxide acid-base trend.

mcqs.q: How does SiO2 show its weakly acidic character?
options: It reacts with HCl to give SiCl4
It dissolves in water to give a strong acid
It reacts with strong bases: SiO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O
It reacts with oxygen to give CO2
mcqs.why: SiO2 is weakly acidic and reacts with strong bases: SiO2 + 2NaOH → Na2SiO3 + H2O, forming sodium silicate and water.

mcqs.q: Which Group 14 dioxide is amphoteric in this lesson's list?
mcqs.why: GeO2 is amphoteric, sitting between weakly acidic SiO2 above and the more basic oxides of tin and lead below it.

mcqs.q: What is the character of SnO and PbO?
options: Basic: they react with acids to form salts
mcqs.why: SnO and PbO are basic oxides that react with acids to form salts, reflecting increased metallic character down the group.

mcqs.q: What is the character of SnO2 and PbO2?
options: Amphoteric: they react with both acids and bases
They do not react at all
mcqs.why: SnO2 and PbO2 are amphoteric, reacting with both acids and bases, as listed in the acid-base behaviour section.

mcqs.q: How does oxide character change down Group 14 and why?
options: More basic, as metallic character increases down the group
mcqs.why: Oxides pass from acidic at the top to basic and amphoteric at the bottom because metallic character increases down the group.

mcqs.q: What does carbon give with steam at high temperature?
options: Water gas: C + H2O → CO + H2
mcqs.why: Carbon does not react with water at ordinary temperature, but with steam at high temperature it gives water gas: C + H2O → CO + H2.

mcqs.q: How does tin react with steam?
options: It does not react at all
mcqs.why: Tin reacts slowly with steam: Sn + 2H2O → SnO2 + 2H2, while germanium is unaffected by water and silicon reacts with steam and alkalis.

mcqs.q: What is plumbosolvency?
options: Lead being unaffected by pure water
Water containing dissolved oxygen slowly attacking lead, forming slightly soluble lead hydroxide
mcqs.why: Plumbosolvency is the slow attack on lead by water containing dissolved oxygen, forming slightly soluble lead hydroxide; pure water does not affect lead.

mcqs.q: How does silicon behave with water?
options: Does not react with cold water but reacts with steam and with alkalis
mcqs.why: Silicon does not react with cold water but reacts with steam and with alkalis, whereas germanium is unaffected by water.

lessons.title: Canning Process and the Use of Metals
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science: Food is preserved in cans made of tinplate, which is steel sheet coated with a thin layer of tin. Tin is used for this coating because it is non-toxic and does not react with the food, and it protects the steel underneath from rusting and from attack by the food acids. In this way the canning process keeps food safe and fresh for a long time. Metals are chosen for such uses because of their special properties: they are strong, can be rolled into thin sheets, conduct heat, and some of them resist corrosion.

Key Points

  • Cans are made of steel coated with a thin layer of tin (tinplate).
  • Tin is non-toxic and unreactive towards food, so it protects both the food and the steel.
  • The tin coating stops the steel from rusting and keeps the food fresh for longer.
  • Metals are selected for uses according to their properties, such as strength, malleability and resistance to corrosion.

mcqs.q: What is tinplate, used for food cans?
options: Steel sheet coated with a thin layer of tin
mcqs.why: Cans are made of tinplate, which is steel sheet coated with a thin layer of tin, as described in the canning process lesson.

mcqs.q: Why is tin used to coat steel for food cans?
options: It is the cheapest metal of all
It is non-toxic and does not react with the food
mcqs.why: Tin is used because it is non-toxic and does not react with the food, and it protects the steel underneath from rusting and food acids.

mcqs.q: What does the tin coating protect the steel from?
options: Rusting and attack by food acids
mcqs.why: The tin coating protects the steel underneath from rusting and from attack by the food acids, keeping food safe and fresh for a long time.

mcqs.q: How does canning keep food?
options: The tin coating stops steel rusting and keeps food safe and fresh for a long time
By adding large amounts of salt only
By removing all metal from the can
mcqs.why: In this way the canning process keeps food safe and fresh for a long time, because the inert tin layer protects both food and steel.

mcqs.q: Which metal properties are given for choosing metals for uses like cans?
options: Strength, ability to be rolled into thin sheets, heat conduction and corrosion resistance for some
mcqs.why: Metals are chosen because they are strong, can be rolled into thin sheets, conduct heat, and some of them resist corrosion.

mcqs.q: What role does corrosion resistance play in canning?
options: It changes the taste of food
The tin layer resists corrosion so the steel does not rust into the food
mcqs.why: Resistance to corrosion is key: tin does not react with food and prevents the steel from rusting, as explained in the key points.

mcqs.q: What is the base metal underneath the tin in a food can?
mcqs.why: Tinplate is steel sheet coated with tin, so steel is the base metal giving the can its strength, protected by the thin tin layer.

mcqs.q: Why is tin's unreactivity towards food important?
options: It protects both the food and the steel
It makes the can lighter than air
It allows steel to dissolve safely
mcqs.why: Tin is non-toxic and unreactive towards food, so it protects both the food from contamination and the steel from attack by food acids.

mcqs.q: Which property lets metal be made into thin can sheets?
options: Low melting point of tin only
Ability to be rolled into thin sheets (malleability in use)
mcqs.why: The notes list that metals can be rolled into thin sheets, a property used to make the steel sheet for tinplate cans.

mcqs.q: What other useful metal property is mentioned besides strength and sheet-forming?
options: They never corrode in any form
mcqs.why: Metals conduct heat is one of the special properties listed, along with strength, rolling into thin sheets and corrosion resistance for some metals.

lessons.title: Group 17 Elements: The Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
The elements of Group 17 (VIIA) — fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br), iodine (I) and astatine (At) — are called halogens, a Greek word meaning salt producers, because they react with metals to form salts. They are the most reactive non-metals and are never found free in nature. They exist as diatomic molecules: F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2.

Halogens have seven electrons in their valence shells, with the general configuration ns2 np5. They need only one electron to complete the octet, so they readily gain an electron to form halide ions, X-, and show an oxidation state of -1. Fluorine shows only the -1 oxidation state, while the other halogens also show positive oxidation states of +1, +3, +5, +6 and +7 in their compounds with more electronegative elements.

Electronic Configuration of Halogens

ElementAtomic NumberElectronic ConfigurationValence Shell Configuration
Fluorine91s2 2s2 2p52s2 2p5
Chlorine171s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p53s2 3p5
Bromine351s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p54s2 4p5
Iodine531s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 3d10 4s2 4p6 4d10 5s2 5p55s2 5p5

Physical States and Colours of Halogens

HalogenState at room temperatureColour
Fluorine, F2GasPale yellow
Chlorine, Cl2GasGreenish yellow
Bromine, Br2LiquidReddish brown
Iodine, I2SolidViolet-black (gives violet vapours on heating)

Key Points

  • Group 17 elements are the halogens: F, Cl, Br, I and At, the most reactive non-metals.
  • They occur as diatomic molecules X2 and are never found free in nature.
  • Valence configuration ns2 np5: they gain one electron to form X- ions (oxidation state -1).
  • Fluorine shows only -1; the others also show positive oxidation states in compounds.
  • F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid at room temperature.

mcqs.q: What does the word 'halogen' mean and why are Group 17 elements so called?
options: Salt producers (Greek); they react with metals to form salts
Gas producers; they are all gases
Acid producers; they are all acids
mcqs.why: Halogen is a Greek word meaning salt producers, because these elements react with metals to form salts, as the lesson explains.

mcqs.q: What is the valence configuration of halogens and what ion do they form?
options: ns2 np5; they gain one electron to form X- ions
mcqs.why: Halogens have ns2 np5, need one electron to complete the octet, readily gain it to form halide ions X- and show oxidation state -1.

mcqs.q: Which oxidation states do halogens other than fluorine also show?
options: Positive +1, +3, +5, +6 and +7 in compounds with more electronegative elements
mcqs.why: Fluorine shows only -1, while other halogens also show positive oxidation states +1, +3, +5, +6 and +7 with more electronegative elements.

mcqs.q: In what molecular form do halogens exist?
options: Diatomic molecules: F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2
mcqs.why: Halogens exist as diatomic molecules X2 — F2, Cl2, Br2 and I2 — and are never found free in nature because they are so reactive.

mcqs.q: What are the states and colours of fluorine and chlorine at room temperature?
options: F2 gas pale yellow; Cl2 gas greenish yellow
mcqs.why: Fluorine is a pale yellow gas and chlorine is a greenish yellow gas at room temperature, as listed in the physical states table.

mcqs.q: What are the state and colour of bromine at room temperature?
mcqs.why: Bromine, Br2, is a reddish brown liquid at room temperature, between gaseous Cl2 above and solid I2 below it in the group.

mcqs.q: What are the state and colour of iodine, and what happens on heating?
options: Solid, violet-black, that gives violet vapours on heating
mcqs.why: Iodine is a violet-black solid at room temperature and gives violet vapours on heating, as described in the halogens table.

mcqs.q: How reactive are halogens and where are they found free?
options: Least reactive non-metals; found free everywhere
Most reactive non-metals; never found free in nature
mcqs.why: Halogens are the most reactive non-metals and are never found free in nature, occurring only in combined forms such as salts.

mcqs.q: What is fluorine's atomic number and valence configuration?
mcqs.why: Fluorine has atomic number 9 with valence shell configuration 2s2 2p5, the first member of Group 17 in the table.

mcqs.q: Which halogen shows ONLY the -1 oxidation state?
mcqs.why: Fluorine shows only the -1 oxidation state, while chlorine, bromine and iodine also show positive oxidation states in some compounds.

lessons.title: Atomic and Physical Properties of the Halogens: Atomic Radius, Electronegativity and Electron Affinity
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in Atomic Radius

The atomic radii of Group VIIA elements go on increasing as we move down the group. This is due to the increase in the number of shells.

ElementFClBrI
Atomic Radii (pm)7299114133

Trends in Electronegativity

Halogens have very high values of electronegativity. These values decrease from fluorine to iodine as the atomic number increases. Fluorine is the most electronegative atom among all the elements.

ElementFClBrI
Electronegativity3.983.002.962.56

Trends in Electron Affinity

Electron affinity values decrease from chlorine to iodine. The electron affinity of fluorine is less than that of chlorine. This is due to the smaller size of fluorine: when an extra electron is added to a fluorine atom, high electron density is produced around the fluoride ion. This high electron density increases the repulsion between the electrons already present in the relatively compact 2p orbitals of fluorine and the electron being added. Due to this electron-electron repulsion, the fluorine atom shows a lesser tendency to attract an electron towards itself to form the fluoride ion, and hence the electron affinity of fluorine becomes less than that of chlorine. The correct order of electron affinity values of the halogens is: Cl > F > Br > I.

ElementFClBrI
Electron Affinity (kJ/mol)-328-349-325-295

Key Points

  • Atomic radius increases down the group (72 pm for F to 133 pm for I) as shells are added.
  • Electronegativity decreases down the group; fluorine (3.98) is the most electronegative element of all.
  • Electron affinity decreases from chlorine to iodine, but fluorine's value is lower than chlorine's.
  • Reason: the small fluorine atom has strong electron-electron repulsion in its compact 2p orbitals.
  • Electron affinity order: Cl > F > Br > I.

mcqs.q: How does halogen atomic radius change down the group, with values?
options: Increases: F 72, Cl 99, Br 114, I 133 pm, as shells increase
mcqs.why: Atomic radii increase down the group due to increase in number of shells: F 72 pm, Cl 99 pm, Br 114 pm and I 133 pm.

mcqs.q: By how much does halogen radius increase from F (72 pm) to I (133 pm)?
mcqs.why: Increase = 133 pm - 72 pm = 61 pm. The radius grows down the group as more electronic shells are added.

mcqs.q: How does electronegativity change down the halogens and which is highest?
options: Decreases F 3.98 to I 2.56; fluorine is most electronegative of all elements
mcqs.why: Electronegativity decreases from fluorine to iodine as atomic number increases; fluorine at 3.98 is the most electronegative atom among all elements.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of halogen electron affinity?
mcqs.why: The correct order is Cl > F > Br > I, because fluorine's electron affinity is anomalously less than chlorine's despite being above it.

mcqs.q: Why is fluorine's electron affinity less than chlorine's?
options: Fluorine is small; high electron density and repulsion in its compact 2p orbitals resist the added electron
mcqs.why: Fluorine's small size gives high electron density; repulsion between existing electrons in compact 2p orbitals and the added electron lowers its electron affinity below chlorine's.

mcqs.q: What are the electron affinity values for F and Cl?
mcqs.why: Fluorine is -328 kJ/mol and chlorine is -349 kJ/mol, so chlorine releases more energy, by 349 - 328 = 21 kJ/mol in magnitude.

mcqs.q: How much greater in magnitude is Cl's electron affinity (-349) than F's (-328)?
mcqs.why: Difference in magnitude = 349 kJ/mol - 328 kJ/mol = 21 kJ/mol. Chlorine's electron affinity is greater because fluorine suffers strong electron-electron repulsion.

mcqs.q: How does electron affinity change from chlorine to iodine?
options: Decreases from chlorine to iodine: -349 to -325 to -295 kJ/mol
mcqs.why: Electron affinity values decrease from chlorine to iodine, with Br at -325 kJ/mol and I at -295 kJ/mol in the table.

mcqs.q: What is iodine's electronegativity in the table?
mcqs.why: Iodine's electronegativity is 2.56, the lowest of the four halogens listed, after F 3.98, Cl 3.00 and Br 2.96.

mcqs.q: Why does atomic radius increase down the halogens?
options: Number of shells increases down the group
Electrons are lost down the group
mcqs.why: Radii increase because the number of shells increases down the group, outweighing the increased nuclear charge, as the notes explain.

lessons.title: Melting and Boiling Points and Bond Enthalpies of the Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Trends in Melting and Boiling Points

Halogens have low melting and boiling points. Their melting and boiling points gradually increase down the group, because the London dispersion forces become stronger as the molecules become larger. This is why F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid at room temperature.

HalogenF2Cl2Br2I2
Melting Point (°C)-220-102-7114
Boiling Point (°C)-188-3559184

Bond Enthalpies in Halogens

The bond enthalpy (bond energy) of the X-X bond generally decreases down the group as the atoms become larger and the bond becomes longer and weaker. Fluorine is an exception: the F-F bond is weaker than the Cl-Cl bond, because the two small fluorine atoms bring their lone pairs very close together, and the strong repulsion between the lone pairs weakens the bond.

BondF-FCl-ClBr-BrI-I
Bond Enthalpy (kJ/mol)158242193151

Bond Enthalpies in Hydrogen Halides

The H-X bond enthalpy decreases steadily down the group, because the halogen atom becomes larger, the bond becomes longer and weaker. This is why the acidic strength and the reducing power of the hydrogen halides increase from HF to HI.

BondH-FH-ClH-BrH-I
Bond Enthalpy (kJ/mol)565432366299

Key Points

  • Melting and boiling points of halogens increase down the group as London dispersion forces strengthen.
  • States at room temperature: F2 gas, Cl2 gas, Br2 liquid, I2 solid.
  • X-X bond enthalpy generally decreases down the group, but F-F (158) is weaker than Cl-Cl (242) due to lone-pair repulsion in the small F2 molecule.
  • H-X bond enthalpy decreases from HF (565) to HI (299 kJ/mol).

mcqs.q: How do halogen melting and boiling points change down the group and why?
options: Increase, London dispersion forces become stronger as molecules become larger
Increase because bonds become covalent networks
mcqs.why: Melting and boiling points gradually increase down the group because London dispersion forces become stronger as the molecules become larger.

mcqs.q: Which halogen states at room temperature follow from this trend?
options: F2 and Cl2 gases, Br2 liquid, I2 solid
mcqs.why: Because forces strengthen down the group, F2 and Cl2 are gases, Br2 is a liquid and I2 is a solid at room temperature.

mcqs.q: Why is the F-F bond weaker than the Cl-Cl bond?
options: Two small fluorine atoms bring lone pairs very close; strong lone-pair repulsion weakens the bond
mcqs.why: Fluorine is the exception: its small atoms bring lone pairs very close together and the strong repulsion between them weakens the F-F bond.

mcqs.q: What are the F-F and Cl-Cl bond enthalpies?
mcqs.why: F-F is 158 kJ/mol and Cl-Cl is 242 kJ/mol, so the F-F bond is weaker despite fluorine being the smaller atom.

mcqs.q: By how much is Cl-Cl bond enthalpy greater than F-F?
mcqs.why: Difference = 242 kJ/mol - 158 kJ/mol = 84 kJ/mol. Cl-Cl is stronger because F-F is weakened by lone-pair repulsion in the small molecule.

mcqs.q: How does X-X bond enthalpy generally change down the group?
options: Generally decreases as atoms become larger and the bond becomes longer and weaker
mcqs.why: Generally X-X bond enthalpy decreases down the group as atoms become larger and the bond becomes longer and weaker, with F-F as the exception below Cl-Cl.

mcqs.q: How does H-X bond enthalpy change and with what values?
options: Decreases steadily: H-F 565, H-Cl 432, H-Br 366, H-I 299 kJ/mol
mcqs.why: H-X bond enthalpy decreases steadily down the group because the halogen atom becomes larger, so the bond becomes longer and weaker.

mcqs.q: What is the fall in H-X bond enthalpy from HF (565) to HI (299)?
mcqs.why: Fall = 565 kJ/mol - 299 kJ/mol = 266 kJ/mol. The much weaker H-I bond explains why HI is a stronger acid and reducing agent than HF.

mcqs.q: What trend in hydrogen halide properties follows from falling H-X enthalpy?
options: Acidic strength and reducing power decrease HF to HI
Acidic strength and reducing power increase from HF to HI
mcqs.why: Because the H-X bond weakens down the group, acidic strength and reducing power of the hydrogen halides increase from HF to HI.

mcqs.q: What are iodine's melting and boiling points in the table?
mcqs.why: Iodine melts at 114 °C and boils at 184 °C, the highest values among the halogens listed, consistent with it being a solid at room temperature.

lessons.title: Strength of Halogens as Oxidizing Agents
lessons.notes_html:
Halogens are strong oxidizing agents because they readily gain an electron to complete their octet and form halide ions. The oxidizing power of the halogens decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2. The oxidizing power of fluorine is maximum among the halogens because of its small size and high electronegativity.

Displacement Reactions

Fluorine can oxidize the chloride, bromide and iodide ions to chlorine, bromine and iodine respectively:

F2 + 2Cl- → 2F- + Cl2

F2 + 2Br- → 2F- + Br2

F2 + 2I- → 2F- + I2

Chlorine can oxidize the bromide and iodide ions, but not the fluoride ion:

Cl2 + 2F- → No action

Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2

Cl2 + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2

Bromine can oxidize only the iodide ions:

Br2 + 2F- → No action

Br2 + 2Cl- → No action

Br2 + 2I- → 2Br- + I2

Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion:

I2 + 2F- → No action; I2 + 2Cl- → No action; I2 + 2Br- → No action.

Key Points

  • Halogens are strong oxidizing agents because they gain an electron to complete the octet.
  • Oxidizing power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.
  • A halogen can displace (oxidize) only the halide ions below it in the group.
  • Fluorine oxidizes all other halide ions; iodine oxidizes none.
  • Fluorine is the strongest oxidizing agent because of its small size and highest electronegativity.

mcqs.q: Why are halogens strong oxidizing agents?
options: They readily gain an electron to complete their octet and form halide ions
They readily lose electrons to form cations
mcqs.why: Halogens gain an electron to complete the octet and form halide ions, so they oxidize other species and are strong oxidizing agents.

mcqs.q: What is the order of oxidizing power of the halogens?
mcqs.why: Oxidizing power decreases down the group: F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2, with fluorine the strongest oxidizing agent among halogens.

mcqs.q: Why is fluorine's oxidizing power maximum?
options: Because it has low electron affinity only
Because of its small size and high electronegativity
mcqs.why: Fluorine's oxidizing power is maximum because of its small size and high electronegativity, as stated in the key points.

mcqs.q: Which halide ions can fluorine oxidize?
mcqs.why: Fluorine can oxidize chloride, bromide and iodide ions to Cl2, Br2 and I2 respectively, e.g. F2 + 2Cl- → 2F- + Cl2.

mcqs.q: What happens when chlorine is added to fluoride ions?
options: ClF is the only product listed
mcqs.why: Chlorine cannot oxidize fluoride ions: Cl2 + 2F- → No action, because fluorine is above chlorine and is a stronger oxidizing agent.

mcqs.q: Which halide ion(s) can bromine oxidize?
mcqs.why: Bromine can oxidize only iodide ions, giving Br2 + 2I- → 2Br- + I2; it has no action on fluoride or chloride ions.

mcqs.q: What can iodine oxidize among halide ions?
mcqs.why: Iodine cannot oxidize any halide ion: it shows no action with F-, Cl- or Br-, because it is the weakest oxidizing halogen in the list.

mcqs.q: What is the displacement rule for halogens?
options: A halogen displaces only halides above it
A halogen can displace (oxidize) only halide ions below it in the group
All halogens displace all halides equally
mcqs.why: A halogen can displace only the halide ions below it in the group, reflecting decreasing oxidizing power F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2.

mcqs.q: What does chlorine do to bromide and iodide ions?
options: Oxidizes both: Cl2 + 2Br- → 2Cl- + Br2 and Cl2 + 2I- → 2Cl- + I2
mcqs.why: Chlorine oxidizes bromide and iodide ions to bromine and iodine respectively, but cannot oxidize fluoride ions.

mcqs.q: What products form when F2 reacts with iodide ions?
mcqs.why: Fluorine oxidizes iodide to iodine: F2 + 2I- → 2F- + I2, one of fluorine's displacement reactions with all three lighter halide ions below it.

lessons.title: The Acidity of Hydrogen Halides
lessons.notes_html:
All the halogens combine with hydrogen to produce hydrogen halides (HF, HCl, HBr, HI), and their aqueous solutions are commonly known as hydrohalic acids or halogen acids. The general formula of hydrogen halides is HX, and all the hydrogen halides are irritant.

H2 + X2 → 2HX

All the hydrogen halide molecules in the gaseous state are essentially covalent and are not able to ionize to give hydrogen ions (protons), but in aqueous solution they ionize to give hydrogen ions. The hydrogen ions combine with water molecules to form hydronium ions, H3O+, and hence hydrogen halide molecules act as acids:

HX + H2O → H3O+ + X-

The acidic strength (proton releasing power) of HX molecules increases from HF to HI, in the order: HF < HCl < HBr < HI. Thus HF is the weakest acid and HI is the strongest acid. HF ionizes only slightly and is therefore a weak acid, whereas HCl, HBr and HI ionize almost completely and are therefore strong acids.

Dissociation Energies of Hydrogen Halides

Hydrogen HalideHFHClHBrHI
Dissociation Energy (kJ/mol)565432366299

The weakest acidic nature of HF is due to the high dissociation energy of the H-F bond: the bond is very strong, so it breaks with great difficulty in water and very few H+ ions are released. Down the group the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, so it breaks more easily and the acid becomes stronger. A related fact: HF cannot be stored in glass containers, because it attacks the silica of glass.

Key Points

  • Hydrogen halides HX dissolve in water to form hydrohalic acids: HX + H2O → H3O+ + X-.
  • Acidic strength increases HF < HCl < HBr < HI.
  • HF is a weak acid; HCl, HBr and HI are strong acids.
  • Reason: the H-X bond weakens down the group (565 to 299 kJ/mol), so H+ is released more easily.
  • HF attacks glass and cannot be stored in glass containers.

mcqs.q: What is the general formation equation for hydrogen halides?
options: HX + H2O → H3O+ + X- is formation
mcqs.why: All halogens combine with hydrogen to produce hydrogen halides: H2 + X2 → 2HX, and all hydrogen halide molecules are irritant.

mcqs.q: How do hydrogen halides behave in aqueous solution?
options: They stay covalent and give no ions
They ionize to give H+, which forms hydronium ions: HX + H2O → H3O+ + X-
mcqs.why: In water they ionize; hydrogen ions combine with water to form hydronium ions H3O+, so HX + H2O → H3O+ + X- and they act as acids.

mcqs.q: What is the order of acidic strength of hydrogen halides?
mcqs.why: Acidic strength increases HF < HCl < HBr < HI, so HF is the weakest acid and HI is the strongest acid among them.

mcqs.q: Which hydrogen halides are strong acids and which is weak?
options: HF, HCl weak; HBr, HI weak
HF is weak (ionizes only slightly); HCl, HBr and HI are strong (ionize almost completely)
HF is strong, HI is weak
mcqs.why: HF ionizes only slightly and is a weak acid, whereas HCl, HBr and HI ionize almost completely and are therefore strong acids.

mcqs.q: Why is HF the weakest hydrohalic acid?
options: The H-F bond has high dissociation energy (565 kJ/mol), is very strong and breaks with difficulty, releasing few H+
Its bond dissociation energy is lowest
HF does not dissolve in water
mcqs.why: HF's high H-F dissociation energy means the strong bond breaks with great difficulty in water and very few H+ ions are released.

mcqs.q: Why does acid strength increase down the HX group?
options: H-X bond becomes shorter and stronger
H-X bond becomes longer and weaker, so it breaks more easily and acid becomes stronger
mcqs.why: Down the group the H-X bond becomes longer and weaker (565 to 299 kJ/mol), so it breaks more easily and the acid becomes stronger.

mcqs.q: In what state are HX molecules essentially covalent and non-ionized?
mcqs.why: In the gaseous state HX molecules are essentially covalent and are not able to ionize to give hydrogen ions; ionization occurs in aqueous solution.

mcqs.q: Why cannot HF be stored in glass containers?
options: It attacks the silica of glass
Glass dissolves in all acids equally
mcqs.why: HF cannot be stored in glass because it attacks the silica of glass, a related fact given at the end of the acidity lesson.

mcqs.q: What are aqueous HX solutions commonly called?
mcqs.why: Their aqueous solutions are commonly known as hydrohalic acids or halogen acids, with general formula HX for the hydrogen halides.

mcqs.q: What are the dissociation energies of HCl and HBr?
mcqs.why: HCl is 432 kJ/mol and HBr is 366 kJ/mol, between HF at 565 and HI at 299 in the decreasing dissociation energy table.

lessons.title: Halide Ions as Reducing Agents and Trends in Reducing Strength of Halide Ions
lessons.notes_html:
A substance that loses electrons during a chemical reaction is called a reducing agent, while a substance that gains electrons is called an oxidizing agent. The reducing agent reduces other substances (decreases their oxidation states) and is itself oxidized (its oxidation state is increased). The halide ions (or hydrogen halides) reduce oxidizing agents and are themselves oxidized to X2 molecules:

4HX + O2 → 2H2O + 2X2

The trend in the reducing ability of halide ions (or hydrogen halides) is opposite to the trend in the oxidizing power of the halogens. The reducing properties increase from fluoride ion (or HF) to iodide ion (or HI), because the ionic radii of the halide ions increase down the group, so the outer electron is held less firmly and is lost more easily. The order is:

F- < Cl- < Br- < I- or HF < HCl < HBr < HI

The fluoride ion (or HF) is the weakest reducing agent; in fact it has no considerable reducing properties at all. It cannot reduce even very strong oxidizing agents such as SO2 and HI, and it cannot reduce any of the halogens (Cl2, Br2 and I2) to their halide ions: 2F- + Cl2 → No action; 2F- + Br2 → No action; 2F- + I2 → No action.

The chloride ion (or HCl) reduces only strong oxidizing agents like F2, and is itself oxidized to Cl2. It can reduce neither Br2 nor I2:

2Cl- + F2 → 2F- + Cl2

2Cl- + Br2 → No action

2Cl- + I2 → No action

The bromide ion (or HBr) reduces F2 and Cl2, but not I2:

2Br- + F2 → 2F- + Br2

2Br- + Cl2 → 2Cl- + Br2

2Br- + I2 → No action

The iodide ion (or HI), being the strongest reducing agent, can reduce all of the other three halogens to their corresponding halide ions:

2I- + F2 → 2F- + I2

2I- + Cl2 → 2Cl- + I2

2I- + Br2 → 2Br- + I2

We may say that a given halide ion (or halogen acid) can reduce only that halogen molecule which lies above it in Group 17 (VIIA) of the periodic table. The halide ion cannot reduce the halogen molecule which lies below it in the group.

Key Points

  • Halide ions act as reducing agents: they lose electrons and are oxidized to X2.
  • Reducing power increases down the group: F- < Cl- < Br- < I-.
  • This trend is opposite to the oxidizing power of the halogens.
  • Reason: the ions get larger down the group, so the outer electron is lost more easily.
  • F- is the weakest reducing agent (practically none); I- is the strongest.
  • A halide ion can reduce only the halogens above it in the group.

mcqs.q: What is a reducing agent in terms of electrons?
options: A substance that loses electrons, reduces others and is itself oxidized
An oxidizing agent in water only
mcqs.why: A reducing agent loses electrons during a reaction, decreases others' oxidation states and is itself oxidized (its oxidation state increases).

mcqs.q: To what are halide ions oxidized when they act as reducing agents?
mcqs.why: Halide ions (or hydrogen halides) reduce oxidizing agents and are themselves oxidized to X2 molecules, e.g. 4HX + O2 → 2H2O + 2X2.

mcqs.q: What is the order of reducing power of halide ions?
options: Cl- is strongest, F- weakest in reverse order given
mcqs.why: Reducing power increases F- < Cl- < Br- < I- (or HF < HCl < HBr < HI), opposite to the oxidizing power of the halogens.

mcqs.q: Why does reducing power increase down the halide group?
options: Ions get smaller and hold electrons tighter
Ionic radii increase, so the outer electron is held less firmly and lost more easily
mcqs.why: Larger halide ions down the group hold the outer electron less firmly, so it is lost more easily and reducing power increases.

mcqs.q: Which halide is the weakest reducing agent, practically with none?
mcqs.why: The fluoride ion (or HF) is the weakest reducing agent; in fact it has no considerable reducing properties at all in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which halogens can chloride ion (or HCl) reduce?
options: Only strong oxidizing agents like F2; it can reduce neither Br2 nor I2
mcqs.why: Chloride reduces only strong oxidizing agents like F2, being oxidized to Cl2 itself; it can reduce neither Br2 nor I2.

mcqs.q: Which halogens can bromide ion (or HBr) reduce?
options: F2 and Cl2, but not I2
mcqs.why: Bromide reduces F2 and Cl2, e.g. 2Br- + Cl2 → 2Cl- + Br2, but it shows no action with I2.

mcqs.q: Which halide is the strongest reducing agent and what can it reduce?
options: I- (or HI), can reduce all other three halogens to their halide ions
mcqs.why: Iodide, the strongest reducing agent, can reduce F2, Cl2 and Br2 all to their corresponding halide ions, e.g. 2I- + Br2 → 2Br- + I2.

mcqs.q: What is the general rule for a halide reducing a halogen?
options: A halide can reduce only the halogen below it
A halide reduces its own halogen only
A halide can reduce only that halogen molecule which lies above it in Group 17
mcqs.why: A given halide ion can reduce only a halogen molecule above it in Group 17; it cannot reduce the halogen below it in the group.

mcqs.q: How does halide reducing trend relate to halogen oxidizing trend?
options: It is opposite to the trend in oxidizing power of the halogens
Both increase for F2 and F-
mcqs.why: The reducing trend of halides is opposite to oxidizing power of halogens: as F2 > Cl2 > Br2 > I2 falls, F- < Cl- < Br- < I- rises.

lessons.title: Properties and Commercial Uses of the Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science:

Properties and Uses of Fluorine

Fluorine is a highly toxic gas. It is the most electronegative and reactive element. It reacts directly with all elements except helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar). It is used in the manufacture of chlorofluorocarbons, commercially known as Freons. Freons are used as refrigerants in refrigerators, as cooling agents in air conditioners, and as aerosol propellants and cleaning agents. Fluorine is also used in the manufacture of Teflon. Teflon is a valuable plastic used for coating electrical wiring; it provides a non-stick surface for frying pans and other cooking-related products.

Properties and Uses of Chlorine

Chlorine (Cl2) is a highly toxic gas with a pale yellow-green colour. Chlorine is chemically less active than fluorine but more active than bromine and iodine. Some of the uses of chlorine depend on its toxic effects: chlorine is used as a disinfectant in swimming pools and water treatment plants. Many organic compounds of chlorine are used in the manufacture of antiseptics, insecticides, weed killers and herbicides. Chlorine is a very strong oxidizing agent and is used commercially as a bleaching agent. Large amounts of chlorine are used to make solvents such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl4), chloroform (CHCl3), dichloroethylene (C2H2Cl2) and trichloroethylene (C2HCl3).

Properties and Uses of Bromine

Bromine (Br2) is a reddish-orange liquid with an unpleasant, choking odour. The vapours of bromine are irritating to the eyes and throat. The liquid is highly corrosive and can cause serious burns if spilled on the skin. Bromine is chemically less active than fluorine and chlorine but more active than iodine. Bromine is used to prepare flame retardants, fire-extinguishing agents, sedatives, germicides, pesticides, fungicides and insecticides. Bromine can also be used as a disinfectant like chlorine.

Properties and Uses of Iodine

Iodine is an intensely coloured solid with an almost metallic lustre. Iodine vapours are irritating to the eyes and respiratory system. Iodine is chemically less active than the other halogens (not counting astatine). Iodine acts as an antioxidant in our blood. It is also used as a cough expectorant and is helpful in treating allergies, dermatitis, bladder infections and moles. The human body uses iodine to make thyroxine, an important hormone (chemical messenger) produced by the thyroid gland, which plays an important role in metabolism. The deficiency of iodine in the human body can lead to goitre, a swelling around the neck. Iodine can be used as a water purifying agent and as a sterilizing agent, and for the preparation of antiseptics such as iodex and tincture.

Properties and Uses of Bleaching Powder

Bleaching powder is also known as calcium hypochlorite, or sometimes calcium oxychloride, and its chemical formula is CaOCl2. It is a pale yellow powder and has a strong smell of chlorine. It loses chlorine when it reacts with carbon dioxide:

CaOCl2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + Cl2

Key Points

  • Fluorine is used to make Freons (refrigerants, propellants) and Teflon (non-stick plastic).
  • Chlorine is a disinfectant for water and a commercial bleaching agent; it is also used to make solvents like CCl4 and CHCl3.
  • Bromine is used in flame retardants, fire-extinguishing agents, sedatives and pesticides.
  • Iodine is needed to make the hormone thyroxine; its deficiency causes goitre. It is used in antiseptics like tincture and iodex.
  • Bleaching powder, CaOCl2, releases chlorine on reacting with CO2.

mcqs.q: With which elements does fluorine NOT react directly?
mcqs.why: Fluorine reacts directly with all elements except helium (He), neon (Ne) and argon (Ar), despite being the most reactive element.

mcqs.q: What are Freons and what are they used for?
options: A plastic for frying pans; non-stick coating
Chlorofluorocarbons made using fluorine; refrigerants, AC cooling agents, aerosol propellants and cleaning agents
mcqs.why: Freons are chlorofluorocarbons manufactured using fluorine, used as refrigerants, cooling agents in air conditioners, aerosol propellants and cleaning agents.

mcqs.q: What is Teflon and its uses?
options: A chlorine solvent for dry cleaning
A valuable plastic from fluorine, for coating electrical wiring and non-stick frying pans/cooking products
mcqs.why: Teflon is a valuable fluorine plastic used for coating electrical wiring and providing a non-stick surface for frying pans and other cooking products.

mcqs.q: What are chlorine's main disinfectant/bleaching uses?
options: Disinfectant in swimming pools and water treatment; strong oxidizing commercial bleaching agent
As a sedative and germicide only
mcqs.why: Chlorine is used as a disinfectant in swimming pools and water treatment plants and, as a very strong oxidizing agent, commercially as a bleaching agent.

mcqs.q: Which solvents are listed as made using large amounts of chlorine?
mcqs.why: Large amounts of chlorine are used to make solvents such as carbon tetrachloride (CCl4), chloroform (CHCl3), dichloroethylene and trichloroethylene.

mcqs.q: What are bromine's appearance and hazards?
options: Reddish-orange liquid, unpleasant choking odour, vapours irritate eyes/throat, corrosive and causes serious burns
mcqs.why: Bromine is a reddish-orange liquid with an unpleasant, choking odour; its vapours irritate eyes and throat and the liquid is highly corrosive.

mcqs.q: What uses are listed for bromine?
options: Flame retardants, fire-extinguishing agents, sedatives, germicides, pesticides, fungicides and insecticides
mcqs.why: Bromine is used to prepare flame retardants, fire-extinguishing agents, sedatives, germicides, pesticides, fungicides and insecticides, and as a disinfectant.

mcqs.q: Why does the human body need iodine, and what does deficiency cause?
options: To make insulin; deficiency causes diabetes in the notes
To make thyroxine by the thyroid gland for metabolism; deficiency can lead to goitre, a swelling around the neck
To make Teflon; deficiency causes fluorosis
To bleach blood; deficiency causes burns
mcqs.why: The body uses iodine to make thyroxine, a thyroid hormone important in metabolism; iodine deficiency can lead to goitre, a swelling around the neck.

mcqs.q: What antiseptic uses of iodine are mentioned?
options: Preparation of antiseptics such as iodex and tincture, and as water purifying/sterilizing agent
mcqs.why: Iodine is used as a water purifying and sterilizing agent and for preparation of antiseptics such as iodex and tincture, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: What is bleaching powder and what does it do with CO2?
options: CaOCl2, calcium hypochlorite/oxychloride, pale yellow with strong Cl smell; CaOCl2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + Cl2
Pure Cl2 gas in a cylinder
mcqs.why: Bleaching powder is CaOCl2, a pale yellow powder with a strong smell of chlorine; it loses chlorine with CO2: CaOCl2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + Cl2.

lessons.title: Fluoride Toxicity and Deficiency
lessons.notes_html:
Society, Technology and Science: A small amount of fluoride is useful for health: fluoride in drinking water (about 1 part per million) and fluoride compounds such as sodium fluoride in toothpaste help to prevent tooth decay by making the enamel of the teeth harder and more resistant to acid attack.

Too much fluoride, however, is harmful; this is called fluoride toxicity. Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis, in which the teeth become mottled (marked with patches) and weak. In more severe cases it causes skeletal fluorosis, in which the bones and joints become stiff and painful. On the other hand, deficiency of fluoride increases tooth decay, because the enamel is not protected.

Key Points

  • About 1 ppm fluoride in drinking water helps prevent tooth decay.
  • Fluoride in toothpaste strengthens the enamel against acid attack.
  • Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis (mottled teeth) and skeletal fluorosis (stiff, painful bones and joints).
  • Fluoride deficiency increases tooth decay.

mcqs.q: How much fluoride in drinking water helps prevent tooth decay?
mcqs.why: About 1 part per million fluoride in drinking water helps prevent tooth decay, as stated at the start of the fluoride lesson.

mcqs.q: How does fluoride help teeth?
options: It whitens teeth only by bleaching
It makes enamel harder and more resistant to acid attack
It replaces all enamel with sodium fluoride
mcqs.why: Fluoride helps prevent decay by making the enamel of the teeth harder and more resistant to acid attack.

mcqs.q: Which fluoride compound example is given in toothpaste?
mcqs.why: Fluoride compounds such as sodium fluoride in toothpaste help prevent tooth decay by strengthening enamel against acid attack.

mcqs.q: What is fluoride toxicity?
options: Harm caused by too much fluoride
mcqs.why: Fluoride toxicity is the harm caused by too much fluoride, even though a small amount of fluoride is useful for health.

mcqs.q: What is dental fluorosis?
options: Teeth become mottled (marked with patches) and weak from excess fluoride
Stiff and painful bones from fluoride
mcqs.why: Excess fluoride causes dental fluorosis, in which the teeth become mottled, marked with patches, and weak, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is skeletal fluorosis?
options: Bones and joints become stiff and painful in more severe excess-fluoride cases
mcqs.why: In more severe cases excess fluoride causes skeletal fluorosis, in which the bones and joints become stiff and painful.

mcqs.q: What happens when fluoride is deficient?
options: Tooth decay increases because enamel is not protected
mcqs.why: Deficiency of fluoride increases tooth decay, because the enamel is not protected against acid attack without enough fluoride.

mcqs.q: What is the balanced conclusion about fluoride in the notes?
options: All fluoride is harmful and must be removed
A small amount is useful for health, but too much is harmful
Only toothpaste fluoride matters, water fluoride is useless
Fluoride has no effect on teeth
mcqs.why: The lesson balances both sides: a small amount of fluoride is useful for preventing decay, while excess causes toxicity and deficiency increases decay.

mcqs.q: Which condition is caused by EXCESS fluoride, not deficiency?
options: Dental fluorosis with mottled, weak teeth
mcqs.why: Dental fluorosis — mottled and weak teeth — is caused by excess fluoride, whereas increased decay is the result of fluoride deficiency.

mcqs.q: How does fluoride in toothpaste act, in the notes' wording?
options: It helps prevent tooth decay by hardening enamel against acid
It causes skeletal fluorosis at normal use in the notes
It is the same as bleaching powder
mcqs.why: Fluoride compounds in toothpaste help prevent tooth decay by making enamel harder and more resistant to acid attack, as the lesson states.

lessons.title: Transition Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Transition elements are the elements in which the d-orbitals are partially filled, either in the atomic state or in any of their common oxidation states. They lie between the s-block and p-block elements. The d-block elements are collectively called transition elements or transition metals, while the f-block elements are called inner transition elements.

Their general electronic configuration is (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2. They are hard, lustrous metals with high melting and boiling points. They show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds, act as catalysts and form alloys.

Series of Transition Elements

SeriesElementsOrbital FilledPeriod
First seriesSc to Zn (10 elements)3d4
Second seriesY to Cd (10 elements)4d5
Third seriesLa and Hf to Hg5d6
Fourth seriesAc and Rf to Cn (incomplete)6d7

The elements of Group 12 (Zn, Cd, Hg) are not counted as transition elements because they have completely filled d-orbitals (d10) in the atomic state and in their common oxidation states. The book also excludes Group 3 elements, whose common ions have an empty d-subshell (d0).

Key Points

  • Transition elements have partially filled d-orbitals in the atom or in a common oxidation state.
  • General configuration: (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2.
  • There are four transition series: 3d, 4d, 5d and 6d series.
  • The first series (Sc to Zn) lies in period 4.
  • Zn, Cd and Hg (d10) are excluded from the transition elements.
  • f-block elements are called inner transition elements.

mcqs.q: What defines a transition element?
options: Its d-orbitals are partially filled in the atomic state or in a common oxidation state
Its s-orbitals are completely filled in every oxidation state
Its p-orbitals are partially filled in the atomic state only
It has a completely filled d-subshell in all common states
mcqs.why: The notes define transition elements by partially filled d-orbitals, either in the atom itself or in any of their common oxidation states.

mcqs.q: Where do transition elements lie in the periodic table?
options: At the far right of the p-block only
Between the s-block and the p-block elements
Between the s-block and the f-block elements
mcqs.why: The notes state that transition elements lie between the s-block and p-block elements, forming the d-block region of the table.

mcqs.q: What is the general electronic configuration of transition elements?
mcqs.why: The notes give the general configuration as (n-1)d1-10 ns1-2, showing that the (n-1)d subshell is being filled gradually.

mcqs.q: Which elements make up the first transition series?
options: Y to Cd, filling the 4d orbitals
La and Hf to Hg, filling the 5d orbitals
Ac and Rf to Cn, filling the 6d orbitals
Sc to Zn, filling the 3d orbitals in period 4
mcqs.why: The first series runs from Sc to Zn, involves filling of the 3d orbital and lies in the fourth period of the periodic table.

mcqs.q: Why are Zn, Cd and Hg not counted as transition elements?
options: They have completely empty d-orbitals in all states
They have completely filled d-orbitals (d10) in the atomic state and common oxidation states
They are not metals and form no compounds
They belong to the f-block instead of the d-block
mcqs.why: Group 12 elements have d10 configurations in the atom and in their common oxidation states, so their d-orbitals are never partially filled.

mcqs.q: What are the f-block elements collectively called?
mcqs.why: The notes distinguish the d-block transition elements from the f-block elements, which are collectively called inner transition elements.

mcqs.q: Which series fills the 5d orbitals?
options: The first series, Sc to Zn, in period 4
The second series, Y to Cd, in period 5
The fourth series, Ac and Rf to Cn, in period 7
The third series, La and Hf to Hg, in period 6
mcqs.why: According to the series table, the third transition series fills the 5d orbital, lies in period 6 and runs through La and Hf to Hg.

mcqs.q: Why does the book also exclude Group 3 elements from the transition elements?
options: Their common ions have an empty d-subshell (d0)
Their common ions have a filled d-subshell (d10)
They have no d-orbitals at all
They show only one oxidation state of +1
mcqs.why: The book excludes Group 3 because their common ions have an empty d-subshell, d0, rather than a partially filled d-subshell.

mcqs.q: Which set lists typical properties of transition elements?
options: Soft dull metals with low melting points and fixed oxidation states
Colourless compounds that never act as catalysts
Hard lustrous metals with high melting points, variable oxidation states and coloured compounds
Non-metals that form alloys only with difficulty
mcqs.why: The notes describe transition elements as hard, lustrous metals with high melting and boiling points that show variable oxidation states, form coloured compounds, act as catalysts and form alloys.

mcqs.q: Which transition series is described as incomplete?
options: The first series, Sc to Zn
The fourth series, Ac and Rf to Cn, filling 6d in period 7
The second series, Y to Cd
The third series, La and Hf to Hg
mcqs.why: The table in the notes marks the fourth series, which fills the 6d orbitals in period 7, as the incomplete transition series.

lessons.title: General Characteristics of Transition Elements
lessons.notes_html:
Almost all transition elements show similar properties because their valence shell configurations are similar. Their important general characteristics are:

  • They have high tensile strength, ductility, malleability and thermal and electrical conductivity.
  • They show variable oxidation states.
  • They form coloured compounds.
  • They are used as catalysts.
  • They form complex compounds (coordination compounds).
  • They form interstitial compounds.
  • They form alloys.
  • Many of their compounds are used in paints.
  • Many of them and their compounds are paramagnetic.

Their metallic character comes from the electrons available for metallic bonding. In the 3d series, chromium and copper contribute the most electrons per atom to the metallic bond, while scandium and zinc contribute the fewest.

Key Points

  • Transition metals are hard, strong, ductile and malleable, and conduct heat and electricity well.
  • Variable oxidation states and coloured compounds are their typical features.
  • They form complexes, alloys and interstitial compounds.
  • They and their compounds are widely used as catalysts.
  • Many transition metal compounds are paramagnetic.

mcqs.q: Why do almost all transition elements show similar properties?
options: Their valence shell configurations are similar
They all have exactly the same atomic number
They all have completely filled d-subshells
They have no electrons available for bonding
mcqs.why: The notes explain the similarity of properties by the similar valence shell configurations shared by almost all transition elements.

mcqs.q: Which set describes the mechanical properties of transition elements?
options: Low tensile strength and brittleness only
High tensile strength, ductility and malleability
Softness with no ductility or malleability
High strength but no ability to be drawn or beaten
mcqs.why: The notes list high tensile strength, ductility and malleability among the general characteristics of transition elements.

mcqs.q: Transition elements conduct which of the following well?
mcqs.why: The notes state that transition elements have good thermal and electrical conductivity, like typical metals used for wires and heating parts.

mcqs.q: Which compound types do transition elements characteristically form?
mcqs.why: Forming complex (coordination) compounds and interstitial compounds are both listed as general characteristics of transition elements.

mcqs.q: What gives transition elements their metallic character, according to the notes?
options: The electrons available for metallic bonding
mcqs.why: The notes say the metallic character of transition elements comes from the electrons that are available to take part in metallic bonding.

mcqs.q: In the 3d series, which pair contributes the most electrons per atom to the metallic bond?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in the 3d series chromium and copper contribute the most electrons per atom to the metallic bond.

mcqs.q: In the 3d series, which pair contributes the fewest electrons per atom to the metallic bond?
mcqs.why: The notes contrast Cr and Cu, which contribute the most, with scandium and zinc, which contribute the fewest electrons per atom.

mcqs.q: Many transition metal compounds are described in the notes as:
mcqs.why: The notes list that many transition elements and their compounds are paramagnetic, one of their typical general characteristics.

mcqs.q: Many compounds of transition metals are used in which application named in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes mention that many transition metal compounds are used in paints because of the colours these compounds display.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly summarises transition elements as catalysts?
options: They never speed up any reaction
They and their compounds are widely used as catalysts
Only one transition metal can act as a catalyst
mcqs.why: Being used as catalysts is one of the listed general characteristics: transition metals and their compounds are widely used as catalysts.

lessons.title: Electronic Configuration
lessons.notes_html:
In d-block elements the (n-1)d subshell is filled gradually. The general configuration is (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2. When ions are formed, the ns electrons are lost before the (n-1)d electrons. For example, Ti2+ is [Ar]3d2, Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6 and Fe3+ is [Ar]3d5.

First Transition Series (3d)

ElementConfigurationElementConfiguration
Sc (21)[Ar]3d1 4s2Mn (25)[Ar]3d5 4s2
Ti (22)[Ar]3d2 4s2Fe (26)[Ar]3d6 4s2
V (23)[Ar]3d3 4s2Co (27)[Ar]3d7 4s2
Cr (24)[Ar]3d5 4s1Ni (28)[Ar]3d8 4s2
Cu (29)[Ar]3d10 4s1Zn (30)[Ar]3d10 4s2

Cr and Cu are exceptions: one 4s electron moves into 3d to give the extra stable half-filled (d5) and completely filled (d10) configurations. Similar exceptions in the 4d series are Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh and Pd (Pd is 4d10 5s0), and in the 5d series Pt (5d9 6s1) and Au (5d10 6s1).

Key Points

  • General configuration of d-block elements: (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2.
  • On forming ions, ns electrons are removed before (n-1)d electrons.
  • Cr is 3d5 4s1 and Cu is 3d10 4s1 because half-filled and filled d-subshells are extra stable.
  • Fe2+ is 3d6 and Fe3+ is 3d5.
  • Pd has the exceptional configuration 4d10 5s0.

mcqs.q: When a d-block element forms an ion, which electrons are lost first?
options: The ns electrons, before the (n-1)d electrons
The (n-1)d electrons, before the ns electrons
Electrons are lost equally from all shells at once
mcqs.why: The notes state clearly that on forming ions the ns electrons are removed before the (n-1)d electrons of a d-block element.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of Fe2+?
mcqs.why: Iron is [Ar]3d6 4s2; forming Fe2+ removes the two 4s electrons first, leaving [Ar]3d6 as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of Fe3+?
mcqs.why: Fe2+ is [Ar]3d6, and removing one more electron, from the 3d subshell, gives Fe3+ as [Ar]3d5, the half-filled arrangement.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of Ti2+?
mcqs.why: Titanium is [Ar]3d2 4s2; the two 4s electrons are lost first on forming the ion, so Ti2+ is [Ar]3d2 as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is chromium's configuration [Ar]3d5 4s1 instead of [Ar]3d4 4s2?
options: Chromium loses an electron to the 4s subshell
One 4s electron moves into 3d to give the extra stable half-filled d5 subshell
The 3d subshell cannot hold more than four electrons
A proton moves from the nucleus into the 3d subshell
mcqs.why: Cr is an exception: one 4s electron shifts into 3d because the half-filled d5 configuration is extra stable, giving 3d5 4s1.

mcqs.q: What is the exceptional configuration of palladium (Pd)?
mcqs.why: The notes single out Pd in the 4d series with the exceptional configuration 4d10 5s0, a completely filled d-subshell and empty 5s.

mcqs.q: Which pair shows exceptional configurations in the 5d series?
mcqs.why: The notes name Pt (5d9 6s1) and Au (5d10 6s1) as the exceptions in the 5d series, each having only one 6s electron.

mcqs.q: What is the configuration of copper, and why?
options: [Ar]3d10 4s1, because a filled d10 subshell is extra stable
mcqs.why: Copper (29) is an exception like chromium: one 4s electron moves into 3d to complete the d10 subshell, giving [Ar]3d10 4s1.

mcqs.q: Which elements are listed as exceptions in the 4d series?
options: Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh and Pd
mcqs.why: The notes list Nb, Mo, Ru, Rh and Pd as the similar exceptions in the 4d series, with Pd being the most extreme case.

mcqs.q: What is the general configuration range given for d-block elements in this lesson?
mcqs.why: This lesson gives the d-block general configuration as (n-1)d1-10 ns0-2, allowing ns to be empty, as in Pd with 5s0.

lessons.title: Binding Energies
lessons.notes_html:
The binding energy of an element is the energy needed to separate its atoms. In transition metals it depends on the number of unpaired electrons taking part in metallic bonding.

Binding energy first increases across a series, reaches a maximum in the middle, and then decreases. Elements in the middle of the series, such as Cr, Mo and W, have the maximum number of unpaired electrons, so they have the highest binding energies and the highest melting points. Towards the end of the series the electrons pair up, bonding becomes weaker, and binding energy and melting point fall. Zn, Cd and Hg, with filled d-subshells, have the lowest melting points and are quite volatile.

The same trend is shown by melting points: they rise up to the middle of the series (Cr, Mo, W) and then decrease, with a small dip at Mn and Tc.

Key Points
