  • Binding energy measures the strength of bonding between metal atoms.
  • It increases up to the middle of a transition series, then decreases.
  • More unpaired d-electrons mean stronger bonding, higher binding energy and higher melting point.
  • Cr, Mo and W have the highest melting points in their series.
  • Zn, Cd and Hg have low melting points because their d-subshells are filled.

mcqs.q: What is the binding energy of an element?
options: The energy needed to separate its atoms
The energy released when its atoms join together
The energy of its outermost electron only
The heat needed to melt one gram of it
mcqs.why: The notes define binding energy as the energy needed to separate the atoms of an element, measuring the strength of bonding between them.

mcqs.q: On what does the binding energy of a transition metal depend?
options: The number of unpaired electrons taking part in metallic bonding
The number of protons in its nucleus only
mcqs.why: The notes state that binding energy in transition metals depends on how many unpaired electrons take part in the metallic bonding.

mcqs.q: How does binding energy change across a transition series?
options: It decreases steadily from start to finish
It increases steadily to the last element
It increases to a maximum in the middle, then decreases
It stays exactly the same for all elements
mcqs.why: Binding energy first increases across a series, reaches a maximum in the middle, and then decreases towards the end of the series.

mcqs.q: Which elements have the highest binding energies and melting points in their series?
options: Zn, Cd and Hg, at the end of their series
Sc, Y and La, at the start of their series
Cu, Ag and Au, the coinage metals
Cr, Mo and W, in the middle of their series
mcqs.why: Elements in the middle such as Cr, Mo and W have the maximum number of unpaired electrons, giving the highest binding energies and melting points.

mcqs.q: Why do binding energy and melting point fall towards the end of a series?
options: More unpaired electrons appear, weakening the bonds
Electrons pair up, so bonding becomes weaker
The atoms lose their d-orbitals completely
mcqs.why: Towards the end of the series the electrons pair up, fewer unpaired electrons bond, bonding weakens, and binding energy and melting point fall.

mcqs.q: Which elements have the lowest melting points and are quite volatile?
options: Cr, Mo and W, with half-filled d-subshells
Fe, Co and Ni, the ferromagnetic metals
Zn, Cd and Hg, with filled d-subshells
Sc, Ti and V, at the start of the series
mcqs.why: Zn, Cd and Hg have filled d-subshells, no unpaired d-electrons for strong bonding, and so the lowest melting points; they are quite volatile.

mcqs.q: The melting point trend across a series shows a small dip at which elements?
mcqs.why: The notes note that melting points rise to the middle (Cr, Mo, W) and then decrease, with a small dip at Mn and Tc.

mcqs.q: More unpaired d-electrons in a transition metal lead to:
options: Stronger bonding, higher binding energy and higher melting point
Weaker bonding and a lower melting point
No bonding between atoms at all
Lower binding energy but higher melting point
mcqs.why: The notes link more unpaired d-electrons with stronger metallic bonding, which raises both the binding energy and the melting point.

mcqs.q: Where in a transition series is binding energy at its maximum?
options: In the middle of the series
It is equal at the start and end only
mcqs.why: Binding energy increases across the first half and reaches its maximum in the middle of the series before decreasing again.

mcqs.q: Which statement about Zn, Cd and Hg follows from their filled d-subshells?
options: Their bonding is the strongest in their series
Their bonding is weak, so their melting points are low
They have the highest binding energies
mcqs.why: Because Zn, Cd and Hg have filled d-subshells with no unpaired electrons, their metallic bonding is weak and their melting points are low.

lessons.title: Variable Oxidation State
lessons.notes_html:
Transition elements show variable oxidation states because the ns and (n-1)d orbitals are very close in energy, so electrons from both can be used in bonding. The maximum oxidation state rises across the series up to the middle (it equals the group number for the early groups) and then falls.

Stable Oxidation States (First Series)

ElementStable Oxidation States
Sc+3
Ti+2, +4
V+2, +3, +4, +5
Cr+2, +3, +6
Mn+2, +4, +6, +7
Fe+2, +3
Co+2, +3
Ni+2
Cu+1, +2
Zn+2

Stability depends on electronic configuration. Sc3+ and Ti4+ are stable because they have the noble gas configuration. Fe3+ (d5, half-filled) is more stable than Fe2+ (d6). Ag+ (4d10, filled) is more stable than Ag2+. In water, however, Cu2+ is more stable than Cu+ because the small Cu2+ ion has a much higher (more negative) hydration enthalpy. Lower oxidation states usually form ionic compounds, while higher oxidation states occur in covalent compounds such as oxides and fluorides (for example V2O5).

Key Points

  • Variable oxidation states arise because ns and (n-1)d electrons are close in energy.
  • The most frequent oxidation states of transition elements are +2 and +3.
  • Half-filled (d5) and filled (d10) configurations give extra stability, e.g. Fe3+ and Ag+.
  • Sc3+ and Ti4+ are stable due to the noble gas configuration.
  • In aqueous solution Cu2+ is more stable than Cu+ due to its high hydration enthalpy.

mcqs.q: Why do transition elements show variable oxidation states?
options: The ns and (n-1)d orbitals are very close in energy, so electrons from both can be used in bonding
Their nuclei change charge from compound to compound
They gain electrons from ligands in every compound
mcqs.why: Variable oxidation states arise because ns and (n-1)d electrons are close in energy, so electrons from both subshells can take part in bonding.

mcqs.q: How does the maximum oxidation state change across a transition series?
options: It falls steadily from the first element
It rises up to the middle of the series and then falls
It rises steadily to the last element
mcqs.why: The notes state that the maximum oxidation state rises across the series up to the middle, equalling the group number for early groups, and then falls.

mcqs.q: Which are the stable oxidation states of manganese listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The table of stable oxidation states lists manganese with +2, +4, +6 and +7, the widest range in the first transition series.

mcqs.q: Why are Sc3+ and Ti4+ especially stable?
options: They have a completely filled d-subshell
They are strongly hydrated in water
They have the noble gas configuration
mcqs.why: Stability depends on configuration: Sc3+ and Ti4+ are stable because losing those electrons leaves them with a noble gas configuration.

mcqs.q: Why is Fe3+ more stable than Fe2+?
options: Fe3+ has a filled d10 configuration
Fe3+ has the half-filled d5 configuration, while Fe2+ is d6
Fe2+ has the noble gas configuration
Fe3+ is smaller and more hydrated in every case
mcqs.why: The notes explain that Fe3+ (d5, half-filled) is more stable than Fe2+ (d6) because a half-filled d-subshell gives extra stability.

mcqs.q: Why is Cu2+ more stable than Cu+ in water, even though Cu+ is d10?
options: Cu2+ has a filled d-subshell in water
Cu+ cannot exist in any compound
The small Cu2+ ion has a much higher (more negative) hydration enthalpy
Water oxidises every Cu+ ion instantly by itself
mcqs.why: Although Ag+ (d10) is favoured by its filled subshell, in water Cu2+ wins because its small size gives a much more negative hydration enthalpy.

mcqs.q: Lower oxidation states of transition elements usually form which type of compound?
mcqs.why: The notes state that lower oxidation states usually form ionic compounds, while higher oxidation states occur in covalent compounds such as oxides and fluorides.

mcqs.q: V2O5 is given in the notes as an example of:
options: A higher oxidation state occurring in a covalent compound
A lower oxidation state in an ionic compound
A complex ion with coordination number 6
mcqs.why: V2O5, with vanadium in the +5 state, is the notes' example of a higher oxidation state found in a covalent compound (an oxide).

mcqs.q: Which oxidation states are the most frequent for transition elements?
mcqs.why: The key points state that the most frequent oxidation states shown by transition elements are +2 and +3.

mcqs.q: Which are the stable oxidation states of vanadium listed in the notes?
mcqs.why: The stable oxidation states table lists vanadium with four states: +2, +3, +4 and +5, showing its variable oxidation behaviour.

lessons.title: Catalytic Behaviour
lessons.notes_html:
Transition metals and their compounds are good catalysts for two reasons:

  • They have variable oxidation states, so they can form unstable intermediate compounds with the reactants and then return to their original state.
  • Their surfaces adsorb reactant molecules, which weakens their bonds and speeds up the reaction (adsorption theory).

Key Reactions

CatalystProcess / Reaction
FeHaber process: manufacture of NH3
V2O5Contact process: manufacture of H2SO4
PtOstwald process: manufacture of HNO3
NiHydrogenation of oils to make ghee
MnO2Decomposition of KClO3 to give O2
FeCl3Manufacture of CCl4 from CS2 and Cl2
Hot CuOxidation of ethanol to ethanal
Pt, RhCatalytic converters in vehicle exhausts

Key Points

  • Transition metals catalyse reactions through variable oxidation states and surface adsorption.
  • Fe is the catalyst in the Haber process and V2O5 in the Contact process.
  • Ni is used for hydrogenation of vegetable oils.
  • MnO2 speeds up the decomposition of KClO3.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used in the Haber process for manufacturing NH3?
mcqs.why: The catalyst table in the notes gives Fe as the catalyst for the Haber process, the manufacture of ammonia, NH3.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used in the Contact process for manufacturing H2SO4?
mcqs.why: The notes list V2O5 as the catalyst in the Contact process used to manufacture sulphuric acid, H2SO4.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used in the Ostwald process for manufacturing HNO3?
mcqs.why: The catalyst table gives Pt as the catalyst for the Ostwald process, the manufacture of nitric acid, HNO3.

mcqs.q: Nickel (Ni) is used as a catalyst for which process?
options: Manufacture of NH3 by the Haber process
Decomposition of KClO3 to give O2
Manufacture of CCl4 from CS2 and Cl2
Hydrogenation of oils to make ghee
mcqs.why: The notes list Ni as the catalyst for the hydrogenation of vegetable oils to make ghee, a classic use of a transition metal catalyst.

mcqs.q: MnO2 speeds up which reaction?
options: Decomposition of KClO3 to give O2
mcqs.why: The table states that MnO2 catalyses the decomposition of potassium chlorate, KClO3, to give oxygen gas.

mcqs.q: One reason transition metals are good catalysts is that they:
options: Have completely filled d-subshells in all states
Never react with the reactants at all
Have variable oxidation states and can form unstable intermediate compounds with reactants
Are always liquids at reaction temperature
mcqs.why: The notes give variable oxidation states as the first reason: the metal forms unstable intermediates with reactants and then returns to its original state.

mcqs.q: The second reason given for catalytic behaviour, the adsorption theory, says that:
options: Reactants dissolve inside the metal lattice permanently
The catalyst surface repels reactant molecules
Adsorption strengthens reactant bonds and slows reactions
Reactant molecules adsorb on the metal surface, which weakens their bonds and speeds up the reaction
mcqs.why: In the adsorption theory, surfaces adsorb reactant molecules; this weakens their bonds and so speeds up the reaction, the second reason in the notes.

mcqs.q: FeCl3 is used as a catalyst in the manufacture of:
mcqs.why: The catalyst table lists FeCl3 for the manufacture of carbon tetrachloride, CCl4, from CS2 and Cl2.

mcqs.q: Hot copper (Cu) catalyses which reaction?
mcqs.why: The notes give hot Cu as the catalyst for oxidising ethanol to ethanal, one of the key catalyst reactions in the table.

mcqs.q: Pt and Rh are used together as catalysts in:
mcqs.why: The table lists Pt and Rh as the catalysts used in catalytic converters fitted to vehicle exhausts to clean the exhaust gases.

lessons.title: Magnetic Behaviour
lessons.notes_html:
The response of a substance to a magnetic field is its magnetic behaviour.

  • Paramagnetic: substances attracted into a magnetic field. They have unpaired electrons, e.g. most transition metal ions.
  • Diamagnetic: substances repelled by a magnetic field. All their electrons are paired, e.g. Zn2+ and Sc3+ compounds.
  • Ferromagnetic: substances that are strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetised, e.g. Fe, Co and Ni.

The magnetic moment is calculated from the number of unpaired electrons (n): μ = √(n(n+2)) BM (Bohr magneton).

IonUnpaired ElectronsMagnetic Moment (BM)
Sc3+00
Ti3+11.73
V3+22.83
Cr3+33.87
Mn2+, Fe3+55.92
Fe2+44.90
Co2+33.87
Ni2+22.83
Cu2+11.73
Zn2+00

Key Points

  • Unpaired electrons make a substance paramagnetic; paired electrons make it diamagnetic.
  • Magnetic moment μ = √(n(n+2)) BM, where n is the number of unpaired electrons.
  • Mn2+ and Fe3+ (5 unpaired electrons) have the highest magnetic moment, 5.92 BM.
  • Cu2+ is paramagnetic (d9) but Zn2+ is diamagnetic (d10).
  • Fe, Co and Ni are ferromagnetic.

mcqs.q: A paramagnetic substance is one that:
options: Is attracted into a magnetic field and has unpaired electrons
Is repelled by a magnetic field and has all electrons paired
Can never be magnetised and has no electrons
Is strongly attracted and permanently magnetised
mcqs.why: The notes define paramagnetic substances as attracted into a magnetic field; they have unpaired electrons, like most transition metal ions.

mcqs.q: Which ions are given as examples of diamagnetic substances?
options: Zn2+ and Sc3+ compounds, with all electrons paired
mcqs.why: Diamagnetic substances are repelled by a magnetic field and have all electrons paired; the notes give Zn2+ and Sc3+ compounds as examples.

mcqs.q: Which metals are ferromagnetic?
mcqs.why: Ferromagnetic substances are strongly attracted and can be permanently magnetised; the notes name iron, cobalt and nickel.

mcqs.q: Using mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) BM, what is the magnetic moment of an ion with 4 unpaired electrons?
mcqs.why: Working: mu = sqrt(4 x (4+2)) = sqrt(24) = 4.90 BM, matching the table value given for Fe2+ with 4 unpaired electrons.

mcqs.q: Mn2+ and Fe3+ have the highest magnetic moment in the table because they have:
mcqs.why: Working: mu = sqrt(5 x (5+2)) = sqrt(35) = 5.92 BM; Mn2+ and Fe3+ each have 5 unpaired electrons, the maximum in the table.

mcqs.q: Using mu = sqrt(n(n+2)) BM, what is the magnetic moment of Cu2+, which has 1 unpaired electron?
mcqs.why: Working: mu = sqrt(1 x (1+2)) = sqrt(3) = 1.73 BM, exactly the value the notes list for Cu2+ with one unpaired electron.

mcqs.q: Why is Zn2+ diamagnetic while Cu2+ is paramagnetic?
options: Zn2+ has more unpaired electrons than Cu2+
Cu2+ is d10 and Zn2+ is d9
Both are d10 but only Cu2+ has unpaired electrons
Zn2+ is d10 with all electrons paired; Cu2+ is d9 with one unpaired electron
mcqs.why: The notes contrast Cu2+ (d9, paramagnetic) with Zn2+ (d10, diamagnetic) because the filled d10 subshell has every electron paired.

mcqs.q: How many unpaired electrons does Ni2+ have, and what is its magnetic moment?
mcqs.why: Working: the table gives Ni2+ 2 unpaired electrons; mu = sqrt(2 x (2+2)) = sqrt(8) = 2.83 BM, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the magnetic moment of Sc3+?
options: 0 BM, because it has no unpaired electrons
mcqs.why: Working: Sc3+ has n = 0 unpaired electrons, so mu = sqrt(0 x (0+2)) = sqrt(0) = 0 BM, and its compounds are diamagnetic.

mcqs.q: Cr3+ and Co2+ both appear in the table with which magnetic moment?
mcqs.why: Working: both ions have 3 unpaired electrons, so mu = sqrt(3 x (3+2)) = sqrt(15) = 3.87 BM, the value listed for both Cr3+ and Co2+.

lessons.title: Alloy Formation
lessons.notes_html:
Transition metals form alloys readily because their atomic sizes are very similar (within about 15% of each other), so atoms of one metal can easily replace atoms of another in the crystal lattice. An alloy is a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal.

Examples: brass (Cu + Zn), bronze (Cu + Sn) and stainless steel (Fe + Cr).

How Alloy Properties Differ from the Pure Metals

  • Alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals.
  • Their melting points are usually lower than those of the component metals.
  • They resist corrosion better, e.g. stainless steel does not rust like iron.
  • Their appearance and colour can differ, e.g. brass looks golden.
  • Their electrical resistance can be much higher, e.g. nichrome is used in heating elements.

Key Points

  • Alloys form easily because transition metal atoms have similar sizes.
  • Brass is Cu + Zn and bronze is Cu + Sn.
  • Alloys are generally harder, stronger and more corrosion-resistant than pure metals.
  • Alloys usually melt lower than their component metals.

mcqs.q: Why do transition metals form alloys readily?
options: Their atomic sizes are very similar, within about 15% of each other
Their atomic sizes differ by more than 50%
They are all liquids at room temperature
mcqs.why: Alloy formation is easy because transition metal atoms are similar in size (within about 15%), so one metal's atoms replace another's in the lattice.

mcqs.q: What is an alloy?
options: A compound with a fixed chemical formula only
A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal
A pure metal with impurities removed
mcqs.why: The notes define an alloy as a homogeneous mixture of two or more metals, or of a metal with a non-metal, such as brass or steel.

mcqs.q: Brass is an alloy of which metals?
mcqs.why: The notes give brass as Cu + Zn; bronze, by contrast, is Cu + Sn, and stainless steel is Fe + Cr.

mcqs.q: Bronze is an alloy of which metals?
mcqs.why: Bronze is listed in the notes as the alloy of copper with tin, Cu + Sn, distinct from brass which uses zinc instead.

mcqs.q: Stainless steel is an alloy of:
mcqs.why: The notes give stainless steel as Fe + Cr, and chromium is what makes it resist corrosion and not rust like pure iron.

mcqs.q: How do the hardness and strength of alloys compare with the pure metals?
options: Alloys are softer and weaker than pure metals
Alloys have exactly the same hardness
Alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals
Alloys are harder but much weaker
mcqs.why: The notes state that alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metals from which they are made, one way their properties differ.

mcqs.q: How do alloy melting points usually compare with those of the component metals?
options: Always higher than every component metal
Exactly equal to the highest component
Usually lower than those of the component metals
mcqs.why: The notes say the melting points of alloys are usually lower than those of the component metals that were mixed to make them.

mcqs.q: Why does stainless steel not rust like iron?
options: Alloys resist corrosion better than pure metals
Stainless steel contains no iron at all
Its melting point is very low
It is painted with chromium oxide
mcqs.why: The notes explain that alloys resist corrosion better, giving stainless steel as the example that does not rust like iron does.

mcqs.q: Nichrome is mentioned in the notes because:
options: It is golden in colour like brass
It never conducts electricity at all
Its electrical resistance is much higher, so it is used in heating elements
It melts at the highest temperature of any alloy
mcqs.why: The notes give nichrome as the example of an alloy whose electrical resistance can be much higher, which is why it is used in heating elements.

mcqs.q: Brass is given as an example of an alloy whose:
options: Melting point is higher than copper and zinc
Appearance and colour differ from its metals; it looks golden
mcqs.why: The notes point out that an alloy's appearance and colour can differ from the pure metals, giving golden-looking brass as the example.

lessons.title: Coordination Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Coordination compounds (complex compounds) contain a central metal atom or ion attached to a group of ligands by coordinate covalent bonds, and the complex can exist independently as a molecule or ion, e.g. [Cu(NH3)4]2+ and [Fe(CN)6]4-.

They differ from double salts: Mohr's salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, gives all its ions (Fe2+, NH4+ and SO4 2-) in solution, but K4[Fe(CN)6] gives only K+ ions and the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4-; it does not give free Fe2+ or CN- ions.

Transition elements form complexes readily because they have small size, high charge, and vacant (n-1)d orbitals that can accept lone pairs from ligands.

Parts of a Complex

  • Central metal atom or ion: the electron-pair acceptor, e.g. Fe in [Fe(CN)6]4-.
  • Ligands: ions or molecules that donate lone pairs to the metal.
  • Coordination sphere: the metal and its ligands, written inside square brackets.
  • Counter-ions: ions outside the brackets that balance the charge.

Types of Ligands

TypeMeaningExamples
MonodentateDonates one lone pairNH3, H2O, Cl-, CN-, OH-
BidentateDonates two lone pairsEthylenediamine (en), oxalate C2O4 2-
PolydentateDonates several lone pairsEDTA (hexadentate)
AmbidentateCan bind through either of two atomsNO2- (through N or O), SCN- (through S or N)
BridgingBinds two metal atoms at onceOH-, Cl- bridges

Key Points

  • A complex has a central metal ion bonded to ligands by coordinate bonds.
  • Unlike double salts, a complex does not give free metal ions in solution.
  • Small size, high charge and vacant d-orbitals favour complex formation.
  • Ligands are classified by the number of lone pairs they donate.
  • EDTA is a hexadentate (chelating) ligand.

mcqs.q: What is a coordination (complex) compound?
options: A compound with a central metal atom or ion attached to ligands by coordinate covalent bonds
A simple mixture of two salts in solution
A metal dissolved in an acid
Any compound containing water of crystallisation
mcqs.why: Coordination compounds contain a central metal atom or ion bonded to a group of ligands by coordinate covalent bonds, e.g. [Cu(NH3)4]2+.

mcqs.q: How does K4[Fe(CN)6] behave in solution compared with a double salt?
options: It gives free Fe2+, CN- and K+ ions separately
It gives only K+ ions and the complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4-, not free Fe2+ or CN- ions
It gives no ions at all in solution
It gives Fe3+ and cyanide ions freely
mcqs.why: Unlike Mohr's salt, which gives all its ions, K4[Fe(CN)6] gives only K+ and the intact complex ion [Fe(CN)6]4- in solution.

mcqs.q: Mohr's salt, FeSO4.(NH4)2SO4.6H2O, is an example of:
options: A complex that gives no metal ions
A double salt that gives all its ions (Fe2+, NH4+, SO4 2-) in solution
mcqs.why: The notes use Mohr's salt as the double-salt contrast: in solution it gives all of its ions, Fe2+, NH4+ and sulphate, separately.

mcqs.q: Why do transition elements form complexes readily?
options: They have large size and low charge
Their d-orbitals are always completely filled
They donate lone pairs to the ligands
They have small size, high charge and vacant (n-1)d orbitals to accept lone pairs
mcqs.why: Complex formation is favoured by the metal's small size, high charge and vacant (n-1)d orbitals that can accept lone pairs from ligands.

mcqs.q: In a complex, what is the role of a ligand?
options: It accepts lone pairs from the central metal
It donates lone pairs of electrons to the central metal
It balances the charge outside the brackets
It is always a positively charged ion
mcqs.why: Ligands are ions or molecules that donate lone pairs to the central metal, which acts as the electron-pair acceptor in the complex.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the coordination sphere?
options: The ions written outside the square brackets
The central metal and its ligands, written inside square brackets
The charge on the whole compound
mcqs.why: The coordination sphere is the metal together with its attached ligands, written inside square brackets; ions outside are counter-ions.

mcqs.q: Which ligand is hexadentate?
mcqs.why: The ligand table lists EDTA as polydentate and specifically hexadentate, donating several (six) lone pairs, so it is a chelating ligand.

mcqs.q: NO2- and SCN- are examples of which type of ligand?
options: Ambidentate ligands, which can bind through either of two atoms
Bidentate ligands, donating two lone pairs at once
Bridging ligands, binding two metals at once
Monodentate ligands, donating one lone pair
mcqs.why: Ambidentate ligands can bind through either of two atoms: NO2- through N or O, and SCN- through S or N, as the notes explain.

mcqs.q: Ethylenediamine (en) and oxalate are which type of ligand?
options: Bridging, binding two metals at once
mcqs.why: The table classifies ethylenediamine (en) and oxalate, C2O4 2-, as bidentate ligands because each donates two lone pairs to the metal.

mcqs.q: Which ligands are given as examples of bridging ligands?
options: OH- and Cl-, which bind two metal atoms at once
mcqs.why: Bridging ligands bind two metal atoms at once; the notes give OH- and Cl- bridges as the examples of this ligand type.

lessons.title: Oxidation State and Coordination Number of Central Metal Ion
lessons.notes_html:
The coordination number is the number of lone pairs of electrons provided by the ligands to the central metal atom or ion, that is, the number of coordinate bonds formed. Common coordination numbers are 2, 4 and 6.

Coordination NumberShapeExample
2Linear[Ag(NH3)2]+
4Tetrahedral[Zn(NH3)4]2+
4Square planar[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]
6Octahedral[Fe(CN)6]4-

Finding the Oxidation State

The sum of the oxidation state of the metal and the charges of the ligands equals the charge on the complex ion.

  • In K4[Fe(CN)6]: the complex ion is [Fe(CN)6]4-. x + 6(-1) = -4, so Fe = +2.
  • In [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2: the complex ion is [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+. x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2, so Co = +3.
  • In [Zn(NH3)4]2+: NH3 is neutral, so Zn = +2.

Key Points

  • Coordination number = number of coordinate bonds to the central metal.
  • Common coordination numbers are 2, 4 and 6.
  • Neutral ligands (NH3, H2O) contribute zero charge in oxidation state calculations.
  • In K4[Fe(CN)6] iron is in the +2 oxidation state.

mcqs.q: The coordination number of a complex is:
options: The number of lone pairs donated by ligands, i.e. the number of coordinate bonds formed
The charge on the central metal ion
The number of counter-ions outside the brackets
The number of ligands minus the charge
mcqs.why: The notes define coordination number as the number of lone pairs provided by the ligands, that is, the number of coordinate bonds to the metal.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of Fe in K4[Fe(CN)6]?
mcqs.why: Working: for [Fe(CN)6]4-, x + 6(-1) = -4, so x = -4 + 6 = +2. Iron is in the +2 oxidation state in this complex.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of Co in [Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2?
mcqs.why: Working: for [Co(NH3)5Cl]2+, x + 5(0) + (-1) = +2, so x = +2 + 1 = +3. Cobalt is in the +3 oxidation state.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of Zn in [Zn(NH3)4]2+?
mcqs.why: Working: NH3 is a neutral ligand contributing 0, so x + 4(0) = +2 and Zn = +2, exactly as worked in the notes.

mcqs.q: A complex with coordination number 2, such as [Ag(NH3)2]+, has which shape?
mcqs.why: The coordination number table gives shape linear for coordination number 2, with [Ag(NH3)2]+ as the example in the notes.

mcqs.q: A complex with coordination number 6, such as [Fe(CN)6]4-, has which shape?
mcqs.why: Coordination number 6 gives an octahedral shape; the notes use [Fe(CN)6]4- as the example of this common arrangement.

mcqs.q: [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] has coordination number 4 and which shape?
mcqs.why: The table pairs coordination number 4 with two shapes; [Pt(NH3)2Cl2] is the notes' example of the square planar arrangement.

mcqs.q: [Zn(NH3)4]2+ has coordination number 4 and which shape?
mcqs.why: The notes list [Zn(NH3)4]2+ as the tetrahedral example for coordination number 4, in contrast to square planar platinum complexes.

mcqs.q: In oxidation state calculations for complexes, neutral ligands such as NH3 and H2O contribute:
options: A charge equal to the metal's charge
mcqs.why: The key points stress that neutral ligands (NH3, H2O) contribute zero charge when finding the metal's oxidation state in a complex.

mcqs.q: Which are the common coordination numbers named in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state that common coordination numbers are 2, 4 and 6, with linear, tetrahedral or square planar, and octahedral shapes respectively.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Coordination Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Rules for Naming

  • The cation is named first, then the anion.
  • Inside the complex, ligands are named first (in alphabetical order, ignoring di, tri, etc.), then the central metal.
  • Anionic ligands end in -o: Cl- chloro, CN- cyano, OH- hydroxo, SO4 2- sulphato, C2O4 2- oxalato.
  • Neutral ligands keep their names, with special names: H2O aqua, NH3 ammine, CO carbonyl, NO nitrosyl.
  • The number of ligands is shown by di, tri, tetra, penta, hexa; bis, tris, tetrakis are used for complex ligand names such as ethylenediamine.
  • The oxidation state of the metal is written in Roman numerals in brackets, e.g. iron(III).
  • If the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate, e.g. ferrate, cobaltate, platinate, argentate, stannate.

Worked Examples (from the book)

FormulaName
[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2Pentaamminechlorocobalt(III) chloride
K3[Fe(CN)6]Potassium hexacyanoferrate(III)
K4[Fe(CN)6]Potassium hexacyanoferrate(II)
[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]Diamminedichloroplatinum(II)
[Cr(H2O)6]Cl3Hexaaquachromium(III) chloride
Na2[Sn(OH)6]Sodium hexahydroxostannate(IV)
Na2[Fe(CN)5NO]Sodium pentacyanonitrosylferrate(II)
[Pt(NH3)2Cl4]Diamminetetrachloroplatinum(IV)

Key Points

  • Name the cation before the anion; ligands before the metal.
  • Anionic ligands end in -o; H2O is aqua and NH3 is ammine.
  • Show the metal's oxidation state in Roman numerals.
  • For anionic complexes the metal name ends in -ate.

mcqs.q: In naming a coordination compound, what is named first?
options: The central metal, then the ligands
The counter-ion last in all cases
mcqs.why: The first naming rule in the notes is that the cation is named first, then the anion, just as in simple ionic compounds.

mcqs.q: Inside a complex, in what order are the parts named?
options: Central metal first, then ligands alphabetically
Ligands first (alphabetically, ignoring di, tri), then the central metal
Ligands in order of their charges
mcqs.why: Within the complex, ligands are named first in alphabetical order (ignoring prefixes like di and tri), followed by the central metal.

mcqs.q: Anionic ligands end in which letter pattern in complex names?
options: They end in -o, e.g. chloro, cyano, hydroxo
mcqs.why: The rules state that anionic ligands end in -o: Cl- is chloro, CN- is cyano, OH- is hydroxo, SO4 2- is sulphato and oxalate is oxalato.

mcqs.q: What are the special names for the neutral ligands H2O and NH3?
options: H2O is hydroxo and NH3 is amino
H2O is aqua and NH3 is nitro
H2O is oxo and NH3 is ammine
H2O is aqua and NH3 is ammine
mcqs.why: Neutral ligands keep their names with special cases: H2O is aqua, NH3 is ammine, CO is carbonyl and NO is nitrosyl.

mcqs.q: When the complex ion is an anion, how does the metal name change?
options: It ends in -ate, e.g. ferrate, cobaltate, platinate
It stays exactly the same as the element
mcqs.why: The rules state that if the complex ion is an anion, the metal name ends in -ate, as in ferrate, cobaltate, platinate, argentate and stannate.

mcqs.q: What is the name of K3[Fe(CN)6]?
mcqs.why: Working: 3 K+ give +3, so the complex is [Fe(CN)6]3-; x + 6(-1) = -3 gives Fe = +3, and as an anion the name is potassium hexacyanoferrate(III).

mcqs.q: What is the name of [Cr(H2O)6]Cl3?
mcqs.why: Working: 3 Cl- give -3, so the complex charge is +3; H2O is neutral, so Cr = +3, giving hexaaquachromium(III) chloride as in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which prefixes are used for complex ligand names such as ethylenediamine?
options: di, tri, tetra in all cases
mcqs.why: The notes state that bis, tris and tetrakis are used instead of di, tri, tetra when the ligand name itself is complex, e.g. ethylenediamine.

mcqs.q: What is the name of [Pt(NH3)2Cl2]?
mcqs.why: Working: the complex is neutral, so x + 2(0) + 2(-1) = 0 gives Pt = +2; ligands first gives diamminedichloroplatinum(II), as in the notes.

mcqs.q: How is the oxidation state of the metal shown in a complex name?
options: As a subscript after the formula
In Roman numerals in brackets after the metal name, e.g. iron(III)
In Arabic numerals before the ligands
It is not shown in the name at all
mcqs.why: The rules require the metal's oxidation state to be written in Roman numerals in brackets, for example iron(III) in a complex name.

lessons.title: Shapes of Complex Compound
lessons.notes_html:
The shape (geometry) of a complex depends on its coordination number.

Coordination NumberShapeExamples
2Linear[Ag(NH3)2]+, [Ag(CN)2]-
4Tetrahedral[Zn(NH3)4]2+, [Ni(CO)4]
4Square planar[Cu(NH3)4]2+, [Ni(CN)4]2-, [AuCl4]-
5Trigonal bipyramidal / square pyramidal[Fe(CO)5]
6Octahedral[Fe(CN)6]4-, [Co(NH3)6]3+

The octahedral shape (coordination number 6) is the most common geometry of coordination compounds.

Key Points

  • Coordination number 2 gives a linear shape.
  • Coordination number 4 gives tetrahedral or square planar shapes.
  • Coordination number 6 gives an octahedral shape, the most common one.
  • [Ag(NH3)2]+ is linear and [Fe(CN)6]4- is octahedral.

mcqs.q: The shape (geometry) of a complex depends on its:
mcqs.why: The notes state that the shape of a complex depends on its coordination number, with each number giving a characteristic geometry.

mcqs.q: [Ag(NH3)2]+ and [Ag(CN)2]- have which shape?
mcqs.why: Coordination number 2 gives a linear shape; both [Ag(NH3)2]+ and [Ag(CN)2]- are listed as linear examples in the notes.

mcqs.q: [Ni(CO)4] has coordination number 4 and which shape?
mcqs.why: The shape table lists [Ni(CO)4] with [Zn(NH3)4]2+ as tetrahedral complexes of coordination number 4.

mcqs.q: Which complexes are given as square planar examples?
mcqs.why: For coordination number 4, the notes list [Cu(NH3)4]2+, [Ni(CN)4]2- and [AuCl4]- as the square planar examples.

mcqs.q: [Fe(CO)5], with coordination number 5, has which shape?
mcqs.why: Coordination number 5 is paired in the table with trigonal bipyramidal / square pyramidal shapes, with [Fe(CO)5] as the example.

mcqs.q: Which is the most common geometry of coordination compounds?
mcqs.why: The key points state that the octahedral shape (coordination number 6) is the most common geometry of coordination compounds.

mcqs.q: [Co(NH3)6]3+ has which shape?
mcqs.why: With six NH3 ligands the coordination number is 6, so [Co(NH3)6]3+ is listed with [Fe(CN)6]4- as an octahedral complex.

mcqs.q: A complex with coordination number 4 can have which two shapes?
mcqs.why: The notes show coordination number 4 giving two possible shapes: tetrahedral, e.g. [Zn(NH3)4]2+, or square planar, e.g. [Ni(CN)4]2-.

mcqs.q: [Fe(CN)6]4- is used in the notes as the standard example of which shape?
mcqs.why: Six CN- ligands give coordination number 6, and [Fe(CN)6]4- is the notes' standard example of an octahedral complex.

mcqs.q: What shape does a coordination number of 2 always give in these notes?
mcqs.why: The shape table pairs coordination number 2 only with the linear shape, as in [Ag(NH3)2]+ and [Ag(CN)2]-.

lessons.title: Colour in Complex Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Most transition metal complexes are coloured. The colour is due to d-d transitions: when ligands surround the metal ion, its five d-orbitals split into two sets of different energy. An electron absorbs visible light and jumps from the lower set to the higher set. The colour absorbed is removed from white light, and we see the complementary colour.

Ions with empty d-orbitals (d0, e.g. Sc3+, Ti4+) or completely filled d-orbitals (d10, e.g. Zn2+) cannot show d-d transitions, so they are colourless. Hydrated copper(II) sulphate, [Cu(H2O)6]2+, is blue, while anhydrous CuSO4 is white. CoCl2 is blue when anhydrous and pink when hydrated.

Iond-ElectronsColour
Sc3+d0Colourless
Ti4+d0Colourless
Ti3+d1Purple (violet)
V4+d1Blue
V3+d2Green
V2+d3Violet

Some very intense colours, such as purple MnO4- and orange Cr2O7 2-, are due to charge-transfer transitions, because Mn(VII) and Cr(VI) have no d-electrons.

Key Points

  • Colour in complexes is caused by d-d transitions between split d-orbitals.
  • The colour seen is complementary to the colour absorbed.
  • d0 and d10 ions (Sc3+, Zn2+) are colourless.
  • [Ti(H2O)6]3+ is violet and [Cu(H2O)6]2+ is blue.
  • The colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligand.

mcqs.q: Colour in transition metal complexes is mainly due to:
options: d-d transitions of electrons between split d-orbitals
Electrons jumping between the metal and counter-ions
Vibration of the ligands around the metal
Reflection of light by the crystal surface
mcqs.why: When ligands surround the metal ion its d-orbitals split into two energy sets, and electrons absorbing light jump between them: d-d transitions.

mcqs.q: When ligands surround a metal ion, its five d-orbitals:
options: All gain exactly the same energy
Split into two sets of different energy
mcqs.why: The notes explain that the ligand field splits the five d-orbitals into two sets of different energy, making d-d transitions possible.

mcqs.q: The colour we see from a complex is:
options: Exactly the colour that was absorbed
The complementary colour to the colour absorbed
mcqs.why: The absorbed colour is removed from white light, and the colour observed is the complementary colour to the one absorbed.

mcqs.q: Why are Sc3+ and Ti4+ compounds colourless?
options: They are d10 with a filled subshell
They are d0, so no d-d transitions are possible
mcqs.why: Ions with empty d-orbitals (d0, e.g. Sc3+, Ti4+) cannot show d-d transitions, so the notes list them as colourless.

mcqs.q: Why is Zn2+ colourless?
options: It is d0 with empty orbitals
It is d10, completely filled, so no d-d transition can occur
mcqs.why: A completely filled d10 subshell, as in Zn2+, leaves no space for a d-d transition, so Zn2+ compounds are colourless.

mcqs.q: Hydrated copper(II) sulphate, [Cu(H2O)6]2+, is blue, while anhydrous CuSO4 is:
mcqs.why: The notes contrast blue hydrated copper(II) sulphate with white anhydrous CuSO4, showing how water ligands produce the colour.

mcqs.q: CoCl2 changes colour with hydration: it is:
options: Pink when anhydrous and blue when hydrated
Blue when anhydrous and pink when hydrated
mcqs.why: The notes state that CoCl2 is blue when anhydrous and pink when hydrated, another example of colour depending on the ligands present.

mcqs.q: Which ion-colour pairing is correct from the notes' table?
options: Ti3+ (d1) is purple (violet) and V3+ (d2) is green
Ti3+ (d1) is colourless and V3+ (d2) is blue
V4+ (d1) is violet and V2+ (d3) is green
Sc3+ (d0) is purple and Ti4+ (d0) is blue
mcqs.why: The table gives Ti3+ d1 as purple (violet), V4+ d1 as blue, V3+ d2 as green and V2+ d3 as violet; d0 ions are colourless.

mcqs.q: The intense purple of MnO4- and orange of Cr2O7 2- are due to:
options: Charge-transfer transitions, because Mn(VII) and Cr(VI) have no d-electrons
Hydration of the ions in solution
mcqs.why: The notes explain these very intense colours by charge-transfer transitions, since Mn(VII) and Cr(VI) have no d-electrons for d-d transitions.

mcqs.q: On what does the colour of a complex depend, according to the notes?
options: The metal, its oxidation state and the ligand
Only the size of the crystal
The temperature of the room only
mcqs.why: The key points state that the colour depends on the metal, its oxidation state and the ligand surrounding the metal ion.

lessons.title: Uses of Transition Metal Compounds in Paints
lessons.notes_html:
Pure transition metals are valued for many reasons. One important reason is their ability to form highly coloured compounds, which are used as pigments in paints.

  • Transition elements such as chromium, iron, copper, cobalt and titanium form numerous coloured compounds with oxygen.
  • Red paint comes from compounds of iron with oxygen.
  • Green and blue paints come from different compounds of copper, chromium and cobalt.
  • Titanium forms a white compound with oxygen, used for white paint.

Key Points

  • Coloured transition metal compounds are used as paint pigments.
  • Iron-oxygen compounds give red paint.
  • Copper, chromium and cobalt compounds give green and blue paints.
  • Titanium gives white paint.

mcqs.q: Why are pure transition metals valued in connection with paints?
options: They form highly coloured compounds used as pigments in paints
They dissolve completely in paint solvents
They prevent any colour from forming
mcqs.why: The lesson states that transition metals are valued for their ability to form highly coloured compounds, which are used as pigments in paints.

mcqs.q: Red paint comes from compounds of which element with oxygen?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that red paint comes from compounds of iron with oxygen, a transition metal oxide pigment.

mcqs.q: Green and blue paints come from compounds of which elements?
mcqs.why: The notes state that green and blue paints come from different compounds of copper, chromium and cobalt with oxygen.

mcqs.q: White paint comes from a compound of which element with oxygen?
mcqs.why: Titanium forms a white compound with oxygen, and the notes state that this white compound is used for white paint.

mcqs.q: Which elements are named as forming numerous coloured compounds with oxygen?
options: Chromium, iron, copper, cobalt and titanium
mcqs.why: The lesson names chromium, iron, copper, cobalt and titanium as transition elements forming numerous coloured compounds with oxygen.

mcqs.q: In paints, the coloured transition metal compounds act as:
mcqs.why: The key points state that coloured transition metal compounds are used as paint pigments, giving the paint its colour.

mcqs.q: Which colour pairing is correct from the lesson?
options: Iron-oxygen compounds give white; titanium gives red
Copper compounds give white paint only
Iron-oxygen compounds give red; titanium-oxygen gives white
mcqs.why: The lesson pairs iron with oxygen for red paint and titanium with oxygen for the white compound used in white paint.

mcqs.q: A paint manufacturer needing a green or blue pigment would use compounds of:
mcqs.why: Green and blue paints come from different compounds of copper, chromium and cobalt, according to the notes on paint pigments.

mcqs.q: The coloured compounds used in paints are mostly compounds of transition elements with:
mcqs.why: The lesson emphasises that these transition elements form numerous coloured compounds with oxygen, and those compounds serve as pigments.

mcqs.q: Which statement best summarises this lesson?
options: All transition metal compounds are white
Coloured transition metal compounds are used as pigments: iron for red, Cu/Cr/Co for green and blue, titanium for white
Only titanium compounds are used in paints
Transition metals are never used in paints
mcqs.why: The key points summarise: iron-oxygen compounds give red paint, copper, chromium and cobalt give green and blue, and titanium gives white paint.

lessons.title: Vanadium
lessons.notes_html:
Vanadium has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d3 4s2. It shows oxidation states from +2 to +5.

Oxidation StateExamplesColour
+5VO3-, V2O5Yellow / orange
+4VO2+, VOCl2Blue
+3V3+, VCl3Green
+2V2+, VCl2Violet

The +5 state is the most stable; stability decreases as the oxidation state falls. Vanadium(II) compounds are strong reducing agents and are quickly oxidised by air to vanadium(III). In acid solution the blue vanadyl ion VO2+ reacts with V2+: VO2+ + 2V2+ + 4H+ → 3V3+ + 2H2O.

Vanadium(V) oxide, V2O5, is amphoteric: it dissolves in acids and in alkalis, forming vanadates. It is used as a catalyst in the Contact process for making sulphuric acid.

Key Reactions

ReactionChange
SO2 + V2O5 → SO3 + 2VO2V(V) oxidises SO2
4VO2 + O2 → 2V2O5Catalyst regenerated
VO2+ + 2V2+ + 4H+ → 3V3+ + 2H2OReaction in acid solution

Key Points

  • Vanadium shows oxidation states +2, +3, +4 and +5, each with a different colour.
  • The +5 state is the most stable; V(II) is a strong reducing agent.
  • V2O5 is amphoteric and forms vanadates with alkalis.
  • V2O5 catalyses the oxidation of SO2 to SO3 in the Contact process.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of vanadium?
mcqs.why: The notes give vanadium's configuration as [Ar]3d3 4s2, from which it shows oxidation states from +2 to +5.

mcqs.q: Which oxidation state of vanadium is the most stable?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the +5 state is the most stable for vanadium, and stability decreases as the oxidation state falls.

mcqs.q: What is the colour of vanadium in the +4 state, e.g. VO2+ and VOCl2?
mcqs.why: The oxidation state table gives the +4 state (VO2+, VOCl2) as blue, between +5 yellow/orange and +3 green.

mcqs.q: What is the colour of vanadium(II) compounds such as VCl2?
mcqs.why: The table lists the +2 state (V2+, VCl2) as violet, the lowest and least stable of vanadium's oxidation states in the notes.

mcqs.q: Vanadium(II) compounds behave as:
options: Strong oxidising agents, reduced by air
Strong reducing agents, quickly oxidised by air to vanadium(III)
mcqs.why: The notes state that vanadium(II) compounds are strong reducing agents and are quickly oxidised by air to vanadium(III).

mcqs.q: V2O5 is described as amphoteric because it:
options: Dissolves in acids and in alkalis, forming vanadates with alkalis
mcqs.why: V2O5 is amphoteric: it dissolves in acids and in alkalis, and with alkalis it forms vanadates, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: In the Contact process, what is the role of V2O5?
options: It is the raw material converted to H2SO4
It catalyses the oxidation of SO2 to SO3
mcqs.why: V2O5 is used as the catalyst in the Contact process for making sulphuric acid, catalysing SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + 2VO2.

mcqs.q: In the reaction SO2 + V2O5 -> SO3 + 2VO2, vanadium(V):
options: Oxidises SO2 and is itself reduced to VO2
Is regenerated unchanged in this step
Takes no part in the reaction
mcqs.why: The reaction table states that V(V) oxidises SO2 to SO3 while V2O5 is converted to VO2; the catalyst is later regenerated by oxygen.

mcqs.q: How is the V2O5 catalyst regenerated in the Contact process?
mcqs.why: The notes give the regeneration step as 4VO2 + O2 -> 2V2O5, restoring the catalyst so the Contact process cycle can continue.

mcqs.q: In acid solution, VO2+ reacts with V2+ to give which product?
mcqs.why: Working: the notes' equation is VO2+ + 2V2+ + 4H+ -> 3V3+ + 2H2O; the coefficients 1:2 give 3 V3+ ions, balancing vanadium atoms (1+2=3).

lessons.title: Chromium
lessons.notes_html:
Chromium has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d5 4s1. Its main oxidation states are +2, +3 and +6.

  • +2 state: chromium(II) compounds are reducing agents and are unstable; they are quickly oxidised to chromium(III).
  • +3 state: the most stable state. Chromium(III) oxide, Cr2O3, is a green solid, and chromium(III) salts such as CrCl3 are violet or green.
  • +6 state: compounds such as K2Cr2O7, K2CrO4 and CrO3 are strong oxidizing agents.

Cr2O3 is amphoteric: it reacts with both acids and alkalis. Chromium gives stainless steel its resistance to rusting.

Chromate-Dichromate Equilibrium

ReactionObservation
2CrO4 2- (yellow) + 2H+ ⇌ Cr2O7 2- (orange) + H2OAcid turns yellow chromate into orange dichromate
Cr2O7 2- + 2OH- → 2CrO4 2- + H2OAlkali turns orange dichromate back to yellow chromate

Key Points

  • Chromium shows +2, +3 and +6 oxidation states; +3 is the most stable.
  • Cr2O3 is green and amphoteric.
  • Cr(VI) compounds are strong oxidizing agents.
  • Yellow chromate and orange dichromate interconvert in acid and alkali.
  • Chromium makes stainless steel rust-resistant.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of chromium?
mcqs.why: Chromium is one of the exceptions: its configuration is [Ar]3d5 4s1, giving the extra stable half-filled d5 arrangement.

mcqs.q: Which oxidation state of chromium is the most stable?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the +3 state is chromium's most stable state, while +2 is unstable and +6 compounds are strong oxidising agents.

mcqs.q: Chromium(II) compounds behave as:
options: Strong oxidising agents like Cr(VI) compounds
Reducing agents that are unstable and quickly oxidised to chromium(III)
Acids that dissolve in alkalis only
mcqs.why: The notes describe chromium(II) compounds as reducing agents that are unstable and quickly oxidised to chromium(III).

mcqs.q: Chromium(III) oxide, Cr2O3, is:
options: An orange solid and a strong oxidiser
A yellow solid and purely basic
A green solid, and it is amphoteric
mcqs.why: Cr2O3 is a green solid in the +3 state, and the notes state that it is amphoteric, reacting with both acids and alkalis.

mcqs.q: Which chromium compounds are strong oxidising agents?
options: Cr(VI) compounds such as K2Cr2O7, K2CrO4 and CrO3
mcqs.why: The notes list the +6 compounds K2Cr2O7, K2CrO4 and CrO3 as strong oxidising agents, unlike the reducing Cr(II) compounds.

mcqs.q: What happens when acid is added to yellow chromate solution?
options: It turns into green Cr3+ solution
It gives a yellow precipitate of Cr2O3
It turns into orange dichromate: 2CrO4 2- + 2H+ -> Cr2O7 2- + H2O
mcqs.why: Working: the equilibrium in the notes is 2CrO4 2- (yellow) + 2H+ ⇌ Cr2O7 2- (orange) + H2O, so acid converts yellow chromate to orange dichromate.

mcqs.q: What happens when alkali is added to orange dichromate solution?
options: It turns back into yellow chromate: Cr2O7 2- + 2OH- -> 2CrO4 2- + H2O
mcqs.why: The notes give Cr2O7 2- + 2OH- -> 2CrO4 2- + H2O: alkali reverses the acid reaction, turning orange dichromate back to yellow chromate.

mcqs.q: Chromium gives stainless steel which useful property?
mcqs.why: The key points state that chromium makes stainless steel rust-resistant, which is why chromium is alloyed with iron.

mcqs.q: Chromium(III) salts such as CrCl3 are described as:
mcqs.why: The notes describe chromium(III) salts such as CrCl3 as violet or green, in the most stable +3 oxidation state.

mcqs.q: Cr2O3 reacting with both acids and alkalis shows that it is:
mcqs.why: An oxide that reacts with both acids and alkalis is amphoteric; the notes state this property explicitly for Cr2O3.

lessons.title: Potassium Dichromate(VI) as an Oxidizing Agent
lessons.notes_html:
Potassium dichromate, K2Cr2O7, is prepared from the mineral chromite, FeCr2O4.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
Roasting chromite4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 → 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2
Acidifying2Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 → Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O
With KClNa2Cr2O7 + 2KCl → K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl

K2Cr2O7 forms orange crystals (melting point 398°C) and is less soluble in water than sodium dichromate. In acid solution it is a powerful oxidizing agent; chromium changes from +6 to +3 and the orange solution turns green:

Cr2O7 2- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O

It oxidises iron(II) to iron(III): K2Cr2O7 + 7H2SO4 + 6FeSO4 → 3Fe2(SO4)3 + Cr2(SO4)3 + K2SO4 + 7H2O. Because of this oxidising action it is used in volumetric analysis.

Key Points

  • K2Cr2O7 is made from chromite ore in three steps.
  • It is an orange crystalline solid, melting point 398°C.
  • In acid it oxidises Fe2+ to Fe3+ and is itself reduced to green Cr3+.
  • Half-equation: Cr2O7 2- + 14H+ + 6e- → 2Cr3+ + 7H2O.
  • It is used as an oxidising agent in volumetric analysis.

mcqs.q: Potassium dichromate, K2Cr2O7, is prepared from which mineral?
mcqs.why: The notes state that K2Cr2O7 is prepared from the mineral chromite, FeCr2O4, in three steps beginning with roasting.

mcqs.q: The first step in preparing K2Cr2O7 is:
options: Roasting chromite with Na2CO3 and O2 to give Na2CrO4
Heating chromite alone in a vacuum
mcqs.why: Step 1 is roasting: 4FeCr2O4 + 8Na2CO3 + 7O2 -> 8Na2CrO4 + 2Fe2O3 + 8CO2, forming sodium chromate.

mcqs.q: The final step uses KCl to convert sodium dichromate into potassium dichromate:
mcqs.why: The notes give the KCl step as Na2Cr2O7 + 2KCl -> K2Cr2O7 + 2NaCl, exchanging sodium for potassium in the dichromate.

mcqs.q: K2Cr2O7 forms which kind of solid, and with what melting point?
options: White crystals with a melting point of 800°C
mcqs.why: The notes describe K2Cr2O7 as orange crystals, melting point 398°C, and less soluble in water than sodium dichromate.

mcqs.q: In acid solution, dichromate is reduced to which ion, with what colour change?
options: Yellow CrO4 2-; the solution stays orange
Green Cr3+; the orange solution turns green
mcqs.why: In acid, chromium changes from +6 to +3 and the orange solution turns green as Cr3+ forms, per the notes' half-equation.

mcqs.q: What is the correct half-equation for dichromate in acid?
mcqs.why: Working: balance Cr (2), O (7 H2O), H (14H+) then charge: left -2+14-6 = +6 = right 2(+3); so 6 electrons are gained, as in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many Fe2+ ions does one dichromate ion oxidise, from the notes' equation?
options: 6 Fe2+ ions are oxidised to Fe3+ per dichromate
mcqs.why: Working: the equation K2Cr2O7 + 7H2SO4 + 6FeSO4 -> products uses 6 FeSO4 per 1 K2Cr2O7, so 6 Fe2+ are oxidised, matching the 6 electrons gained.

mcqs.q: Compared with sodium dichromate, K2Cr2O7 is:
mcqs.why: The notes state that potassium dichromate is less soluble in water than sodium dichromate, which is why the KCl conversion step works.

mcqs.q: Because of its oxidising action in acid, K2Cr2O7 is used in:
mcqs.why: The key points state that K2Cr2O7 is used as an oxidising agent in volumetric analysis, oxidising Fe2+ to Fe3+ quantitatively.

mcqs.q: The acidifying step in the preparation converts sodium chromate using:
mcqs.why: Step 2 in the notes is acidifying with sulphuric acid: 2Na2CrO4 + H2SO4 -> Na2Cr2O7 + Na2SO4 + H2O, before the KCl step.

lessons.title: Manganese
lessons.notes_html:
Manganese has the electronic configuration [Ar]3d5 4s2. It shows oxidation states from +2 to +7. The common states are +2 (d5), +4 (d3) and +7 (d0).

The +2 state is the most stable because of the half-filled d5 configuration. Manganese(II) salts such as MnCl2 and MnSO4 are pale pink. Compounds in higher oxidation states, such as potassium manganate(VI), K2MnO4 (+6), and potassium permanganate, KMnO4 (+7), are strong oxidizing agents.

Oxides of Manganese

OxideFormulaOxidation StateNature
Manganese(II) oxideMnO+2Basic
Manganese(IV) oxideMnO2+4Amphoteric
Manganese(VII) oxideMn2O7+7Acidic

The acidic character of manganese oxides increases, and the basic character decreases, as the oxidation state increases.

Key Points

  • Manganese shows oxidation states +2 to +7.
  • Mn2+ (d5) is the most stable state; its salts are pale pink.
  • K2MnO4 and KMnO4 are strong oxidizing agents.
  • MnO is basic, MnO2 is amphoteric and Mn2O7 is acidic.
  • Acidic character of the oxides increases with oxidation state.

mcqs.q: What is the electronic configuration of manganese?
mcqs.why: The notes give manganese's configuration as [Ar]3d5 4s2, and it shows oxidation states from +2 to +7.

mcqs.q: Why is the +2 state the most stable for manganese?
options: Mn2+ has a filled d10 configuration
Mn2+ has the half-filled d5 configuration
Mn2+ has the noble gas configuration
Mn2+ is the most strongly hydrated ion
mcqs.why: Mn2+ keeps the half-filled 3d5 arrangement after losing the 4s electrons, and the notes state this makes +2 the most stable state.

mcqs.q: What colour are manganese(II) salts such as MnCl2 and MnSO4?
mcqs.why: The notes describe manganese(II) salts such as MnCl2 and MnSO4 as pale pink, in the stable +2 oxidation state.

mcqs.q: Which manganese compounds are strong oxidising agents?
mcqs.why: Compounds in higher oxidation states, potassium manganate(VI) K2MnO4 and potassium permanganate KMnO4, are strong oxidising agents.

mcqs.q: MnO, manganese(II) oxide, is which type of oxide?
mcqs.why: The oxide table lists MnO (+2) as basic, MnO2 (+4) as amphoteric and Mn2O7 (+7) as acidic, showing the trend with oxidation state.

mcqs.q: MnO2, manganese(IV) oxide, is which type of oxide?
mcqs.why: The notes classify MnO2, with manganese in the +4 state, as amphoteric, between basic MnO and acidic Mn2O7.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of Mn in Mn2O7?
mcqs.why: Working: 2x + 7(-2) = 0, so 2x = 14 and x = +7. Mn2O7 is manganese(VII) oxide, the acidic oxide in the table.

mcqs.q: What is the oxidation state of Mn in KMnO4?
mcqs.why: Working: x + (+1) + 4(-2) = 0, so x = 8 - 1 = +7. KMnO4 contains Mn(VII), matching the notes' +7 state (d0).

mcqs.q: How does the character of manganese oxides change as oxidation state increases?
options: Basic character increases and acidic character decreases
Acidic character increases and basic character decreases
mcqs.why: The notes state that the acidic character of manganese oxides increases, and basic character decreases, as the oxidation state increases.

mcqs.q: The common oxidation states of manganese highlighted in the notes are:

lessons.title: Potassium Manganate(VII) as an Oxidizing Agent in Organic Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Potassium manganate(VII), KMnO4 (potassium permanganate), is a powerful oxidizing agent and probably the most useful one in organic chemistry. It can work in acidic, basic or neutral medium. In acid it is reduced to manganese(II) ions, while in alkaline or neutral medium MnO2 is formed.

Oxidizing Properties in Alkaline Medium (Baeyer's Test)

When an alkene is passed through cold 1% alkaline KMnO4 solution (Baeyer's reagent), a vicinal diol (glycol) is formed. The pink colour is discharged and dark brown MnO2 appears. This is Baeyer's test for unsaturation.

3CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 4H2O → 3CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) + 2KOH + 2MnO2

Oxidizing Properties in Acidic Medium

With acidified KMnO4 an alkene also gives a glycol, but the pink colour disappears because colourless manganese(II) ions are formed:

5CH2=CH2 + 2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 2H2O → 5CH2(OH)-CH2(OH) + 2MnSO4 + K2SO4

Use in Titrations

Acidified KMnO4 is used in redox titrations. It acts as its own indicator (self-indicator): the end point is the first permanent pink colour. It oxidises iron(II) ions and oxalic acid:

ReactionUse
MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ → Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2OEstimation of iron(II)
2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 5(COOH)2 → K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 8H2O + 10CO2Estimation of oxalates

Key Points

  • KMnO4 oxidises in acid, alkaline and neutral media.
  • In acid it gives Mn2+; in alkaline or neutral medium it gives MnO2.
  • Cold alkaline KMnO4 converts alkenes to glycols (Baeyer's test for unsaturation).
  • KMnO4 is a self-indicator in redox titrations.
  • It is used to estimate iron(II) and oxalates volumetrically.

mcqs.q: In acidic medium, KMnO4 is reduced to which product?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in acid KMnO4 is reduced to manganese(II) ions, while in alkaline or neutral medium MnO2 is formed instead.

mcqs.q: In alkaline or neutral medium, KMnO4 is reduced to which product?
mcqs.why: The key points state that in alkaline or neutral medium permanganate gives MnO2, seen as a dark brown solid in Baeyer's test.

mcqs.q: Baeyer's test uses which reagent?
mcqs.why: Baeyer's reagent is cold 1% alkaline KMnO4 solution; an alkene passed through it forms a vicinal diol (glycol).

mcqs.q: What is observed when an alkene undergoes Baeyer's test?
options: The solution turns deep blue permanently
The pink colour is discharged and dark brown MnO2 appears
mcqs.why: In Baeyer's test the pink colour is discharged and dark brown MnO2 appears as the alkene is converted to a glycol, showing unsaturation.

mcqs.q: Baeyer's test is a test for:
mcqs.why: The notes call Baeyer's test the test for unsaturation, because alkenes decolourise cold alkaline KMnO4 and form glycols.

mcqs.q: With acidified KMnO4, an alkene gives a glycol and the pink colour disappears because:
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the media: with acidified KMnO4 the pink disappears because colourless Mn2+ ions form, not brown MnO2.

mcqs.q: Why is KMnO4 called a self-indicator in titrations?
options: It changes colour at the start of the titration
It is colourless throughout the titration
It indicates its own concentration on the bottle
Its end point is the first permanent pink colour, so no separate indicator is needed
mcqs.why: Acidified KMnO4 acts as its own indicator: the end point is the first permanent pink colour from a slight excess of permanganate.

mcqs.q: From the titration equation, how many Fe2+ ions react with one MnO4- ion?
mcqs.why: Working: MnO4- + 8H+ + 5Fe2+ -> Mn2+ + 5Fe3+ + 4H2O, so the ratio is 1 MnO4- : 5 Fe2+, used in estimating iron(II).

mcqs.q: Acidified KMnO4 is used volumetrically to estimate:
mcqs.why: The notes list two titration uses: estimation of iron(II) and estimation of oxalates, both using acidified KMnO4 as a self-indicator.

mcqs.q: From the oxalate equation, how many CO2 molecules are produced from 5 oxalic acid molecules?
mcqs.why: Working: 2KMnO4 + 3H2SO4 + 5(COOH)2 -> K2SO4 + 2MnSO4 + 8H2O + 10CO2; each oxalic acid gives 2 CO2, so 5 x 2 = 10 CO2.

lessons.title: Iron
lessons.notes_html:
Iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust. It is highly reactive, corrodes easily and occurs only in the combined state. Its important ores are magnetite (Fe3O4), haematite (Fe2O3) and limonite (2Fe2O3.3H2O). In Pakistan, iron ore deposits are found at Kalabagh (the largest), Nokundi and Chiniot. The largest world producers are China, Australia, Brazil, India and Russia.

Oxidation States

Iron, [Ar]3d6 4s2, shows oxidation states from -2 to +6; the most common are +2 and +3. Iron(II) compounds such as [Fe(H2O)6]2+ and FeSO4.7H2O are reducing agents. Fe2+ (3d6) is easily oxidised to Fe3+ (3d5) because the half-filled d-subshell is extra stable; this is why a cut apple turns brown in air and why Fe2O3 is more stable than FeO.

Iron as Catalyst in Haber's Process

N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3 (Fe catalyst). Nitrogen comes from air and hydrogen from methane in natural gas. The reaction is reversible and slow, so a catalyst is used to reach equilibrium quickly. The catalyst is magnetite (Fe3O4) mixed with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3. The gases are purified first so the catalyst is not poisoned. Iron is cheap, so it lowers the cost of the process.

Iron as Catalyst in the Reaction between Persulphate and Iodide Ions

Persulphate ions oxidise iodide ions only slowly: S2O8 2- + 2I- → 2SO4 2- + I2. Iron(II) or iron(III) ions catalyse the reaction in two steps:

StepReaction
1S2O8 2- + 2Fe2+ → 2SO4 2- + 2Fe3+
22Fe3+ + 2I- → 2Fe2+ + I2

The iron(II) catalyst is regenerated at the end of the second step.

Key Points

  • Iron's main ores are magnetite, haematite and limonite; Kalabagh has Pakistan's largest deposits.
  • The common oxidation states of iron are +2 and +3.
  • Fe3+ (d5) is extra stable, so Fe2+ compounds are reducing agents.
  • Iron (magnetite) catalyses the Haber process for ammonia.
  • Fe2+/Fe3+ ions catalyse the persulphate-iodide reaction and are regenerated.

mcqs.q: Iron is which in abundance in the Earth's crust?
options: A rare element found only in ores abroad
mcqs.why: The notes state that iron is the fourth most abundant element in the Earth's crust, though it occurs only in the combined state.

mcqs.q: Which set gives iron's important ores correctly?
mcqs.why: The notes name magnetite (Fe3O4), haematite (Fe2O3) and limonite (2Fe2O3.3H2O) as iron's important ores.

mcqs.q: Where are Pakistan's largest iron ore deposits found?
mcqs.why: The notes state that in Pakistan iron ore is found at Kalabagh (the largest), Nokundi and Chiniot, with Kalabagh the biggest deposit.

mcqs.q: Which are the largest world producers of iron named in the notes?
options: China, Australia, Brazil, India and Russia
mcqs.why: The notes list China, Australia, Brazil, India and Russia as the largest world producers of iron.

mcqs.q: Why is Fe2+ easily oxidised to Fe3+?
options: Fe3+ has a filled d10 subshell
Fe3+ has the extra stable half-filled 3d5 subshell, while Fe2+ is 3d6
Fe2+ has the noble gas configuration
mcqs.why: Fe2+ (3d6) loses one more electron to reach Fe3+ (3d5, half-filled and extra stable), which is why Fe2O3 is more stable than FeO.

mcqs.q: In the Haber process, the iron catalyst is actually:
options: Magnetite (Fe3O4) mixed with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3
mcqs.why: The notes state the Haber catalyst is magnetite (Fe3O4) mixed with KOH, SiO2 and Al2O3, and the gases are purified so it is not poisoned.

mcqs.q: In the Haber equation N2 + 3H2 ⇌ 2NH3, how many moles of NH3 form from 3 moles of H2?
mcqs.why: Working: the equation ratio H2 : NH3 is 3 : 2, so 3 moles of hydrogen reacting with 1 mole of nitrogen produce exactly 2 moles of ammonia.

mcqs.q: Where do the Haber process gases come from, according to the notes?
options: Nitrogen from air and hydrogen from methane in natural gas
Nitrogen from ammonia and hydrogen from water electrolysis only
Nitrogen from fertilisers and hydrogen from acids
mcqs.why: The notes state that nitrogen comes from air and hydrogen comes from methane in natural gas for the Haber process.

mcqs.q: The persulphate-iodide reaction without a catalyst is:
mcqs.why: The notes say persulphate ions oxidise iodide ions only slowly, S2O8 2- + 2I- -> 2SO4 2- + I2, until iron ions catalyse it.

mcqs.q: How do Fe2+/Fe3+ ions catalyse the persulphate-iodide reaction?
options: Fe2+ is consumed completely in the first step
Fe2+ is oxidised to Fe3+ by persulphate, then Fe3+ oxidises I- and Fe2+ is regenerated
Fe3+ reacts with sulphate to give iodine
The iron ions only warm the mixture
mcqs.why: Step 1: S2O8 2- + 2Fe2+ -> 2SO4 2- + 2Fe3+; step 2: 2Fe3+ + 2I- -> 2Fe2+ + I2, so the iron(II) catalyst is regenerated at the end.

lessons.title: Reactions of Hexaaquairon(II) and Hexaaquairon(III) Ions
lessons.notes_html:
Reaction with Water

The pale green hexaaquairon(II) ion, [Fe(H2O)6]2+, and the yellow hexaaquairon(III) ion, [Fe(H2O)6]3+, are both acidic: they donate hydrogen ions to water. The greater the charge density on the metal ion, the more acidic it is, so hexaaquairon(III) is more acidic than hexaaquairon(II).

[Fe(H2O)6]2+ + H2O ⇌ [Fe(H2O)5(OH)]+ + H3O+

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + H2O ⇌ [Fe(H2O)5(OH)]2+ + H3O+

Reaction with Ammonia

Ammonia is a stronger base than water and removes protons from the hexaaqua ions, forming hydroxide precipitates:

[Fe(H2O)6]2+ + 2NH3 ⇌ [Fe(H2O)4(OH)2] + 2NH4+

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3NH3 ⇌ [Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3NH4+

Reaction with Carbonate Ions

The less acidic iron(II) complex gives a green precipitate of iron(II) carbonate: [Fe(H2O)6]2+ + CO3 2- → FeCO3 + 6H2O. The more acidic iron(III) complex instead forms the hydrated hydroxide with effervescence of CO2: 2[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3CO3 2- → 2[Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3H2O + 3CO2.

Reaction with Thiocyanate Ions

This is a ligand exchange reaction. Adding thiocyanate ions to a solution of hexaaquairon(III) ions gives an intense blood-red solution of [Fe(H2O)5(SCN)]2+:

[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + SCN- → [Fe(H2O)5(SCN)]2+ + H2O

Hexaaquairon(II) ions do not give this reaction, so it is a test for iron(III).

Key Points

  • Hexaaqua iron ions are acidic; Fe(III) is more acidic than Fe(II) due to higher charge density.
  • Ammonia precipitates the hydrated hydroxides of both ions.
  • Carbonate gives green FeCO3 precipitate with Fe(II), but hydroxide precipitate and CO2 gas with Fe(III).
  • Thiocyanate gives a blood-red colour with Fe(III) only.

mcqs.q: What are the colours of the hexaaquairon(II) and hexaaquairon(III) ions?
options: [Fe(H2O)6]2+ is pale green and [Fe(H2O)6]3+ is yellow
Fe(II) is yellow and Fe(III) is pale green
Fe(II) is deep blue and Fe(III) is pink
mcqs.why: The notes state that the hexaaquairon(II) ion is pale green and the hexaaquairon(III) ion is yellow, and both are acidic in water.

mcqs.q: Why is hexaaquairon(III) more acidic than hexaaquairon(II)?
options: It has greater charge density on the metal ion
It is yellow rather than green
It has a smaller charge than Fe(II)
mcqs.why: Both ions donate H+ to water; the notes explain that the greater the charge density on the metal ion, the more acidic, so Fe(III) is more acidic.

mcqs.q: What does ammonia do to hexaaqua iron ions?
options: It dissolves them to deep blue solutions
It reduces them to iron metal
It removes protons, forming hydroxide precipitates
It gives a blood-red colour with both
mcqs.why: Ammonia is a stronger base than water and removes protons from the hexaaqua ions, forming precipitates of the hydrated hydroxides.

mcqs.q: How many NH3 molecules react with one [Fe(H2O)6]3+ ion in the notes' equation?
mcqs.why: Working: [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3NH3 ⇌ [Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3NH4+; three protons are removed, so 3 ammonia molecules form 3 NH4+ ions.

mcqs.q: What does carbonate solution give with hexaaquairon(II) ions?
options: A green precipitate of iron(II) carbonate, FeCO3
mcqs.why: The less acidic iron(II) complex gives a green precipitate: [Fe(H2O)6]2+ + CO3 2- -> FeCO3 + 6H2O, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: What does carbonate solution give with hexaaquairon(III) ions?
options: Hydrated iron(III) hydroxide precipitate with effervescence of CO2
mcqs.why: The more acidic iron(III) complex forms the hydrated hydroxide with CO2 effervescence: 2[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3CO3 2- -> 2[Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3H2O + 3CO2.

mcqs.q: Thiocyanate ions added to hexaaquairon(III) give:
mcqs.why: This ligand exchange, [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + SCN- -> [Fe(H2O)5(SCN)]2+ + H2O, gives the intense blood-red colour described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is the thiocyanate reaction a test for iron(III)?
options: Hexaaquairon(II) ions do not give this reaction
Iron(II) gives an even deeper red colour
Thiocyanate reacts with every metal ion identically
Iron(III) is the only coloured ion
mcqs.why: The notes state that hexaaquairon(II) ions do not give the blood-red reaction, so thiocyanate distinguishes and tests for iron(III).

mcqs.q: The acidity of hexaaqua iron ions is shown by their reaction with water, in which they:
options: Donate hydrogen ions to water, forming H3O+
Split water into H2 and O2
mcqs.why: Both ions are acidic because they donate hydrogen ions to water: [Fe(H2O)6]3+ + H2O ⇌ [Fe(H2O)5(OH)]2+ + H3O+, and similarly for Fe(II).

mcqs.q: In the carbonate reaction of Fe(III), how many CO2 molecules form from 3 carbonate ions?
mcqs.why: Working: 2[Fe(H2O)6]3+ + 3CO3 2- -> 2[Fe(H2O)3(OH)3] + 3H2O + 3CO2; the 3 carbonate ions give 3 CO2, matching the effervescence observed.

lessons.title: Copper
lessons.notes_html:
Copper is a reddish-orange, soft, malleable and ductile metal with high thermal and electrical conductivity. It tarnishes to a dull brownish colour in air. It is used in electrical cables and appliances and in alloys such as brass and bronze. It occurs native and in combined form; in Pakistan it is found at Reko Diq, Balochistan.

Important Ores

OreFormulaCopper Content
CupriteCu2OAbout 88%
ChalcociteCu2SAbout 80%
Azurite (blue)2CuCO3.Cu(OH)2About 65%
Malachite (green)CuCO3.Cu(OH)2About 57%
ChalcopyriteCuFeS2About 34%

Chalcopyrite is the most common source of copper and accounts for about 50% of world copper production.

Oxidation States

Copper, [Ar]3d10 4s1, shows +1 (cuprous, d10) and +2 (cupric, d9) states, e.g. Cu2O and CuO. Copper is the only transition metal for which +1 is important. Copper(II) is the most stable and abundant state in solution and in solids, while copper(I) is more stable in some solids at moderate temperatures. In aqueous solution copper(I) is readily oxidised, Cu+ → Cu2+ + e-, so Cu+ acts as a reducing agent.

Reactions of Hexaaquacopper(II) Ions

  • With hydroxide ions: a pale blue precipitate of copper(II) hydroxide forms: [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH- → [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] + 2H2O.
  • With ammonia: a little ammonia gives the same pale blue precipitate; excess ammonia dissolves it to a deep blue solution of tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ions: [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] + 4NH3 → [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ + 2OH- + 2H2O.
  • With carbonate ions: an insoluble precipitate of copper(II) carbonate forms: [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + CO3 2- → CuCO3 + 6H2O.

Key Points

  • Copper is a reddish-orange metal used in cables and alloys; its Pakistani source is Reko Diq.
  • Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is its most common ore.
  • Common oxidation states are +1 (cuprous) and +2 (cupric); Cu(II) is most stable in solution.
  • Cu+ is a reducing agent in aqueous solution.
  • Excess ammonia gives a deep blue tetraamminecopper(II) solution.

A silvery, hard and brittle metal with low conductivity
A green metal that never tarnishes in air
A pale pink metal used only in coins
mcqs.why: The notes describe copper as reddish-orange, soft, malleable and ductile, with high thermal and electrical conductivity, used in cables and appliances.

mcqs.q: In Pakistan, copper is found at:
mcqs.why: The notes state that copper occurs native and combined, and in Pakistan it is found at Reko Diq in Balochistan.

mcqs.q: Which copper ore is the most common source, providing about 50% of world production?
mcqs.why: Chalcopyrite (CuFeS2) is the most common source of copper and accounts for about 50% of world copper production, per the notes.

mcqs.q: Which ore has the highest copper content in the notes' table?
mcqs.why: The ore table gives cuprite (Cu2O) about 88% copper, higher than chalcocite 80%, azurite 65%, malachite 57% and chalcopyrite 34%.

mcqs.q: How much copper is in 100 g of malachite ore, using the notes' figure?
mcqs.why: Working: malachite is listed as about 57% copper, so 100 g of malachite contains 57/100 x 100 g = about 57 g of copper.

mcqs.q: Copper's oxidation states and names are:
mcqs.why: Copper, [Ar]3d10 4s1, shows +1 (cuprous, d10) as in Cu2O and +2 (cupric, d9) as in CuO; it is the only transition metal where +1 is important.

mcqs.q: Which copper state is most stable and abundant in solution and in solids?
mcqs.why: The notes state that copper(II) is the most stable and abundant state in solution and in solids, while Cu(I) is more stable in some solids at moderate temperatures.

mcqs.q: In aqueous solution, Cu+ acts as a reducing agent because:
options: It is readily oxidised: Cu+ -> Cu2+ + e-
It is readily reduced to copper metal
It gains an electron to become Cu2+

mcqs.why: The notes give Cu+ -> Cu2+ + e- in aqueous solution: Cu+ loses an electron, so it reduces other species and acts as a reducing agent.

mcqs.q: Excess ammonia added to hexaaquacopper(II) gives:
options: A deep blue solution of tetraamminediaquacopper(II) ions
mcqs.why: A little ammonia gives the pale blue hydroxide precipitate, but excess ammonia dissolves it to a deep blue [Cu(NH3)4(H2O)2]2+ solution.

mcqs.q: What do hydroxide and carbonate ions give with [Cu(H2O)6]2+?
options: OH- gives a pale blue Cu(OH)2 precipitate; CO3 2- gives an insoluble CuCO3 precipitate
OH- gives CuCO3 and CO3 2- gives Cu(OH)2
mcqs.why: The notes give [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + 2OH- -> [Cu(H2O)4(OH)2] + 2H2O (pale blue precipitate) and [Cu(H2O)6]2+ + CO3 2- -> CuCO3 + 6H2O.

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.notes_html:
In the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, chemists classified compounds into two classes: organic compounds, obtained from plants or animals (living sources), and inorganic compounds, obtained from non-living sources. For example, acetic acid (from vinegar) and tartaric acid (from grapes) were called organic, while marble and sodium chloride (from rocks) were called inorganic.

Today, organic compounds are the chemical compounds containing carbon, usually with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and the halogens. A few carbon compounds are not counted as organic: carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, cyanides, cyanates, CO, CO2 and CS2.

Carbon is essential to life; all living things are made of carbon compounds. Because carbon can link with itself and with other elements in many ways, there are more than 16 million carbon compounds, and chemists make thousands of new ones every year. More than 90% of all known compounds contain carbon.

The most useful definition is: hydrocarbons and their derivatives are called organic compounds. Compounds of carbon and hydrogen only are hydrocarbons; compounds containing other elements along with carbon and hydrogen are their derivatives. The branch of chemistry in which we study hydrocarbons and their derivatives is called organic chemistry.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds were originally defined as compounds from living sources.
  • Today organic compounds are compounds of carbon; carbonates, CO, CO2 and similar compounds are excluded.
  • More than 16 million carbon compounds are known.
  • Hydrocarbons and their derivatives are called organic compounds.
  • Organic chemistry is the study of hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

options: Compounds obtained from plants or animals (living sources)
Compounds containing carbon and hydrogen only
Compounds obtained from rocks and minerals
