mcqs.why: The notes state chemists first classified compounds from plants or animals as organic, while those from non-living sources were inorganic.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is counted as an organic compound under the modern definition given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Acetic acid from vinegar is given as an organic example, whereas carbonates, carbides, CO and CO2 are explicitly excluded from organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Which set is EXCLUDED from organic compounds in the notes?
options: Carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, cyanides, CO, CO2 and CS2
Compounds of carbon with hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen
mcqs.why: The notes list carbonates, bicarbonates, carbides, cyanides, cyanates, CO, CO2 and CS2 as carbon compounds not counted as organic.

mcqs.q: What is the most useful definition of organic compounds given in the notes?
options: Compounds obtained only from living things
mcqs.why: The notes give the most useful definition as: hydrocarbons and their derivatives are called organic compounds.

mcqs.q: Compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen are called:
mcqs.why: By definition in the notes, compounds of carbon and hydrogen only are hydrocarbons; adding other elements gives their derivatives.

mcqs.q: How many carbon compounds are known, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state there are more than 16 million carbon compounds and chemists make thousands of new ones every year.

mcqs.q: What percentage of all known compounds contain carbon, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes state more than 90% of all known compounds contain carbon, which is why carbon chemistry is so vast.

mcqs.q: Organic chemistry is the branch that studies:
mcqs.why: The notes define organic chemistry as the branch in which we study hydrocarbons and their derivatives.

mcqs.q: Which pair was given as examples of inorganic compounds from non-living sources?
options: Marble and sodium chloride from rocks
mcqs.why: Marble and sodium chloride, obtained from rocks, are given in the notes as examples of inorganic compounds from non-living sources.

mcqs.q: Besides carbon and hydrogen, which elements are usually present in organic compounds in the notes?
options: Oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and the halogens
mcqs.why: Today organic compounds are described as containing carbon, usually with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulphur, phosphorus and the halogens.

lessons.title: Sources of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
There are two main sources of organic compounds: (i) natural sources and (ii) synthetic sources. Natural organic compounds are present in our environment and do not need to be made, while synthetic organic compounds are man-made and do not occur naturally. The natural sources are: (i) fossil remains, i.e. coal, petroleum and natural gas, (ii) plants, and (iii) animals.

Fossil Remains: Coal, Petroleum and Natural Gas

The three major fossil remains are formed by the decay of plants and animals over millions of years.

  • Coal: a black solid fuel formed from plants buried under the Earth's surface for about 300 million years at high temperature and pressure. On destructive distillation it yields coke (mostly carbon) and coal tar (a complex mixture of organic compounds). Its main types, by carbon content, are lignite (about 70% C), bituminous (about 80% C) and anthracite (92-98% C). Higher carbon content means better quality, and older coal has more carbon.
  • Petroleum: formed by bacterial decomposition of plants and animals buried deep under porous rocks by heat and pressure; its deposits are younger than coal. It is a mixture of gaseous and liquid hydrocarbons. Fractional distillation gives gasoline, kerosene, diesel, lubricating oil and paraffin wax.
  • Natural gas: a mixture of low molecular mass hydrocarbons (methane, ethane, propane, butane); methane is nearly 85%. It is formed by decay of organic matter and is found in porous rocks near petroleum deposits. It is used as a fuel and as a raw material for fertilizers and petrochemicals.

Key Points

  • Organic compounds come from natural and synthetic sources.
  • Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil remains of plants and animals.
  • Anthracite has the highest carbon content (92-98%) and is the best quality coal.
  • Petroleum gives gasoline, kerosene and diesel on fractional distillation.
  • Natural gas contains nearly 85% methane.

lessons.title: Plants and Natural Products Chemistry
lessons.notes_html:
Plants and animals are major sources of organic compounds. Many compounds are obtained directly from them by suitable methods of isolation. Compounds obtained from living organisms are called natural products, and the study of such compounds is called natural product chemistry.

Important natural products from animals include proteins, hormones, animal fats, urea and insulin. From plants we get carbohydrates (cellulose, sugars, starches), vitamins, alcohols, acetone, acids, esters, vegetable oils, dyes, drugs, perfumes and fibres (cotton, jute).

lessons.title: Partial and Total Synthesis
lessons.notes_html:
Many useful organic compounds, including ether, glycol, drugs, rubber, fibres, dyes and plastics, are synthesized in the laboratory. Today synthesis is the most important source of organic compounds. Compounds synthesized in the laboratory are called synthetic compounds, and the study of such compounds is called synthetic chemistry.

Synthesis is of two types, and the difference between them is the starting material:

  • Partial synthesis (semi-synthesis): the desired product is obtained from an intermediate product of a reaction. For example, ethanoic acid is obtained by the oxidation of ethanal (an intermediate), instead of starting from the alkane: CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH (K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4).
  • Total synthesis: the starting material is converted into the desired product through various steps. For example, ethanoic acid can be obtained from ethane through several steps: ethane → ethanol → ethanal → ethanoic acid.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
1CH3-CH3 + [O] → CH3CH2OH (ethane to ethanol, Cu catalyst)
2CH3CH2OH + [O] → CH3CHO (ethanol to ethanal, K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4)
3CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH (ethanal to ethanoic acid, K2Cr2O7 / H2SO4)

Key Points

  • Laboratory-made compounds are called synthetic compounds.
  • Synthesis is now the most important source of organic compounds.
  • Partial synthesis starts from an intermediate product.
  • Total synthesis builds the product from a simple starting material through many steps.

lessons.title: Products of Biotechnology
lessons.notes_html:
Biotechnology involves the use of living organisms, especially microorganisms, or other biological systems in the manufacture of products and in industrial, agricultural, medical and technological applications. The compounds obtained by means of biotechnology are called products of biotechnology.

Important products of biotechnology include ethylene glycol, ethyl alcohol, hormones, acids, vitamins, vaccines and antibiotics. Genetically engineered bacteria are used to make medicines such as insulin, and fermentation by yeast gives alcohol and bread.

Key Points

  • Biotechnology uses living organisms or biological systems to manufacture products.

  • Vaccines and antibiotics are also products of biotechnology.

lessons.title: Destructive Distillation of Coal
lessons.notes_html:
Coal is a most important source of organic compounds. When coal is heated strongly at 500-1000°C in the absence of air, it is converted into various useful organic and inorganic products. This process is called destructive distillation of coal. The major products are coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor and coke.

Products

  • Coal gas: a mixture of hydrogen (H2), methane (CH4), carbon monoxide (CO) and other gases. It is an excellent fuel; in the past it was used for domestic cooking and lighting, and nowadays as an industrial fuel.
  • Coal tar: a liquid product containing more than 215 organic compounds. On fractional distillation it yields benzene, toluene, xylene, phenol, cresol, naphthalene and anthracene, which are used in explosives, pesticides, perfumes, synthetic fibres, naphthalene balls, dyes and paints. The residue left is called pitch, used for metalling roads and as a binder in roof making.
  • Ammoniacal liquor: ammonium compounds obtained during the distillation dissolve in water to form ammoniacal liquor. It is used to make nitrogenous fertilizers such as ammonium sulphate and ammonium superphosphate.
  • Coke: the solid product, an almost pure form of carbon. It is an excellent fuel that burns without smoke. It is used in the manufacture of steel, calcium carbide, graphite, silicon carbide and carbon disulphide, as a reducing agent, and for making fuel gases such as water gas (CO + H2) and producer gas (CO + N2).

Key Points

  • Destructive distillation is heating coal strongly (500-1000°C) without air.
  • Its four products are coal gas, coal tar, ammoniacal liquor and coke.
  • Coal tar is a source of benzene, toluene, phenol and naphthalene.
  • Ammoniacal liquor is used to make nitrogenous fertilizers.
  • Coke is almost pure carbon and burns without smoke.

lessons.title: Conversion of Coal to Petroleum
lessons.notes_html:
Coal can be converted into liquid fuels such as gasoline, kerosene and diesel by the Fischer-Tropsch process. In this process, the coal gas obtained during the destructive distillation of coal is converted into high quality, ultraclean liquid fuel products.

The Fischer-Tropsch process is a collection of chemical reactions that converts water gas into liquid hydrocarbons. The water gas is mixed with half its volume of hydrogen. The reactions occur at 150-300°C and at pressures of 1 to 10 atmospheres, in the presence of metal catalysts such as cobalt, iron, nickel and ruthenium.

Key Reactions

ReactionConditions
CO + H2 → Mixture of hydrocarbons + H2OCobalt catalyst, 150-300°C, 1-10 atm

Liquid coal can become a petroleum substitute (gasoline, kerosene or diesel) for the transportation industry. It is also used in synthetic lubricants and synthetic waxes.

Key Points

  • Coal is converted to liquid fuels by the Fischer-Tropsch process.
  • Water gas (CO + H2) is converted into liquid hydrocarbons.
  • Extra hydrogen, equal to half the volume of water gas, is mixed in.
  • Conditions: 150-300°C, 1-10 atm pressure, Co, Fe, Ni or Ru catalyst.
  • The products can replace petroleum in transport.

lessons.title: Characteristic of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Organic compounds obey all the fundamental laws of chemistry, just like inorganic compounds, and there is no clear-cut division between their properties. Even so, organic compounds are studied as a separate branch because of the following characteristic features:

  • Catenation: the self-linking property by which an atom combines with other atoms of the same element to form long chains and cyclic structures. Carbon forms long chains, loops, sheets and rings.
  • Isomerism: compounds with the same molecular formula but different structural formulas are isomers; organic compounds show this phenomenon widely.
  • Non-polar character: most organic compounds are non-polar and are poor conductors of heat and electricity.
  • Solubility: most organic compounds do not dissolve in water but dissolve in organic solvents such as ether, benzene, alcohol and acetone.
  • Rate of reactions: organic compounds are generally covalent, so their reactions are usually slow and may need heating, thorough mixing and a catalyst.
  • Melting and boiling points: generally low, because of weak intermolecular forces; such compounds also have high vapour pressure.
  • Flammability: they are generally volatile and flammable; fuels such as natural gas, coal and oil burn to give energy as heat and light.
  • Stability: most organic compounds are thermally unstable and decompose on heating (above 500°C).

Key Points

  • Catenation and isomerism are special features of carbon compounds.
  • Organic compounds are mostly non-polar covalent compounds.
  • They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
  • Weak intermolecular forces give them low melting and boiling points.
  • Their reactions are slow and they decompose on strong heating.
  • Most organic compounds are flammable.

lessons.title: New Allotrope of Carbon: Bucky Balls (Fullerenes)
lessons.notes_html:
Until the mid-1980s, scientists thought that pure carbon existed in only two allotropic forms: diamond and graphite. In 1985 a new allotropic form, buckminsterfullerene, commonly called a bucky ball, was discovered by Richard Smalley, Robert Curl and Harry Kroto. The 1996 Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to them for this discovery.

Fullerenes (bucky balls) consist of molecules composed entirely of carbon atoms arranged in the form of hollow spheres, ellipsoids or tubes. Each molecule generally has both pentagonal and hexagonal faces.

  • The most common bucky ball is C60: 60 carbon atoms joined in a shape like a soccer ball, with 32 faces — 12 pentagons and 20 hexagons.
  • The smallest fullerene has 20 carbon atoms (C20); fullerenes up to 100 carbon atoms are commonly obtained, and the largest has more than 600 carbon atoms.
  • Fullerenes are rare in nature. Small amounts of C60, C70, C76, C82 and C84 have been found in soot and in the residue of carbon arc lamps; they are also formed by lightning discharges in the atmosphere.
  • Bucky balls are a new family of aromatic organic molecules and are soft like graphite. Doped fullerenes can conduct electricity and even act as superconductors at low temperature.

Key Points

  • Bucky ball (buckminsterfullerene) is the third allotrope of carbon, after diamond and graphite.
  • It was discovered in 1985 by Smalley, Curl and Kroto (Nobel Prize 1996).
  • C60 has 32 faces: 12 pentagonal and 20 hexagonal, like a soccer ball.
  • Fullerenes are hollow spheres, ellipsoids or tubes of carbon atoms.
  • They occur in small amounts in soot and arc-lamp residue.

mcqs.why: In 1985 a new allotropic form, buckminsterfullerene, was discovered by Richard Smalley, Robert Curl and Harry Kroto.

mcqs.why: Working: total faces = 12 pentagons + 20 hexagons = 32 faces, in a shape like a soccer ball as stated in the notes.

lessons.title: Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Carbon forms millions of compounds, so they are divided into families on the basis of their functional groups to make their study easy. A functional group is an atom or group of atoms in a molecule that is mainly responsible for the chemical behaviour of the molecule. Double and triple bonds are also functional groups.

Compounds with the same functional group have similar chemical properties, whatever the rest of the molecule is. For example, methanol (CH3OH), ethanol (CH3CH2OH) and propanol have similar properties because all contain the -OH group. Replacing one functional group by another changes the properties: methanol (CH3OH) and methanoic acid (HCOOH) behave differently. The functional group is the reactive part of the molecule, while the hydrocarbon portion is inert. A compound with two or more functional groups is called a polyfunctional compound.

Common Functional Groups

ClassFunctional GroupExample (IUPAC Name)Suffix / Prefix
AlkanesR-HCH3-CH3 (Ethane)-ane
AlkenesC=CH2C=CH2 (Ethene)-ene
AlkynesC≡CCH≡CH (Ethyne)-yne
ArenesAryl ringBenzene-ene
Alkyl halidesR-XCH3-CH2Cl (Chloroethane)halo-
AlcoholsR-OHCH3CH2-OH (Ethanol)-ol
PhenolsAr-OHPhenol-ol
EthersR-O-RCH3-O-CH3 (Methoxymethane)-
AldehydesR-CHOCH3-CHO (Ethanal)-al
KetonesRR'C=O2-Propanone-one
Carboxylic acidsR-COOHCH3-COOH (Ethanoic acid)-oic acid
Acyl halidesR-CO-XEthanoyl chloride-oyl halide
EstersR-COO-R'Methyl ethanoate-oate
AmidesR-CONH2Ethanamide-amide
Acid anhydrides(RCO)2OEthanoic anhydride-oic anhydride
AminesR-NH2CH3-NH2 (Methanamine)-amine

Amino acids are polyfunctional compounds: they contain an amino group (-NH2) and a carboxylic acid group (-COOH).

Key Points

  • A functional group decides the chemical behaviour of a molecule.
  • Compounds with the same functional group have similar chemical properties.
  • The functional group is the reactive part; the hydrocarbon part is inert.
  • Compounds with two or more functional groups are polyfunctional.
  • Examples: -OH alcohols (-ol), -COOH acids (-oic acid), -NH2 amines (-amine).

lessons.title: Homologous Series
lessons.notes_html:
A group of organic compounds in which each member differs from the next member by a methylene group (-CH2-) is called a homologous series. Its members are called homologs. For example, butane (CH3CH2CH2CH3) and pentane (CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3) are homologs. Removing one hydrogen atom from an alkane gives an alkyl group, CnH2n+1.

Homologous Series of Alkanes

AlkaneC AtomsMolecular FormulaCondensed Structural Formula
Methane1CH4CH4
Ethane2C2H6CH3CH3
Propane3C3H8CH3CH2CH3
Butane4C4H10CH3(CH2)2CH3
Pentane5C5H12CH3(CH2)3CH3
Hexane6C6H14CH3(CH2)4CH3
Heptane7C7H16CH3(CH2)5CH3
Octane8C8H18CH3(CH2)6CH3
Nonane9C9H20CH3(CH2)7CH3
Decane10C10H22CH3(CH2)8CH3

General Characteristics of a Homologous Series

  • All members have the same functional group and the same general formula.
  • They have similar chemical properties because of the same functional group.
  • Their physical properties differ because their molecular masses differ.
  • Successive members differ by a CH2 group, so their molecular masses differ by 14 units (CH2 = 12 + 2 = 14).
  • All members contain the same type of elements and are prepared by the same methods.

Key Formulae

SeriesGeneral Formula
AlkaneCnH2n+2
AlkeneCnH2n
AlkyneCnH2n-2
AlcoholCnH2n+1OH
Alkyl halideCnH2n+1X

Key Points

  • Members of a homologous series differ from each other by one -CH2- group.
  • Successive homologs differ in molecular mass by 14 units.
  • All members share one functional group and one general formula.
  • Chemical properties are similar; physical properties change gradually.
  • Alkanes follow the general formula CnH2n+2.

lessons.title: Preparation of Lassaigne's Solution and Detection of Nitrogen
lessons.notes_html:
All organic compounds contain carbon, and most of them (except CCl4, CS2, etc.) contain hydrogen, so these two elements are usually not tested. Oxygen is generally present, but there is no direct method for its detection. Other elements that may be present — nitrogen, sulphur, halogens and phosphorus — are detected by Lassaigne's test.

Preparation of Lassaigne's Solution (Sodium Extract)

  • Take a small, freshly cut piece of sodium metal (pea size) in a fusion tube and heat it until the sodium melts. Sodium is stored under kerosene oil and must never be touched with fingers; use forceps.
  • Add a small amount of the unknown organic compound and heat, first gently and then strongly, until the bottom of the tube becomes red hot.
  • Plunge the red-hot tube into a china dish containing about 10-15 mL of cold distilled water.
  • Crush the contents, boil and filter. The filtrate is Lassaigne's solution (sodium extract).

Fusion with sodium converts the covalently bound elements into ionic sodium salts that can be tested. The extract is divided into portions for the detection of nitrogen, sulphur and halogens.

Key Reactions

ReactionProduct
Na + C + N → NaCNSodium cyanide
Na + C + N + S → NaCNSSodium sulphocyanide
2Na + S → Na2SSodium sulphide
Na + X → NaXSodium halide

Detection of Nitrogen

Boil the sodium extract with freshly prepared ferrous sulphate solution and a little sodium hydroxide. Cool the mixture, then add a few drops of ferric chloride solution and excess concentrated hydrochloric acid. A green or Prussian blue colour confirms nitrogen. Fresh FeSO4 is used because Fe2+ is easily oxidised by air to Fe3+.

ReactionNote
FeSO4 + 2NaOH → Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4Green precipitate
Fe(OH)2 + 6NaCN → Na4[Fe(CN)6] + 2NaOHSodium ferrocyanide
3Na4[Fe(CN)6] + 4FeCl3 → Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 + 12NaClFerric ferrocyanide, Prussian blue

Key Points

  • Lassaigne's test detects nitrogen, sulphur and halogens in organic compounds.
  • The compound is fused with sodium to form ionic sodium salts.
  • The filtrate of the fused mixture is called the sodium extract.
  • Prussian blue colour with FeSO4 and FeCl3 confirms nitrogen.
  • Sodium is handled with forceps and stored under kerosene oil.

mcqs.why: Other elements that may be present - nitrogen, sulphur, halogens and phosphorus - are detected by Lassaigne's test in the notes.

mcqs.why: Fusion with sodium converts the covalently bound elements into ionic sodium salts that can be tested; the filtrate is the sodium extract.

mcqs.why: The filtrate is Lassaigne's solution, also called the sodium extract, divided into portions for detecting nitrogen, sulphur and halogens.

options: All organic compounds contain carbon and most (except CCl4, CS2 etc.) contain hydrogen

lessons.title: Detection of Sulphur and Halogens
lessons.notes_html:
Detection of Sulphur

Sodium nitroprusside test: add sodium nitroprusside solution to the sodium extract. A deep violet colour confirms sulphur:

Na2S + Na2[Fe(CN)5NO] → Na4[Fe(CN)5NOS] (deep violet)

Lead acetate test: add freshly prepared lead acetate solution to the extract in the presence of dilute acetic acid. A black precipitate of lead sulphide confirms sulphur:

Na2S + (CH3COO)2Pb → PbS (black) + 2CH3COONa

If sulphur is present along with nitrogen, the extract contains NaCNS, which gives a blood-red colouration of ferric sulphocyanide with FeCl3: 3NaCNS + FeCl3 → Fe(CNS)3 + 3NaCl.

Detection of Halogens

Boil the sodium extract with concentrated nitric acid for some time to expel HCN or H2S, which would otherwise give a white precipitate of silver cyanide or a black precipitate of silver sulphide with silver nitrate. Cool the mixture and add silver nitrate solution:

Precipitate with AgNO3Solubility in NH4OHHalogen Present
White (AgCl)Soluble in cold NH4OHChlorine
Light yellow (AgBr)Sparingly soluble in cold, soluble in hot concentrated NH4OHBromine
Yellow (AgI)Insoluble in NH4OHIodine

Key Reactions

ReactionNote
2Na + X2 → 2NaXFusion forms sodium halide
NaX + AgNO3 → AgX↓ + NaNO3Silver halide precipitate
AgCl + 2NH4OH → [Ag(NH3)2]Cl + 2H2OSoluble complex
AgBr + 2NH4OH → [Ag(NH3)2]Br + 2H2OSparingly soluble

Key Points

  • Deep violet colour with sodium nitroprusside confirms sulphur.
  • Black PbS precipitate with lead acetate also confirms sulphur.
  • Before the halogen test, the extract is boiled with conc. HNO3 to remove HCN and H2S.
  • White AgCl soluble in NH4OH shows chlorine; yellow AgI insoluble in NH4OH shows iodine.
  • Nitrogen and sulphur together give a blood-red colour with FeCl3.

mcqs.why: Sodium nitroprusside test: Na2S + Na2[Fe(CN)5NO] -> Na4[Fe(CN)5NOS] (deep violet), confirming sulphur.

mcqs.q: A black precipitate with lead acetate in dilute acetic acid confirms sulphur because it is:
mcqs.why: Lead acetate test gives a black precipitate of lead sulphide: Na2S + (CH3COO)2Pb -> PbS (black) + 2CH3COONa.

mcqs.q: If nitrogen and sulphur are present together, FeCl3 gives:
options: Blood-red colour of ferric sulphocyanide Fe(CNS)3
mcqs.why: With NaCNS in the extract, 3NaCNS + FeCl3 -> Fe(CNS)3 + 3NaCl gives a blood-red colouration of ferric sulphocyanide.

mcqs.why: Boiling with conc. HNO3 expels HCN or H2S, which would otherwise give white AgCN or black Ag2S precipitate with silver nitrate.

mcqs.why: The table lists white AgCl, soluble in cold NH4OH, for chlorine; light yellow AgBr is sparingly soluble and yellow AgI is insoluble.

mcqs.q: Yellow AgI that is insoluble in NH4OH shows:
mcqs.why: Yellow precipitate of AgI, insoluble in NH4OH, indicates iodine in the halogen detection table.

mcqs.q: Light yellow AgBr is described as:
options: Sparingly soluble in cold, soluble in hot concentrated NH4OH
mcqs.why: AgBr is light yellow and sparingly soluble in cold, soluble in hot concentrated NH4OH, indicating bromine.

mcqs.q: The silver nitrate test for halogens forms:
options: AgX precipitate plus NaNO3: NaX + AgNO3 -> AgX + NaNO3
mcqs.why: Key reactions give NaX + AgNO3 -> AgX precipitate + NaNO3, the basis of halogen detection with silver nitrate.

mcqs.q: AgCl dissolves in NH4OH by forming:
mcqs.why: AgCl + 2NH4OH -> [Ag(NH3)2]Cl + 2H2O is listed as the soluble complex explaining AgCl solubility in ammonium hydroxide.

mcqs.why: Key reactions list 2Na + X2 -> 2NaX for fusion forming sodium halide, which is then tested with silver nitrate.

lessons.title: Types of Hydrocarbons
lessons.notes_html:
Hydrocarbons are the simplest organic compounds. They are made of carbon and hydrogen only, joined by covalent bonds. Examples are methane (CH4), ethylene (C2H4), acetylene (C2H2) and benzene (C6H6). They are classified as aliphatic or aromatic, depending on whether a benzene ring is present or not.

Two Main Types

  • Aliphatic hydrocarbons: straight chained, branched or non-aromatic compounds. They may be linear or cyclic. Most of them are volatile and flammable.
  • Aromatic hydrocarbons: compounds that contain at least one benzene ring in their structure.

Saturated and Unsaturated Hydrocarbons

  • Saturated hydrocarbons contain carbon-carbon single bonds only. They include the alkanes and the cycloalkanes.
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons contain at least one carbon-carbon double bond or triple bond. They include the alkenes and the alkynes.

In a straight chain, a carbon atom is never bonded to more than two other carbon atoms. In a branched chain, a carbon atom may be bonded to three or four carbon atoms at a time.

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons contain carbon and hydrogen only, joined by covalent bonds.
  • They are classified as aliphatic (no benzene ring) or aromatic (at least one benzene ring).
  • Saturated hydrocarbons have single bonds only: alkanes and cycloalkanes.
  • Unsaturated hydrocarbons have at least one double or triple bond: alkenes and alkynes.
  • Most aliphatic hydrocarbons are volatile and flammable.

lessons.title: Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkanes are hydrocarbons that contain only single bonds. They are also called paraffins, from the Latin words parum (little) and affin (affinity): paraffins have little affinity, so they are the least reactive hydrocarbons. Petroleum and natural gas are composed of alkanes.

General Formula of Alkanes

The general formula of alkanes is CnH2n+2, where n is the number of carbon atoms.

AlkanenHydrogen atoms (2n + 2)Molecular formula
Methane12 × 1 + 2 = 4CH4
Ethane22 × 2 + 2 = 6C2H6
Propane32 × 3 + 2 = 8C3H8
Butane42 × 4 + 2 = 10C4H10

Cycloalkanes

Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which the carbon atoms are linked by single covalent bonds to form a ring. They are also called cycloparaffins. Their general formula is CnH2n: a cycloalkane has two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane, because of the ring formation.

Key Points

  • Alkanes contain single bonds only and are called paraffins (little affinity, least reactive).
  • General formula of alkanes: CnH2n+2.
  • Petroleum and natural gas are composed of alkanes.
  • Cycloalkanes are ring compounds with single bonds only; general formula CnH2n.
  • A cycloalkane has two hydrogens less than the alkane with the same number of carbons.

mcqs.q: Alkanes are also called paraffins because they have:
mcqs.why: Paraffin comes from parum (little) and affin (affinity); paraffins have little affinity and are the least reactive hydrocarbons.

mcqs.why: The notes give the general formula of alkanes as CnH2n+2, where n is the number of carbon atoms in the molecule.

mcqs.why: Hydrogens = 2n + 2 = 2 x 3 + 2 = 8, so propane is C3H8, exactly as shown in the table in the notes.

mcqs.why: The notes state directly that petroleum and natural gas are composed of alkanes, the single-bonded hydrocarbons.

mcqs.why: The general formula of cycloalkanes is CnH2n, which is two hydrogens less than the corresponding alkane CnH2n+2.

mcqs.why: Because of ring formation, a cycloalkane has two hydrogen atoms less than the corresponding alkane, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.why: Hydrogens = 2n = 2 x 5 = 10, so the formula is C5H10, following the cycloalkane general formula CnH2n.

mcqs.why: Hydrogens = 2n + 2 = 2 x 4 + 2 = 10, so butane is C4H10, matching the alkane table given in the notes.

mcqs.why: Cycloalkanes are saturated hydrocarbons in which carbon atoms are linked by single covalent bonds to form a ring.

lessons.title: Nomenclature: Common and IUPAC Systems
lessons.notes_html:
Nomenclature is the system used for naming chemical compounds. There are two systems: the common system and the IUPAC system.

The Common System

  • In early days, compounds were named after the plants or animals from which they were obtained, or sometimes after their discoverer.
  • Methane was called marsh gas because it was found in marshy places.
  • Acetic acid got its name from the Latin word acetum, meaning vinegar.
  • Methyl alcohol was called wood spirit because it was obtained by the destructive distillation of wood.
  • Barbituric acid was supposedly named by Adolf von Baeyer after a girl called Barbara.
  • The common system follows no formal rules. It is impossible to give common names to the millions of compounds now known, and impossible to remember them all. Common names are still in wide use today.
  • Common names are useful when the IUPAC name is lengthy and complicated: for example, tartaric acid instead of 2,3-dihydroxybutanedioic acid.

The IUPAC System

  • A commission of 34 chemists from nine countries met at Geneva (Switzerland) in 1892 and developed a system of nomenclature, called the Geneva system.
  • The group later became the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), pronounced “eye-you-pack”.
  • The IUPAC rules have been continually revised and improved since 1892.
  • The fundamental principle is that each different compound should have a different and unambiguous (clear, single-meaning) name.

Key Points

  • Nomenclature is the system of naming chemical compounds.
  • Common names come from sources or discoverers and follow no formal rules.
  • Examples: methane = marsh gas; methyl alcohol = wood spirit; acetic acid from acetum (vinegar).
  • The IUPAC system began at Geneva in 1892; its rules are still revised today.
  • IUPAC principle: every different compound gets one different, unambiguous name.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Straight Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
The first four alkanes are known by their common names: methane, ethane, propane and butane. The names of alkanes with more than four carbons are formed from a Latin or Greek prefix that shows the number of carbon atoms, plus the suffix -ane.

Parts of an IUPAC Name

  • Root: shows the number of carbon atoms in the longest continuous chain.
  • Suffix: shows the family of the compound; for alkanes the suffix is -ane.
  • Prefix: shows the identity, position and number of substituents (side groups).

Parent Names of Alkanes

1MethMethane11UndecUndecane
2EthEthane12DodecDodecane
3PropPropane13TridecTridecane
4ButButane14TetradecTetradecane
5PentPentane15PentadecPentadecane
6HexHexane16HexadecHexadecane
7HeptHeptane17HeptadecHeptadecane
8OctOctane18OctadecOctadecane
9NonNonane19NonadecNonadecane
10DecDecane20IcosIcosane

Common Prefixes n-, iso- and neo-

  • In the common system, all isomeric alkanes have the same parent name: the three isomeric C5H12 alkanes are all pentanes. The prefixes n, iso and neo show which isomer is meant.
  • n- (normal): all carbon atoms are joined in one continuous, unbranched chain, e.g. n-pentane, CH3CH2CH2CH2CH3.
  • iso-: one methyl group is bonded to the second carbon of the continuous chain, e.g. isopentane, isohexane.
  • neo-: two methyl groups are bonded to the second carbon of the continuous chain, e.g. neohexane, neoheptane.

Alkyl Groups

A group formed by the removal of one hydrogen atom from an alkane is called an alkyl group. It is represented by the symbol R (R-H → R- on removal of H). An alkyl group is named by replacing “ane” with “yl”: methane gives methyl (CH3-), ethane gives ethyl (CH3CH2-). From propane, removal of H from a primary (1°) carbon gives n-propyl (CH3CH2CH2-), and from a secondary (2°) carbon gives isopropyl.

A primary carbon is bonded to only one other carbon, a secondary carbon to two, a tertiary carbon to three and a quaternary carbon to four other carbons.

Key Points

  • Alkane name = root (number of carbons in longest chain) + suffix -ane.
  • An IUPAC name has three parts: prefix, root and suffix.
  • Common prefixes: n- = unbranched chain; iso- = one methyl on carbon 2; neo- = two methyls on carbon 2.
  • Alkyl group = alkane minus one H; named by changing -ane to -yl (methyl, ethyl).
  • Primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary carbons are bonded to 1, 2, 3 and 4 other carbons.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Branched Chain Alkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Branched chain alkanes are named by the following IUPAC rules.

Rules

  • Rule 1: Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms and name it as the parent (stem) name. The longest chain is not always in a straight line; sometimes it “turns a corner”.
  • Rule 2: Show the position of each substituent by the number of the carbon atom to which it is bonded, e.g. a methyl branch on carbon 4 of octane gives 4-methyloctane.
  • Rule 3: Number the longest chain from the end nearer to the substituents, so that the substituents get the lowest numbers: 3-methylhexane is correct, not 4-methylhexane.
  • Rule 4: For two or more identical substituents, use the prefixes di, tri, tetra or penta, e.g. 2,4-dimethylpentane.
  • Rule 5: If the first substituent is at the same distance from both ends, number the chain so that the second substituent gets the lower number. Always look for the first point of difference: 2,4,7-trimethyloctane is correct, not 2,5,7-trimethyloctane.
  • Rule 6: Name different substituents in alphabetical order, e.g. 3-ethyl-5-methylheptane. The prefixes di, tri, tetra, penta, sec and tert are ignored in alphabetizing, but iso and cyclo are not ignored.
  • If the same set of numbers is obtained in both directions, number from the end that gives the lower number to the substituent that comes first alphabetically.
  • Rule 7: If two or more chains of equal length can be selected, choose the chain with the greater number of substituents: 3-ethyl-2-methylheptane is correct, not 3-isopropylheptane.

The branch name and the parent name are written as a single word, with a hyphen after the number. Numbers for identical substituents are separated by commas, and a hyphen is placed between a number and a word.

Key Points

  • The parent is the longest continuous carbon chain, even if it turns a corner.
  • Number from the end nearer the substituents; use the first point of difference for ties.
  • Identical substituents take di, tri, tetra; different substituents are listed alphabetically.
  • di, tri, sec, tert are ignored in alphabetizing; iso and cyclo are counted.
  • Between equal-length chains, choose the one with more substituents.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Rules

  • Rule 1: Add the prefix cyclo- to the name of the corresponding alkane with the same number of carbons as the ring: cyclopropane, cyclobutane, cyclopentane, cyclohexane. A cycloalkane is drawn as a geometric figure (triangle, square, pentagon, hexagon); each corner stands for one carbon atom and two hydrogen atoms.
  • Rule 2: For a ring with only one substituent, no position number is needed, because all positions of the ring are equivalent: methylcyclopropane, ethylcyclobutane.
  • Rule 3: For two or more substituents, number the ring so that the substituent carbons get the lowest possible numbers, and name the substituents in alphabetical order: 1,2-dimethylcyclopropane; 1,3-dimethylcyclopentane; 1-ethyl-2-methylcyclopentane; 1-ethyl-2,5-dimethylcyclohexane.
  • Rule 4: If the substituent has more carbon atoms than the ring, the substituent is taken as the parent and the ring is named as a substituent: 1-cyclopropylbutane; 2-cyclobutylpentane.

Key Points

  • Cycloalkane name = cyclo- + alkane name for the ring size.
  • One substituent on a ring needs no locant (number).
  • With two or more substituents, number for the lowest locants and list alphabetically.
  • If the side chain is longer than the ring, the chain is the parent and the ring is a substituent (cyclopropyl, cyclobutyl).

mcqs.why: Rule 3 requires numbering the ring so substituent carbons get the lowest possible numbers, listed alphabetically.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties of Alkanes

  • The first four members (methane to butane) are colourless, odourless gases at room temperature. They are used as fuels.
  • Members with 5 to 17 carbons are colourless, odourless liquids at room temperature. They are found in gasoline, kerosene, diesel and jet fuels.
  • Members with 18 or more carbons are colourless waxy solids, used as lubricants. Vaseline is a semisolid mixture of alkanes having more than 25 carbon atoms.
  • Alkanes are mostly non-polar. They are insoluble in polar solvents like water, but soluble in solvents like benzene, ether, carbon tetrachloride and acetone.
  • Boiling points and melting points increase with the number of carbon atoms; the rise in melting point is not very regular. The boiling point increases by 20-30°C for each added methylene group (-CH2-).
  • A straight chain alkane has a higher boiling point than its branched isomer, because its larger surface area of contact gives stronger van der Waals forces: n-butane boils at -0.5°C, isobutane at -10.2°C.
  • Densities increase gradually with the number of carbons, from about 0.62 g/mL to about 0.79 g/mL. Alkanes are less dense than water (1.0 g/mL), so they float on water.
  • Viscosity increases with molecular mass.

Solid alkanes are used in the waxy coatings of fruits such as apples, plums, oranges and pears, and of vegetables such as cucumber, turnips and green tomatoes. The coating prevents loss of water (keeping firmness and juiciness), improves appearance and freshness, and slows down microbial degradation.

Physical Properties of Cycloalkanes

  • Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are gases at room temperature; cycloalkanes with five or more carbons are liquids.
  • They are soluble in non-polar solvents like benzene and ether, and insoluble in polar solvents.
  • Their melting and boiling points increase gradually with molecular mass.
  • They have low densities, like alkanes; alkanes and cycloalkanes are the least dense of all groups of organic compounds.
  • Liquid cycloalkanes are soluble in one another.

Key Points

  • Alkanes: C1-C4 gases, C5-C17 liquids, C18 and above waxy solids; all colourless and odourless.
  • Alkanes are insoluble in water, soluble in organic solvents, and less dense than water.
  • Boiling point rises 20-30°C per -CH2- group; straight chains boil higher than branched isomers.
  • Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are gases; higher cycloalkanes are liquids.
  • Melting point, boiling point and density of cycloalkanes rise gradually with molecular mass.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Structure of Alkanes

The simplest alkane is methane, CH4. Its four hydrogen atoms are arranged around the central carbon atom as far apart from each other as possible. Methane therefore has a tetrahedral geometry, with bond angles of 109.5°. In the higher alkanes too, the four bonds about each carbon atom are still tetrahedral, and all bond angles are nearly 109.5°.

Structure of Cycloalkanes

The simplest cycloalkane is cyclopropane. The line-angle formula of a cycloalkane is drawn as a regular polygon with the same number of sides as the number of carbon atoms in the ring: a triangle for cyclopropane, a square for cyclobutane, a pentagon for cyclopentane and a hexagon for cyclohexane.

Key Points

  • Methane is tetrahedral; the H-C-H bond angle is 109.5°.
  • Every carbon in every alkane is tetrahedral, with bond angles near 109.5°.
  • Cycloalkanes are drawn as regular polygons (line-angle formulas).
  • The number of sides of the polygon equals the number of carbons in the ring.

lessons.title: Relative Stability and Reactivity of Alkanes and Cycloalkanes
lessons.notes_html:
Relative Stability

  • Alkanes are relatively stable compounds. Branched chain alkanes are more stable than straight chain alkanes: 2-methylpropane is more stable than n-butane.
  • Cycloalkanes are also stable, except cyclopropane and cyclobutane.

Why Alkanes Are Inert

  • The C-H bond is the least polar bond.
  • The C-C bond is completely non-polar.
  • There is no unshared pair of electrons.
  • There is no point of unsaturation.
  • There is no electrophilic or nucleophilic centre.

Reactivity

Alkanes contain only strong sigma bonds. The electrons in the C-H and C-C sigma bonds are shared equally between the atoms, so no atom carries a significant charge. An alkane is therefore neither an electrophile nor a nucleophile, and alkanes are the least reactive organic compounds. They do not react with acids, bases, strong oxidizing agents or other reagents at room temperature. Their most useful reactions take place under drastic conditions and are of two types: (i) substitution reactions and (ii) thermal and catalytic reactions.

Cycloalkanes behave like alkanes, except cyclopropane and cyclobutane. The reactivity of cyclopropane and cyclobutane is due to their largest ring strain.

Key Points

  • Branched alkanes are more stable than straight chain alkanes.
  • Alkanes are inert: non-polar bonds, no lone pairs, no unsaturation, no electrophilic or nucleophilic centre.
  • Alkanes do not react with acids, bases or strong oxidizers at room temperature.
  • Useful alkane reactions need drastic conditions: substitution, and thermal and catalytic reactions.
  • Cyclopropane and cyclobutane are reactive because of ring strain.

lessons.title: Radical Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
A radical (free radical) is a highly reactive species that contains an atom with an unpaired electron. It is formed by the homolysis (homolytic cleavage) of a covalent bond: A-B → A• + B•. Each atom keeps one electron of the shared pair. Free radicals are electrically neutral, but very reactive and unstable because of their incomplete octet. A radical process involves a single electron, and the movement of one electron is shown by a half-headed arrow.

In heterolytic cleavage (heterolysis), both electrons of the bond stay with one atom: A-B → A+ + :B-, or A:- + B+.

Overview of Radical Substitution

  • In a substitution reaction, an atom or group of atoms in a molecule is replaced by another atom or group.
  • Alkanes react with Cl2 or Br2 to form alkyl chlorides and alkyl bromides.
  • Reactivity order of alkanes: tertiary → secondary → primary → methyl (tertiary most reactive).
  • Reactivity order of halogens: F2 → Cl2 → Br2 → I2 (F2 most reactive).
  • Chlorination gives the less stable radical; bromination gives the most stable radical.
  • The reaction proceeds by a radical chain mechanism involving radical intermediates.
  • Termination steps have a low probability, because the concentration of radical species is low, so the chances of collision between radicals are very low.

Key Points

  • A free radical has an unpaired electron and an incomplete octet; it is neutral, reactive and unstable.
  • Homolysis: each atom keeps one electron. Heterolysis: one atom takes both electrons, giving ions.
  • Alkane reactivity: tertiary, then secondary, then primary, then methyl.
  • Halogen reactivity: F2, then Cl2, then Br2, then I2.
  • Halogenation of alkanes follows a radical chain mechanism.

lessons.title: Reaction Mechanism of Free Radical Halogenation
lessons.notes_html:
The halogenation of alkanes proceeds by a free radical mechanism in three steps, shown here for the chlorination of methane.

Step 1: Initiation

The Cl-Cl bond of a chlorine molecule breaks by homolytic fission in the presence of heat or light, giving two chlorine free radicals: Cl2 →(Heat or Light) 2Cl•.

Step 2: Propagation

  • The chlorine radical abstracts (removes) a hydrogen atom from methane, forming HCl and a methyl radical: Cl• + CH3-H → HCl + •CH3.
  • The methyl radical abstracts a chlorine atom from a chlorine molecule, forming chloromethane and a new chlorine radical: •CH3 + Cl-Cl → CH3-Cl + Cl•.
  • These two steps repeat again and again, so the reaction is a chain reaction. They are called propagation steps because they propagate (carry forward) the reaction.

Step 3: Termination

Two radicals combine to form a neutral molecule, and the chain ends: •CH3 + •CH3 → CH3-CH3; Cl• + Cl• → Cl2; •CH3 + Cl• → CH3-Cl. Termination ends the reaction by decreasing the number of radicals available to propagate the chain.

Chlorination of methane also produces more highly halogenated products: CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4, together with more HCl.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
InitiationCl2 →(Heat or Light) 2Cl•
Propagation 1Cl• + CH4 → HCl + •CH3
Propagation 2•CH3 + Cl2 → CH3Cl + Cl•
Termination•CH3 + •CH3 → C2H6; Cl• + Cl• → Cl2; •CH3 + Cl• → CH3Cl

Key Points

  • Initiation: heat or light splits Cl2 into two chlorine radicals.
  • Propagation: each step consumes one radical and produces a new one, so the chain continues.
  • Termination: two radicals combine; the supply of radicals falls and the reaction stops.
  • Further chlorination of methane gives CH2Cl2, CHCl3 and CCl4.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Organic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Oxidation means an increase in the oxygen content, or a decrease in the hydrogen content, of a compound. The reverse process is reduction. Oxidation and reduction always take place simultaneously; such a reaction is a redox reaction.

Complete Oxidation (Combustion)

Alkanes such as natural gas, gasoline and diesel burn readily in oxygen to produce carbon dioxide, water vapours and energy. Burning in oxygen is called combustion. Methane, the main part of natural gas used for cooking and heating, burns as: CH4(g) + 2O2(g) → CO2(g) + 2H2O(g), ΔH = -891 kJ/mol. The heat of combustion is the heat evolved when one mole of a hydrocarbon is completely burnt to carbon dioxide and water.

Incomplete Oxidation

When the supply of oxygen or air is insufficient, alkanes burn incompletely and produce carbon monoxide, water vapours and carbon black (soot): 3CH4(g) + 4O2(g) → 2CO(g) + 6H2O(g) + C(s) + Energy.

Catalytic Oxidation

When lower alkanes are burnt in the presence of a metallic catalyst at high temperature and pressure, many useful products are formed. With a copper catalyst at 400°C and 200 atm, methane is oxidized in stages to methyl alcohol, then formaldehyde, then formic acid.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
Complete combustion of methaneCH4 + 2O2 → CO2 + 2H2O (ΔH = -891 kJ/mol)
Incomplete combustion of methane3CH4 + 4O2 → 2CO + 6H2O + C
Catalytic oxidation, step 1CH4 + [O] →(Cu catalyst, 400°C, 200 atm) CH3OH
Catalytic oxidation, step 2CH3OH + [O] → HCHO + H2O
Catalytic oxidation, step 3HCHO + [O] → HCOOH

Key Points

  • Oxidation = gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen; reduction is the reverse; together they form a redox reaction.
  • Complete combustion gives CO2 + H2O + energy; methane gives ΔH = -891 kJ/mol.
  • Incomplete combustion (less oxygen) gives CO + H2O + carbon black.
  • Catalytic oxidation of methane (Cu, 400°C, 200 atm) gives methanol, then formaldehyde, then formic acid.
  • Heat of combustion is measured for one mole of hydrocarbon burnt completely.

lessons.title: Alkenes and Their Nomenclature
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain one or more carbon-carbon double bonds. They are also called olefins, from the French word olefiant (oil forming), because the lower members react with chlorine or bromine to give oily products. Alkenes occur in small amounts in natural gas, coal gas and gasoline, and are produced in large amounts by the cracking of petroleum. Alkenes with one double bond (monoenes) have the general formula CnH2n. Ethylene is the first member of the series.

Nomenclature of Alkenes

  • Alkenes are normally named by the IUPAC system, but older common names are still used: ethene is called ethylene, and propene is called propylene.
  • The IUPAC name is formed by replacing the ending “ane” of the corresponding alkane with “ene”: CH2=CH2 is ethene; CH3CH=CH2 is propene.
  • Step 1: Select the longest chain that contains the double bond, and name it (for example, a five-carbon chain gives pentene).
  • Step 2: Number the longest chain from the end closer to the double bond. Alkenes of two or three carbons do not need numbers.
  • Step 3: Show the position of the double bond by the number of the lower-numbered carbon of the double bond: a double bond between carbons 2 and 3 gives 2-pentene (pent-2-ene).
  • Step 4: Name substituents as for alkanes, before the parent name and with their numbers. The double bond suffix must get the lowest possible number: 4-methyl-2-pentene (4-methylpent-2-ene).
  • Step 5: For two or more double bonds, replace “ene” with diene, triene or tetraene: CH2=CH-CH=CH2 is 1,3-butadiene (buta-1,3-diene).

Key Points

  • Alkenes contain at least one C=C double bond; general formula CnH2n; also called olefins.
  • Large amounts of alkenes come from the cracking of petroleum.
  • The parent chain must contain the double bond, and it is numbered from the end nearer the double bond.
  • The double bond position is shown by its lower-numbered carbon.
  • Two or three double bonds are shown by diene and triene.

lessons.title: Relative Stability of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The stability of an alkene depends on three factors.

Degree of Substitution

The stability of alkenes increases with an increase in the number of R (alkyl) groups attached to the doubly bonded carbons: CH2=CH2 → RCH=CH2 → RCH=CHR → R2C=CHR → R2C=CR2, in order of increasing stability. Ethene is the least stable and the tetra-substituted alkene is the most stable.

Stereochemistry

Trans alkenes are more stable than cis alkenes. A cis alkene has more steric hindrance, because its bulky groups lie on the same side of the double bond and crowd each other. A trans alkene has less steric hindrance, because its bulky groups lie on opposite sides. For example, trans-2-butene is more stable than cis-2-butene.

Conjugation

Conjugated alkenes are more stable than isolated alkenes: 1,3-pentadiene (conjugated) is more stable than 1,4-pentadiene (isolated).

Key Points

  • More alkyl groups on the C=C carbons means a more stable alkene.
  • Trans isomers are more stable than cis isomers (less steric hindrance).
  • Conjugated alkenes are more stable than isolated alkenes.
  • Order: CH2=CH2 is least stable; R2C=CR2 is most stable among substituted ethenes.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
In ethene, the carbon-carbon double bond consists of one sigma bond and one pi bond. The doubly bonded carbons are sp2 hybridized. Each such carbon has three sp2 hybrid orbitals and one pure p-orbital.

  • The sp2 orbitals overlap with the orbitals of other atoms to form sigma bonds. A sigma bond is formed by the head-to-head overlap of hybrid orbitals.
  • The remaining pure p-orbitals overlap sideways (side-to-side) to form the pi bond.
  • All six atoms of ethene lie in the same plane; the molecule is trigonal planar.
  • The HCH and HCC bond angles are approximately 120°.
  • The C=C bond length is 134 pm and the C-H bond length is 109 pm.

Key Points

  • A C=C double bond = one sigma bond + one pi bond.
  • Double-bonded carbons are sp2 hybridized: three sp2 orbitals plus one pure p-orbital.
  • Sigma bonds form by head-to-head overlap; the pi bond by side-to-side overlap of p-orbitals.
  • Ethene is planar (trigonal planar), with angles near 120°.
  • C=C = 134 pm; C-H = 109 pm.

mcqs.why: Difference = 134 - 109 = 25 pm; C=C is 134 pm and C-H is 109 pm, so C=C exceeds C-H by 25 pm.

lessons.title: Preparation of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are generally prepared by β-elimination reactions: two atoms or groups present on adjacent (neighbouring) carbon atoms are removed, and a double bond is formed between those carbons.

Dehydration of Alcohols

  • Water is removed from adjacent carbons by heating the alcohol with a dehydrating agent. The best dehydrating reagents are conc. H2SO4, Al2O3 and P2O3, and all of them work at high temperature.
  • The -OH group is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon.
  • Ease of dehydration: tertiary (3°) alcohols dehydrate most easily, then secondary (2°), then primary (1°).
  • Primary: ethyl alcohol with conc. H2SO4 at 170-180°C gives ethene: CH3CH2OH → CH2=CH2 + H2O.
  • Secondary: 75% H2SO4 at 100-140°C (the book's example works at 108°C).
  • Tertiary: tert-butyl alcohol with only 5% H2SO4 at 50°C gives 2-methylpropene + H2O.

Dehydrohalogenation of Alkyl Halides

  • Hydrogen halide (HX) is removed from adjacent carbons by heating the alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH.
  • The halogen (X) is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon.
  • Example: chloroethane + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) CH2=CH2 + KCl + H2O.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
Dehydration (1° alcohol)CH3CH2OH →(Conc. H2SO4, 170-180°C) CH2=CH2 + H2O
Dehydration (3° alcohol)tert-Butyl alcohol →(5% H2SO4, 50°C) 2-methylpropene + H2O
DehydrohalogenationCH3CH2Cl + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) CH2=CH2 + KCl + H2O

Key Points

  • Alkene preparations are β-eliminations: groups leave from adjacent carbons.
  • Dehydration removes -OH from the α-carbon and H from the β-carbon.
  • Ease of dehydration: 3° alcohols, then 2°, then 1°; stronger acid and higher temperature are needed for 1° alcohols.
  • Dehydrohalogenation removes HX with hot alcoholic KOH.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkenes: Hydrogenation, Hydrohalogenation, Hydration and Halogenation
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes are more reactive than alkanes because of the pi bond. The pi bond is formed by the parallel overlap of p-orbitals, so its electrons lie much farther from the carbon nuclei and are less firmly bound. The pi bond is weaker than the sigma bond and breaks easily when an electrophilic reagent attacks. The most important reactions of alkenes are addition reactions, in which two molecules combine to form a single product molecule, and the double bond changes into a single bond.

Catalytic Hydrogenation

Hydrogen adds to the double bond in the presence of a catalyst (Pt, Ni or Pd) at moderate pressure (1-5 atm), giving the saturated hydrocarbon (alkane): CH2=CH2 + H2 →(Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C) CH3-CH3. The heat of hydrogenation is the heat evolved when one mole of an alkene is hydrogenated; it is about 120 kJ/mol for each double bond. The reaction is used in industry to convert vegetable oil into vegetable ghee with a nickel catalyst.

Hydrohalogenation

Hydrogen halides (HX) add to alkenes to form alkyl halides. The reaction is carried out in a solvent such as acetic acid, or by passing dry gaseous HX over the alkene: CH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3-CH2Br (ethyl bromide). The reactivity order of HX is HI → HBr → HCl (in decreasing order). The mechanism has two steps: first the alkene and HBr form a carbocation and Br-; then the carbocation combines with Br- (the nucleophile) to give the alkyl bromide.

Markovnikov's rule: when an unsymmetrical molecule (polar reagent) such as HX is added to an unsymmetrical alkene like propene, the negative part of the adding molecule goes to the carbon atom that has the least number of hydrogen atoms. So propene + HBr gives 2-bromopropane.

Hydration

Water adds to alkenes in the presence of H2SO4 at 100°C to form alcohols. In step 1, ethene reacts with sulphuric acid (H-OSO3H) to form ethyl hydrogensulphate. In step 2, ethyl hydrogensulphate reacts with water (H-OH) to give ethyl alcohol, and the sulphuric acid is regenerated.

Halogenation

Chlorine and bromine add to alkenes in an inert solvent (CCl4) in the dark, giving vicinal dihalides (halogens on adjacent carbons): propene + Cl2 → 1,2-dichloropropane. The mechanism has two steps: first the alkene and X2 form a halonium ion and X-; then the halonium ion combines with X- to give the vicinal dihalide.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HydrogenationCH2=CH2 + H2 →(Ni, 1-5 atm, 250-300°C) CH3-CH3
HydrohalogenationCH2=CH2 + HBr → CH3CH2Br; propene + HBr → 2-bromopropane (Markovnikov)
HydrationCH2=CH2 + H2O →(H2SO4, 100°C) CH3CH2OH
HalogenationPropene + Cl2 →(CCl4, dark) 1,2-dichloropropane

Key Points

  • The weak, exposed pi bond makes alkenes reactive; their main reactions are additions.
  • Hydrogenation (Ni/Pt/Pd, 1-5 atm) gives alkanes; heat of hydrogenation ≈ 120 kJ/mol per double bond.
  • HX addition follows Markovnikov's rule; HX order: HI, then HBr, then HCl.
  • Hydration with H2SO4 at 100°C gives alcohols, through ethyl hydrogensulphate.
  • Halogenation in CCl4 in the dark gives vicinal dihalides through a halonium ion.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alkenes: Halohydration, Epoxidation, Ozonolysis and Polymerization
lessons.notes_html:
Halohydration

This is the addition of a hypohalous acid to an alkene. Aqueous solutions of halogens (Cl2 or Br2) react with alkenes to form halohydrins, which carry a halo group and a hydroxyl group on adjacent carbons: propene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloro-2-propanol + HCl.

Epoxidation

This is the addition of oxygen (O2) to an alkene. Alkenes react with oxygen in the presence of a silver catalyst under high pressure and temperature to form epoxides: 2CH2=CH2 + O2 →(Ag, 300°C) 2 ethylene oxide. Propene similarly gives propylene oxide.

Ozonolysis

Ozonolysis is the reaction of ozone (O3) with an alkene, in which the C=C double bond is broken. In an inert solvent such as ether, ozone first forms an unstable molozonide, which rearranges into an ozonide. Ozonides are explosive and are not isolated. Decomposition of the ozonide with zinc and water gives an aldehyde and/or a ketone: ethylene ozonide + Zn →(H2O, 100°C) 2HCHO (formaldehyde) + ZnO. Ozonolysis is used to find the position of the double bond, because the molecule is cleaved at the double bond.

Polymerization

Polymerization is the process in which small molecules (monomers) combine to form large molecules (polymers). Ethylene polymerizes in the presence of a catalyst at high temperature and pressure to form polythene (polyethylene): n CH2=CH2 →(400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2) -[CH2-CH2]n-. Polythene is a plastic used for toys, bags, boxes, purses, carpet backing, buckets, rain coats, dustbins, shoe soles and pipes.

The reaction of ethene with bromine is very important: it is used for the detection of unsaturation in a compound.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HalohydrationPropene + Cl2 + H2O → 1-chloro-2-propanol + HCl
Epoxidation2CH2=CH2 + O2 →(Ag, 300°C) 2 ethylene oxide
OzonolysisEthylene ozonide + Zn →(H2O, 100°C) 2HCHO + ZnO
Polymerizationn CH2=CH2 →(400°C, 100 atm, 0.01% O2) polythene

Key Points

  • Halohydration gives halohydrins: -X and -OH on adjacent carbons.
  • Epoxidation with O2 and a silver catalyst gives epoxides such as ethylene oxide.
  • Ozonolysis cleaves the double bond and gives aldehydes and/or ketones; it locates the double bond.
  • Polymerization joins monomers into polymers: ethene gives polythene.
  • Bromine water reaction with ethene is the test for unsaturation.

lessons.title: Conjugation in Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
The word conjugation comes from Latin and means “to link together”. It describes conjugated (pi) systems, such as double bonds, that are linked together. The focus here is on dienes, alkenes with two double bonds. Dienes are divided into three classes by the closeness of their pi bonds.

Three Classes of Dienes

  • Cumulated dienes (cumulenes or allenes): the two double bonds are adjacent (next to each other), e.g. 1,2-pentadiene, CH2=C=CH-CH2-CH3. They are relatively rare.
  • Isolated dienes (non-conjugated): the double bonds are separated by more than one single bond, e.g. 1,4-pentadiene, CH2=CH-CH2-CH=CH2.
  • Conjugated dienes: the double bonds are separated by exactly one single bond, e.g. 1,3-pentadiene, CH2=CH-CH=CH-CH3. The simplest conjugated diene is 1,3-butadiene, CH2=CH-CH=CH2.

Why Conjugation Gives Stability

Conjugation takes place whenever p-orbitals overlap on three or more adjacent atoms. In 1,3-butadiene, all four carbons are sp2 hybridized and each carries a pure p-orbital with an unpaired electron. The four p-orbitals on adjacent carbons overlap, so the pi electrons are delocalized over the whole molecule. The electron density of the pi bonds is spread over all four atoms, which lowers the energy and makes the molecule more stable. In 1,4-pentadiene, the pi bonds are separated by more than one sigma bond; they are too far apart to conjugate, so it behaves differently from 1,3-butadiene.

Key Points

  • Dienes have two double bonds: cumulated (adjacent), isolated (far apart) or conjugated (one single bond between them).
  • Conjugation needs p-orbitals overlapping on three or more adjacent atoms.
  • In 1,3-butadiene the pi electrons delocalize over all four carbons, lowering the energy.
  • Conjugated dienes are more stable than isolated dienes.

lessons.title: Isomerism and Chiral Centres
lessons.notes_html:
Compounds that have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas are called isomers, and the phenomenon is called isomerism. For example, n-butane and isobutane are isomers: both have the formula C4H10 but different structures. Isomers have different physical, chemical and biological properties. The number of isomers of a compound depends on the number of carbon atoms, and it increases as the number of carbon atoms increases: butane has 2 isomers, pentane 3, heptane 9 and decane 75.

There are two main types of isomerism: constitutional isomerism and stereoisomerism.

Chiral Centres

  • Tetrahedral atoms, usually carbon, that carry four different substituents are called chiral centres (or stereogenic centres).
  • A molecule that contains a chiral centre will be chiral; a molecule without a chiral centre will be achiral.
  • A molecule with a single chiral centre is always chiral. A molecule with two or more chiral centres may or may not be chiral.
  • Example: in the amino acid alanine, the central carbon is bonded to four different groups (CH3, H, COOH and NH2), so it is a chiral centre and the molecule is chiral.
  • The word chiral comes from the Greek word cheir, meaning “hand”. Left and right hands are chiral: each is the mirror image of the other, and the two do not superimpose (do not fit exactly on each other).

Key Points

  • Isomers: same molecular formula, different structural formulas, different properties.
  • The number of isomers grows quickly with carbon number (decane has 75).
  • Two main types: constitutional isomerism and stereoisomerism.
  • A chiral centre is a tetrahedral atom (usually C) with four different substituents.
  • One chiral centre always makes a molecule chiral; two or more may or may not.

lessons.title: Optical Activity and Optical Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Optical Activity

  • Ordinary light consists of waves vibrating in many planes. When it passes through a polarizer (a Nicol prism or a Polaroid lens), it vibrates in one plane only; this is plane polarized light.
  • Compounds that can rotate the plane of polarized light clockwise or anticlockwise are called optically active compounds, and this property is called optical activity. It is measured with an instrument called a polarimeter.
  • When plane polarized light passes through a solution of a chiral (optically active) compound, the beam is rotated by a certain number of degrees.
  • Dextrorotatory: rotates the plane clockwise; shown by the prefix d or (+). Dextro is Latin for “to the right”.
  • Levorotatory: rotates the plane anticlockwise; shown by the prefix l or (-). Levo is Latin for “to the left”. Sometimes d and l are used rather than (+) and (-).

Optical Isomers

  • Optically active compounds that have the same molecular formulas and the same structural formulas, but differ in their interaction with plane polarized light, are called optical isomers; the phenomenon is optical isomerism.
  • Optical isomers have the same physical and chemical properties; they differ only in their behaviour towards plane polarized light.
  • Lactic acid has two optical isomers: (+) lactic acid is dextrorotatory and (-) lactic acid is levorotatory. The (+) form is the mirror image of the (-) form.
  • An equal mixture of the (+) and (-) forms is called a racemic mixture or racemate, written (±). In it, the two rotations cancel each other, so no rotation is observed.

Key Points

  • Plane polarized light vibrates in one plane only; optical activity is measured by a polarimeter.
  • Dextrorotatory = clockwise rotation, d or (+); levorotatory = anticlockwise, l or (-).
  • Optical isomers share formula and structure and all physical and chemical properties, except the direction of rotation.
  • (+) and (-) lactic acid are mirror images of each other.
  • An equal mixture of both forms is a racemate (±), which shows no rotation.

lessons.title: Stereoisomers and Geometrical Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Stereoisomers (configurational isomers) have the same molecular formulas and the same structural formulas, but differ in the arrangement of their atoms or groups in space. They are of two types: geometrical isomers and optical isomers.

Geometrical (Cis-Trans) Isomers

  • Geometrical isomers have the same formulas but restricted rotation in the molecule. Restricted rotation is produced by carbon-carbon double bonds, or by carbon-carbon single bonds in cyclic compounds.
  • Cis (from Latin cisoid, same side): the similar groups lie on the same side of the double bond.
  • Trans (from Latin transoid, opposite side): the similar groups lie on opposite sides of the double bond.
  • In cis-2-butene the two hydrogen atoms are on the same side; in trans-2-butene they are on opposite sides.
  • Cis and trans isomers are different compounds with different physical and chemical properties. The trans isomer is more stable, because in the cis isomer the bulky groups on the same side repel each other.
  • Cyclic compounds with two substituents on different carbons also show cis-trans isomerism: in cis-1,2-dimethylcyclopropane both methyl groups are on the same side of the ring; in the trans form they are on opposite sides.

Conditions for Geometrical Isomerism

  • The compound must have a double bond.
  • Two different atoms or groups must be bonded to each carbon of the double bond.

Key Points

  • Stereoisomers differ only in the arrangement of atoms in space; they are geometrical or optical.
  • Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation (double bond or ring).
  • Cis = similar groups on the same side; trans = on opposite sides.
  • Trans isomers are more stable than cis isomers.
  • Each double-bond carbon must carry two different atoms or groups.

lessons.title: Constitutional Isomers
lessons.notes_html:
Constitutional isomers (structural isomers) have the same molecular formula but different structural formulas; they differ in the arrangement of atoms within the molecule. There are five types.

Chain Isomers (Skeleton Isomers)

These have different carbon chains or skeletons. The three chain isomers of pentane (C5H12) are n-pentane (a five-carbon chain), isopentane (longest chain of four carbons) and neopentane (longest chain of three carbons).

Position Isomers

These differ in the position of the same functional group. Examples: 1-chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane (C4H9Cl); 1-butene and 2-butene (C4H8), which differ in the position of the double bond.

Functional Group Isomers

These have different functional groups. Examples: ethyl alcohol, CH3CH2OH, and dimethyl ether, CH3OCH3 (both C2H6O); methyl acetate and propionic acid (both C3H6O2).

Metamers

These have the same molecular formula and the same functional group, but differ in the distribution of carbon atoms on either side of the functional group. Diethyl ether, CH3CH2OCH2CH3, and methyl-n-propyl ether, CH3OCH2CH2CH3, are metamers; trimethylamine and ethylmethylamine are also metamers. Metamers belong to the same homologous series.

Tautomers

Tautomers are two forms of the same compound that differ in the position of protons and electrons; the phenomenon is called tautomerism. The keto and enol forms are readily interconvertible and exist in dynamic equilibrium. In ethyl acetoacetate at 25°C, the keto form is 93% and the enol form is 7%. Usually the keto form is more stable, but in some cases the enol form is more stable.

Key Points

  • Constitutional isomers differ in the arrangement of atoms: chain, position, functional group, metamers, tautomers.
  • Chain isomers: different carbon skeletons (n-pentane, isopentane, neopentane).
  • Position isomers: same group at different positions (1-butene and 2-butene).
  • Functional group isomers: different functional groups (ethanol and dimethyl ether).
  • Metamers: different carbon distribution around the same functional group.
  • Tautomers: keto and enol forms in dynamic equilibrium (ethyl acetoacetate: 93% keto, 7% enol at 25°C).

mcqs.why: Constitutional (structural) isomers share a molecular formula but differ in the arrangement of atoms, giving different structural formulas.

lessons.title: Alkynes and Their Nomenclature
lessons.notes_html:
Alkynes are unsaturated hydrocarbons that contain one or more carbon-carbon triple bonds. The simplest alkyne is ethyne, commonly called acetylene, and the common name of the alkyne family is acetylenes, after this simplest member. The general formula of alkynes is CnH2n-2, where n = 2, 3, 4, 5, ... Acetylene has the structure H-C#C-H (# shows a triple bond). Alkynes are less common in nature than alkenes, although more than 1000 different alkynes have been isolated from natural sources. They are also produced during the cracking of petroleum.

Nomenclature of Alkynes

  • Alkynes are named like alkenes: replace the ending “ane” with “yne”. CH#CH is ethyne; CH3C#CH is propyne.
  • Step 1: Select the longest chain that contains the triple bond.
  • Step 2: Number the chain from the end closer to the triple bond. Alkynes of two or three carbons do not need numbers.
  • Step 3: Show the position of the triple bond by the number of its lower-numbered carbon, e.g. 2-hexyne.
  • Step 4: Name substituents as for alkanes; the triple bond suffix must get the lowest possible number, e.g. 4-methyl-2-hexyne.
  • Step 5: For two or more triple bonds, use diyne, triyne or tetrayne: HC#C-C#CH is 1,3-butadiyne (buta-1,3-diyne).

Alkenynes

Hydrocarbons that contain both double and triple bonds are called alkenynes. If the double and triple bonds are at different positions from the two ends, number from the end closer to a double or triple bond (3-penten-1-yne; 1-penten-3-yne). If they are at the same positions from the ends, the double bond is given preference in numbering (1-penten-4-yne).

Key Points

  • Alkynes contain at least one C#C triple bond; general formula CnH2n-2.
  • Ethyne (acetylene) is the first member; the family is also called acetylenes.
  • The parent chain must contain the triple bond and is numbered from the end nearer it.
  • Two triple bonds are shown by diyne; compounds with both bond types are alkenynes.
  • In alkenynes, a tie in numbering is given to the double bond.

mcqs.why: Step 1 of alkyne nomenclature is to select the longest chain that contains the triple bond, then number from the end closer to it.

mcqs.q: HC#C-C#CH, with two triple bonds, is named:
mcqs.why: Two triple bonds are shown by diyne: HC#C-C#CH is 1,3-butadiyne (buta-1,3-diyne), using locants 1 and 3 for the triple bonds.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbons containing both double and triple bonds are called:
mcqs.why: Compounds with both double and triple bonds are alkenynes, e.g. 3-penten-1-yne and 1-penten-3-yne in the notes.

mcqs.q: In an alkenyne, if double and triple bonds are equidistant from the ends, numbering preference goes to:
mcqs.why: If the double and triple bonds are at the same positions from the ends, the double bond is given preference in numbering, e.g. 1-penten-4-yne.

mcqs.q: 4-methyl-2-hexyne shows that in alkyne naming:
options: The triple bond suffix must get the lowest possible number
The methyl group is numbered first alphabetically in all cases
mcqs.why: Substituents are named as for alkanes, and the triple bond must receive the lowest possible locant, as in 4-methyl-2-hexyne where the triple bond is at carbon 2.

lessons.title: Relative Stability and Structure of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Relative Stability of Alkynes

The book relates the stability of alkynes to the smaller bond length of the triple bond. Two factors decide the stability of an alkyne.

  • Position of the triple bond: internal alkynes, in which the triple bond is at a position other than the end of the chain, are more stable than terminal alkynes, in which the triple bond is at the end. 2-Pentyne is more stable than 1-pentyne.
  • Number of substituents: branched alkynes are more stable than unbranched alkynes. 2,5-Dimethyl-3-hexyne is more stable than 3-hexyne.

Structure of Alkynes

  • In acetylene, the triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The carbon atoms are sp hybridized; each carbon has two sp hybrid orbitals and two pure p-orbitals.
  • One sp orbital of each carbon overlaps with the half-filled s orbital of a hydrogen atom, forming a C-H sigma bond. The other sp orbital overlaps with the sp orbital of the second carbon, forming the C-C sigma bond.
  • The two remaining pure p-orbitals form two pi bonds by sidewise overlapping.
  • Acetylene is a linear molecule; all bond angles are 180°.
  • The C#C bond length is 120 pm and the C-H bond length is 106 pm.

Key Points

  • Internal alkynes are more stable than terminal alkynes; branched alkynes are more stable than unbranched ones.
  • A triple bond = one sigma bond + two pi bonds; the carbons are sp hybridized.
  • Acetylene is linear, with bond angles of 180°.
  • C#C = 120 pm; C-H = 106 pm.

mcqs.q: Internal alkynes are more stable than terminal alkynes. An internal alkyne has its triple bond:
options: At a position other than the end of the chain
At the very end of the chain
mcqs.why: Internal alkynes, with the triple bond not at the end, are more stable than terminal alkynes; 2-pentyne is more stable than 1-pentyne.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly shows the stability comparison from the notes?
options: Unbranched alkynes always more stable than branched
mcqs.why: The notes state 2-pentyne (internal) is more stable than 1-pentyne (terminal), and branched alkynes are more stable than unbranched ones.

mcqs.q: A carbon-carbon triple bond consists of:
options: Two sigma bonds and one pi bond
One sigma bond and two pi bonds
mcqs.why: In acetylene the triple bond is one sigma bond plus two pi bonds, formed by the two pure p-orbitals overlapping sidewise.

mcqs.q: The carbons in acetylene are hybridized as:
mcqs.why: Acetylene carbons are sp hybridized: each carbon has two sp hybrid orbitals and two pure p-orbitals, giving the linear structure.

mcqs.q: Acetylene is a linear molecule with all bond angles of:
mcqs.why: Because acetylene is linear with sp hybridization, all its bond angles are 180 degrees, unlike trigonal planar ethene at about 120 degrees.

mcqs.q: The C#C bond length and C-H bond length in acetylene are:
mcqs.why: The notes give C#C = 120 pm and C-H = 106 pm in acetylene; these are shorter than the C=C 134 pm values for ethene.

mcqs.q: How do the two pi bonds in acetylene form?
options: By head-to-head overlap of sp orbitals
By overlap with hydrogen s orbitals only
They do not form bonds at all
By sidewise overlapping of the two pure p-orbitals
mcqs.why: The C-C sigma bond forms from sp-sp overlap, while the two remaining pure p-orbitals form two pi bonds by sidewise overlapping.

mcqs.q: Which C-H sigma bond formation is described for acetylene?
options: s orbital of carbon with s orbital of carbon
One sp orbital of carbon overlaps the half-filled s orbital of hydrogen
mcqs.why: One sp orbital of each carbon overlaps with the half-filled s orbital of a hydrogen atom, forming a C-H sigma bond in acetylene.

mcqs.q: Branched alkynes compared with unbranched alkynes are:
options: Identical in stability in all cases
Not mentioned in relation to stability
mcqs.why: The number of substituents affects stability: branched alkynes are more stable, e.g. 2,5-dimethyl-3-hexyne is more stable than 3-hexyne.

mcqs.q: The book relates alkyne stability in this lesson partly to:
options: The larger bond length of the triple bond
The presence of a benzene ring
The smaller bond length of the triple bond
Free rotation about the triple bond
mcqs.why: The lesson opens by relating alkyne stability to the smaller bond length of the triple bond, then discusses position and substituents.

lessons.title: Physical Properties and Preparation of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties of Alkynes

  • The first three members are gases, the next eight members are liquids, and the higher members are solids.
  • They are colourless and odourless, except acetylene, which has a garlic-like smell.
  • They are generally non-polar compounds, soluble in non-polar solvents like ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride.
  • Their melting points, boiling points and densities increase gradually with molecular mass.

Preparation of Alkynes

Alkynes are prepared by the elimination of atoms or groups from adjacent carbon atoms.

Dehydrohalogenation of Dihalides

  • A vicinal dihalide is heated with alcoholic KOH. The reaction takes place in two steps: in the first step one HX is removed and a vinyl halide is formed; in the second step a second HX is removed and the alkyne is formed.
  • Step 1: 1,2-dibromoethane + alcoholic KOH →(Heat) vinyl bromide + KBr + H2O.
  • Step 2: vinyl bromide + alcoholic KOH →(Heat) acetylene + KBr + H2O. Removal of the second HX is difficult and needs a strong base.
  • This method is useful because vicinal dihalides are readily prepared from alkenes by the addition of halogens.

Dehalogenation of Tetrahalides

  • A vicinal tetrahalide is heated with zinc dust in ethanol. The reaction again takes place in two steps: 1,1,2,2-tetrabromoethane + Zn →(Heat) 1,2-dibromoethene + ZnBr2; then 1,2-dibromoethene + Zn →(Heat) acetylene + ZnBr2.
  • This method is not used in practice, because tetrahalides themselves are prepared by the halogenation of alkynes.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
From vicinal dihalide, step 11,2-Dibromoethane + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) vinyl bromide + KBr + H2O
From vicinal dihalide, step 2Vinyl bromide + KOH →(Alcohol, Heat) acetylene + KBr + H2O
From tetrahalide1,1,2,2-Tetrabromoethane + 2Zn →(Heat) acetylene + 2ZnBr2 (in two steps)

Key Points

  • Alkynes: first three gases, next eight liquids, higher members solids; colourless and non-polar.
  • Melting point, boiling point and density rise gradually with molecular mass.
  • Dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide removes two HX in two steps; the second step needs a strong base.
  • Dehalogenation of a tetrahalide uses zinc dust in ethanol, but the method is not used in practice.

mcqs.q: The physical states of alkynes are: first three members, next eight, higher members are respectively:
mcqs.why: The first three alkynes are gases, the next eight are liquids and higher members are solids; they are colourless and generally non-polar.

mcqs.q: Acetylene differs from other alkynes in having:
