mcqs.why: Alkynes are colourless and odourless except acetylene, which has a garlic-like smell, as noted in the physical properties.

mcqs.q: Alkynes are soluble in:
options: Non-polar solvents like ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride
mcqs.why: Being generally non-polar, alkynes dissolve in non-polar solvents such as ether, benzene and carbon tetrachloride, not in polar water.

mcqs.q: As molecular mass of alkynes increases, melting point, boiling point and density:
mcqs.why: Their melting points, boiling points and densities increase gradually with molecular mass, following the trend described in the notes.

mcqs.q: Dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal dihalide to an alkyne removes:
mcqs.why: A vicinal dihalide heated with alcoholic KOH loses one HX to give a vinyl halide, then a second HX to give the alkyne, in two steps.

mcqs.q: In step 1 from 1,2-dibromoethane with alcoholic KOH, the product is:
mcqs.why: Step 1: 1,2-dibromoethane + alcoholic KOH (heat) gives vinyl bromide + KBr + H2O; step 2 then converts vinyl bromide to acetylene.

mcqs.q: Removal of the second HX in alkyne preparation is difficult and needs:
mcqs.why: The second HX removal is difficult and needs a strong base, which is why the two-step dehydrohalogenation conditions matter.

mcqs.q: Dehalogenation of a vicinal tetrahalide uses:
mcqs.why: A vicinal tetrahalide is heated with zinc dust in ethanol in two steps, e.g. tetrabromoethane to dibromoethene and then to acetylene.

mcqs.q: Why is the tetrahalide method not used in practice?
options: Tetrahalides themselves are prepared by halogenation of alkynes
It produces no alkyne at all
mcqs.why: The method is not used in practice because tetrahalides themselves are made by halogenating alkynes, so it is a circular route.

mcqs.q: Vicinal dihalides for alkyne preparation are readily prepared from:
mcqs.why: The dihalide method is useful because vicinal dihalides are readily prepared from alkenes by the addition of halogens.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alkynes and Acidity of Terminal Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Reactivity of Alkynes

  • The triple bond consists of one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The electron density between the carbon atoms is very high, and this draws the atoms very close to each other.
  • The electrons of the triple bond are less exposed than the electrons of a double bond.
  • Therefore alkynes are less reactive towards electrophilic reagents than alkenes.

Acidity of Terminal Alkynes

  • The triply bonded carbon atom is sp hybridized. An sp hybridized carbon is highly electronegative and strongly electron withdrawing.
  • Because of this, the hydrogen attached to a terminal triple-bonded carbon is slightly acidic (the carbon carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogen a partial positive charge).
  • This hydrogen is replaced readily by metals such as Na, Ag and Cu, forming ionic compounds (metal acetylides).

Key Points

  • High electron density in the triple bond holds its electrons close, so they are less exposed than double-bond electrons.
  • Alkynes react with electrophiles more slowly than alkenes.
  • The sp carbon of a terminal alkyne is highly electronegative, so its hydrogen is weakly acidic.
  • Terminal alkyne hydrogen is replaced by Na, Ag or Cu to form ionic acetylides.

mcqs.q: Compared with alkenes, alkynes towards electrophilic reagents are:
mcqs.why: The triple-bond electrons are less exposed than double-bond electrons, so alkynes are less reactive towards electrophiles than alkenes.

mcqs.q: Why are triple-bond electrons less exposed?
options: The triple bond has no pi electrons
High electron density draws the carbon atoms very close together
Hydrogen atoms shield every bond completely
mcqs.why: Very high electron density between the carbons draws them close, so the electrons are held tightly and are less exposed than in a double bond.

mcqs.q: The carbon of a terminal alkyne is sp hybridized and is described as:
options: Highly electronegative and strongly electron withdrawing
mcqs.why: An sp hybridized carbon is highly electronegative and strongly electron withdrawing, making its attached hydrogen slightly acidic.

mcqs.q: In a terminal alkyne C-H bond, the partial charges are:
options: Carbon partial positive, hydrogen partial negative
Both atoms neutral with no polarity
Carbon partial negative, hydrogen partial positive
mcqs.why: Because the sp carbon withdraws electrons, carbon carries a partial negative charge and the terminal hydrogen a partial positive charge.

mcqs.q: The hydrogen of a terminal alkyne is replaced readily by metals such as:
mcqs.why: Terminal alkyne hydrogen is replaced by metals such as Na, Ag and Cu, forming ionic compounds called metal acetylides.

mcqs.q: Compounds formed when terminal alkyne hydrogen is replaced by a metal are called:
mcqs.why: Replacing the acidic terminal hydrogen with Na, Ag or Cu gives ionic metal acetylides, a key property of terminal alkynes.

mcqs.q: A terminal alkyne is one whose triple bond is:
options: In the middle of the chain
At the end of the chain
mcqs.why: Terminal means at the end of the chain; only terminal alkynes have the acidic hydrogen attached directly to a triply bonded carbon.

mcqs.q: The triple bond in alkynes consists of:
options: One sigma and one pi bond
Two sigma and one pi bond
One sigma and two pi bonds
mcqs.why: As in the structure lesson, the triple bond is one sigma bond and two pi bonds, with high electron density between the carbons.

mcqs.q: Internal alkynes do not show the same metal-replacement acidity because they:
options: Lack a hydrogen attached to a triply bonded carbon
mcqs.why: Internal alkynes have no hydrogen on the triple-bond carbons, so there is no acidic terminal hydrogen to be replaced by Na, Ag or Cu.

mcqs.q: The acidity of terminal alkyne hydrogen is described as:
options: Strongly acidic like a mineral acid
mcqs.why: The notes call the terminal hydrogen slightly acidic: it is replaced readily by metals, but the alkyne is not a strong acid.

lessons.title: Addition Reactions of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkynes undergo addition reactions like alkenes, but they add two molecules of the reagent instead of one. The reaction takes place in two steps: in the first step the triple bond changes into a double bond, and in the second step the double bond changes into a single bond.

Hydrogenation (Addition of H2)

Hydrogen adds in the presence of a finely divided metal catalyst (Ni, Pt or Pd) at or above room temperature, in two steps: HC#CH + H2 →(Ni, 250-300°C) CH2=CH2 (ethene); then CH2=CH2 + H2 → CH3-CH3 (ethane).

Dissolving Metal Reduction

This is one of the most useful and oldest reduction methods. The reduction uses a solution of a strongly electropositive metal (Na, K or Zn) in an inert solvent such as liquid ammonia or THF, containing a proton source. With sodium in liquid ammonia, acetylene forms sodium acetylide: HC#CH + Na →(Liquid NH3) HC#CNa + 1/2 H2. Sodium acetylides are used to convert lower alkynes into higher alkynes: HC#CNa + CH3I → HC#C-CH3 + NaI. In these reactions the “H2” is added as 2e- and 2H+.

Hydrohalogenation (Addition of HX)

Alkynes add HX to form dihaloalkanes. The reaction follows Markovnikov's rule: the halogen adds to the carbon with the lesser number of hydrogen atoms. It takes place in two steps: propyne + HBr → 2-bromopropene; then 2-bromopropene + HBr → 2,2-dibromopropane. The reactivity order of HX is HI → HBr → HCl → HF (in decreasing order).

Hydration (Addition of H2O)

Alkynes react with water in the presence of mercuric sulphate and sulphuric acid to form unstable enols, which rearrange to carbonyl compounds. Acetylene gives an aldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones. The addition follows Markovnikov's rule: propyne + H2O →(HgSO4, H2SO4) propen-2-ol (enol), which rearranges to propanone (acetone).

Bromination (Addition of Br2)

With less bromine, alkynes form dibromides; with excess bromine they form tetrabromides: propyne + Br2 → 1,2-dibromopropene; then + Br2 → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane.

Ozonolysis (Addition of O3)

Ozone breaks the carbon-carbon triple bond. First, ozone adds across the pi bond (in CCl4) to form a molozonide, which rearranges into an ozonide. The ozonide is then hydrolysed by water to a 1,2-dicarbonyl compound and H2O2, and the dicarbonyl compound is cleaved by the H2O2 into a mixture of carboxylic acids. Ozonolysis is used to find the position of the triple bond, because the molecule is cleaved at the triple bond.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HydrogenationHC#CH + 2H2 →(Ni, 250-300°C) CH3-CH3 (through CH2=CH2)
Sodium acetylide formationHC#CH + Na →(Liquid NH3) HC#CNa + 1/2 H2
HydrohalogenationPropyne + 2HBr → 2,2-dibromopropane (Markovnikov, two steps)
HydrationPropyne + H2O →(HgSO4, H2SO4) propanone (through propen-2-ol)
BrominationPropyne + 2Br2 → 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane (through 1,2-dibromopropene)

Key Points

  • Alkynes add two molecules of reagent in two steps: triple bond, then double bond, is saturated.
  • Full hydrogenation gives the alkane; the first step gives the alkene.
  • HX addition follows Markovnikov's rule twice and gives a geminal dihalide.
  • Hydration (HgSO4/H2SO4) gives an enol that rearranges: acetylene to an aldehyde, other alkynes to ketones.
  • Bromination gives dibromides or tetrabromides; ozonolysis cleaves the triple bond to carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: Alkynes add how many molecules of a reagent in addition reactions?
mcqs.why: Alkynes add two molecules of reagent in two steps: first the triple bond becomes a double bond, then the double bond becomes single.

mcqs.q: Full hydrogenation of acetylene with Ni at 250-300°C gives finally:
mcqs.why: HC#CH + H2 gives CH2=CH2 (ethene) first, then CH2=CH2 + H2 gives CH3-CH3 (ethane), so full hydrogenation gives the alkane ethane.

mcqs.q: With sodium in liquid ammonia, acetylene forms:
mcqs.why: HC#CH + Na in liquid NH3 gives HC#CNa (sodium acetylide) + 1/2 H2; acetylides are used to build higher alkynes.

mcqs.q: Sodium acetylide reacting with CH3I gives:
options: Only NaI and no carbon product
A higher alkyne, HC#C-CH3, plus NaI
mcqs.why: HC#CNa + CH3I → HC#C-CH3 + NaI, converting a lower alkyne into a higher alkyne, as described for dissolving metal reduction.

mcqs.q: Hydrohalogenation of propyne with 2 HBr following Markovnikov's rule gives:
mcqs.why: Propyne + HBr gives 2-bromopropene, then + HBr gives 2,2-dibromopropane: both halogens add to the carbon with fewer hydrogens, a geminal dihalide.

mcqs.q: The reactivity order of HX towards alkynes is:
mcqs.why: The notes give HX reactivity in decreasing order HI, then HBr, then HCl, then HF, for addition to alkynes.

mcqs.q: Hydration of propyne with HgSO4 and H2SO4 gives, after rearrangement:
mcqs.why: Propyne + H2O gives propen-2-ol (an enol) by Markovnikov addition, which rearranges to propanone (acetone), a ketone.

mcqs.q: Hydration of alkynes gives aldehydes or ketones as follows:
options: Acetylene gives an aldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones
Acetylene gives a ketone; others give aldehydes
mcqs.why: Water adds to give unstable enols that rearrange: acetylene gives an aldehyde, while all other alkynes give ketones.

mcqs.q: With excess bromine, propyne forms:
mcqs.why: Propyne + Br2 gives 1,2-dibromopropene, then + Br2 gives 1,1,2,2-tetrabromopropane; excess bromine gives the tetrabromide.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis of alkynes is used to find:
options: The melting point of the alkyne
The position of the triple bond
Whether the alkyne is a gas
mcqs.why: Ozonolysis cleaves the molecule at the triple bond and finally gives carboxylic acids, so it locates the position of the triple bond.

lessons.title: Benzene and Substituted Benzenes
lessons.notes_html:
Michael Faraday, an English scientist, isolated benzene from whale oil in 1825. Twenty years later, in 1845, benzene was found in coal tar by Hoffman.

Benzene is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon (arene). Its formula is C6H6: it consists of a ring of six carbon atoms, with one hydrogen atom bonded to each carbon. It is represented by the Kekulé structure (a hexagon with alternating double bonds) or by a hexagon with a circle inside it. Compounds that contain a benzene ring are called aromatic compounds, because many benzene compounds had fragrant odours.

Types of Substituted Benzene Derivatives

  • Monosubstituted: one hydrogen of benzene is replaced by another atom or group.
  • Disubstituted: two hydrogens are replaced.
  • Polysubstituted: more than two hydrogens are replaced.

Key Points

  • Faraday isolated benzene from whale oil in 1825; it was found in coal tar in 1845.
  • Benzene, C6H6, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon: a six-carbon ring, one H on each carbon.
  • It is drawn as a hexagon with alternating double bonds, or with a circle inside.
  • Derivatives are mono-, di- or polysubstituted, according to how many hydrogens are replaced.

mcqs.q: Who isolated benzene from whale oil, and in which year?
mcqs.why: Michael Faraday, an English scientist, isolated benzene from whale oil in 1825; twenty years later in 1845 it was found in coal tar by Hoffman.

mcqs.q: Benzene was found in coal tar in 1845 by:
mcqs.why: Twenty years after Faraday's 1825 isolation, benzene was found in coal tar by Hoffman in 1845, as recorded in the notes.

mcqs.q: The molecular formula and structure of benzene are:
options: C6H6, a ring of six carbons with no hydrogens
C6H6, a ring of six carbons each with one hydrogen
mcqs.why: Benzene, C6H6, is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon: a ring of six carbon atoms with one hydrogen bonded to each carbon.

mcqs.q: Benzene is represented by a hexagon with alternating double bonds, called the:
mcqs.why: Benzene is represented by the Kekulé structure (hexagon with alternating double bonds) or by a hexagon with a circle inside it.

mcqs.q: Compounds containing a benzene ring are called aromatic because:
options: They all smell sweet in every case
Many benzene compounds had fragrant odours
mcqs.why: They are called aromatic compounds because many benzene compounds had fragrant odours; benzene itself is the simplest arene.

mcqs.q: A monosubstituted benzene derivative has:
options: One hydrogen replaced by another atom or group
mcqs.why: Monosubstituted means one hydrogen of benzene is replaced; disubstituted means two, and polysubstituted means more than two are replaced.

mcqs.q: If three hydrogens of benzene are replaced, the derivative is:
mcqs.why: Polysubstituted derivatives have more than two hydrogens replaced, so replacing three hydrogens gives a polysubstituted benzene.

mcqs.q: Benzene belongs to the family of hydrocarbons called:
mcqs.why: Benzene is the simplest aromatic hydrocarbon, also called an arene, distinct from aliphatic alkanes, alkenes and alkynes.

mcqs.q: The alternative drawing of benzene uses what inside the hexagon?
mcqs.why: Besides the Kekulé form, benzene is drawn as a hexagon with a circle inside it, representing the delocalized pi electrons.

mcqs.q: How many carbon atoms and hydrogen atoms are in one benzene molecule?
mcqs.why: Working: formula C6H6 means 6 carbon atoms and 6 hydrogen atoms, one hydrogen on each ring carbon, as the notes state.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Monosubstituted and Disubstituted Benzene Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
The nomenclature of aromatic hydrocarbons is more complex than that of aliphatic hydrocarbons.

Monosubstituted Benzene Derivatives

  • They are named by placing the name of the substituent in front of the word benzene: chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, ethylbenzene.
  • Some monosubstituted derivatives have common names that are accepted by IUPAC. These names have to be memorized.
SubstituentCommon nameSubstituentCommon name
-CH3Toluene-CHOBenzaldehyde
-OHPhenol-COCH3Acetophenone
-OCH3Anisole-COC6H5Benzophenone
-NH2Aniline-CH=CH2Styrene
-COOHBenzoic acid-CNBenzonitrile
IsopropylCumene-SO3HBenzenesulphonic acid

Disubstituted Benzene Derivatives

  • A disubstituted benzene has three isomers, with substitution at the 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4- positions. They are designated by the prefixes ortho, meta and para: 1,2- is ortho (Greek: correct or straight), 1,3- is meta (Greek: between, in the middle) and 1,4- is para (Greek: beyond). They are abbreviated o-, m- and p-.
  • Relative to one substituent, a benzene ring has two ortho positions, two meta positions and one para position.
  • Positions are shown either by the ortho, meta and para descriptors or by locants (1,2- for ortho). For two identical substituents the prefix di is used. The dimethyl derivatives of benzene are called xylenes: 1,2-dimethylbenzene (o-xylene), 1,3-dimethylbenzene (m-xylene) and 1,4-dimethylbenzene (p-xylene).
  • For two different substituents, position 1 is given to the group of higher priority. The priority order is: -COOH, -CN, -CHO, -COCH3, -OH, -NH2, -OR, -R. Examples: 2-aminobenzaldehyde, 3-hydroxybenzoic acid, 4-methylanisole.
  • If there is no priority order, the substituents are named in alphabetical order, and the last-named substituent is assumed to be at position 1: 2-bromochlorobenzene, 3-fluoronitrobenzene, 4-chloroiodobenzene.
  • If one substituent is part of a common root, the compound is named as a derivative of that monosubstituted benzene: 2-bromophenol, 3-nitroaniline, 4-chlorobenzenesulphonic acid.
  • Some disubstituted derivatives are better known by common names: catechol (1,2-dihydroxybenzene), resorcinol (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) and hydroquinone (1,4-dihydroxybenzene).

Key Points

  • Monosubstituted: substituent name + benzene (chlorobenzene), or an accepted common name (toluene, phenol, aniline).
  • Disubstituted positions: 1,2- = ortho (o-), 1,3- = meta (m-), 1,4- = para (p-).
  • Dimethylbenzenes are the three xylenes.
  • With two different groups, position 1 goes to the higher-priority group: -COOH has the highest priority in the book's list.
  • Without a priority order, name alphabetically with the last-named group at position 1.

mcqs.q: Chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene and ethylbenzene are named by:
options: Placing the substituent name in front of the word benzene
Numbering the ring from 1 to 6 in all cases
mcqs.why: Monosubstituted benzenes are named by placing the substituent name before benzene: chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene, ethylbenzene.

mcqs.q: The common name for benzene with a -CH3 substituent is:
mcqs.why: The table of accepted common names gives -CH3 as toluene, -OH as phenol, -NH2 as aniline and -CH=CH2 as styrene.

mcqs.q: Phenol is benzene carrying which substituent?
mcqs.why: Phenol is the accepted common name for hydroxybenzene, the -OH derivative; -NH2 gives aniline and -COOH gives benzoic acid.

mcqs.q: The three positions for disubstituted benzene are designated ortho, meta and para for:
mcqs.why: 1,2- is ortho (o-), 1,3- is meta (m-) and 1,4- is para (p-); relative to one substituent there are two ortho, two meta and one para position.

mcqs.q: The dimethyl derivatives of benzene are collectively called:
mcqs.why: Dimethylbenzenes are the xylenes: 1,2- is o-xylene, 1,3- is m-xylene and 1,4- is p-xylene, three isomers in total.

mcqs.q: For two different substituents, position 1 is given to the group with:
options: Smallest number of atoms in all cases
mcqs.why: Position 1 goes to the higher-priority group; the priority order begins -COOH, -CN, -CHO, -COCH3, -OH, -NH2, -OR, -R.

mcqs.q: Which group has the highest priority in the book's list?
mcqs.why: The priority order listed is -COOH, -CN, -CHO, -COCH3, -OH, -NH2, -OR, -R, so -COOH is highest and takes position 1.

mcqs.q: Catechol, resorcinol and hydroquinone are respectively:
mcqs.why: Catechol is 1,2-dihydroxybenzene, resorcinol is 1,3-dihydroxybenzene and hydroquinone is 1,4-dihydroxybenzene, common names given in the notes.

mcqs.q: 2-bromophenol and 3-nitroaniline are named as derivatives of a common root because:
options: One substituent is part of a common root (phenol, aniline)
mcqs.why: If one substituent is part of a common root, the compound is named as a derivative of that monosubstituted benzene, e.g. 2-bromophenol, 3-nitroaniline.

mcqs.q: The substituent -OCH3 on benzene gives the common name:
mcqs.why: The table gives -OCH3 as anisole, -COCH3 as acetophenone, -CN as benzonitrile and isopropyl as cumene.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Polysubstituted Benzene Derivatives
lessons.notes_html:
Rules

  • Identical substituents: when the ring has more than two identical substituents, use the prefix tri for three, tetra for four, penta for five and hexa for six, and assign the lowest possible numbers: 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene; 1,3,5-tribromobenzene; 1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene.
  • Different substituents: when the ring has more than two different substituents, name them in alphabetical order; the last-named substituent is assumed to be at position 1: 4-bromo-3-chloroiodobenzene; 3-bromo-5-fluoronitrobenzene; 2,4-dichloro-5-iodonitrobenzene.
  • Common roots: if the substituents are part of common roots, name the compound as a derivative of that monosubstituted benzene, and the substituent that includes the common root is placed at position 1: 2,4,6-trinitrophenol; 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene; 2,4,6-triiodophenol.
  • Some polysubstituted derivatives are better known by common names: phloroglucinol (1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene), mesitylene (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene), durene (1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene), picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) and TNT (2,4,6-trinitrotoluene).

Key Points

  • More than two identical groups: tri, tetra, penta, hexa, with the lowest locants.
  • More than two different groups: alphabetical order, last-named group at position 1.
  • With a common root (phenol, toluene), the compound is named as its derivative.
  • Picric acid = 2,4,6-trinitrophenol; TNT = 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene.

mcqs.q: For more than two identical substituents on benzene, the prefixes used are:
options: Tri, tetra, penta and hexa for 3, 4, 5 and 6
mcqs.why: Identical polysubstituents use tri for three, tetra for four, penta for five and hexa for six, with the lowest possible numbers assigned.

mcqs.q: 1,3,5-tribromobenzene illustrates which rule?
options: Lowest possible locants for identical substituents
mcqs.why: With three identical bromo groups, locants 1,3,5 are the lowest possible set, as also in 1,2,4-trichlorobenzene given in the notes.

mcqs.q: When a ring has more than two different substituents, they are named:
options: In alphabetical order, with the last-named substituent at position 1
mcqs.why: Different substituents are named alphabetically and the last-named substituent is assumed to be at position 1, e.g. 4-bromo-3-chloroiodobenzene.

mcqs.q: If substituents are part of common roots, the compound is named:
options: With the root at the highest locant
As a derivative of that monosubstituted benzene, root substituent at position 1
mcqs.why: With common roots the name is a derivative of the monosubstituted benzene and the root substituent is placed at position 1, e.g. 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.

mcqs.q: Picric acid is the common name for:
mcqs.why: Picric acid is 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, while TNT is 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene and phloroglucinol is 1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene.

mcqs.q: TNT stands for the compound:
mcqs.why: TNT is 2,4,6-trinitrotoluene: a toluene ring carrying three nitro groups at positions 2, 4 and 6, a polysubstituted benzene.

mcqs.q: Mesitylene and durene are respectively:
mcqs.why: Mesitylene is 1,3,5-trimethylbenzene and durene is 1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene, common names listed for polysubstituted benzenes.

mcqs.q: Phloroglucinol is:
mcqs.why: Phloroglucinol is the common name for 1,3,5-trihydroxybenzene, with three -OH groups at the 1, 3 and 5 positions.

mcqs.q: 2,4-dichloro-5-iodonitrobenzene shows naming of different substituents in:
mcqs.why: The substituents chloro, iodo and nitro are listed alphabetically, with the last-named (nitro) group taken at position 1 in this name.

mcqs.q: 1,2,4,5-tetramethylbenzene has how many methyl substituents?
mcqs.why: Working: the prefix tetra means four substituents; locants 1,2,4,5 list four positions, so the ring carries four methyl groups (durene).

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
• Benzene is a colourless liquid with a peculiar smell.
  • It has a burning taste.
  • Its melting point is 5.5°C and its boiling point is 80.1°C.
  • It is insoluble in water.
  • It is highly inflammable and burns with a luminous and smoky flame.
  • It is miscible with alcohol and ether in all proportions.
  • Its specific gravity is 0.884 g/cm3 at 15°C.
  • It is a good solvent for many organic and inorganic substances, such as fats, resins, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.
  • Its vapours are highly toxic: on inhalation they produce loss of consciousness, and in the long run they destroy the red and white blood cells.

Key Points

  • Benzene is a colourless liquid, melting point 5.5°C, boiling point 80.1°C.
  • It is insoluble in water but miscible with alcohol and ether.
  • It burns with a luminous, smoky flame and is highly inflammable.
  • Specific gravity 0.884 g/cm3 at 15°C; a good solvent for fats, resins, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine.
  • Benzene vapours are highly toxic and damage blood cells.

mcqs.q: Benzene at room conditions is described as:
options: A colourless liquid with a peculiar smell
A colourless gas with no smell
A white solid with a sweet taste
A blue liquid insoluble in ether
mcqs.why: Benzene is a colourless liquid with a peculiar smell and a burning taste; it is insoluble in water but miscible with alcohol and ether.

mcqs.q: The melting point and boiling point of benzene are:
mcqs.why: The notes give benzene melting point 5.5°C and boiling point 80.1°C, values that identify it as a liquid over the usual room range.

mcqs.q: Benzene burns with a flame that is:
options: Blue and soot-free in all cases
mcqs.why: Benzene is highly inflammable and burns with a luminous and smoky flame, reflecting its high carbon content as an aromatic hydrocarbon.

mcqs.q: The specific gravity of benzene at 15°C is:
mcqs.why: Benzene has specific gravity 0.884 g/cm3 at 15°C, so it is lighter than water, in which it is insoluble.

mcqs.q: Benzene is a good solvent for substances such as:
options: Fats, resins, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine
mcqs.why: Benzene dissolves many organic and inorganic substances such as fats, resins, sulphur, phosphorus and iodine, making it a useful solvent.

mcqs.q: Benzene is miscible with which liquids in all proportions?
mcqs.why: Benzene is insoluble in water but miscible with alcohol and ether in all proportions, consistent with its non-polar character.

mcqs.q: Benzene vapours are dangerous because they are:
options: Highly toxic, causing loss of consciousness and destroying blood cells
mcqs.why: Benzene vapours are highly toxic: inhalation produces loss of consciousness and in the long run destroys red and white blood cells.

mcqs.q: Benzene's taste is described in the notes as:
mcqs.why: Along with its peculiar smell, benzene has a burning taste; it should never actually be tasted because its vapours and liquid are toxic.

mcqs.q: Compared with water, a separate benzene layer would be expected to:
options: Float because its specific gravity is 0.884, less than 1
mcqs.why: Working: specific gravity 0.884 < 1.000 for water, so benzene is less dense than water and, being insoluble, forms a layer that floats.

mcqs.q: Which property makes benzene hazardous to handle near flames?
mcqs.why: Benzene is highly inflammable and burns with a luminous smoky flame, so it is a fire hazard as well as a toxic substance.

lessons.title: Structure of Benzene (Molecular Orbital Aspects)
lessons.notes_html:
The hexagonal planar structure of benzene is best explained by molecular orbital theory.

The Sigma Framework

  • Each carbon in benzene has three sp2 hybrid orbitals, which are half filled and are used in bond formation.
  • Two sp2 orbitals of each carbon form sigma bonds with the adjacent carbon atoms (sp2-sp2 overlapping), and the third sp2 orbital forms a sigma bond with a hydrogen atom (sp2-s overlapping).
  • All the sigma bonds lie in the same plane and all bond angles are 120°, which confirms the regular hexagonal structure of benzene.

The Pi System

  • Each carbon also has one pure p-orbital with an unpaired electron, so there are six p-orbitals in all. They stand perpendicular to the plane of the sigma bonds.
  • The six pure p-orbitals form pi-molecular orbitals. One half of this pi molecular orbital lies above the plane of the sigma bonds and the other half lies below it.
  • The six electrons of the p-orbitals cover all six carbon atoms; they are said to be delocalized.
  • Delocalization forms stronger pi bonds and a more stable molecule. It makes benzene less reactive, so benzene undergoes substitution reactions rather than addition.
  • Because of delocalization, all the bond lengths in benzene are equal. The delocalization of the six pi electrons is shown by a circle in the ring.

Key Points

  • Each benzene carbon is sp2 hybridized; the sigma framework is planar with 120° angles.
  • Six p-orbitals, one on each carbon, stand perpendicular to the ring plane.
  • They form pi-molecular orbitals above and below the plane, holding six delocalized electrons.
  • Delocalization gives equal bond lengths, extra stability and low reactivity.
  • Benzene therefore prefers substitution over addition.

mcqs.q: In benzene, each carbon atom is hybridized as:
mcqs.why: Each benzene carbon has three sp2 hybrid orbitals used in sigma bonds, plus one pure p-orbital for the pi system.

mcqs.q: The sigma framework of benzene uses sp2 orbitals to form bonds with:
options: Two adjacent carbons and one hydrogen atom
mcqs.why: Two sp2 orbitals of each carbon form sigma bonds with adjacent carbons (sp2-sp2) and the third forms a sigma bond with hydrogen (sp2-s).

mcqs.q: All sigma bonds in benzene lie in one plane with bond angles of:
mcqs.why: All sigma bonds are in the same plane and all bond angles are 120 degrees, confirming the regular hexagonal planar structure of benzene.

mcqs.q: How many pure p-orbitals are there in total in benzene?
mcqs.why: Each of the six carbons has one pure p-orbital with an unpaired electron, so there are six p-orbitals standing perpendicular to the ring plane.

mcqs.q: The pi molecular orbitals in benzene lie:
options: Half above and half below the plane of the sigma bonds
mcqs.why: The six p-orbitals form pi-molecular orbitals, one half above the plane of the sigma bonds and the other half below that plane.

mcqs.q: The six pi electrons in benzene are said to be:
options: Delocalized over all six carbon atoms
mcqs.why: The six p-orbital electrons cover all six carbons and are delocalized, which forms stronger pi bonds and a more stable molecule.

mcqs.q: Because of delocalization, all bond lengths in benzene are:
options: The same as in ethane only
mcqs.why: Delocalization makes all bond lengths in benzene equal, which is shown by drawing a circle inside the hexagonal ring.

mcqs.q: Delocalization makes benzene prefer which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: Delocalization gives extra stability and low reactivity, so benzene undergoes substitution reactions rather than addition reactions.

mcqs.q: The molecular orbital explanation is used for which structure of benzene?
mcqs.why: The hexagonal planar structure of benzene is best explained by molecular orbital theory, with its planar sigma framework and pi system.

mcqs.q: The delocalization of the six pi electrons is represented in diagrams by:
mcqs.why: A circle drawn inside the hexagon represents the delocalized six pi electrons spread over all six carbon atoms of benzene.

lessons.title: Resonance, Resonance Energy and Stabilization
lessons.notes_html:
Resonance

  • Resonance is another term used for delocalization. The process in which two or more structures are written for a compound, differing only in the arrangement of electrons, is called resonance.
  • The different structures are called resonance structures, also known as canonical structures or contributing structures.
  • No single structure alone can explain the characteristics of such a molecule. The actual structure is a hybrid of all the resonance structures.
  • Resonance structures are hypothetical; they cannot be isolated. In writing them, we are allowed to move electrons, not atoms. Resonance is shown by a double-headed arrow (↔) between the structures.
  • For benzene, the two major contributing structures are the two Kekulé forms. Each carbon-carbon bond is single in one structure and double in the other, so the actual bond length, 139 pm, is intermediate between a carbon-carbon single bond (153 pm) and a carbon-carbon double bond (134 pm). The three alternate single and double bonds are called conjugate bonds or resonating bonds.
  • The resonance hybrid (drawn with a circle in the hexagon) is more stable than either structure, because in a single canonical form the pi-electrons are localized, while in the hybrid they are delocalized over the six atoms of the ring.

Resonance Energy and Stability of Benzene

  • The difference between the energy of the actual molecule (the resonance hybrid) and the energy of the most stable resonance structure is called resonance energy. It is also known as delocalization energy.
  • Resonance energy explains the unusual stability of benzene and its lack of reactivity towards addition. It is found from the difference between the calculated and experimental heats of hydrogenation.
  • The heat of hydrogenation of cyclohexene (one double bond) is -120 kJ/mol.
  • For 1,3-cyclohexadiene (two double bonds) the expected value is 2 × -120 = -240 kJ/mol; the observed value is -232 kJ/mol, slightly smaller because a conjugated diene is more stable than two isolated double bonds.
  • For benzene, treated as 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene (three double bonds), the expected value is 3 × -120 = -360 kJ/mol, but the observed value is only -208 kJ/mol.
  • The observed value is 152 kJ/mol less than expected. This difference is the resonance energy of benzene: benzene is resonance stabilized by 152 kJ/mol, which makes it more stable than the other unsaturated hydrocarbons.

Key Formulae

QuantityValue
Heat of hydrogenation, cyclohexene-120 kJ/mol
Expected for benzene (3 × -120)-360 kJ/mol
Observed for benzene-208 kJ/mol
Resonance energy of benzene360 - 208 = 152 kJ/mol
C-C bond length in benzene139 pm (single 153 pm, double 134 pm)

Key Points

  • Resonance structures differ only in electron arrangement; the real molecule is their hybrid.
  • Resonance is shown by a double-headed arrow; structures cannot be isolated.
  • All C-C bonds in benzene are equal at 139 pm, between single and double bond lengths.
  • Resonance energy = energy of most stable structure minus energy of the hybrid.
  • Benzene's resonance energy is 152 kJ/mol, from heats of hydrogenation.

mcqs.q: Resonance structures of a compound differ only in:
mcqs.why: Resonance structures differ only in electron arrangement; atoms are not moved, and the actual structure is a hybrid of all of them.

mcqs.q: Resonance is shown between structures by which symbol?
mcqs.why: Resonance is shown by a double-headed arrow between the structures; the structures are hypothetical and cannot be isolated.

mcqs.q: For benzene, the two major contributing structures are:
mcqs.why: Benzene's two major resonance structures are the two Kekulé forms, each bond being single in one and double in the other.

mcqs.q: The actual C-C bond length in benzene, 139 pm, is intermediate between:
mcqs.why: Each C-C bond is single in one Kekulé form and double in the other, so the actual length 139 pm lies between single 153 pm and double 134 pm.

mcqs.q: Resonance energy is defined as the difference between:
options: The energy of the actual hybrid and the energy of the most stable resonance structure
Heats of combustion of two alkanes
Bond lengths of single and double bonds
mcqs.why: Resonance energy (delocalization energy) is the energy difference between the resonance hybrid and the most stable resonance structure.

mcqs.q: The heat of hydrogenation of cyclohexene (one double bond) is:
mcqs.why: Cyclohexene with one double bond has heat of hydrogenation -120 kJ/mol, the basis for calculating expected values for dienes and benzene.

mcqs.q: The expected heat of hydrogenation for benzene as three double bonds is:
mcqs.why: Working: 3 double bonds x -120 kJ/mol per bond = -360 kJ/mol expected for 1,3,5-cyclohexatriene, but the observed value is only -208 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: The resonance energy of benzene, from observed -208 and expected -360 kJ/mol, is:
mcqs.why: Working: resonance energy = 360 - 208 = 152 kJ/mol. Benzene releases 152 kJ/mol less than expected, so it is stabilized by 152 kJ/mol.

mcqs.q: For 1,3-cyclohexadiene the observed heat of hydrogenation -232 kJ/mol versus expected -240 kJ/mol shows:
options: A conjugated diene is slightly more stable than two isolated double bonds
It is less stable than expected
mcqs.why: Working: expected 2 x -120 = -240 kJ/mol; observed -232 is 8 kJ/mol smaller in magnitude, because a conjugated diene is more stable than two isolated bonds.

mcqs.q: Resonance structures are described as hypothetical because they:
options: Cannot be isolated; only the hybrid exists
Are the same as isomers that can be bottled
mcqs.why: Resonance (canonical) structures are hypothetical and cannot be isolated; the real molecule is the resonance hybrid with delocalized electrons.

lessons.title: Reactivity and Reactions of Benzene: Addition Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Reactivity of Benzene

Benzene is highly unsaturated and has six pi-electrons delocalized in six p-orbitals, yet it does not undergo addition reactions as readily as other unsaturated hydrocarbons such as alkenes and alkynes. In alkenes and alkynes the pi-electrons are localized and easily available for addition reactions; in benzene they are delocalized and not easily available. Benzene is therefore less reactive than alkenes and alkynes towards electrophilic addition. The most common reactions of benzene are electrophilic substitution reactions. Benzene does undergo two addition reactions.

Addition of Hydrogen (Catalytic Hydrogenation)

Benzene reacts with hydrogen in the presence of a catalyst such as Pt, Pd or Ni at high temperature and pressure to produce cyclohexane: C6H6 + 3H2 →(Ni, 200°C, 25 atm) cyclohexane.

Addition of Halogens

Benzene reacts with Cl2 (or Br2) in the presence of sunlight to form benzene hexachloride, which is used as an insecticide: C6H6 + 3Cl2 →(Sunlight) C6H6Cl6. The reaction of F2 with benzene is vigorous, and the reaction of I2 with benzene is very slow. These addition reactions indicate that benzene is unsaturated and contains three double bonds.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
HydrogenationC6H6 + 3H2 →(Ni, 200°C, 25 atm) cyclohexane
Chlorine additionC6H6 + 3Cl2 →(Sunlight) benzene hexachloride, C6H6Cl6

Key Points

  • Delocalized pi-electrons make benzene less reactive towards addition than alkenes and alkynes.
  • Benzene's common reactions are electrophilic substitutions, not additions.
  • Hydrogenation (Ni, 200°C, 25 atm) gives cyclohexane.
  • Chlorine adds in sunlight to give benzene hexachloride, an insecticide.
  • Addition reactions show that benzene is unsaturated, with three double bonds.

mcqs.q: Why does benzene not undergo addition as readily as alkenes and alkynes?
options: Its pi electrons are delocalized and not easily available
Its pi electrons are localized and exposed
mcqs.why: In alkenes and alkynes pi electrons are localized and available for addition; in benzene they are delocalized, so benzene is less reactive towards electrophilic addition.

mcqs.q: The most common reactions of benzene are:
mcqs.why: Benzene's most common reactions are electrophilic substitutions, preserving the aromatic ring, though it does undergo two addition reactions.

mcqs.q: Catalytic hydrogenation of benzene with Ni at 200°C and 25 atm gives:
mcqs.why: C6H6 + 3H2 with Ni at 200°C and 25 atm produces cyclohexane, fully saturating the ring in an addition reaction.

mcqs.q: How many moles of H2 add to one mole of benzene in its hydrogenation?
mcqs.why: Working: equation C6H6 + 3H2 → cyclohexane shows 3 moles of H2 per mole of benzene, one for each of the three double bonds.

mcqs.q: Benzene reacts with Cl2 in sunlight to form:
mcqs.why: C6H6 + 3Cl2 in sunlight gives benzene hexachloride C6H6Cl6, an addition product used as an insecticide.

mcqs.q: Benzene hexachloride is used as:
mcqs.why: Benzene hexachloride, formed by chlorine addition to benzene in sunlight, is used as an insecticide, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: The addition reactions of benzene indicate that benzene is:
options: Unsaturated and contains three double bonds
mcqs.why: Hydrogenation and halogen addition show benzene is unsaturated and contains three double bonds, even though it resists addition.

mcqs.q: The reaction of fluorine with benzene is described as vigorous, while iodine's reaction is:
options: Instant and explosive in all cases
Not a reaction at all with any halogen
mcqs.why: The notes contrast halogens: F2 reacts vigorously with benzene and I2 reacts very slowly, in the addition reactions section.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst and conditions are given for benzene hydrogenation?
mcqs.why: Benzene hydrogenation uses a catalyst such as Pt, Pd or Ni at high temperature and pressure; the equation specifies Ni, 200°C, 25 atm.

mcqs.q: How many moles of Cl2 add to one mole of benzene to give C6H6Cl6?
mcqs.why: Working: C6H6 + 3Cl2 → C6H6Cl6; 3 moles of Cl2 supply 6 chlorine atoms, matching the six Cl atoms in the product formula.

lessons.title: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
The most important reactions of benzene are electrophilic substitution reactions. In these reactions, one hydrogen atom (proton) of the benzene ring is replaced by an electrophile. They are carried out in the presence of a Lewis acid catalyst such as FeX3 or AlX3, which helps in the generation of the electrophile. The electrophile is either a positive ion or the slightly positive end of a polar molecule.

General Mechanism

  • Step 1: Formation of the arenium ion. The electrophile attacks the pi-electrons of the benzene ring and forms a sigma bond with one carbon atom. This generates a positively charged intermediate (a cyclohexadienyl carbocation) called the arenium ion or sigma complex. The sigma complex is not aromatic, because the carbon that bonds to the electrophile becomes sp3 hybridized and has no p-orbital; only five carbons remain sp2 with p-orbitals, so there is no continuous system of overlapping p-orbitals. The positive charge is distributed over three carbon atoms by resonance, which makes the ion partially stable.
  • Step 2: Regeneration of catalyst and formation of product. The sigma complex is highly reactive and loses its proton from the sp3 carbon to a Lewis base. The electrons that held the proton move into the ring and restore its aromaticity. The proton is always removed from the carbon that formed the new bond with the electrophile.
  • Step 1 is the rate determining step and is relatively slow, because an aromatic compound is being converted into a much less stable non-aromatic intermediate. Step 2 is fast, because the aromaticity of the ring is restored.

The five most useful electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions are nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and Friedel-Crafts acylation.

Key Points

  • In electrophilic substitution, a ring hydrogen is replaced by an electrophile; the aromatic ring survives.
  • Lewis acid catalysts (FeX3, AlX3) generate the electrophile.
  • Step 1 forms the arenium ion (sigma complex): slow and rate determining; aromaticity is lost.
  • Step 2 removes the proton and restores aromaticity: fast.
  • The five key reactions: nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation.

mcqs.q: In electrophilic aromatic substitution, a ring hydrogen is replaced by:
mcqs.why: One hydrogen atom of the benzene ring is replaced by an electrophile, which is a positive ion or the slightly positive end of a polar molecule.

mcqs.q: Lewis acid catalysts such as FeX3 or AlX3 are used in these reactions to:
mcqs.why: Electrophilic substitutions are carried out with Lewis acid catalysts like FeX3 or AlX3, which help in generating the electrophile.

mcqs.q: The positively charged intermediate formed in step 1 is called:
mcqs.why: Step 1 forms the arenium ion or sigma complex, a cyclohexadienyl carbocation whose charge is distributed over three carbons by resonance.

mcqs.q: Why is the sigma complex not aromatic?
options: The carbon bonded to the electrophile becomes sp3 with no p-orbital, breaking the continuous p-orbital system
mcqs.why: The attacked carbon becomes sp3 and has no p-orbital; only five carbons remain sp2, so there is no continuous overlapping p-orbital system.

mcqs.q: Which step of electrophilic substitution is slow and rate determining?
options: Step 1, formation of the arenium ion
mcqs.why: Step 1 is slow and rate determining because an aromatic compound is converted into a much less stable non-aromatic intermediate.

mcqs.q: Step 2 is fast because it:
options: Restores the aromaticity of the ring
mcqs.why: In step 2 the sigma complex loses its proton from the sp3 carbon, the electrons move into the ring and aromaticity is restored, so it is fast.

mcqs.q: The proton removed in step 2 always comes from:
options: A carbon far from the attack site
The carbon that formed the new bond with the electrophile
mcqs.why: The proton is always removed from the carbon that formed the new bond with the electrophile, by a Lewis base in step 2.

mcqs.q: How many key electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions are listed as most useful?
mcqs.why: The five most useful reactions are nitration, sulphonation, halogenation, Friedel-Crafts alkylation and Friedel-Crafts acylation.

mcqs.q: The positive charge of the arenium ion is distributed over how many carbon atoms by resonance?
options: All six equally in a ring current
mcqs.why: The positive charge is distributed over three carbon atoms by resonance, which makes the arenium ion partially stable.

mcqs.q: An electrophile in these reactions may be:
options: A positive ion or the slightly positive end of a polar molecule
mcqs.why: The notes define the electrophile as either a positive ion or the slightly positive (delta positive) end of a polar molecule.

lessons.title: Nitration and Sulphonation of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
Nitration

  • The replacement of a hydrogen of an organic compound by a nitro group is called nitration.
  • Benzene reacts with a mixture of conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 at 50-55°C to produce nitrobenzene: C6H6 + HONO2 →(Conc. H2SO4, 50-55°C) C6H5NO2 + H2O.
  • Conc. H2SO4 acts as a catalyst and increases the rate by increasing the concentration of the electrophile, NO2+ (the nitronium ion).
  • Mechanism: the NO2+ electrophile is produced by an acid-base reaction between HNO3 and H2SO4. Step 1: nitric acid acts as a base and accepts a proton from the stronger sulphuric acid, forming protonated nitric acid. Step 2: protonated nitric acid dissociates to form the nitronium ion and water. Step 3: the electrophile attacks the benzene ring to form the arenium ion (slow). Step 4: the arenium ion loses a proton to a Lewis base, producing nitrobenzene (fast).

Sulphonation

  • The replacement of a hydrogen of an organic compound by a sulphonic acid (-SO3H) group is called sulphonation.
  • Benzene reacts with fuming sulphuric acid (H2SO4 + SO3) at room temperature to give benzenesulphonic acid: C6H6 + SO3 →(Conc. H2SO4, 25°C) C6H5SO3H.
  • Mechanism: Step 1: sulphuric acid ionizes in water to produce hydrogen sulphate and hydronium ions: H2SO4 + H2O → HSO4- + H3O+. Step 2: the electrophile (SO3) attacks the benzene ring to form the arenium ion (slow). Step 3: a Lewis base removes the proton from the arenium ion to produce the benzenesulphonate ion (fast). Step 4: the benzenesulphonate ion accepts a proton from a hydronium ion to produce benzenesulphonic acid (fast).

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation and electrophile
NitrationC6H6 + HNO3 →(Conc. H2SO4, 50-55°C) C6H5NO2 + H2O; electrophile NO2+
SulphonationC6H6 + SO3 →(Fuming H2SO4, 25°C) C6H5SO3H; electrophile SO3

Key Points

  • Nitration: conc. HNO3 + conc. H2SO4 at 50-55°C gives nitrobenzene; electrophile is NO2+.
  • H2SO4 in nitration raises the concentration of the nitronium ion.
  • Sulphonation: fuming sulphuric acid at room temperature gives benzenesulphonic acid; electrophile is SO3.
  • Both mechanisms pass through the arenium ion: attack (slow), then loss of proton (fast).

mcqs.q: Nitration of benzene uses which reagents and temperature?
options: Conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 at 50-55°C
mcqs.why: Benzene with conc. HNO3 and conc. H2SO4 at 50-55°C gives nitrobenzene: C6H6 + HONO2 → C6H5NO2 + H2O.

mcqs.q: The electrophile in nitration of benzene is:
mcqs.why: Conc. H2SO4 increases the concentration of the electrophile NO2+, the nitronium ion, formed from protonated nitric acid dissociating.

mcqs.q: In nitration, conc. H2SO4 acts to:
options: Increase the rate by increasing the concentration of NO2+
mcqs.why: Sulphuric acid is the stronger acid: nitric acid accepts a proton from it, then loses water to give NO2+, so the electrophile concentration rises.

mcqs.q: Sulphonation of benzene uses fuming sulphuric acid at room temperature to give:
mcqs.why: C6H6 + SO3 with conc. H2SO4 at 25°C gives benzenesulphonic acid C6H5SO3H, replacing a hydrogen by the -SO3H group.

mcqs.q: The electrophile in sulphonation of benzene is:
mcqs.why: In sulphonation the electrophile SO3 attacks the ring to form the arenium ion (slow step), followed by fast proton removal.

mcqs.q: Fuming sulphuric acid is described as:
mcqs.why: Fuming sulphuric acid is H2SO4 + SO3; the SO3 it contains is the electrophile that attacks benzene in sulphonation.

mcqs.q: In the nitration mechanism, nitric acid in step 1 acts as:
options: A stronger acid than sulphuric acid
A base, accepting a proton from sulphuric acid
mcqs.why: Step 1: nitric acid acts as a base and accepts a proton from the stronger sulphuric acid, forming protonated nitric acid.

mcqs.q: Both nitration and sulphonation mechanisms pass through which intermediate?
mcqs.why: Both pass through the arenium ion: electrophile attack is slow, then loss of a proton is fast, restoring aromaticity.

mcqs.q: Sulphonation replaces a ring hydrogen with which group?
mcqs.why: Sulphonation is replacement of hydrogen by a sulphonic acid group -SO3H; nitration replaces it by a nitro group -NO2.

mcqs.q: The final step of sulphonation mechanism produces benzenesulphonic acid when the benzenesulphonate ion:
options: Accepts a proton from a hydronium ion
mcqs.why: Step 4: the benzenesulphonate ion accepts a proton from a hydronium ion (fast) to produce benzenesulphonic acid.

lessons.title: Halogenation and Friedel-Crafts Alkylation of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
Halogenation

  • The replacement of a hydrogen of an organic compound by a halogen is called halogenation.
  • Benzene reacts with halogens (Cl2 or Br2) in the presence of Lewis acids such as ferric chloride or ferric bromide to produce a halobenzene: C6H6 + Cl2 →(FeCl3, 25°C) chlorobenzene + HCl; C6H6 + Br2 →(FeBr3, Heat) bromobenzene + HBr.
  • The reactions of iodine and fluorine are not synthetically useful, because iodine reacts too slowly and fluorine too fast.
  • Mechanism (chlorination): Step 1: chlorine reacts with FeCl3 to produce a Lewis acid-base complex (the electrophile); the complex has a weak, polar Cl-Cl bond and acts as a source of the chloronium ion (Cl+). Step 2: the benzene ring donates an electron pair to the terminal chlorine, forming a new carbon-chlorine sigma bond and the arenium ion, along with the base FeCl4- (slow). Step 3: the base FeCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion to form chlorobenzene and regenerate the catalyst (fast).

Friedel-Crafts Alkylation

  • Charles Friedel, a French chemist, and James Crafts, an American chemist, discovered new methods for the preparation of alkylbenzenes and acylbenzenes in 1877; these are the Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation reactions.
  • The replacement of a hydrogen of benzene by an alkyl group (-R) is called alkylation. Benzene reacts with an alkyl halide in the presence of a Lewis acid such as aluminium chloride to produce an alkylbenzene: C6H6 + R-Cl →(AlCl3) C6H5-R + HCl.
  • Mechanism: Step 1: the Lewis acid AlCl3 reacts with the alkyl chloride to produce a Lewis acid-base complex, which serves as a source of the electrophile. Step 2: the benzene ring donates an electron pair to the alkyl group, forming the arenium ion and the base AlCl4- (slow). Step 3: the base AlCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion to form the alkylbenzene and regenerate the catalyst (fast).

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
ChlorinationC6H6 + Cl2 →(FeCl3, 25°C) C6H5Cl + HCl
BrominationC6H6 + Br2 →(FeBr3, Heat) C6H5Br + HBr
Friedel-Crafts alkylationC6H6 + R-Cl →(AlCl3) C6H5-R + HCl

Key Points

  • Halogenation needs a Lewis acid (FeCl3 or FeBr3); iodine is too slow and fluorine too fast to be useful.
  • In chlorination, the FeCl3 complex supplies the Cl+ electrophile.
  • Friedel-Crafts alkylation (1877) puts an alkyl group on the ring using R-Cl and AlCl3.
  • Both mechanisms follow the same pattern: complex formation, arenium ion (slow), proton removal (fast).

mcqs.q: Halogenation of benzene with Cl2 needs which catalyst and gives chlorobenzene at 25°C?
mcqs.why: C6H6 + Cl2 with FeCl3 at 25°C gives chlorobenzene + HCl; bromination uses FeBr3 with heat to give bromobenzene.

mcqs.q: Why are iodine and fluorine not synthetically useful for benzene halogenation?
options: Both react at a perfect rate
Iodine reacts too slowly and fluorine too fast
They give no product at all
mcqs.why: Iodine is too slow and fluorine too fast, so only chlorine and bromine with Lewis acid catalysts are useful for halobenzenes.

mcqs.q: In chlorination mechanism step 1, chlorine reacts with FeCl3 to produce:
options: A Lewis acid-base complex acting as a source of Cl+
mcqs.why: Cl2 + FeCl3 forms a complex with a weak polar Cl-Cl bond that acts as a source of the chloronium ion Cl+, the electrophile.

mcqs.q: In step 3 of benzene chlorination, the base FeCl4- does what?
options: Removes the proton from the arenium ion, forming chlorobenzene and regenerating the catalyst
mcqs.why: FeCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion (fast step), forming chlorobenzene and regenerating FeCl3 catalyst.

mcqs.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation were discovered in 1877 by:
mcqs.why: Charles Friedel (French) and James Crafts (American) discovered these methods in 1877 for preparing alkylbenzenes and acylbenzenes.

mcqs.q: Friedel-Crafts alkylation replaces a benzene hydrogen with:
mcqs.why: Alkylation puts an alkyl group -R on the ring: C6H6 + R-Cl with AlCl3 gives C6H5-R + HCl, an alkylbenzene.

mcqs.q: The Lewis acid used in Friedel-Crafts alkylation with R-Cl is:
mcqs.why: Benzene reacts with an alkyl halide in the presence of aluminium chloride AlCl3 to produce an alkylbenzene plus HCl.

mcqs.q: In alkylation mechanism step 2, formation of the arenium ion is:
mcqs.why: Step 2, where the ring donates an electron pair to the alkyl group forming the arenium ion and AlCl4-, is the slow step.

mcqs.q: Bromination of benzene gives bromobenzene using:
options: Br2 in CCl4 in the dark only
mcqs.why: C6H6 + Br2 with FeBr3 and heat gives bromobenzene + HBr, a substitution, unlike alkene bromination in CCl4 in the dark.

mcqs.q: The general mechanism pattern for both halogenation and alkylation is:
options: Complex formation, arenium ion (slow), proton removal (fast)
mcqs.why: Both follow: Lewis acid-base complex formation, arenium ion formation (slow), then proton removal by the base (fast), regenerating catalyst.

lessons.title: Friedel-Crafts Acylation of Benzene
lessons.notes_html:
• The replacement of a hydrogen of benzene by an acyl group (-COR) is called acylation.
  • Benzene reacts with acyl halides (also called acid halides) or with an acid anhydride, in the presence of a Lewis acid, to produce an acylbenzene: C6H6 + R-COCl →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + HCl; and C6H6 + (RCO)2O →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + R-COOH.
  • Mechanism: Step 1: the Lewis acid AlCl3 reacts with the acyl chloride to produce a Lewis acid-base complex, which serves as a source of the electrophile. Step 2: the benzene ring donates an electron pair to the carbon of the carbonyl group of the complex, forming the arenium ion and the base AlCl4- (slow). Step 3: the base AlCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion to form the acylbenzene and regenerate the catalyst (fast).

Key Reactions

ReagentEquation
Acyl chlorideC6H6 + R-COCl →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + HCl
Acid anhydrideC6H6 + (RCO)2O →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + R-COOH

Key Points

  • Acylation replaces a ring hydrogen with an acyl group (-COR).
  • Reagents: an acyl halide or an acid anhydride, with AlCl3 as Lewis acid.
  • The product is an acylbenzene (an aromatic ketone).
  • Mechanism: complex formation, arenium ion (slow), proton removal by AlCl4- (fast).

mcqs.q: Acylation of benzene replaces a ring hydrogen with which group?
mcqs.why: Acylation is replacement of a benzene hydrogen by an acyl group -COR, giving an acylbenzene (an aromatic ketone).

mcqs.q: The reagents for Friedel-Crafts acylation are an acyl halide or acid anhydride with:
mcqs.why: Benzene reacts with acyl halides or an acid anhydride in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl3 to produce an acylbenzene.

mcqs.q: Benzene + R-COCl with AlCl3 gives:
mcqs.why: C6H6 + R-COCl →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + HCl: the acyl chloride supplies the -COR group that replaces a ring hydrogen.

mcqs.q: Benzene + acid anhydride (RCO)2O with AlCl3 gives, besides the acylbenzene:
mcqs.why: C6H6 + (RCO)2O →(AlCl3) C6H5-COR + R-COOH, so the anhydride route produces a carboxylic acid as the second product.

mcqs.q: The product of Friedel-Crafts acylation is best described as:
mcqs.why: The product is an acylbenzene (an aromatic ketone), because the -COR group contains a carbonyl attached to the ring.

mcqs.q: In acylation mechanism step 1, AlCl3 reacts with the acyl chloride to produce:
options: A Lewis acid-base complex that serves as a source of the electrophile
mcqs.why: Step 1 forms a Lewis acid-base complex from AlCl3 and the acyl chloride, which serves as the source of the electrophile.

mcqs.q: In step 2 of acylation, the benzene ring donates an electron pair to:
options: The chlorine atom of the complex
The carbon of the carbonyl group of the complex
mcqs.why: The ring donates an electron pair to the carbonyl carbon of the complex, forming the arenium ion and AlCl4- in the slow step.

mcqs.q: Step 3 of acylation is fast because AlCl4- removes the proton and:
options: Regenerates the catalyst and forms the acylbenzene
mcqs.why: AlCl4- removes the proton from the arenium ion (fast), forming the acylbenzene and regenerating the AlCl3 catalyst.

mcqs.q: Acyl halides are also called:
mcqs.why: The notes state acyl halides are also called acid halides; they react with benzene and AlCl3 in Friedel-Crafts acylation.

mcqs.q: Which pair distinguishes alkylation from acylation products?
options: Alkylbenzene carries -R; acylbenzene carries -COR with a carbonyl
mcqs.why: Alkylation installs an alkyl group -R giving an alkylbenzene, while acylation installs -COR giving an acylbenzene, an aromatic ketone.

lessons.title: Substituent Effects on Benzene Ring
lessons.notes_html:
Electrophilic substitution on benzene itself gives only one product, because all the available sites of the ring are equivalent. On a ring that already has a substituent, the substituent affects the reaction in two ways: (a) it affects the reactivity of the ring, and (b) it affects the orientation of the reaction.

A) The Effect of Substituents on Reactivity

  • An activating group donates electrons to the ring. It makes the ring more electron rich, so the ring becomes more reactive towards electrophilic aromatic substitution and the reaction occurs faster. For example, in aromatic nitration the hydroxyl group (-OH) makes the ring 1000 times more reactive than benzene.
  • A deactivating group withdraws electrons from the ring. It makes the ring electron poor, so the ring becomes less reactive and the reaction occurs slower. For example, in aromatic nitration the nitro group (-NO2) makes the ring more than 10 million times less reactive than benzene.
  • The hydrogen atom is taken as the standard and is regarded as having no effect.
  • Activating groups are alkyl groups or phenyl groups, or they have an atom, especially N or O, with a lone pair of electrons attached directly to the ring. Deactivating groups are either halogens, or they have an atom with a full or partial positive charge attached to the ring.
Activating: StrongActivating: ModerateActivating: WeakDeactivating: StrongDeactivating: ModerateDeactivating: Weak
-O-, -NR2, -NH2, -OH, -OR-NHCOR, -OCOR-R, -C6H5, -CH=CR2-NO2, -NR3+, -SO3H, -CN, -CF3-COCl, -COOH, -COOR, -COR, -CHO-X (halogens)

B) The Effect of Substituents on Orientation

  • Orientation is the process of determining the position of the second incoming substituent on a monosubstituted benzene. It depends on the nature of the first substituent already present.
  • Ortho-para directing groups direct the incoming electrophile towards the ortho and para positions. They are electron releasing groups and activate primarily the ortho and para positions. All activating substituents, and the weakly deactivating halogens, are ortho-para directors. Example: nitration of toluene gives o-nitrotoluene (59%), m-nitrotoluene (4%) and p-nitrotoluene (37%), so the methyl group is ortho-para directing.
  • Meta directing groups direct the incoming electrophile towards the meta positions. They are electron withdrawing groups; they deactivate primarily the ortho and para positions, so attack occurs at the meta positions. All moderately and strongly deactivating substituents are meta directors. Example: nitration of benzoic acid at 100°C gives about 80% m-nitrobenzoic acid, 18% o-nitrobenzoic acid and 2% p-nitrobenzoic acid, so the carboxyl group is meta directing.
  • Monosubstituted benzenes that give mainly ortho and para products usually react faster than benzene; those that give mainly the meta product always react more slowly than benzene.

Key Points

  • A substituent changes both the reactivity of the ring and the position of the next substitution.
  • Activating groups donate electrons (faster reaction); deactivating groups withdraw electrons (slower reaction).
  • -OH activates strongly (1000 times benzene in nitration); -NO2 deactivates strongly (over 10 million times slower).
  • Ortho-para directors: all activators plus halogens. Meta directors: moderate and strong deactivators.
  • Toluene nitration: 59% ortho, 4% meta, 37% para. Benzoic acid nitration: 80% meta.

mcqs.q: A substituent already on benzene affects electrophilic substitution in two ways: it affects reactivity and it affects:
mcqs.why: The substituent affects (a) the reactivity of the ring and (b) the orientation, i.e. the position where the next substituent enters.

mcqs.q: An activating group makes the ring more reactive by:
options: Donating electrons to the ring, making it more electron rich
mcqs.why: Activating groups donate electrons, making the ring electron rich and more reactive towards electrophiles, so the reaction is faster.

mcqs.q: In aromatic nitration, the -OH group makes the ring how much more reactive than benzene?
mcqs.why: The hydroxyl group makes the ring 1000 times more reactive than benzene in nitration, a strong activating effect given in the notes.

mcqs.q: In nitration, the -NO2 group makes the ring:
options: More than 10 million times less reactive than benzene
mcqs.why: The nitro group is strongly deactivating: in nitration it makes the ring more than 10 million times less reactive than benzene.

mcqs.q: The standard substituent taken as having no effect on reactivity is:
mcqs.why: The hydrogen atom is taken as the standard and is regarded as having no effect, against which activators and deactivators are compared.

mcqs.q: Ortho-para directing groups are mostly:
options: Electron releasing groups, plus the halogens
mcqs.why: Ortho-para directors are electron releasing groups: all activating substituents and the weakly deactivating halogens are ortho-para directors.

mcqs.q: Meta directing groups are:
mcqs.why: All moderately and strongly deactivating substituents are meta directors; they deactivate ortho and para positions, so attack occurs at meta.

mcqs.q: Nitration of toluene gives o-, m- and p-nitrotoluene in percentages:
mcqs.why: Working: 59 + 4 + 37 = 100%. Toluene nitration gives 59% ortho, 4% meta and 37% para, showing methyl is ortho-para directing.

mcqs.q: Nitration of benzoic acid at 100°C gives mainly m-nitrobenzoic acid, about:
mcqs.why: Working: 80 + 18 + 2 = 100%. Benzoic acid gives about 80% meta, 18% ortho and 2% para product, so -COOH is meta directing.

mcqs.q: Monosubstituted benzenes giving mainly meta product, compared with benzene, react:
mcqs.why: Compounds giving mainly ortho/para products usually react faster than benzene, while those giving mainly meta product always react more slowly.

lessons.title: Formation of Polysubstituted Benzenes
lessons.notes_html:
The substitution pattern of electrophilic substitution reactions can be controlled by the substituent group already present on the benzene ring. An activating group such as methyl, hydroxyl or methoxy directs the electrophile to the ortho and para positions, whereas deactivating groups such as nitro, carboxyl and aldehyde (except halogens) direct the electrophile to the meta positions. If there is competition between ortho-para and meta directing groups, the ortho-para directing groups predominate.

Formation of Disubstituted Benzenes

  • The position of the second substituent depends on the nature of the first substituent bonded to the ring.
  • Example: in the nitration of anisole, the methoxy group is an electron releasing, ortho-para directing group. It sends the second substituent (the electrophile) mostly to the ortho and para positions, giving o-nitroanisole and p-nitroanisole as the major products.
  • The ortho and para products can be separated by several methods, because they have different physical properties.

Formation of Trisubstituted Benzenes

  • The position of the third substituent depends on the nature of both substituents already bonded to the ring.
  • Example 1 (both groups direct to the same positions): neither group dominates. In p-nitrotoluene, the methyl group is an ortho-para director and the nitro group is a meta director. The methyl group directs the incoming substituent to its ortho positions only (its para position is already blocked), and the nitro group directs it to the position meta to itself. Both groups direct to the same positions, and the two positions are identical, so only one product is formed: nitration gives 2,4-dinitrotoluene.
  • Example 2 (groups direct to different positions): the more powerful group predominates. In m-nitroanisole, the methoxy group is a stronger activating group than the nitro group, so substitution takes place ortho and para to the methoxy group. The isomer with the sulphonic acid group (-SO3H) between the -OCH3 and -NO2 groups is a very minor product, because of steric hindrance.

Key Points

  • Existing groups control where the next electrophile goes: activators to ortho/para, deactivators (except halogens) to meta.
  • In a competition, ortho-para directors predominate over meta directors.
  • Anisole nitration gives o- and p-nitroanisole as major products.
  • If both groups direct to the same position, one product forms (p-nitrotoluene → 2,4-dinitrotoluene).
  • If groups direct differently, the stronger group wins; crowded positions are avoided (steric hindrance).

mcqs.q: Activating groups such as methyl, hydroxyl or methoxy direct an incoming electrophile to:
mcqs.why: Activators direct to ortho and para positions, whereas deactivators such as nitro, carboxyl and aldehyde (except halogens) direct to meta.

mcqs.q: If ortho-para and meta directing groups compete on the same ring, which predominates?
mcqs.why: In a competition between ortho-para and meta directing groups, the ortho-para directing groups predominate in controlling substitution.

mcqs.q: Nitration of anisole gives as major products:
mcqs.why: The methoxy group of anisole is electron releasing and ortho-para directing, giving o- and p-nitroanisole as the major products.

mcqs.q: The ortho and para products of a substitution can be separated because they have:
options: The same melting point in all cases
mcqs.why: Ortho and para products can be separated by several methods because they have different physical properties, as noted for anisole nitration.

mcqs.q: Nitration of p-nitrotoluene gives only one product, 2,4-dinitrotoluene, because:
options: Both groups direct the incoming group to different positions
Both groups direct to the same positions, which are identical
mcqs.why: Methyl directs to its ortho positions (para is blocked) and nitro directs meta to itself; both point to the same identical positions, so one product forms.

mcqs.q: In m-nitroanisole, substitution occurs ortho and para to the methoxy group because:
options: The methoxy group is a stronger activating group than the nitro group
mcqs.why: When groups direct to different positions, the more powerful group predominates: methoxy is stronger, so substitution is ortho/para to -OCH3.

mcqs.q: The isomer with -SO3H between -OCH3 and -NO2 in m-nitroanisole substitution is a very minor product because of:
mcqs.why: The crowded position between the -OCH3 and -NO2 groups is avoided because of steric hindrance, making that isomer a very minor product.

mcqs.q: For a trisubstituted benzene, the position of the third substituent depends on:
options: The nature of both substituents already on the ring
mcqs.why: Formation of trisubstituted benzenes depends on both existing substituents: if they direct to the same positions one product forms; if differently, the stronger wins.

mcqs.q: Halogens are an exception among deactivating groups because they direct to:
options: Only the para position in every case
mcqs.why: Deactivating groups direct to meta except halogens, which are weakly deactivating yet ortho-para directors, as recalled in this lesson.

mcqs.q: The substitution pattern in polysubstituted benzene formation can be controlled by:
options: The substituent group already present on the ring
mcqs.why: The pattern is controlled by the group already present: activators send electrophiles ortho/para and deactivators (except halogens) send them meta.

lessons.title: Importance of Various Hydrocarbons as Fuels for the Future Energy Needs
lessons.notes_html:
Fuels are naturally occurring combustible substances that act as a source of heat energy, or as raw materials for the chemical industry. Hydrocarbons (compounds of hydrogen and carbon) are mainly used as fuels. Fuels include hydrocarbons from methane up to higher hydrocarbons containing seventeen carbon atoms. Important hydrocarbon fuels are LPG, natural gas, gasoline, kerosene oil and diesel. Higher hydrocarbons with more than seventeen carbon atoms are present in heavy oil fractions; they can be cracked to get gasoline and other hydrocarbons that can be used as fuel in various sectors. Energy is obtained from fuels through the combustion (burning) process.

Uses of Hydrocarbons as Fuels

  • LPG (liquefied petroleum gas): a refined petroleum gas, used as a camping and domestic fuel.
  • Natural gas: a fossil fuel that exists in a gaseous state and is composed mainly of methane (CH4). It is used as a fuel in industries, electric power stations and homes.
  • CNG (compressed natural gas): natural gas under pressure. It can be used as a cheaper, greener and more efficient alternative to the traditional petrol and diesel fuels for vehicles.
  • Gasoline: used as a fuel for cars, motorbikes, trucks, boats and other transport vehicles.
  • Kerosene oil: widely used to power the jet engines of aeroplanes and some rocket engines. It is used to fuel lamps and lanterns because it has a low explosion hazard and burns relatively cleanly, and it is also used in stoves for cooking.
  • Diesel: used as a fuel for trucks, buses, tractors, tanks and central heating systems, and in diesel engine generators to generate electricity.
  • Coal: not a hydrocarbon; it is made up almost entirely of carbon. It is mainly used in power generation, and also as a household fuel for cooking and heating.
  • Fuel oil: derived from crude petroleum, either as a distillate or as a residue at the oil refinery. It is the most widely used liquid fuel for power generation and ships. Fuel oil has more than sixteen carbon atoms.
  • Paraffin wax: an alkane with approximately 25 carbon atoms, used as a fuel for candles.

Key Points

  • Hydrocarbons from methane to C17 compounds are the main fuels; heavier fractions are cracked into fuel-range hydrocarbons.
  • Natural gas is mainly methane; CNG is its compressed form for vehicles.
  • Gasoline runs road vehicles; kerosene runs jet engines; diesel runs trucks, buses and generators.
  • Coal is not a hydrocarbon: it is almost entirely carbon.
  • Paraffin wax (about C25) is the candle fuel.

mcqs.q: Fuels are defined as naturally occurring combustible substances that act as:
options: A source of heat energy, or raw materials for the chemical industry
mcqs.why: Fuels are combustible substances acting as a source of heat energy or as raw materials for the chemical industry; hydrocarbons are mainly used as fuels.

mcqs.q: Hydrocarbon fuels range mainly from methane up to hydrocarbons containing:
mcqs.why: Fuels include hydrocarbons from methane up to C17 compounds; heavier fractions with more carbons are cracked to get gasoline and other fuels.

mcqs.q: Natural gas is composed mainly of:
mcqs.why: Natural gas is a fossil fuel in a gaseous state composed mainly of methane CH4, used in industries, power stations and homes.

mcqs.q: CNG is natural gas that is:
options: Under pressure (compressed), a cheaper, greener vehicle fuel alternative
mcqs.why: CNG is compressed natural gas: natural gas under pressure, used as a cheaper, greener and more efficient alternative to petrol and diesel for vehicles.

mcqs.q: LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) is described as a refined petroleum gas used as:
mcqs.why: LPG is a refined petroleum gas used as a camping and domestic fuel, distinct from gasoline, kerosene and diesel uses listed.

mcqs.q: Kerosene oil is widely used to power:
options: Jet engines of aeroplanes and some rocket engines
mcqs.why: Kerosene powers jet engines of aeroplanes and some rocket engines, and also fuels lamps and stoves because it burns relatively cleanly.

mcqs.q: Diesel is used as a fuel for:
options: Trucks, buses, tractors, tanks, central heating and generator engines
mcqs.why: Diesel fuels trucks, buses, tractors and tanks, central heating systems, and diesel engine generators that generate electricity.

mcqs.q: Coal is not a hydrocarbon because it is:
options: Made up almost entirely of carbon
mcqs.why: Coal is not a hydrocarbon; it is made up almost entirely of carbon and is mainly used in power generation and as a household fuel.

mcqs.q: Fuel oil, derived from crude petroleum as a distillate or residue, has:
mcqs.why: Fuel oil is the most widely used liquid fuel for power generation and ships, and it has more than sixteen carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Paraffin wax, used as a fuel for candles, is an alkane with approximately:
mcqs.why: Paraffin wax is an alkane with approximately 25 carbon atoms used for candles, heavier than the methane-to-C17 main fuel range.

lessons.title: Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are organic compounds containing a halogen atom covalently bonded to one of the saturated carbon atoms of an alkyl group. They are also called haloalkanes.

Classification

Alkyl halides are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary according to the nature of the carbon atom to which the halogen is attached.

  • Primary (1°) alkyl halide: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to only one other carbon atom, e.g. R-CH2-X.
  • Secondary (2°) alkyl halide: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to two other carbon atoms.
  • Tertiary (3°) alkyl halide: the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to three other carbon atoms.

The general formula of alkyl halides is CnH2n+1X, where X may be fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br) or iodine (I).

Key Points

  • Alkyl halides have a halogen atom covalently bonded to a saturated carbon of an alkyl group.
  • They are also known as haloalkanes.
  • They are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary by the carbon bearing the halogen.
  • Their general formula is CnH2n+1X, where X = F, Cl, Br or I.

mcqs.q: What is an alkyl halide?
options: A compound with a halogen covalently bonded to a saturated carbon of an alkyl group
A compound with a halogen bonded to a benzene ring only
An alcohol containing a halogen in its OH group
A salt formed by a metal and a halogen
mcqs.why: The notes define alkyl halides as compounds containing a halogen atom covalently bonded to one of the saturated carbon atoms of an alkyl group.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halides are also called:
mcqs.why: The notes state that alkyl halides are also called haloalkanes, because they are halogen-substituted alkanes.

mcqs.q: In a primary (1°) alkyl halide, the halogen-bearing carbon is attached to how many other carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: A primary alkyl halide has the halogen-bearing carbon attached to only one other carbon atom, as in the general example R-CH2-X given in the notes.

mcqs.q: A halogen-bearing carbon attached to two other carbon atoms belongs to which class?
mcqs.why: By the notes' classification, attachment to two other carbon atoms makes the alkyl halide secondary, or 2°, in nature.

mcqs.q: Which description fits a tertiary (3°) alkyl halide?
options: Halogen carbon attached to three other carbons
Halogen carbon attached to one other carbon
Three halogen atoms on one carbon
mcqs.why: A tertiary alkyl halide is defined by a halogen-bearing carbon attached to three other carbon atoms, according to the classification in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of an alkyl halide?
mcqs.why: The notes give the general formula CnH2n+1X, where X represents the halogen atom attached to the alkyl group.

mcqs.q: Using CnH2n+1X, what is the hydrogen count for an alkyl halide with n = 4?
mcqs.why: Full working: hydrogen count = 2n + 1 = 2(4) + 1 = 8 + 1 = 9, so the formula is C4H9X, as verified by substitution into the general formula.

mcqs.q: Which set contains only halogens represented by X in CnH2n+1X?
mcqs.why: The notes specify that X may be fluorine (F), chlorine (Cl), bromine (Br) or iodine (I), and no other element is listed for X.

mcqs.q: Classification of alkyl halides as 1°, 2° or 3° is based on:
options: The number of halogen atoms present
The nature of the carbon atom to which the halogen is attached
The boiling point of the compound
mcqs.why: The notes classify alkyl halides according to the nature of the carbon atom to which the halogen is attached, not according to the halogen itself.

mcqs.q: Which example represents the pattern of a primary alkyl halide given in the notes?
