mcqs.why: The notes give R-CH2-X as the example pattern for a primary alkyl halide, whose halogen-bearing CH2 carbon is attached to one other carbon group.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are named by two systems: the common system and the IUPAC system.

Common System

The names consist of two words. The first word is the name of the alkyl group and the second word is fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide. Examples: CH3Cl = methyl chloride, CHCl3 = chloroform, CH2Cl2 = methylene chloride, CCl4 = carbon tetrachloride, (CH3)3CBr = tert-butyl bromide, (CH3)2CHCl = isopropyl chloride.

IUPAC System

In this system alkyl halides are named as haloalkanes and the names consist of one word only.

  • Select the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the halogen atom.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer to the halogen atom.
  • Name the halogen as a prefix: fluoro, chloro, bromo or iodo.
  • Show the position of the halogen by a number before its name.
  • If different substituents are present, name them in alphabetical order.

Examples: chloromethane, fluoroethane, 1-iodopropane, 2-chloropropane, 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, tetrachloromethane, 2-bromo-3-chlorobutane, 2,4-dibromopentane, 3-bromo-5-chloro-2-methylhexane.

Key Points

  • Common names have two words: alkyl group name + fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide.
  • IUPAC names are one-word haloalkane names.
  • The longest chain containing the halogen is selected and numbered from the end nearer the halogen.
  • Halogens are named fluoro, chloro, bromo and iodo as prefixes, with position numbers.
  • Different substituents are listed in alphabetical order.

mcqs.q: In the common system, an alkyl halide name consists of:
options: The alkyl group name followed by fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide
A number followed by the halogen name only
The halogen name followed by the word alkane
mcqs.why: Common names have two words: the first is the alkyl group name and the second is fluoride, chloride, bromide or iodide, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the common name of CH3Cl?
mcqs.why: The notes list CH3Cl as methyl chloride in the common system: methyl is the alkyl group and chloride is the halide word.

mcqs.q: CHCl3 is given the common name:
mcqs.why: The examples in the notes identify CHCl3 as chloroform, distinguishing it from CH2Cl2 and CCl4 by its formula.

mcqs.q: Which formula corresponds to methylene chloride in the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes pair CH2Cl2 with the common name methylene chloride, while CHCl3 is chloroform and CCl4 is carbon tetrachloride.

mcqs.q: (CH3)3CBr is named in the common system as:
mcqs.why: The notes give (CH3)3CBr as tert-butyl bromide, using tert-butyl for the branched alkyl group attached to bromine.

mcqs.q: In the IUPAC system, alkyl halides are named as:
mcqs.why: The IUPAC system names alkyl halides as haloalkanes, and the notes emphasise that these names consist of one word only.

mcqs.q: Which chain is selected for IUPAC naming of an alkyl halide?
options: The longest continuous carbon chain containing the halogen atom
Any chain that excludes the halogen
The chain with the most hydrogen atoms
mcqs.why: IUPAC naming begins by selecting the longest continuous carbon chain that contains the halogen atom, according to the rules in the notes.

mcqs.q: The selected chain is numbered from:
options: The end farther from the halogen
The end nearer to the halogen atom
The end with the longest alkyl branch
mcqs.why: The notes require numbering from the end nearer to the halogen atom, so the halogen receives the lowest possible position number.

mcqs.q: How are different substituents ordered in an IUPAC alkyl halide name?
options: By the order in which they appear in the formula
Halogens always come last regardless of name
mcqs.why: When different substituents are present, the notes state that they are named in alphabetical order in the IUPAC name.

mcqs.q: Which is an IUPAC-style example from the notes?
mcqs.why: 2-Bromo-3-chlorobutane is listed among the IUPAC haloalkane examples, with position numbers and substituents ordered alphabetically: bromo before chloro.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
• The lower members of the series (CH3Cl, CH3Br, CH3F and CH3CH2Cl) are gases at room temperature. Alkyl halides up to C18 are colourless liquids, and beyond C18 they are colourless solids.
  • Alkyl halides are practically insoluble in water, because they cannot form hydrogen bonds with water. They are, however, soluble in organic solvents.
  • For a given halogen, the boiling point increases with the increase in the size and mass of the alkyl group.
  • For a given alkyl group, the boiling points follow the order RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
  • For a given halogen, the density decreases with the increase in the size and mass of the alkyl group.

Key Points

  • Lower alkyl halides are gases; members up to C18 are liquids; higher members are solids.
  • They are insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents.
  • Boiling point rises with the size and mass of the alkyl group.
  • For the same alkyl group, boiling points follow RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
  • Density falls as the alkyl group becomes larger and heavier.

mcqs.q: Which lower alkyl halides are gases at room temperature according to the notes?
options: All alkyl halides up to C18
mcqs.why: The notes name CH3Cl, CH3Br, CH3F and CH3CH2Cl as the lower members that are gases at room temperature.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halides up to C18 are generally:
mcqs.why: The notes state that alkyl halides up to C18 are colourless liquids, whereas members beyond C18 are colourless solids.

mcqs.q: Members beyond C18 in the alkyl halide series are:
mcqs.why: Beyond C18, the notes describe alkyl halides as colourless solids, marking the change from the liquid range up to C18.

mcqs.q: Why are alkyl halides practically insoluble in water?
options: They cannot form hydrogen bonds with water
mcqs.why: The notes explain their practical insolubility by the fact that alkyl halides cannot form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halides are soluble in:
mcqs.why: Although practically insoluble in water, alkyl halides are soluble in organic solvents, as stated directly in the physical-properties notes.

mcqs.q: For a given halogen, boiling point changes with alkyl group size and mass as follows:
options: It decreases as size and mass increase
It increases with increase in size and mass of the alkyl group
mcqs.why: The notes state that for a given halogen, the boiling point increases with the increase in the size and mass of the alkyl group.

mcqs.q: For a given alkyl group, the boiling-point order is:
mcqs.why: For the same alkyl group, the notes give the boiling-point order RI > RBr > RCl > RF, with the iodide highest and fluoride lowest.

mcqs.q: For a given halogen, density changes as the alkyl group becomes larger and heavier by:
mcqs.why: The notes state that for a given halogen, density decreases with the increase in the size and mass of the alkyl group.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly combines the physical properties in the notes?
options: Alkyl halides dissolve in water but not organic solvents
Lower members are gases and higher members beyond C18 are solids
All members are solids at room temperature
Boiling point falls as the alkyl group grows
mcqs.why: The notes describe lower members as gases, members up to C18 as liquids and members beyond C18 as solids, so the combined statement is correct.

mcqs.q: Which alkyl halide has the highest boiling point for a fixed alkyl group R?
mcqs.why: The fixed-R boiling-point order RI > RBr > RCl > RF places RI at the top, so the iodide has the highest boiling point.

lessons.title: Structure of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
The structure of alkyl halides can be explained by taking methyl chloride as an example. The carbon atom of an alkyl halide is sp3 hybridized.

  • The carbon-halogen sigma bond is formed by the overlap of an sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon with the half-filled p-orbital of the halogen atom.
  • The carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds are formed by the overlap of sp3 hybrid orbitals of carbon with the s-orbitals of hydrogen atoms.
  • The H-C-H and H-C-X bond angles are approximately 109.5°.
  • The molecule therefore has a tetrahedral shape around carbon.

Key Points

  • The carbon atom in an alkyl halide is sp3 hybridized.
  • The C-X sigma bond forms from an sp3 orbital of carbon and a p-orbital of the halogen.
  • Bond angles are about 109.5°, so the shape around carbon is tetrahedral.

mcqs.q: The carbon atom in an alkyl halide is:
mcqs.why: Using methyl chloride as the example, the notes state that the carbon atom of an alkyl halide is sp3 hybridized.

mcqs.q: The carbon-halogen sigma bond is formed by overlap of:
options: Carbon sp3 orbital with halogen half-filled p-orbital
Carbon s orbital with halogen s orbital
Carbon p orbital with hydrogen s orbital
mcqs.why: The notes say the C-X sigma bond forms by overlap of an sp3 hybrid orbital of carbon with the half-filled p-orbital of the halogen atom.

mcqs.q: Carbon-hydrogen sigma bonds in methyl chloride are formed by overlap of:
options: Carbon p orbitals with halogen orbitals
Carbon sp3 orbitals with hydrogen s-orbitals
Hydrogen p orbitals with carbon s orbital
mcqs.why: The C-H sigma bonds form from sp3 hybrid orbitals of carbon overlapping with the s-orbitals of hydrogen atoms, according to the structure notes.

mcqs.q: The H-C-H and H-C-X bond angles in an alkyl halide are approximately:
mcqs.why: The notes give both H-C-H and H-C-X bond angles as approximately 109.5°, the tetrahedral angle associated with sp3 carbon.

mcqs.q: The shape around carbon in an alkyl halide is:
mcqs.why: Because carbon is sp3 hybridized with bond angles near 109.5°, the molecule has a tetrahedral shape around carbon, as the notes conclude.

mcqs.q: Which molecule is used as the example to explain alkyl halide structure?
mcqs.why: The structure section explicitly explains alkyl halides by taking methyl chloride as the example molecule.

mcqs.q: The bond formed between carbon and halogen in methyl chloride is a:
mcqs.why: The notes describe the carbon-halogen linkage as a sigma bond formed by orbital overlap along the bond axis.

mcqs.q: How many sigma-bonding arrangements around carbon are implied by its tetrahedral sp3 structure?
mcqs.why: Full working: sp3 carbon forms four sigma bonds in a tetrahedral arrangement; in CH3Cl these are 3 C-H bonds + 1 C-Cl bond = 4 sigma bonds in total.

mcqs.q: If the bond angle were about 109.5°, which hybridization is consistent with the notes?
mcqs.why: The notes connect the approximately 109.5° angles and tetrahedral shape with sp3 hybridization of the carbon atom.

mcqs.q: The half-filled orbital of the halogen used in C-X bond formation is a:
mcqs.why: For the C-X sigma bond, the notes specify overlap with the half-filled p-orbital of the halogen atom, not an s- or d-orbital.

lessons.title: Preparation of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
From Alcohols and Hydrogen Halides

Alcohols react with hydrogen halides in the presence of anhydrous ZnCl2, which acts as a dehydrating agent: CH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O (with ZnCl2). The reactivity of the hydrogen halides is in the order HI > HBr > HCl, and the reactivity of alcohols is 3° > 2° > 1°.

From Alcohols and Other Halogenating Agents (SOCl2, PX3)

Alkyl halides are prepared by heating alcohols with thionyl chloride (SOCl2) in the presence of pyridine: CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl. This is the best method for preparing alkyl halides, because both by-products (SO2 and HCl) are gases and can be removed easily. Alcohols also react with phosphorus halides (PX3): 3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3.

Radical Halogenation of Alkanes

Alkanes react with halogens in diffused sunlight or UV light: CH3CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + HCl (UV light). This is not a good method, because halogen derivatives containing two or more halogen atoms are also formed along with the alkyl halide.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
Alcohol + HXCH3CH2OH + HCl → CH3CH2Cl + H2O (ZnCl2)
Alcohol + SOCl2CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 → CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl (pyridine)
Alcohol + PCl33CH3CH2OH + PCl3 → 3CH3CH2Cl + H3PO3
Alkane + halogenCH3CH3 + Cl2 → CH3CH2Cl + HCl (UV light)

Key Points

  • Alcohols react with HX in the presence of anhydrous ZnCl2 to give alkyl halides.
  • Reactivity of HX: HI > HBr > HCl; reactivity of alcohols: 3° > 2° > 1°.
  • The SOCl2 method is the best, because SO2 and HCl are gases and escape easily.
  • Phosphorus halides (PX3) also convert alcohols into alkyl halides.
  • Radical halogenation of alkanes is a poor method because polyhalogen products are also formed.

mcqs.q: Alcohols react with hydrogen halides to give alkyl halides in the presence of:
mcqs.why: The alcohol-HX method uses anhydrous ZnCl2, which the notes identify as acting as a dehydrating agent in the reaction.

mcqs.q: In the reaction CH3CH2OH + HCl -> CH3CH2Cl + H2O, ZnCl2 acts as a:
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly state that anhydrous ZnCl2 acts as a dehydrating agent when ethanol reacts with HCl to form ethyl chloride and water.

mcqs.q: The reactivity order of hydrogen halides toward alcohols is:
mcqs.why: The preparation notes give the hydrogen-halide reactivity order as HI > HBr > HCl, with hydrogen iodide the most reactive.

mcqs.q: The reactivity order of alcohols toward hydrogen halides is:
mcqs.why: The notes state that alcohol reactivity follows 3° > 2° > 1°, so tertiary alcohols react most readily with hydrogen halides.

mcqs.q: Why is the SOCl2 method called the best method for preparing alkyl halides?
options: It forms no by-products at all
Both by-products SO2 and HCl are gases and are removed easily
It works only for tertiary alcohols
mcqs.why: The notes call the thionyl chloride method best because both by-products, SO2 and HCl, are gases and can be removed easily from the product.

mcqs.q: Ethanol with SOCl2 in pyridine gives ethyl chloride plus:
mcqs.why: The given reaction is CH3CH2OH + SOCl2 -> CH3CH2Cl + SO2 + HCl, carried out in the presence of pyridine.

mcqs.q: The reaction 3CH3CH2OH + PCl3 -> 3CH3CH2Cl + ? has which other product?
mcqs.why: The phosphorus trichloride reaction in the notes produces H3PO3 along with three molecules of ethyl chloride from three molecules of ethanol.

mcqs.q: Radical halogenation of alkanes requires:
mcqs.why: Alkanes react with halogens in diffused sunlight or UV light, as shown by CH3CH3 + Cl2 -> CH3CH2Cl + HCl under UV light.

mcqs.q: Why is radical halogenation of alkanes not a good preparation method?
options: Halogen derivatives with two or more halogen atoms are also formed
The product is always a gas
mcqs.why: The notes say this is not a good method because polyhalogen derivatives containing two or more halogen atoms form along with the desired alkyl halide.

mcqs.q: Which preparation route is represented by CH3CH3 + Cl2 under UV light?
mcqs.why: Ethane reacting with chlorine under UV light is the radical halogenation example in the notes, producing ethyl chloride and HCl.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Alkyl halides are very reactive compounds. The extent of their reactivity depends on two factors: (i) the bond polarity of the carbon-halogen bond, and (ii) the bond energy of the carbon-halogen bond.

Bond Polarity of the Carbon-Halogen Bond

The halogen atom is more electronegative than carbon, so the alkyl halide molecule is polarized: carbon carries a partial positive charge and the halogen a partial negative charge. The greater the electronegativity difference (ΔEN) between carbon and the halogen, the greater is the polarity of the C-X bond. Greater polarity means greater bond strength and lesser reactivity of RX.

HalomethaneElectronegativity of halogenEN difference (C and X)Dipole moment (Debye)
CH3F3.981.481.85
CH3Cl3.000.501.87
CH3Br2.960.461.81
CH3I2.560.061.62

Bond Energy of the Carbon-Halogen Bond

Bond energy is the measure of bond strength. The greater the bond energy, the greater is the bond strength and the lesser is the reactivity of the C-X bond.

BondBond energy (kJ/mol)
C-F467
C-Cl346
C-Br290
C-I228

From the bond energies, the order of reactivity of alkyl halides is: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

Key Points

  • Reactivity of alkyl halides depends on C-X bond polarity and C-X bond energy.
  • The C-X bond is polarized because the halogen is more electronegative than carbon.
  • Bond energies fall in the order C-F (467) > C-Cl (346) > C-Br (290) > C-I (228) kJ/mol.
  • The weakest bond (C-I) breaks most easily, so reactivity is RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

mcqs.q: Reactivity of alkyl halides depends on which two factors?
options: Bond polarity and bond energy of the C-X bond
mcqs.why: The notes state that the extent of reactivity depends on the bond polarity of the carbon-halogen bond and the bond energy of that bond.

mcqs.q: In a polarized C-X bond, the partial charges are:
mcqs.why: Because the halogen is more electronegative than carbon, carbon carries a partial positive charge and the halogen a partial negative charge.

mcqs.q: Greater electronegativity difference between C and X leads to:
options: Greater polarity, greater bond strength and lesser reactivity of RX
mcqs.why: The notes state that a greater ΔEN gives greater C-X polarity, and greater polarity means greater bond strength and lesser reactivity of RX.

mcqs.q: For CH3F, the notes give the halogen electronegativity and EN difference as:
mcqs.why: The halomethane table lists fluorine electronegativity as 3.98 and the C-F electronegativity difference as 1.48, the largest difference in the table.

mcqs.q: What is the dipole moment listed for CH3Cl?
mcqs.why: The table in the notes gives CH3Cl a dipole moment of 1.87 Debye, slightly higher than the values listed for CH3F, CH3Br and CH3I.

mcqs.q: Which halomethane has the smallest EN difference in the table?
mcqs.why: CH3I is listed with an EN difference of only 0.06, smaller than 0.46 for CH3Br, 0.50 for CH3Cl and 1.48 for CH3F.

mcqs.q: The bond energy of C-F is:
mcqs.why: The bond-energy table gives C-F as 467 kJ/mol, the highest bond energy and therefore the strongest carbon-halogen bond listed.

mcqs.q: How much greater is the C-F bond energy than the C-I bond energy?
mcqs.why: Full working: difference = bond energy(C-F) - bond energy(C-I) = 467 kJ/mol - 228 kJ/mol = 239 kJ/mol, verified from the table values.

mcqs.q: The correct order of C-X bond energies is:
mcqs.why: The listed energies are C-F 467, C-Cl 346, C-Br 290 and C-I 228 kJ/mol, giving the order C-F > C-Cl > C-Br > C-I.

mcqs.q: From bond energies, the reactivity order of alkyl halides is:
mcqs.why: The weakest bond, C-I at 228 kJ/mol, breaks most easily, so the notes conclude the reactivity order RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

lessons.title: Nucleophilic Substitution Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
The reactions in which an electron-rich nucleophile replaces another nucleophile (the leaving group) to form a new molecule are called nucleophilic substitution reactions, or SN reactions: Nu- + R-C-X → R-C-Nu + X-.

  • In these reactions the nucleophile is always a Lewis base. It may be neutral or negatively charged.
  • The substrate is frequently an alkyl halide, and the leaving group is a halide ion.
  • The partial positive carbon atom of the alkyl halide acts as an electrophile and accepts a pair of electrons from the attacking nucleophile. In this way a new bond is formed between the nucleophile and the carbon of the alkyl halide.
  • SN reactions take place by two mechanisms: SN1 and SN2.

Key Points

  • In an SN reaction a nucleophile replaces a leaving group on carbon.
  • The nucleophile is a Lewis base and may be neutral or negatively charged.
  • The substrate is usually an alkyl halide and the leaving group is a halide ion.
  • The partially positive carbon is the electrophile that accepts the electron pair.
  • SN reactions occur by the SN1 or the SN2 mechanism.

mcqs.q: A nucleophilic substitution reaction is one in which:
options: A nucleophile replaces a leaving group to form a new molecule
Two groups are removed from adjacent carbons only
A metal replaces carbon in the chain
Hydrogen is added across a double bond
mcqs.why: The notes define SN reactions as reactions where an electron-rich nucleophile replaces another nucleophile, the leaving group, to form a new molecule.

mcqs.q: In the general SN equation Nu- + R-C-X -> R-C-Nu + X-, X- is:
mcqs.why: In the general equation, X- departs from the substrate and is therefore the leaving group, while Nu- is the attacking nucleophile.

mcqs.q: In every SN reaction, the nucleophile acts as a:
mcqs.why: The notes state that in these reactions the nucleophile is always a Lewis base, because it donates an electron pair.

mcqs.q: A nucleophile in an SN reaction may be:
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly say the nucleophile may be neutral or negatively charged, provided it is electron-rich and can donate a pair.

mcqs.q: The usual substrate and leaving group in the SN reactions described are:
mcqs.why: The substrate is frequently an alkyl halide and the leaving group is a halide ion, according to the introduction to SN reactions.

mcqs.q: The partial positive carbon of an alkyl halide acts as:
mcqs.why: The partially positive carbon acts as an electrophile and accepts a pair of electrons from the attacking nucleophile, forming the new bond.

mcqs.q: What happens when the nucleophile attacks the electrophilic carbon?
options: A new bond forms between the nucleophile and carbon
Carbon loses all its bonds permanently
The nucleophile becomes the leaving group before bonding
mcqs.why: The notes explain that a new bond is formed between the nucleophile and the carbon of the alkyl halide as carbon accepts the electron pair.

mcqs.q: SN reactions take place by which two mechanisms?
mcqs.why: The notes state that SN reactions take place by two mechanisms: SN1 and SN2, which are treated in the following lessons.

mcqs.q: The species that replaces the leaving group is best described as:
mcqs.why: The definition in the notes calls the replacing species an electron-rich nucleophile, which distinguishes it from the electron-deficient electrophilic carbon.

mcqs.q: In R-C-X, the atom directly attacked by the nucleophile is:
mcqs.why: The nucleophile donates its electron pair to the partial positive carbon atom of the alkyl halide, which is the electrophilic centre of the substrate.

lessons.title: Important Concepts: Carbocations, Nucleophiles and Leaving Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Carbocations and Their Stability

Carbocations are very reactive, unstable, electron-deficient species. Anything that donates electron density to the electron-deficient centre helps to stabilize them. Alkyl groups are weak electron-donating groups, so they stabilize a nearby carbocation. More substituted carbocations are therefore more stable: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl (the methyl carbocation is the least stable).

Nucleophile and Base

Both nucleophiles and Lewis bases are electron-pair donor species. A base is a species that donates an electron pair to hydrogen (a proton), while a nucleophile donates an electron pair to an atom other than hydrogen, particularly a carbon atom. For example, the hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile in a substitution reaction (it donates electrons to carbon) but as a base in an elimination reaction (it donates electrons to hydrogen).

Reactivity classNucleophileRelative reactivity
Very good nucleophileI-, HS-> 10^5
Good nucleophileBr-, HO-, RO-, CN-10^4
Fair nucleophileNH3, Cl-, F-10^3
Weak nucleophileH2O, ROH10^0
Very weak nucleophileRCOOH10^-2

Substrate and Leaving Group

The substrate is the carbon-containing compound on which substitution takes place: it is the reactant to which the nucleophile becomes bonded and from which the leaving group departs. The leaving group is the species that departs from the substrate and takes a pair of electrons with it. The best leaving groups are those that become the most stable ions after they depart; they are weakly basic. Halide ions are weak bases, so they are good leaving groups. Poor leaving groups are strongly basic, e.g. hydroxide and amide ions.

ClassLeaving group
Good leaving groupsI-, Br-, Cl-, H2O
Moderate leaving groupsHS-, CN-, NH3
Poor leaving groupsF-, HO-, RO-
Very poor leaving groupsNH2-, H-, R-

Key Points

  • Carbocations are reactive, unstable and electron deficient.
  • Carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl.
  • A base donates its electron pair to a proton; a nucleophile donates its pair to carbon.
  • I- and HS- are very good nucleophiles; RCOOH is a very weak nucleophile.
  • The substrate is the molecule attacked; the leaving group departs with the bonding electron pair.
  • Good leaving groups are weak bases; strongly basic groups leave poorly.

mcqs.q: Carbocations are best described as:
mcqs.why: The notes describe carbocations as very reactive, unstable and electron-deficient species whose stability increases when electron density is donated to them.

mcqs.q: The stability order of carbocations is:
mcqs.why: Alkyl groups donate electron density, so the notes give carbocation stability as tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl, with methyl least stable.

mcqs.q: Why do alkyl groups stabilize a nearby carbocation?
options: They form hydrogen bonds with it
They remove its positive charge completely
mcqs.why: The notes say alkyl groups are weak electron-donating groups, and donation of electron density to the electron-deficient centre helps stabilize the carbocation.

mcqs.q: A base differs from a nucleophile because a base donates its electron pair to:
mcqs.why: A base donates an electron pair to hydrogen, a proton, whereas a nucleophile donates an electron pair to an atom other than hydrogen, particularly carbon.

mcqs.q: Hydroxide ion acts as a nucleophile in substitution but as a base in elimination because:
options: It changes into a different ion
In substitution it donates electrons to carbon; in elimination it donates electrons to hydrogen
It is neutral in one reaction and charged in the other
mcqs.why: The notes use hydroxide as the example: it donates electrons to carbon in substitution, making it a nucleophile, and to hydrogen in elimination, making it a base.

mcqs.q: Which pair is classed as very good nucleophiles with relative reactivity > 10^5?
mcqs.why: The reactivity table lists I- and HS- as very good nucleophiles with relative reactivity greater than 10^5, the highest class given.

mcqs.q: RCOOH is classed as which type of nucleophile?
mcqs.why: The table classifies RCOOH as a very weak nucleophile with relative reactivity 10^-2, the lowest value listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: The substrate in a substitution reaction is:
options: The species that departs with the electron pair
The carbon-containing compound on which substitution takes place
mcqs.why: The notes define the substrate as the carbon-containing reactant to which the nucleophile becomes bonded and from which the leaving group departs.

mcqs.q: The best leaving groups are those that:
options: Become the most stable ions after departure and are weakly basic
mcqs.why: Good leaving groups become stable ions after departing and are weakly basic; halide ions are weak bases and therefore good leaving groups.

mcqs.q: Which group is a very poor leaving group according to the table?
mcqs.why: The table lists NH2-, along with H- and R-, as very poor leaving groups, whereas I-, Cl- and H2O are good leaving groups.

lessons.title: SN1 Mechanism
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation SN1, S stands for substitution, N for nucleophilic and 1 for unimolecular: only one molecule is involved in the rate-determining step. In this mechanism, the breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group is fully completed before bond making with the nucleophile starts. The reaction of a tertiary alkyl halide occurs in two steps.

Step 1 (Slow, Rate-Determining)

The tert-alkyl halide ionizes in a polar solvent to produce a planar carbocation and the leaving group: R3C-X → R3C+ + X-. The tertiary carbocation is stable because of its three electron-donating alkyl groups. This step involves the breakage of a covalent bond, so it is slow and rate-determining.

Step 2 (Fast)

The nucleophile attacks the planar carbocation to produce the tert-alkyl product. This step is fast because it is a combination of a cation and an anion.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [R3CX], so Rate = k[R3CX]. The rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate (tert-alkyl halide), not on the concentration of the nucleophile. Doubling the concentration of the tert-alkyl halide doubles the rate; changing the nucleophile concentration has no effect. The reaction is first order overall.

Stereochemical Evidence

The positively charged carbon of the carbocation is sp2 hybridized, with an empty p-orbital having one lobe on each side of the plane. The nucleophile can attack from either side of the plane, so some product has retained configuration and some has inverted configuration.

Key Points

  • SN1 is a two-step, unimolecular mechanism typical of tertiary alkyl halides.
  • Step 1 is the slow ionization to a planar carbocation; it is the rate-determining step.
  • Step 2 is the fast attack of the nucleophile on the carbocation.
  • Rate = k[R3CX]: first order, independent of nucleophile concentration.
  • Attack from either side gives products with retained and inverted configurations.

lessons.title: SN2 Mechanism
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation SN2, S stands for substitution, N for nucleophilic and 2 for bimolecular: two molecules (the alkyl halide and the nucleophile) are involved in the rate-determining step. The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group and the formation of the bond between the nucleophile and the electrophile occur simultaneously. The reaction of a primary alkyl halide occurs in one step.

The Transition State

In the transition state, the bond to the nucleophile is partially formed and the bond to the leaving group (halide) is partially broken. The transition state has a very short-lived existence. This single step is the slow, rate-determining step.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [RH2CX][Nu-], so Rate = k[RH2CX][Nu-]. The rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the nucleophile. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate; doubling both quadruples it. The reaction is first order in each reactant and second order overall.

Stereochemical Evidence

In a primary alkyl halide the electrophilic carbon carries one alkyl group and two small hydrogen atoms, so there is no steric hindrance. The nucleophile attacks from the back side of the leaving group, because the leaving group blocks the front side. The product therefore has an inverted configuration compared with the reactant alkyl halide. (Keep in mind: methyl and primary alkyl halides undergo SN2 only; tertiary alkyl halides undergo SN1 only; secondary alkyl halides can undergo both, depending on the solvent and the alkyl groups.)

Comparison of SN1 and SN2 Mechanisms

SN1SN2
Two-step mechanismOne-step mechanism
Unimolecular, first-order kineticsBimolecular, second-order kinetics
Proceeds through a carbocationProceeds through a transition state
Rate depends on [RX] only: Rate ∝ [RX]Rate depends on [RX] and [Nu-]: Rate ∝ [RX][Nu-]
Reactivity order: 3° > 2° > 1° > methyl; methyl and primary halides fail to reactReactivity order: methyl > 1° > 2° > 3°; tertiary halides fail to react
Products have both retained and inverted configurationsProduct has the inverted configuration
Favoured by polar solventsFavoured by non-polar solvents
Favoured by weaker nucleophilesFavoured by stronger nucleophiles

Key Points

  • SN2 is a one-step, bimolecular mechanism typical of primary alkyl halides.
  • Bond breaking and bond making happen at the same time, through a transition state.
  • Rate = k[RX][Nu-]: second order overall.
  • The nucleophile attacks from the back side, so the product is inverted.
  • Complete inversion in a substitution shows the mechanism is SN2, not SN1.

mcqs.why: The comparison notes state that complete inversion in a substitution shows the mechanism is SN2, not SN1, because SN1 gives retained and inverted products.

mcqs.why: The SN1-SN2 comparison table lists SN2 as favoured by non-polar solvents and stronger nucleophiles, while SN1 is favoured by polar solvents and weaker nucleophiles.

lessons.title: 1,2-Elimination Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
In addition to SN reactions, alkyl halides also undergo elimination reactions. An elimination reaction is a type of organic reaction in which two substituents are removed from two adjacent saturated carbon atoms of a substrate molecule.

When an alkyl halide undergoes elimination, the halogen atom is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen is removed from the β-carbon. As a result, a double bond is formed between the α-carbon and the β-carbon, and the product is an alkene. The removal of a proton (hydrogen ion) and a halide ion is called dehydrohalogenation.

The most common bases used in elimination reactions are HO-, RO- and H2N-. There are two important mechanisms for elimination reactions: E1 and E2, just like the SN reactions.

Key Points

  • Elimination removes two substituents from two adjacent saturated carbons.
  • The halogen leaves from the α-carbon and a hydrogen from the β-carbon.
  • A double bond forms between the α- and β-carbons, giving an alkene.
  • Removal of H+ and halide ion together is called dehydrohalogenation.
  • Common bases are HO-, RO- and H2N-; the mechanisms are E1 and E2.

mcqs.why: In alkyl halide elimination the halogen atom is removed from the α-carbon and a hydrogen is removed from the β-carbon.

mcqs.why: The notes state that a hydrogen is removed from the β-carbon while the halogen leaves the α-carbon, allowing a double bond to form between them.

mcqs.why: A double bond forms between the α- and β-carbons during elimination, so the organic product is an alkene.

options: A proton (hydrogen ion) and a halide ion

lessons.title: E1 Mechanism (Unimolecular Elimination)
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation E1, E stands for elimination and 1 for unimolecular: only one molecule is involved in the rate-determining step. The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group is fully completed before any reaction occurs with the base to lose a hydrogen. The reaction of a tert-alkyl halide with a base occurs in two steps.

Step 1 (Slow, Rate-Determining)

The tert-butyl halide ionizes in a polar solvent to produce a planar carbocation and the leaving group. The bond breaks between the halogen atom and the α-carbon atom. This step involves the breakage of a covalent bond, so it is slow and rate-determining.

Step 2 (Fast)

The base (HO-) removes a proton from one of the β-carbons, and a new π-bond is formed between the α- and β-carbons, giving the alkene.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [(CH3)3CX], so Rate = k[(CH3)3CX]. The rate depends only on the concentration of the substrate (tert-butyl halide) and not on the concentration of the base. The reaction is first order overall.

Key Points

  • E1 is a two-step, unimolecular elimination through a carbocation.
  • Step 1 is the slow ionization of the tert-alkyl halide; it is rate-determining.
  • Step 2 is the fast removal of a β-proton by the base, forming the π-bond.
  • Rate = k[(CH3)3CX]: first order, independent of base concentration.

mcqs.q: In E1, the number 1 indicates:
mcqs.why: E1 stands for elimination unimolecular: only one molecule is involved in the rate-determining step, according to the notes.

options: Completed before any reaction with the base to lose hydrogen
Done by the base in the same transition state
mcqs.why: The notes state that in E1 the C-leaving group bond breaking is fully completed before any reaction occurs with the base to lose a hydrogen.

options: A planar carbocation and the leaving group
A transition state with partial bonds only
mcqs.why: Step 1 is ionization in a polar solvent to produce a planar carbocation and the leaving group, with the bond breaking between halogen and the α-carbon.

options: It combines a cation and an anion
It involves breakage of a covalent bond
The base removes a proton quickly
A π-bond forms in that step
mcqs.why: As in SN1, the ionization step involves breakage of a covalent bond, so the notes identify it as slow and rate-determining.

mcqs.why: The fast second step has the base, HO-, remove a proton from one of the β-carbons while the π-bond forms between α- and β-carbons.

mcqs.why: Kinetic evidence gives Rate = k[(CH3)3CX], depending only on substrate concentration and not on base concentration; the reaction is first order overall.

mcqs.why: Because the E1 rate law contains only the tert-butyl halide concentration, changing base concentration does not change the rate.

mcqs.why: Full working: Rate2/Rate1 = k(2[(CH3)3CX]) / k[(CH3)3CX] = 2, so doubling the substrate concentration doubles the first-order E1 rate.

mcqs.why: E1 is described as a two-step unimolecular elimination through a carbocation formed by ionization of the tert-alkyl halide.

mcqs.why: The π-bond forms in the fast second step as the base removes a β-proton and the α-β double bond of the alkene is created.

lessons.title: E2 Mechanism (Bimolecular Elimination)
lessons.notes_html:
In the designation E2, E stands for elimination and 2 for bimolecular: both the alkyl halide and the base are involved in the rate-determining step. The breaking of the bond between carbon and the leaving group and the reaction with the base to lose a proton (hydrogen) occur simultaneously. The reaction of a primary alkyl halide with a base occurs in one step.

The Transition State

In the transition state, the bond of the base to one of the β-hydrogens and the bond between the α- and β-carbon atoms are partially formed, while the bond of the β-hydrogen to carbon and the bond between the α-carbon and the leaving group are partially broken. This is the slow, rate-determining step. The product is an alkene, e.g. ethene from a primary halide.

Kinetic Evidence

Rate ∝ [RH2CX][OH-], so Rate = k[RH2CX][OH-]. The rate depends on the concentrations of both the substrate and the base. Doubling either reactant doubles the rate; doubling both quadruples it. The reaction is second order. (Keep in mind: primary alkyl halides undergo E2 reactions only; secondary and tertiary alkyl halides undergo both E1 and E2 reactions.)

Key Points

  • E2 is a one-step, bimolecular elimination.
  • Proton removal and leaving-group departure happen at the same time.
  • The reaction passes through a single transition state.
  • Rate = k[RX][OH-]: second order overall.
  • Primary halides follow E2 only; secondary and tertiary halides can follow E1 and E2.

mcqs.why: E2 stands for elimination bimolecular because both the alkyl halide and the base are involved in the rate-determining step.

mcqs.why: The single E2 transition-state step is identified in the notes as the slow, rate-determining step of the reaction.

mcqs.why: Kinetic evidence gives Rate = k[RH2CX][OH-], depending on both substrate and base concentrations, so the reaction is second order.

mcqs.q: If both [RX] and [OH-] are doubled in E2, the rate becomes:
mcqs.why: Full working: new rate = k(2[RX])(2[OH-]) = 4k[RX][OH-], so doubling both reactants quadruples the second-order E2 rate.

mcqs.why: The notes state that the product is an alkene, for example ethene from a primary halide undergoing E2 elimination.

mcqs.why: The notes remind that primary alkyl halides undergo E2 reactions only, unlike secondary and tertiary halides which can follow both pathways.

mcqs.why: The notes state that secondary and tertiary alkyl halides undergo both E1 and E2 reactions, depending on the conditions.

lessons.title: Substitution versus Elimination
lessons.notes_html:
All nucleophiles are possible bases and all bases are possible nucleophiles, because the reactive part of both is an unshared electron pair. Elimination reactions therefore occur simultaneously with substitution reactions: there is always a competition between them, and the reaction of a nucleophile (base) with an alkyl halide produces a mixture of elimination (alkene) and substitution products.

If the nucleophile attacks the α-carbon, substitution occurs. If it attacks a β-hydrogen, elimination occurs. The ratio of products depends on the relative rates of the two reactions, which are affected by these factors:

  • Nature of solvent: polar solvents favour substitution, while non-polar solvents favour elimination. In an aqueous medium (more polar), substitution is the main reaction and elimination is a side reaction; in an alcoholic medium (less polar), elimination is the main reaction and substitution is a side reaction.
  • Nature of base: strong bases favour elimination reactions.
  • Effect of temperature: an increase in temperature favours elimination over substitution.
  • Nature of substrate: crowding within the substrate favours elimination over substitution.
  • Nature of alkyl halide: primary alkyl halides favour mainly substitution; tertiary alkyl halides favour mainly elimination; secondary alkyl halides favour both.

Alkyl Halides as Precursors

A compound that participates in a chemical reaction and produces another compound is called a precursor. Alkyl halides act as precursors and produce many other organic chemicals in the laboratory, such as thiols, Grignard reagents and dialkyl disulphides.

  • R-X + KOH + H2S → R-SH + H2O + KX (thiols).
  • R-X + Mg → R-Mg-X in pure diethyl ether, in the absence of moisture, CO2 or O2 (Grignard reagents).
  • R-X + thiourea, with triethylamine (Et3N) in CCl4 at 50°C for about 12 hours → R-S-S-R (dialkyl disulphides), which are used to make other chemicals.

Key Points

  • Substitution and elimination always compete; a mixture of products is formed.
  • Attack at the α-carbon gives substitution; attack at a β-hydrogen gives elimination.
  • Polar (aqueous) solvents favour substitution; less polar (alcoholic) media favour elimination.
  • Strong bases, high temperature and a crowded substrate favour elimination.
  • Primary halides favour substitution; tertiary halides favour elimination.
  • Alkyl halides are precursors for thiols, Grignard reagents and dialkyl disulphides.

lessons.title: Organometallic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Compounds that have a metal-carbon bond are called organometallic compounds. For example, alkyl magnesium halides (RMgX) are organometallic compounds because they have metal-carbon bonds.

Alkyl magnesium halides are also known as Grignard reagents. They are named after the French chemist Victor Grignard, who discovered them in 1900 and received the Nobel Prize in 1912. Grignard reagents are used in the preparation of alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids. Their general formula is RMgX, where R is an alkyl or aryl group and X is chlorine, bromine or iodine.

Key Points

  • Organometallic compounds contain a direct metal-carbon bond.
  • Alkyl magnesium halides, RMgX, are called Grignard reagents.
  • They are named after Victor Grignard (discovered 1900; Nobel Prize 1912).
  • They are used to prepare alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids.
  • In RMgX, R is an alkyl or aryl group and X is Cl, Br or I.

lessons.title: Preparation of Grignard Reagents
lessons.notes_html:
Grignard reagents are prepared in the laboratory by the reaction of an alkyl or aryl halide with magnesium metal in the presence of pure diethyl ether, in the absence of moisture, CO2 or O2.

Key Reactions

ReactantsProduct
R-X + Mg (ether)RMgX (Grignard reagent)
CH3-Cl + Mg (ether)CH3-MgCl (methylmagnesium chloride)

Key Points

  • An alkyl or aryl halide reacts with magnesium metal to form a Grignard reagent.
  • The reaction is carried out in pure diethyl ether.
  • Moisture, CO2 and O2 must be absent, because the reagent reacts with them.
  • General equation: R-X + Mg → RMgX.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Grignard Reagents
lessons.notes_html:
Grignard reagents are highly reactive compounds because of the highly polar carbon-magnesium bond. Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so carbon has a partial negative charge (δ-) and magnesium a partial positive charge (δ+): R(δ-)-Mg(δ+)-X.

The partial negative charge on carbon makes the alkyl group highly reactive towards electrophiles, and the reagent acts as a source of a nucleophile (the carbon is nucleophilic, not electrophilic).

  • For the same alkyl group, the order of reactivity of halides towards magnesium is: RI > RBr > RCl. Alkyl iodide is more reactive than alkyl bromide, which is more reactive than alkyl chloride.
  • For a given halogen, the order of reactivity of alkyl groups is: CH3X > C2H5X > C3H7X. Methyl halide is more reactive than ethyl halide, which is more reactive than propyl halide.

Key Points

  • The C-Mg bond is highly polar: carbon is δ- and magnesium is δ+.
  • The negatively charged carbon attacks electrophiles; the reagent is a source of nucleophile.
  • Halide reactivity towards Mg: RI > RBr > RCl.
  • Alkyl group reactivity: CH3X > C2H5X > C3H7X.

mcqs.q: Why are Grignard reagents highly reactive?
options: Because the C-Mg bond is highly polar
Because magnesium is more electronegative than carbon
Because the reagent contains a halogen
Because ether makes the bond ionic
mcqs.why: The notes attribute the high reactivity to the highly polar carbon-magnesium bond, which makes the alkyl carbon strongly reactive towards electrophiles.

mcqs.q: What are the partial charges in R-Mg-X?
options: Carbon is δ+ and magnesium is δ-
Carbon is δ- and magnesium is δ+
Both carbon and magnesium are δ-
Both carbon and magnesium are δ+
mcqs.why: Carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, so carbon carries a partial negative charge δ- and magnesium carries a partial positive charge δ+.

mcqs.q: The carbon of a Grignard reagent behaves as:
mcqs.why: The partial negative charge on carbon makes it nucleophilic, not electrophilic, so the reagent acts as a source of a nucleophile that attacks electrophiles.

mcqs.q: For the same alkyl group, the reactivity of halides towards magnesium is:
mcqs.why: The notes give the order RI > RBr > RCl for the same alkyl group, so alkyl iodide is most reactive and alkyl chloride is least reactive towards magnesium.

mcqs.q: Which halide is most reactive towards magnesium for a given alkyl group?
mcqs.why: According to the order RI > RBr > RCl given in the notes, the alkyl iodide reacts most readily with magnesium to form the Grignard reagent.

mcqs.q: For a given halogen, the reactivity order of alkyl groups is:
mcqs.why: The notes state CH3X > C2H5X > C3H7X for a given halogen, so methyl halide is most reactive and propyl halide is least reactive in this series.

mcqs.q: Which alkyl halide is least reactive for a given halogen, according to the notes?
mcqs.why: In the order CH3X > C2H5X > C3H7X, propyl halide C3H7X comes last, so it is the least reactive of the three alkyl groups listed.

mcqs.why: The notes say carbon is more electronegative than magnesium, which is why carbon becomes δ- and magnesium becomes δ+ in the polar C-Mg bond.

mcqs.why: Because its carbon carries a partial negative charge, the Grignard reagent supplies a nucleophilic carbon that attacks electron-deficient electrophilic centres.

mcqs.why: The notes state the negatively charged alkyl carbon is highly reactive towards electrophiles, which are the electron-deficient species it attacks.

lessons.title: Reactions of Grignard Reagents with Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Grignard reagents react with organic and inorganic compounds to form a variety of valuable compounds. Their reactions with carbonyl compounds first give an addition product, which on acid hydrolysis gives an alcohol. These reactions can be used to increase the length of the carbon chain.

  • With formaldehyde: the addition product on acid hydrolysis forms a primary alcohol. Example: HCHO + CH3MgCl → addition product → (H2O/H+) CH3CH2OH, ethyl alcohol, a 1° alcohol.
  • With other aldehydes: the addition products on acid hydrolysis form secondary alcohols. Example: CH3CHO + CH3MgCl → addition product → (H2O/H+) isopropyl alcohol, a 2° alcohol.
  • With ketones: the addition products on acid hydrolysis form tertiary alcohols. Example: CH3COCH3 (acetone) + CH3MgCl → addition product → (H2O/H+) tert-butyl alcohol, a 3° alcohol.

Key Reactions

Carbonyl compoundProduct after hydrolysis
Formaldehyde (HCHO)Primary (1°) alcohol
Other aldehydes (RCHO)Secondary (2°) alcohol
Ketones (RCOR)Tertiary (3°) alcohol

Key Points

  • Grignard reagents add to the carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones.
  • Acid hydrolysis of the addition product gives an alcohol.
  • Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol; other aldehydes give secondary alcohols; ketones give tertiary alcohols.
  • These reactions increase the length of the carbon chain.

mcqs.why: The notes say reactions with carbonyl compounds first give an addition product, which only on acid hydrolysis gives the alcohol product.

mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is the special case in the notes: its addition product on acid hydrolysis forms a primary, or 1°, alcohol.

mcqs.why: The worked example is HCHO + CH3MgCl → addition product → CH3CH2OH, ethyl alcohol, which is a primary alcohol with two carbons.

mcqs.q: Other aldehydes (besides formaldehyde) with Grignard reagents give, after hydrolysis:
mcqs.why: The notes distinguish other aldehydes RCHO from formaldehyde: their addition products on hydrolysis form secondary, or 2°, alcohols.

mcqs.q: CH3CHO + CH3MgCl, after hydrolysis, gives:
mcqs.why: The example in the notes is CH3CHO + CH3MgCl → addition product → isopropyl alcohol, a secondary alcohol, after acid hydrolysis.

mcqs.q: Ketones with Grignard reagents, after hydrolysis, give:
mcqs.why: Ketones RCOR give tertiary, or 3°, alcohols after addition of a Grignard reagent and acid hydrolysis of the addition product.

mcqs.why: The notes give acetone + CH3MgCl → addition product → tert-butyl alcohol on H2O/H+ hydrolysis, a tertiary alcohol product.

options: Increase the length of the carbon chain
Decrease the carbon chain by one
Remove the carbonyl oxygen as CO2
mcqs.why: The notes explicitly say these reactions can be used to increase the length of the carbon chain, because the Grignard alkyl group adds to the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.why: In every example the addition product is converted to the alcohol by acid hydrolysis, written as H2O/H+ in the notes.

mcqs.why: The summary table is formaldehyde → 1° alcohol, other aldehydes → 2° alcohol, ketones → 3° alcohol, so only the other-aldehyde to secondary pairing is correct here.

lessons.title: Reactions of Grignard Reagents with Esters
lessons.notes_html:
The reaction of a Grignard reagent with an ester takes place in two steps.

Step 1

Ethyl formate reacts with the Grignard reagent to produce an unstable intermediate, which expels an alkoxide ion to produce an aldehyde. Example: ethyl formate + CH3MgCl → unstable intermediate → CH3CHO (acetaldehyde).

Step 2

The acetaldehyde reacts with a second molecule of the Grignard reagent to produce an unstable intermediate, which on acid hydrolysis forms a secondary alcohol: CH3CHO + CH3MgCl → intermediate → (H2O/H+) isopropyl alcohol, a 2° alcohol.

Keep in mind: esters other than ethyl formate react in the same way with an excess of Grignard reagent to form tertiary alcohols.

Key Points

  • Ethyl formate reacts with a Grignard reagent in two steps.
  • Step 1 gives an aldehyde through an unstable intermediate.
  • Step 2 adds a second Grignard molecule; hydrolysis gives a secondary alcohol.
  • Other esters with excess Grignard reagent give tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: How many steps are described for the reaction of a Grignard reagent with an ester?
mcqs.why: The notes describe the ester reaction in two steps: first formation of an aldehyde, then addition of a second Grignard molecule to that aldehyde.

mcqs.q: In step 1, ethyl formate + Grignard reagent produces, via an unstable intermediate:
mcqs.why: Step 1 in the notes: ethyl formate reacts to give an unstable intermediate which expels an alkoxide ion to produce an aldehyde.

mcqs.q: Ethyl formate + CH3MgCl gives in step 1:
mcqs.why: The specific example is ethyl formate + CH3MgCl → unstable intermediate → CH3CHO, which is acetaldehyde, before the second step occurs.

mcqs.q: What is expelled when the step 1 unstable intermediate forms the aldehyde?
mcqs.why: The notes say the unstable intermediate expels an alkoxide ion to produce the aldehyde in the first step of the ester reaction.

options: A second molecule of Grignard reagent
mcqs.why: Step 2 is the reaction of the acetaldehyde with a second molecule of the Grignard reagent to produce another unstable intermediate.

mcqs.q: Ethyl formate + CH3MgCl, after step 2 and acid hydrolysis, gives:
mcqs.why: The full example ends CH3CHO + CH3MgCl → intermediate → isopropyl alcohol on H2O/H+ hydrolysis, a secondary alcohol.

mcqs.q: The final alcohol from ethyl formate in the example is classified as:
mcqs.why: Isopropyl alcohol obtained from ethyl formate and CH3MgCl is stated in the notes to be a 2°, or secondary, alcohol.

mcqs.q: Esters other than ethyl formate, with excess Grignard reagent, form:
mcqs.why: The notes add a keep-in-mind point: esters other than ethyl formate react in the same way with excess Grignard reagent to form tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: What condition is needed for other esters to give tertiary alcohols?
mcqs.why: The notes specify excess Grignard reagent for esters other than ethyl formate, because two Grignard additions are needed to reach the tertiary alcohol.

mcqs.q: The second unstable intermediate in the ester reaction gives the alcohol on:
mcqs.why: As with aldehydes and ketones, the intermediate from the second addition forms the alcohol only on acid hydrolysis, as shown in the notes.

lessons.title: Reactions of Grignard Reagents with Carbon Dioxide
lessons.notes_html:
A Grignard reagent reacts with CO2 to produce an unstable intermediate, which on acid hydrolysis forms a carboxylic acid. Example: CH3MgCl + CO2 → unstable intermediate → (H2O/H+) CH3COOH, acetic acid. The product acid has one carbon more than the alkyl group of the reagent.

Organometallic Compounds in Medicines

Organometallic compounds play an important role in medicines, mainly in cancer therapy. Salvarsan, the first important organometallic medicine, was discovered in 1908 and used as an anti-syphilis drug. Cisplatin is a chemotherapy drug, highly effective in treating several cancers such as ovarian and testicular cancers. Carboplatin is used to treat ovarian cancer. Thimerosal (trade name merthiolate) is used as a preservative in vaccines, some cosmetics and eye drops, and as a disinfectant in pharmaceuticals. Merbromin (mercurochrome) is a weak antiseptic for minor cuts, bedsores and abrasions. Ferroquine is a next-generation drug with good antimalarial activity, and vanadoceneacetylacetonate (VDacac) shows anti-HIV properties.

Haemoglobin and Chlorophyll

Haemoglobin and chlorophyll are both pigments found in organisms, and both have a metallic element at the centre of the molecule. They differ in important ways: chlorophyll has magnesium at its centre, while haemoglobin has iron. Chlorophyll is found in the chloroplast of plant cells and gives the green colour to leaves, seaweed, algae and vegetables; it absorbs light energy from the sun and changes it into chemical energy by photosynthesis, so it is called the blood of plants. Haemoglobin is found in the blood of all vertebrates and some invertebrates; it gives the red colour to the blood (in RBCs) and transports oxygen from the lungs to various parts of the body.

Key Points

  • Grignard reagent + CO2, followed by acid hydrolysis, gives a carboxylic acid.
  • Example: CH3MgCl + CO2 → CH3COOH (acetic acid) after hydrolysis.
  • Organometallic compounds are used in medicines, e.g. salvarsan, cisplatin and carboplatin.
  • Chlorophyll has magnesium at its centre; haemoglobin has iron.
  • Chlorophyll absorbs light for photosynthesis; haemoglobin transports oxygen.

lessons.title: Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

Classification

  • Primary amine: one alkyl group is bonded to the nitrogen atom, R-NH2.
  • Secondary amine: two alkyl groups are bonded to the nitrogen atom, R2NH.
  • Tertiary amine: three alkyl groups are bonded to the nitrogen atom, R3N.

Amines are classified as primary, secondary or tertiary depending on the number of alkyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom.

Key Points

  • Amines are derivatives of ammonia with one or more H atoms replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.
  • Primary amines have one alkyl group on nitrogen.
  • Secondary amines have two alkyl groups on nitrogen.
  • Tertiary amines have three alkyl groups on nitrogen.

mcqs.q: Amines are derivatives of which compound?
mcqs.why: Amines are defined as derivatives of ammonia in which one or more hydrogen atoms have been replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

mcqs.why: A primary amine has one alkyl group bonded to nitrogen, written R-NH2 in the notes, with two hydrogens still on nitrogen.

mcqs.why: Secondary amines have two alkyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom, giving the form R2NH as stated in the classification.

mcqs.q: A tertiary amine is represented as:
mcqs.why: A tertiary amine has three alkyl groups bonded to nitrogen and no N-H hydrogen, so it is written R3N in the notes.

options: The number of alkyl groups bonded to nitrogen
The number of carbon atoms in the chain
mcqs.why: Classification depends on the number of alkyl groups bonded to the nitrogen atom: one gives primary, two secondary, and three tertiary.

mcqs.why: The definition specifies replacement by alkyl or aryl groups, not by halogens, oxygen or metals, to form amines from ammonia.

mcqs.why: R2NH has two R groups on nitrogen and one hydrogen remaining, which matches the secondary amine definition in the notes.

mcqs.why: A primary amine, R-NH2, has exactly one alkyl group bonded to the nitrogen atom, as stated in the classification section.

mcqs.why: R3N has three alkyl groups replacing all three hydrogens of ammonia, so no hydrogen remains directly bonded to nitrogen.

mcqs.why: Two alkyl groups on nitrogen define a secondary amine, R2NH, regardless of the identity of the particular alkyl groups present.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Common Names

Common names are obtained by adding the suffix amine to the name of the alkyl or aryl group; the whole name is written as one word. If there are two or more identical alkyl or aryl groups, the prefix di- or tri- is used. If there are two or more different groups, their names are arranged in alphabetical order. Examples: methylamine, ethylamine, ethylmethylamine, ethyldimethylamine, trimethylamine. In the common system, most primary amines are named as alkylamines.

IUPAC Names: Primary Amines

Primary amines with more complex groups are named as alkanamines.

  • Select the longest continuous chain of carbon atoms containing the amino group.
  • Replace the ending -e of the parent alkane by the suffix amine.
  • Number the parent chain from the end nearer to the amino group.
  • When another functional group is present, the amino group is generally listed as a substituent (amino-).

Examples: methanamine, ethanamine, 2-propanamine, 3-amino-2-butanol, 2-methyl-2-butanamine, 2,3-dimethyl-2-pentanamine.

IUPAC Names: Secondary and Tertiary Amines

  • They are named as derivatives of primary amines.
  • The longest chain bonded to the nitrogen atom is taken as the parent chain; the remaining alkyl groups are named as substituents.
  • The locant N is used to show substituents bonded to the nitrogen atom.
  • If the same alkyl group appears more than once, the prefix di or tri is used; different groups are named individually in alphabetical order.
  • Secondary amines are named as N-alkylalkanamines; tertiary amines as N,N-dialkylalkanamines (same groups) or N-alkyl-N-alkylalkanamines (different groups).

Examples: N-methylethanamine, N-ethylethanamine, N,N-dimethylmethanamine, N-ethyl-N-methyl-2-propanamine.

Key Points

  • Common names: alkyl group name + amine, written as one word.
  • IUPAC primary amines are alkanamines: longest chain with -NH2, -e replaced by -amine.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer the amino group.
  • Substituents on nitrogen are shown by the locant N.
  • Secondary amines are N-alkylalkanamines; tertiary amines are N,N-dialkylalkanamines.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Physical State

Lower amines are gases. Higher amines with three or more carbon atoms are liquids, and still higher ones are solids.

Odour

Methylamine and ethylamine have an ammoniacal smell, but higher amines have a fishy smell.

Boiling Points

Amines are polar compounds; their polarity is due to the nitrogen atom. Primary and secondary amines form intermolecular hydrogen bonds. The hydrogen bonds in alcohols are much stronger than in amines, because oxygen is more electronegative than nitrogen. Amines therefore have higher boiling points than the corresponding hydrocarbons, but lower boiling points than the corresponding alcohols or carboxylic acids. Tertiary amines do not form hydrogen bonds with each other, so their boiling points are similar to those of the corresponding alkanes.

Solubility

Lower amines are soluble in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl group (the hydrophobic part) increases, and higher members are predominantly insoluble in water. Amines are more soluble in water than the corresponding alcohols and ethers, which may be due to the increased basicity of the amines.

Key Points

  • Lower amines are gases, C3 and higher members are liquids, and the highest are solids.
  • Lower amines smell ammoniacal; higher amines smell fishy.
  • Primary and secondary amines hydrogen-bond with each other; tertiary amines do not.
  • Amines boil higher than hydrocarbons but lower than alcohols and carboxylic acids.
  • Lower amines are miscible with water; solubility falls as the alkyl group grows.

lessons.title: Structure of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
The nitrogen atom in amines is sp3 hybridized. Nitrogen has five electrons in its valence shell: three unpaired electrons and one lone pair of electrons. The three unpaired electrons form sigma bonds with hydrogen atoms or with carbon atoms of alkyl groups.

According to VSEPR theory, a molecule with three bond pairs and one lone pair has a trigonal pyramidal shape. Hence the structure of amines is trigonal pyramidal. The C-N-C angle in amines is less than 109.5°; the angles in amines are approximately 108°.

Key Points

  • The nitrogen atom of an amine is sp3 hybridized.
  • Nitrogen forms three sigma bonds and carries one lone pair.
  • With three bond pairs and one lone pair, the shape is trigonal pyramidal.
  • The C-N-C bond angle is about 108°, less than the tetrahedral 109.5°.

mcqs.q: The nitrogen atom in amines is hybridized as:
mcqs.why: The structure section states the nitrogen atom in amines is sp3 hybridized, with three bond pairs and one lone pair around it.

mcqs.q: Nitrogen in amines has in its valence shell:
options: Five electrons: three unpaired and one lone pair
mcqs.why: Nitrogen has five valence electrons: three unpaired electrons that form sigma bonds and one lone pair of electrons, as described in the notes.

mcqs.q: The three unpaired electrons on nitrogen form:
options: Sigma bonds with H or C atoms
mcqs.why: The unpaired electrons form sigma bonds with hydrogen atoms or with carbon atoms of alkyl groups, giving three sigma bonds around nitrogen.

mcqs.q: According to VSEPR, three bond pairs and one lone pair give:
mcqs.why: VSEPR theory predicts a trigonal pyramidal shape for three bond pairs plus one lone pair, which is the structure stated for amines.

mcqs.q: The C-N-C angle in amines is approximately:
mcqs.why: The notes give the C-N-C angle as approximately 108°, which is less than the ideal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.

mcqs.q: The amine bond angle is less than 109.5° by how much if it is 108°?
mcqs.why: Arithmetic check: 109.5 - 108 = 1.5, so the observed angle of about 108° is 1.5° less than the tetrahedral 109.5° value.

mcqs.q: The shape of amines is described as:
mcqs.why: Because of the lone pair, the arrangement of atoms is trigonal pyramidal, even though the electron-pair geometry is based on sp3 hybridization.

mcqs.why: Nitrogen forms three sigma bonds, using its three unpaired electrons, and retains one lone pair, totalling four electron pairs.

mcqs.why: The lone pair is one of the four sp3 electron pairs; it compresses the C-N-C angle to about 108°, below the 109.5° tetrahedral value.

options: N is sp2 and angle is 120°

mcqs.why: Both facts in this option match the notes: nitrogen is sp3 hybridized and, with a lone pair, the molecular shape is trigonal pyramidal.

lessons.title: Basicity of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are basic in nature because of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. Alkanamines are more basic than ammonia because of the electron-releasing alkyl groups: the alkyl groups concentrate the electron density on nitrogen and make the lone pair more easily available for sharing with acids. The expected order of basicity is therefore 3° alkylamines > 2° alkylamines > 1° alkylamines.

The methylamines follow this expected order in the gas phase. In aqueous solution, however, they do not follow the expected trend, and the order changes to: (CH3)2NH (pKb = 3.29) > CH3NH2 (pKb = 3.36) > (CH3)3N (pKb = 4.28). The larger the value of pKb, the smaller is the tendency to accept a proton from water. Basic strength in aqueous solution depends not only on the electron-releasing effect of the alkyl groups, but also on the steric effect and the hydration effect: due to the high steric effect, a 3° alkylamine cannot easily donate its electron pair to a proton.

Key Points

  • Amines are basic because nitrogen carries a lone pair of electrons.
  • Alkyl groups release electrons, so alkanamines are more basic than ammonia.
  • Expected (gas phase) order: 3° > 2° > 1° alkylamines.
  • In water the order is (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N, by their pKb values 3.29, 3.36 and 4.28.
  • A larger pKb means a weaker base (less tendency to accept a proton).
  • Steric and hydration effects also control basic strength in aqueous solution.

mcqs.q: Amines are basic because of:
options: The lone pair of electrons on nitrogen
mcqs.why: Basicity is due to the lone pair of electrons on nitrogen, which can be shared with a proton from an acid or from water.

mcqs.q: Alkanamines are more basic than ammonia because alkyl groups:
options: Release electrons and concentrate density on nitrogen
mcqs.why: Alkyl groups are electron-releasing: they concentrate electron density on nitrogen and make the lone pair more easily available for sharing with acids.

mcqs.q: The expected (gas phase) basicity order for alkylamines is:
mcqs.why: Based only on the electron-releasing effect, the expected order is 3° alkylamines > 2° alkylamines > 1° alkylamines, followed in the gas phase by methylamines.

mcqs.q: In aqueous solution, the methylamine basicity order by pKb is:
mcqs.why: In water the order is (CH3)2NH (pKb 3.29) > CH3NH2 (pKb 3.36) > (CH3)3N (pKb 4.28), with lower pKb meaning stronger base.

mcqs.q: A larger pKb value means:
options: A weaker base with smaller tendency to accept a proton
Greater tendency to accept a proton
mcqs.why: The notes state the larger the pKb, the smaller is the tendency to accept a proton from water, so larger pKb corresponds to a weaker base.

mcqs.q: Which methylamine is the strongest base in aqueous solution?
mcqs.why: Dimethylamine has the smallest pKb, 3.29, among the three, and smaller pKb means stronger base, so (CH3)2NH is strongest in water.

mcqs.q: What is the pKb difference between (CH3)3N (4.28) and (CH3)2NH (3.29)?
mcqs.why: Arithmetic check: 4.28 - 3.29 = 0.99, so trimethylamine's pKb is 0.99 higher than dimethylamine's, making it the weaker base in water.

mcqs.q: Basic strength in aqueous solution depends, besides the electron-releasing effect, on:
mcqs.why: The notes add steric effect and hydration effect: due to high steric effect, a 3° amine cannot easily donate its electron pair to a proton.

mcqs.q: Why does a 3° alkylamine donate its pair less easily in water?
options: Due to high steric effect around nitrogen
mcqs.why: The steric effect explanation is that crowding around nitrogen in a 3° alkylamine hinders donation of its electron pair to a proton.

mcqs.q: The methylamines follow the expected 3° > 2° > 1° order in:
mcqs.why: The notes contrast the phases: methylamines follow the expected order in the gas phase, but they do not follow it in aqueous solution.

lessons.title: Alkylation of Ammonia by Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
An alkyl halide reacts with an aqueous or alcoholic solution of ammonia in a sealed tube on heating to produce primary, secondary and tertiary amines. This is a nucleophilic substitution (SN2) reaction. The process of cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond by an ammonia molecule is known as ammonolysis.

Key Reactions

StepReaction
1NH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI
2CH3NH2 + CH3I → (CH3)2NH + HI
3(CH3)2NH + CH3I → (CH3)3N + HI
4(CH3)3N + CH3I → [(CH3)4N]+ I- (quaternary ammonium salt)

The primary amine is the major product when ammonia is present in excess. Conversely, the tertiary amine is the major product when the alkyl halide is present in excess. The resulting ammonium salt, on treatment with a base, regenerates the amine: [(CH3)4N]+I- + NaOH → (CH3)3N + NaI + CH3OH.

Key Points

  • Alkyl halides react with ammonia (aqueous or alcoholic, sealed tube, heating) to give amines.
  • This cleavage of the C-X bond by ammonia is called ammonolysis; it is an SN2 reaction.
  • The reaction continues stepwise: 1° amine → 2° amine → 3° amine → quaternary ammonium salt.
  • Excess ammonia makes the primary amine the major product.
  • Excess alkyl halide makes the tertiary amine the major product.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halide + ammonia in a sealed tube on heating gives:
mcqs.why: Heating an alkyl halide with aqueous or alcoholic ammonia in a sealed tube produces primary, secondary and tertiary amines in succession.

mcqs.q: The cleavage of the C-halogen bond by ammonia is called:
mcqs.why: The process of cleavage of the carbon-halogen bond by an ammonia molecule is known as ammonolysis, and it is an SN2 reaction.

mcqs.q: The alkylation of ammonia by alkyl halides is which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: The notes classify this reaction as a nucleophilic substitution, specifically SN2, in which ammonia attacks the alkyl halide carbon.

mcqs.q: Step 4, (CH3)3N + CH3I, gives:
mcqs.why: The fourth step forms the quaternary ammonium salt [(CH3)4N]+ I- from trimethylamine and methyl iodide, completing the stepwise sequence.

mcqs.q: The primary amine is the major product when:
mcqs.why: The notes state the primary amine is major when ammonia is present in excess; conversely tertiary amine is major when alkyl halide is in excess.

mcqs.q: The tertiary amine is the major product when:
mcqs.why: With excess alkyl halide, further alkylation is favoured and the tertiary amine becomes the major product, opposite to the excess-ammonia case.

mcqs.q: The sequence of products in ammonolysis is:
mcqs.why: The stepwise reactions go NH3 → CH3NH2 → (CH3)2NH → (CH3)3N → [(CH3)4N]+ I-, i.e. 1° to 2° to 3° to quaternary salt.

mcqs.q: Treatment of the quaternary ammonium salt with a base such as NaOH regenerates:
mcqs.why: The notes say the resulting ammonium salt, on treatment with a base, regenerates the amine, illustrated with NaOH in the given equation.

mcqs.q: In step 1, NH3 + CH3I gives:
mcqs.why: Step 1 in the table is NH3 + CH3I → CH3NH2 + HI, forming the primary amine methylamine as the first product.

mcqs.q: Conditions for alkylation of ammonia are:
options: Aqueous or alcoholic ammonia, sealed tube, heating
mcqs.why: The reaction uses an aqueous or alcoholic solution of ammonia in a sealed tube on heating, distinct from Grignard or reduction conditions.

lessons.title: Reduction of Nitrogen Containing Functional Groups
lessons.notes_html:
Amines are obtained by the reduction of nitrogen-containing functional groups such as nitriles, nitro compounds and amides.

Reduction of Nitriles

Nitriles are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4 or by catalytic hydrogenation: CH3CN + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 (LiAlH4); CH3CN + 2H2 → CH3CH2NH2 (Ni). This method is used for increasing the length of the carbon chain.

Reduction of Nitro Compounds

Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4, or Zn/HCl, or H2/Ni, or H2/Pt: CH3NO2 + 6[H] → CH3NH2 + 2H2O (LiAlH4); CH3NO2 + 3H2 → CH3NH2 + 2H2O (Pt).

Reduction of Amides

Amides are reduced to primary amines by LiAlH4: CH3CONH2 (acetamide) + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 + H2O (LiAlH4).

Key Reactions

Starting materialReagentProduct
CH3CN (nitrile)LiAlH4 or H2/NiCH3CH2NH2
CH3NO2 (nitro compound)LiAlH4 or H2/PtCH3NH2
CH3CONH2 (amide)LiAlH4CH3CH2NH2

Key Points

  • Reduction of nitriles, nitro compounds and amides gives primary amines.
  • Nitriles are reduced by LiAlH4 or catalytic hydrogenation; the chain grows by one carbon.
  • Nitro compounds are reduced by LiAlH4, Zn/HCl, H2/Ni or H2/Pt.
  • Amides are reduced by LiAlH4.

mcqs.q: Reduction of nitriles gives which type of amine?
mcqs.why: Reduction of nitriles, nitro compounds and amides all give primary amines, as summarised in the key reactions table.

mcqs.q: Nitriles are reduced to primary amines by:
mcqs.why: Nitriles are reduced by LiAlH4 or by catalytic hydrogenation, e.g. CH3CN + 2H2 → CH3CH2NH2 with Ni catalyst.

mcqs.q: CH3CN + 2H2 with Ni gives:
mcqs.why: Catalytic hydrogenation of CH3CN adds hydrogen across the nitrile to give CH3CH2NH2, ethylamine, a primary amine with a longer chain.

mcqs.q: Reduction of nitriles is used for:
options: Increasing the length of the carbon chain
mcqs.why: The notes say nitrile reduction is used for increasing the length of the carbon chain, because the nitrile carbon becomes the CH2NH2 carbon.

mcqs.q: Nitro compounds are reduced to primary amines by:
mcqs.why: Nitro compound reduction can use LiAlH4, or Zn/HCl, or H2/Ni, or H2/Pt, all listed as reagents giving primary amines.

mcqs.q: CH3NO2 + 3H2 with Pt gives:
mcqs.why: The equation is CH3NO2 + 3H2 → CH3NH2 + 2H2O with Pt, so nitromethane is reduced to methylamine plus two waters.

mcqs.q: Amides are reduced to primary amines by:
mcqs.why: Amide reduction in the notes uses LiAlH4: CH3CONH2 + 4[H] → CH3CH2NH2 + H2O, giving a primary amine.

mcqs.q: Acetamide CH3CONH2 on reduction with LiAlH4 gives:
mcqs.why: Acetamide, CH3CONH2, plus 4[H] from LiAlH4 gives CH3CH2NH2 plus H2O, as shown in the reduction of amides section.

mcqs.q: Which starting material gives CH3NH2 on reduction, not CH3CH2NH2?
mcqs.why: CH3NO2 reduces to CH3NH2, while both CH3CN and CH3CONH2 reduce to CH3CH2NH2, according to the summary table.

mcqs.q: All three reductions in this lesson (nitrile, nitro, amide) give:
mcqs.why: The unifying point of the lesson is that reduction of nitriles, nitro compounds and amides gives primary amines as products.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Amines
lessons.notes_html:
Amines can act both as bases and as nucleophiles. Their main reactions are due to the presence of the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom. These electrons attack the electron-deficient centres (positive or slightly positive parts) of other molecules.

Important Reactions of Amines as Nucleophiles

  • Amines are alkylated by alkyl halides through nucleophilic substitution, forming a mixture of products (higher amines and quaternary salts).
  • Amines react with acid halides (or acid anhydrides) through nucleophilic acyl substitution to form substituted amides.
  • Amines react with aldehydes and ketones to form carbinolamines, which dehydrate to imines.
  • Acting as bases, amines react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts.

Key Points

  • The lone pair on nitrogen makes amines both bases and nucleophiles.
  • Amines attack electron-deficient centres of other molecules.
  • With alkyl halides they are alkylated by nucleophilic substitution.
  • With acid halides they form substituted amides by nucleophilic acyl substitution.
  • With nitrous acid they form diazonium salts.

mcqs.q: Amines can act both as bases and as:
mcqs.why: Amines act both as bases and as nucleophiles, and both roles are due to the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom.

mcqs.q: The main reactions of amines are due to:
options: The lone pair of electrons on nitrogen
mcqs.why: The reactivity section states the main reactions are due to the lone pair on nitrogen, which attacks electron-deficient centres.

mcqs.q: The lone pair of an amine attacks:
options: Electron-deficient centres (positive or slightly positive parts)
mcqs.why: These electrons attack the electron-deficient centres, i.e. positive or slightly positive parts, of other molecules, acting as a nucleophile.

mcqs.q: With alkyl halides, amines undergo:
mcqs.why: As nucleophiles, amines are alkylated by alkyl halides through nucleophilic substitution, forming higher amines and quaternary salts.

mcqs.q: With acid halides, amines form substituted amides by:
mcqs.why: Amines react with acid halides or anhydrides through nucleophilic acyl substitution to form substituted amides, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: With aldehydes and ketones, amines first form:
mcqs.why: Amines react with aldehydes and ketones to form carbinolamines, which dehydrate to imines, according to the important reactions list.

mcqs.q: Acting as bases, amines react with nitrous acid to form:
mcqs.why: The notes list that, acting as bases, amines react with nitrous acid to form diazonium salts, a key reaction of primary amines.

mcqs.q: Which reagent gives a substituted amide with an amine?
mcqs.why: Acid halides (or acid anhydrides) give substituted amides with amines by nucleophilic acyl substitution at the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: Which reagent gives an imine (via carbinolamine) with an amine?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones are the carbonyl partners that form carbinolamines with amines, which then dehydrate to imines.

mcqs.q: The dual base/nucleophile character of amines comes from nitrogen's:
mcqs.why: Both basic and nucleophilic behaviour trace to the same feature emphasised throughout: the lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom.

lessons.title: Alkylation of Amines by Alkyl Halides
lessons.notes_html:
Amines react with primary alkyl halides to form alkylated ammonium halides. The alkylation proceeds step by step: each product amine reacts further with more alkyl halide.

Key Reactions

StepReactionProduct type
1CH3NH2 + CH3CH2Br → CH3-NH-CH2CH3 + HBr2° amine
2CH3-NH-CH2CH3 + CH3CH2Br → CH3-N(CH2CH3)2 + HBr3° amine
3CH3-N(CH2CH3)2 + CH3CH2Br → [CH3-N(CH2CH3)3]+ Br-Quaternary salt

Key Points

  • Amines are alkylated by primary alkyl halides in a stepwise manner.
  • A primary amine gives a secondary amine, then a tertiary amine.
  • Further alkylation of a tertiary amine gives a quaternary ammonium salt.
  • Because the reaction does not stop at one stage, a mixture of products is obtained.
