mcqs.q: Amines react with primary alkyl halides to form:
mcqs.why: The lesson states amines react with primary alkyl halides to form alkylated ammonium halides, proceeding step by step.

mcqs.q: Alkylation of amines proceeds:
options: Step by step, each product reacting further
mcqs.why: Each product amine reacts further with more alkyl halide, so alkylation proceeds in a stepwise manner through successive stages.

mcqs.q: CH3NH2 + CH3CH2Br gives, as the organic amine product type:
mcqs.why: Step 1 is CH3NH2 + CH3CH2Br → CH3-NH-CH2CH3 + HBr, classified in the table as a 2° (secondary) amine product.

mcqs.q: Step 2, CH3-NH-CH2CH3 + CH3CH2Br, gives a product of type:
mcqs.why: Step 2 adds a second ethyl group to nitrogen to give CH3-N(CH2CH3)2, which the table classifies as a 3° (tertiary) amine.

mcqs.q: Further alkylation of a tertiary amine gives:
mcqs.why: Step 3 forms [CH3-N(CH2CH3)3]+ Br-, a quaternary ammonium salt, when the tertiary amine reacts with another alkyl halide.

mcqs.q: Why is a mixture of products obtained in amine alkylation?
options: The reaction does not stop at one stage
mcqs.why: Because the reaction does not stop at one stage, each amine product can be alkylated again, so a mixture of products is obtained.

mcqs.q: In step 3, the counter-ion in the quaternary salt from CH3CH2Br is:
mcqs.why: The alkyl halide used is CH3CH2Br, so the quaternary salt formed is [CH3-N(CH2CH3)3]+ Br-, with bromide as the anion.

mcqs.q: The starting amine in the stepwise example is:
mcqs.why: The sequence starts from CH3NH2, methylamine, which is ethylated stepwise to secondary, tertiary and finally quaternary products.

mcqs.q: Each alkylation step in the table also produces:
mcqs.why: Each of the first two steps is written with HBr as the by-product, e.g. CH3NH2 + CH3CH2Br → secondary amine + HBr.

mcqs.q: A primary amine, after one alkylation with a primary alkyl halide, becomes:
mcqs.why: One alkylation replaces one N-H hydrogen with an alkyl group, converting a primary amine into a secondary amine, as in step 1.

lessons.title: Reaction of Amines with Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes react with primary amines to form a carbinolamine, which dehydrates to produce an aldimine (a Schiff's base). Example: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3CHO → carbinolamine → (heat) CH3CH2-N=CH-CH3 + H2O.

Ketones react with primary amines in the same way: they form a carbinolamine, which dehydrates to produce a ketimine (a Schiff's base). Example: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3COCH3 → carbinolamine → (heat) CH3CH2-N=C(CH3)2 + H2O.

Key Points

  • Primary amines add to aldehydes and ketones to form carbinolamines.
  • The carbinolamine loses water (dehydrates) on heating.
  • Aldehydes give aldimines; ketones give ketimines.
  • Aldimines and ketimines are called Schiff's bases.

mcqs.q: Aldehydes react with primary amines to first form:
mcqs.why: Aldehydes add to primary amines to form a carbinolamine, which then dehydrates to produce the final imine product.

mcqs.q: The carbinolamine dehydrates to produce, from an aldehyde:
mcqs.why: From an aldehyde the dehydration product is an aldimine, while from a ketone it is a ketimine; both are called Schiff's bases.

mcqs.q: Ketones react with primary amines to form, after dehydration:
mcqs.why: Ketones form a carbinolamine which dehydrates to a ketimine, exemplified by CH3CH2-N=C(CH3)2 from ethylamine and acetone.

mcqs.q: Aldimines and ketimines are collectively called:
mcqs.why: The key points state aldimines and ketimines are called Schiff's bases, the dehydration products of carbinolamines.

mcqs.q: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3CHO, on heating, gives:
mcqs.why: The aldehyde example is CH3CH2NH2 + CH3CHO → carbinolamine → CH3CH2-N=CH-CH3 + H2O on heating, an aldimine.

mcqs.q: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3COCH3, on heating, gives:
mcqs.why: The ketone example uses acetone: ethylamine + CH3COCH3 → carbinolamine → CH3CH2-N=C(CH3)2 + H2O, a ketimine.

mcqs.q: Dehydration of the carbinolamine occurs on:
mcqs.why: The arrows in both examples show the carbinolamine loses water on heating (heat written over the arrow) to give the imine.

mcqs.q: What is lost when a carbinolamine becomes an imine?
mcqs.why: Dehydration means loss of water: the carbinolamine loses H2O to form the C=N double bond of the aldimine or ketimine.

mcqs.q: Which amine type is used in the aldehyde/ketone examples?
mcqs.why: Both examples start from a primary amine, CH3CH2NH2 (ethylamine), reacting with the carbonyl compound to give the Schiff's base.

mcqs.q: The intermediate between the amine + carbonyl and the imine is:
mcqs.why: The carbinolamine is the named intermediate formed by addition, before it dehydrates to the aldimine or ketimine product.

lessons.title: Preparation of Amides
lessons.notes_html:
Amines attack the carbonyl group of an acid chloride and form amides (nucleophilic acyl substitution). A base such as NaOH or pyridine is used to neutralize the HCl produced.

Key Reactions

ReactionProduct
CH3CH2NH2 + CH3COCl (NaOH)CH3CO-NH-CH2CH3 (N-ethylethanamide) + HCl
NaOH + HClNaCl + H2O (the base neutralizes the acid)

Key Points

  • Amines react with acid chlorides to form substituted amides.
  • The reaction is a nucleophilic acyl substitution at the carbonyl carbon.
  • HCl is formed as a by-product.
  • NaOH or pyridine is added to neutralize the HCl.

mcqs.q: Amines attack the carbonyl group of an acid chloride to form:
mcqs.why: Amines attack the carbonyl group of an acid chloride and form amides by nucleophilic acyl substitution, as stated in the lesson.

mcqs.q: The reaction of an amine with an acid chloride is classified as:
mcqs.why: The reaction is explicitly a nucleophilic acyl substitution at the carbonyl carbon, not a simple alkyl substitution or elimination.

mcqs.q: CH3CH2NH2 + CH3COCl (with NaOH) gives:
mcqs.why: The key reaction gives CH3CO-NH-CH2CH3, named N-ethylethanamide, plus HCl which is neutralized by the base present.

mcqs.q: What by-product acid is formed in amide preparation from acid chlorides?
mcqs.why: HCl is formed as a by-product when the amine displaces chloride from the acid chloride to form the substituted amide.

mcqs.q: Why is NaOH or pyridine used in this reaction?
mcqs.why: A base such as NaOH or pyridine is used to neutralize the HCl produced, e.g. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O.

mcqs.q: NaOH + HCl in this preparation gives:
mcqs.why: The neutralization equation given is NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H2O, removing the acid by-product as salt and water.

mcqs.q: The amine in the worked example is:
mcqs.why: The example uses CH3CH2NH2, ethylamine, reacting with CH3COCl to give N-ethylethanamide, a substituted amide.

mcqs.q: The acid chloride in the worked example is:
mcqs.why: CH3COCl, ethanoyl chloride, provides the CH3CO- acyl group that ends up in the product N-ethylethanamide.

mcqs.q: The product N-ethylethanamide is a:
mcqs.why: The product contains the -CO-NH- linkage formed by acyl substitution and is named as a substituted amide in the notes.

mcqs.q: The site attacked by the amine in acid chloride is:
mcqs.why: Amines attack the carbonyl group, specifically its carbon, in nucleophilic acyl substitution, displacing chloride to form the amide.

lessons.title: Preparation of Diazonium Salts
lessons.notes_html:
Amines react with nitrous acid to produce diazonium salts: R-NH2 + HNO2 + HCl → [R-N≡N]+Cl- + 2H2O.

The diazonium salts are highly unstable. They decompose spontaneously by losing nitrogen to give carbocations: [R-N≡N]+Cl- → R+ + Cl- + N2. The carbocations then change into mixtures of products:

  • Alkenes (by loss of H+).
  • Alcohols (by reaction with H2O, with H+ formed).
  • Alkyl halides (by reaction with Cl-).

Key Points

  • Primary amines react with nitrous acid (HNO2 + HCl) to form diazonium salts.
  • Diazonium salts are highly unstable.
  • They decompose spontaneously, losing N2 to give carbocations.
  • The carbocations give mixtures of alkenes, alcohols and alkyl halides.

mcqs.q: Primary amines react with nitrous acid to produce:
mcqs.why: The reaction R-NH2 + HNO2 + HCl → [R-N≡N]+Cl- + 2H2O produces a diazonium salt from a primary amine.

mcqs.q: The reagents for diazonium salt preparation are:
mcqs.why: Diazonium salts are prepared using nitrous acid together with HCl, as shown in the general equation in the notes.

mcqs.q: How many water molecules are in the diazonium formation equation?
mcqs.why: The balanced form given is R-NH2 + HNO2 + HCl → [R-N≡N]+Cl- + 2H2O, so two water molecules are produced.

mcqs.q: Diazonium salts are described as:
mcqs.why: The notes emphasise diazonium salts are highly unstable and decompose spontaneously by losing nitrogen.

mcqs.q: Diazonium salts decompose spontaneously by losing nitrogen to give:
mcqs.why: Decomposition is [R-N≡N]+Cl- → R+ + Cl- + N2, so loss of N2 leaves a carbocation R+ as the reactive intermediate.

mcqs.q: The gas lost on decomposition of a diazonium salt is:
mcqs.why: Nitrogen gas N2 is expelled when the diazonium salt decomposes, driving formation of the carbocation product mixture.

mcqs.q: Carbocations from diazonium decomposition give alkenes by:
mcqs.why: The product list says alkenes are formed by loss of H+ from the carbocation, one of three product pathways listed.

mcqs.q: Carbocations from diazonium decomposition give alcohols by:
mcqs.why: Alcohols arise by reaction of the carbocation with H2O, with H+ formed, according to the mixture-of-products list.

mcqs.q: Carbocations from diazonium decomposition give alkyl halides by:
mcqs.why: Alkyl halides are formed by reaction of the carbocation with Cl-, the chloride present from the diazonium chloride salt.

mcqs.q: The overall result of diazonium decomposition is:
options: A mixture of alkenes, alcohols and alkyl halides
mcqs.why: Because the carbocation can lose H+, react with water, or react with Cl-, the carbocations change into mixtures of products.

lessons.title: Introduction
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols, phenols and ethers are hydrocarbon derivatives whose functional groups contain one oxygen atom in two single bonds. They all contain the hydroxyl group (—OH) or an oxygen atom like the oxygen of water, so they are also called the oxygen family of organic compounds.

Their structures are derived from the structure of water (H—O—H). If one hydrogen of water is replaced by an alkyl group, an alcohol (R—O—H) is formed. If it is replaced by a phenyl group, a phenol (C6H5—O—H) is formed. If both hydrogens are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, an ether (R—O—R) is formed.

Alcohols and phenols both have a hydroxyl (—OH) group, but alcohols are the hydroxyl derivatives of alkanes, while phenols are the hydroxyl derivatives of benzene. These compounds occur widely in nature and have many pharmaceutical, biological and industrial applications.

Key Points

  • Alcohols, phenols and ethers form the oxygen family of organic compounds.
  • All three are derived from water: alcohol = R—O—H, phenol = C6H5—O—H, ether = R—O—R.
  • Alcohols are hydroxyl derivatives of alkanes.
  • Phenols are hydroxyl derivatives of benzene.
  • They are widely used in medicines, biology and industry.

mcqs.q: Alcohols, phenols and ethers are together called which family of organic compounds?
mcqs.why: The notes state that because they contain hydroxyl or water-like oxygen, they are called the oxygen family of organic compounds.

mcqs.q: The functional groups of alcohols, phenols and ethers contain one oxygen atom in how many single bonds?
mcqs.why: The introduction says their functional groups contain one oxygen atom in two single bonds, like the oxygen of water.

mcqs.q: From which compound are the structures of alcohols, phenols and ethers derived?
mcqs.why: Their structures are derived from water, H-O-H, by replacing one or both hydrogen atoms with other groups.

mcqs.q: Replacing one hydrogen of water by an alkyl group gives which compound?
mcqs.why: If one hydrogen of water is replaced by an alkyl group, an alcohol with formula R-O-H is formed.

mcqs.q: What is the general representation of a phenol given in the notes?
mcqs.why: A phenol is formed when one hydrogen of water is replaced by a phenyl group, giving C6H5-O-H.

mcqs.q: Replacing both hydrogens of water by alkyl or aryl groups gives which compound?
mcqs.why: If both hydrogens of water are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups, an ether, R-O-R, is formed.

mcqs.q: Alcohols are described as hydroxyl derivatives of which compounds?
mcqs.why: The notes define alcohols as the hydroxyl derivatives of alkanes, whereas phenols come from benzene.

mcqs.q: Phenols are hydroxyl derivatives of which compound?
mcqs.why: Phenols are the hydroxyl derivatives of benzene, which distinguishes them from alcohols derived from alkanes.

mcqs.q: Which group is present in both alcohols and phenols?
mcqs.why: Alcohols and phenols both have a hydroxyl (-OH) group, even though the group is attached differently in each.

mcqs.q: Alcohols, phenols and ethers are widely used in which areas?
mcqs.why: The notes say these compounds occur widely in nature and have many pharmaceutical, biological and industrial applications.

lessons.title: Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are the compounds in which a hydroxyl (—OH) group is bonded to a saturated carbon atom. Their general formula is R—OH.

Classification of Alcohols

Alcohols are classified in two ways.

1. By the number of hydroxyl groups:

  • Monohydric alcohols have only one —OH group, e.g. ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol.
  • Polyhydric alcohols have two or more —OH groups, e.g. glycol (two —OH groups) and glycerol (three —OH groups).

2. By the type of carbon bearing the —OH group (for monohydric alcohols):

  • Primary (1°) alcohol: the —OH group is on a carbon attached to only one other carbon.
  • Secondary (2°) alcohol: the —OH group is on a carbon attached to two other carbons.
  • Tertiary (3°) alcohol: the —OH group is on a carbon attached to three other carbons.

Key Points

  • In alcohols, the —OH group is bonded to a saturated carbon atom.
  • Monohydric alcohols have one —OH group; polyhydric alcohols have two or more.
  • Glycol and glycerol are polyhydric alcohols.
  • Monohydric alcohols are primary, secondary or tertiary according to the carbon bearing the —OH group.

mcqs.q: In an alcohol, the hydroxyl group is bonded to which type of carbon atom?
mcqs.why: Alcohols are compounds in which a hydroxyl (-OH) group is bonded to a saturated carbon atom, with general formula R-OH.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of alcohols?
mcqs.why: The notes give the general formula of alcohols as R-OH, where R is an alkyl group attached through carbon to oxygen.

mcqs.q: A monohydric alcohol contains how many hydroxyl groups?
mcqs.why: Monohydric alcohols have only one -OH group; ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol are given as examples.

mcqs.q: Polyhydric alcohols contain how many hydroxyl groups?
mcqs.why: Polyhydric alcohols have two or more -OH groups, unlike monohydric alcohols which have only one such group.

mcqs.q: Glycol and glycerol differ in that glycerol has how many -OH groups?
mcqs.why: The notes state glycol has two -OH groups and glycerol has three -OH groups, so glycerol has three.

mcqs.q: In a primary (1°) alcohol, the carbon bearing -OH is attached to how many other carbons?
mcqs.why: A primary alcohol has the -OH on a carbon attached to only one other carbon atom.

mcqs.q: In a secondary (2°) alcohol, the carbon bearing -OH is attached to how many other carbons?
mcqs.why: A secondary alcohol has the -OH group on a carbon attached to two other carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: In a tertiary (3°) alcohol, the carbon bearing -OH is attached to how many other carbons?
mcqs.why: A tertiary alcohol has the -OH group on a carbon attached to three other carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Which pair are both given as monohydric alcohols?
options: Ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol
mcqs.why: Ethyl alcohol and tertiary butyl alcohol are listed as monohydric examples, while glycol and glycerol are polyhydric.

mcqs.q: Alcohols are classified in how many ways in the notes?
mcqs.why: Classification is by number of hydroxyl groups and, for monohydric alcohols, by the type of carbon bearing the -OH group: two ways.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are named by two systems: the common system and the IUPAC system.

Common System

The name of the alkyl group is written first, followed by the word alcohol, e.g. methyl alcohol, ethyl alcohol, n-propyl alcohol, isopropyl alcohol and tert-butyl alcohol. Common names are generally used for simple alcohols with one to four carbon atoms.

IUPAC System

In the IUPAC system, alcohols are called alkanols. The rules are:

  • Select the longest carbon chain containing the —OH group.
  • Drop the ending -e of the alkane name and add the suffix -ol.
  • Number the chain from the end nearer to the —OH group. The —OH group gets precedence over alkyl groups, halogens and double or triple bonds.
  • Show the position of the —OH group and of all other substituents by numbers.
  • For two, three or four —OH groups, use the suffixes -diol, -triol and -tetraol.
  • In compounds containing a carbonyl group (aldehydes, ketones, carboxylic acids and their derivatives), the —OH group is only a side group and is named as hydroxy with its position number.

Examples: methanol, ethanol, 1-propanol, 3-methyl-1-butanol, 2,4-pentanediol, 4-penten-2-ol, 3-hydroxybutanal.

Isomerism in Alcohols

  • Functional isomerism: alcohols with two or more carbon atoms are functional isomers of ethers, e.g. ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether (both C2H6O).
  • Position isomerism: alcohols with three or more carbon atoms show position isomerism, e.g. 1-propanol and 2-propanol.

Key Points

  • Common name = alkyl group + alcohol.
  • IUPAC name = alkanol: longest chain with —OH, -e replaced by -ol.
  • Number the chain so that the —OH group gets the lowest number.
  • Diols, triols and tetraols have two, three and four —OH groups.
  • Alcohols are functional isomers of ethers and also show position isomerism.

mcqs.q: In the common system, an alcohol is named as alkyl group followed by which word?
mcqs.why: The common name is written as the alkyl group first, followed by the word alcohol, as in methyl alcohol and ethyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: In the IUPAC system, alcohols are called by which name?
mcqs.why: In the IUPAC system alcohols are called alkanols, formed by replacing the ending -e of the alkane with -ol.

mcqs.q: Which chain is selected for IUPAC naming of an alcohol?
options: The longest chain containing the -OH group
mcqs.why: Rule one is to select the longest carbon chain containing the -OH group as the parent chain for naming.

mcqs.q: The IUPAC suffix -ol replaces which ending of the alkane name?
mcqs.why: The ending -e of the alkane name is dropped and the suffix -ol is added to give the alkanol name.

mcqs.q: Numbering of an alcohol chain starts from the end nearer to which group?
mcqs.why: The chain is numbered from the end nearer to the -OH group, so the -OH group gets the lowest possible number.

mcqs.q: The -OH group gets precedence in numbering over which groups?
options: Alkyl groups, halogens and double or triple bonds
mcqs.why: The notes state the -OH group gets precedence over alkyl groups, halogens and double or triple bonds in numbering.

mcqs.q: Suffixes for two, three and four -OH groups are respectively which?
mcqs.why: For two, three or four -OH groups the suffixes -diol, -triol and -tetraol are used respectively.

mcqs.q: When a carbonyl group is present, the -OH group is named as which prefix?
mcqs.why: In aldehydes, ketones and carboxylic acids the -OH is only a side group and is named as hydroxy with its position number.

mcqs.q: Ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether, both C2H6O, are examples of which isomerism?
mcqs.why: Alcohols with two or more carbons are functional isomers of ethers; ethyl alcohol and dimethyl ether both have formula C2H6O.

mcqs.q: 1-Propanol and 2-propanol illustrate which type of isomerism?
mcqs.why: Alcohols with three or more carbons show position isomerism, illustrated by 1-propanol and 2-propanol differing in -OH position.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
• Lower alcohols are colourless liquids; higher alcohols are colourless waxy solids.
  • They have a characteristic alcoholic smell and a burning taste.
  • They are volatile in nature and inflammable.
  • Their boiling points are higher than those of the corresponding alkanes, ethers and haloalkanes.
  • Alcohols with up to four carbon atoms are readily soluble in water. From five carbon atoms onwards, they are insoluble in water.
  • Water solubility is due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding with water. Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl group increases, and increases with branching of the chain.
  • Alcohols are lighter than water. The density of methanol is 0.792 g/mL and that of ethanol is 0.789 g/mL at 20°C, while the density of water is 0.998 g/mL at 20°C.

Key Points

  • Lower alcohols are colourless liquids with an alcoholic smell and burning taste.
  • Hydrogen bonding gives alcohols high boiling points and water solubility.
  • Alcohols up to C4 dissolve readily in water; C5 and above do not.
  • Solubility falls as the alkyl group grows and rises with branching.
  • Alcohols are less dense than water.

mcqs.q: Lower alcohols and higher alcohols are respectively described as what?
options: Colourless liquids and colourless waxy solids
mcqs.why: Lower alcohols are colourless liquids while higher alcohols are colourless waxy solids, with alcoholic smell and burning taste.

mcqs.q: Alcohols have boiling points higher than which corresponding compounds?
mcqs.why: Their boiling points are higher than those of the corresponding alkanes, ethers and haloalkanes because of hydrogen bonding.

mcqs.q: Alcohols with up to how many carbon atoms are readily soluble in water?
mcqs.why: Alcohols with up to four carbon atoms are readily soluble in water; from five carbons onwards they are insoluble.

mcqs.q: Water solubility of alcohols is due to which interaction?
mcqs.why: Solubility is due to intermolecular hydrogen bonding with water, which is possible for the smaller alcohols.

mcqs.q: As the size of the alkyl group increases, water solubility of alcohols does what?
mcqs.why: Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl group increases, and it increases with branching of the chain.

mcqs.q: Branching of the carbon chain has what effect on alcohol solubility in water?
mcqs.why: The notes state solubility increases with branching of the chain, opposite to the effect of increasing alkyl size.

mcqs.q: Compared with water, alcohols are generally what?
mcqs.why: Alcohols are lighter than water; methanol and ethanol densities are both below the density of water given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What is the density difference between water (0.998 g/mL) and methanol (0.792 g/mL) at 20°C?
mcqs.why: Working: 0.998 - 0.792 = 0.206 g/mL. Water is denser than methanol by 0.206 g/mL at 20°C.

mcqs.q: What is the density difference between water (0.998 g/mL) and ethanol (0.789 g/mL) at 20°C?
mcqs.why: Working: 0.998 - 0.789 = 0.209 g/mL. Ethanol at 0.789 g/mL is less dense than water by 0.209 g/mL.

mcqs.q: Which description matches the nature of alcohols?
mcqs.why: Alcohols are volatile in nature and inflammable, with a characteristic alcoholic smell and a burning taste.

lessons.title: Structure of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
In alcohols, the oxygen atom is sp3 hybridized. It has four sp3 hybrid orbitals. Two of them form sigma (σ) bonds, one with carbon and one with hydrogen. The other two orbitals contain the lone pairs of electrons of oxygen.

Because of the lone pairs, the molecule has a bent shape around oxygen. In methanol, the C—O—H bond angle is 108.9°. The C—O bond length is 142 pm and the O—H bond length is 96 pm.

Key Points

  • The oxygen of an alcohol is sp3 hybridized.
  • Oxygen forms two sigma bonds (to C and to H) and carries two lone pairs.
  • The C—O—H angle in methanol is 108.9°.
  • C—O bond length is 142 pm and O—H bond length is 96 pm.

mcqs.q: The oxygen atom in alcohols is hybridized in which way?
mcqs.why: In alcohols the oxygen atom is sp3 hybridized and has four sp3 hybrid orbitals in total.

mcqs.q: How many sp3 hybrid orbitals does the oxygen in an alcohol have?
mcqs.why: Oxygen has four sp3 hybrid orbitals: two form sigma bonds and the other two contain the lone pairs.

mcqs.q: The two sigma bonds formed by oxygen in an alcohol are to which atoms?
mcqs.why: Two orbitals form sigma (sigma) bonds, one with carbon and one with hydrogen, in the C-O-H unit of an alcohol.

mcqs.q: The remaining two orbitals on oxygen in an alcohol contain what?
mcqs.why: The other two orbitals contain the lone pairs of electrons of oxygen, which cause the bent shape around oxygen.

mcqs.q: Because of its lone pairs, the shape around oxygen in an alcohol is what?
mcqs.why: Because of the lone pairs, the molecule has a bent shape around oxygen, similar to the shape in water.

mcqs.q: What is the C-O-H bond angle in methanol?
mcqs.why: The notes give the C-O-H bond angle in methanol specifically as 108.9 degrees.

mcqs.q: What is the C-O bond length in methanol as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The C-O bond length is 142 pm, while the shorter O-H bond length is given as 96 pm.

mcqs.q: What is the O-H bond length in methanol as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: The O-H bond length is 96 pm, which is shorter than the 142 pm C-O bond length in methanol.

mcqs.q: By how much is the C-O bond (142 pm) longer than the O-H bond (96 pm)?
mcqs.why: Working: 142 pm - 96 pm = 46 pm. The C-O bond is longer than the O-H bond by 46 pm.

mcqs.q: How many lone pairs does the oxygen atom in an alcohol carry?
mcqs.why: Oxygen carries two lone pairs in the two sp3 orbitals that are not used for the C and H sigma bonds.

lessons.title: Acidity of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are acidic in nature because of the polar O—H bond. The greater the polarity of the —OH group, the greater is the acidity of the alcohol.

Alkyl groups are electron-releasing. They push electrons towards oxygen, decrease the polarity of the O—H bond and make the alcohol a weaker acid. More alkyl groups on the alpha carbon means lower acidity, so the order of acidity is:

Primary alcohol > secondary alcohol > tertiary alcohol

For example, tert-butyl alcohol is a weaker acid than methyl alcohol or ethyl alcohol.

Compared with water, methanol is more acidic than water, ethanol is almost as acidic as water, and alcohols with more than two carbon atoms are slightly weaker acids than water. Overall, alcohols are only weak acids.

Key Points

  • Alcohols are acidic because the O—H bond is polar.
  • Greater polarity of the O—H bond means greater acidity.
  • Electron-releasing alkyl groups decrease acidity.
  • Acidity order: primary > secondary > tertiary.
  • Methanol is more acidic than water; higher alcohols are weaker acids than water.

mcqs.q: Alcohols are acidic because of which feature?
mcqs.why: Alcohols are acidic in nature because of the polar O-H bond; greater polarity means greater acidity.

mcqs.q: Greater polarity of the -OH group leads to what?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly: the greater the polarity of the -OH group, the greater is the acidity of the alcohol.

mcqs.q: Alkyl groups affect acidity because they are what?
mcqs.why: Alkyl groups are electron-releasing; they push electrons towards oxygen and decrease the polarity of the O-H bond.

mcqs.q: More alkyl groups on the alpha carbon makes an alcohol what?
mcqs.why: More alkyl groups on the alpha carbon means lower acidity, so the alcohol becomes a weaker acid.

mcqs.q: What is the correct order of acidity for alcohols?
mcqs.why: Acidity order is primary alcohol > secondary alcohol > tertiary alcohol, as alkyl substitution increases.

mcqs.q: tert-Butyl alcohol compared with methyl or ethyl alcohol is what?
mcqs.why: tert-Butyl alcohol, a tertiary alcohol, is a weaker acid than methyl alcohol or ethyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: Compared with water, methanol is what?
mcqs.why: The notes state methanol is more acidic than water, while ethanol is almost as acidic as water.

mcqs.q: Ethanol compared with water is described as what?
mcqs.why: Ethanol is almost as acidic as water, between methanol which is more acidic and higher alcohols which are weaker.

mcqs.q: Alcohols with more than two carbon atoms are, compared with water, what?
mcqs.why: Alcohols with more than two carbon atoms are slightly weaker acids than water, and overall alcohols are only weak acids.

mcqs.q: Overall, alcohols are best described as which kind of acids?
mcqs.why: Overall alcohols are only weak acids, even though methanol is slightly more acidic than water.

lessons.title: Preparations of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Hydration of Alkenes

Alkenes react with cold concentrated H2SO4 and then give alcohols on hydrolysis. The addition follows Markovnikov's rule.

Hydrolysis of Alkyl Halides

Alkyl halides are hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH or KOH to give alcohols.

CH3CH2Br + KOH → CH3CH2OH + KBr

Reaction of Grignard Reagents with Aldehydes and Ketones

Grignard reagents (RMgX) add to aldehydes and ketones. The addition product gives an alcohol on protonation with aqueous acid.

  • Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol, e.g. HCHO + CH3MgCl → (addition product) → CH3CH2OH (ethyl alcohol).
  • Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols, e.g. acetaldehyde + CH3MgCl gives isopropyl alcohol.
  • Ketones give tertiary alcohols, e.g. acetone + CH3MgCl gives tert-butyl alcohol.

Reduction of Aldehydes and Ketones

Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols by NaBH4 or LiAlH4. Aldehydes give primary alcohols and ketones give secondary alcohols. NaBH4 is commonly used in polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol.

Reaction of Grignard Reagents with Esters

  • Formate esters first give aldehydes, which react with another molecule of Grignard reagent to give secondary alcohols.
  • Other esters first give ketones, which react further with Grignard reagent to give tertiary alcohols.

Reduction of Carboxylic Acids and Esters

Carboxylic acids and esters are reduced to alcohols by LiAlH4, a strong reducing agent, e.g. acetic acid gives ethyl alcohol, and methyl acetate gives ethyl alcohol and methyl alcohol.

Key Reactions

MethodReaction
Hydrolysis of alkyl halidesCH3CH2Br + KOH → CH3CH2OH + KBr
Grignard + formaldehydeHCHO + CH3MgCl → CH3CH2OH (1° alcohol)
Reduction of acidsCH3COOH + 4[H] (LiAlH4) → CH3CH2OH + H2O

Key Points

  • Alkenes give alcohols by acid-catalysed hydration (Markovnikov addition).
  • Aqueous KOH or NaOH hydrolyzes alkyl halides to alcohols.
  • Grignard reagents give 1° alcohols from formaldehyde, 2° from other aldehydes and 3° from ketones.
  • NaBH4 or LiAlH4 reduces aldehydes to 1° alcohols and ketones to 2° alcohols.
  • Formate esters give 2° alcohols and other esters give 3° alcohols with Grignard reagents.
  • LiAlH4 reduces carboxylic acids and esters to alcohols.

mcqs.q: Hydration of alkenes to alcohols follows which rule?
mcqs.why: Alkenes react with cold concentrated H2SO4 and give alcohols on hydrolysis, with addition following Markovnikov's rule.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halides are hydrolyzed to alcohols by which reagents?
mcqs.why: Alkyl halides are hydrolyzed by aqueous NaOH or KOH to give alcohols, as in CH3CH2Br + KOH giving ethanol and KBr.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde with a Grignard reagent gives which type of alcohol?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde gives a primary alcohol; for example HCHO with CH3MgCl ultimately gives ethyl alcohol, CH3CH2OH.

mcqs.q: Other aldehydes (not formaldehyde) with Grignard reagents give which alcohols?
mcqs.why: Other aldehydes give secondary alcohols; acetaldehyde with CH3MgCl is given as giving isopropyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: Ketones with Grignard reagents give which type of alcohol?
mcqs.why: Ketones give tertiary alcohols with Grignard reagents; acetone with CH3MgCl gives tert-butyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: Reduction of aldehydes and ketones to alcohols uses which reagents?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones are reduced to alcohols by NaBH4 or LiAlH4; aldehydes give primary and ketones give secondary alcohols.

mcqs.q: NaBH4 is commonly used in which kind of solvents?
options: Polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol
mcqs.why: NaBH4 is commonly used in polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol for reducing aldehydes and ketones.

mcqs.q: Formate esters with Grignard reagents finally give which alcohols?
mcqs.why: Formate esters first give aldehydes, which react with another Grignard molecule to give secondary alcohols.

mcqs.q: Other esters (not formates) with Grignard reagents finally give which alcohols?
mcqs.why: Other esters first give ketones, which react further with Grignard reagent to give tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: LiAlH4 reduction of acetic acid gives which product?
mcqs.why: LiAlH4, a strong reducing agent, reduces carboxylic acids and esters; acetic acid gives ethyl alcohol in the example.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols are reactive compounds. They can act both as electrophiles and as nucleophiles, because:

  • Both the C—O and O—H bonds are polar, as oxygen is an electronegative element.
  • Oxygen is an electron-rich centre because it has two lone pairs of electrons.

Alcohols react with polar or ionic reagents in two ways:

  • When a nucleophile attacks the alcohol, the C—O bond breaks.
  • When an electrophile attacks the alcohol, the O—H bond breaks.

The reactivity order for breaking of the C—O bond is: tertiary > secondary > primary > CH3OH.

The reactivity order for breaking of the O—H bond is the reverse: CH3OH > primary > secondary > tertiary.

Key Points

  • Alcohols act as both electrophiles and nucleophiles.
  • Nucleophilic attack breaks the C—O bond; electrophilic attack breaks the O—H bond.
  • C—O bond breaking is easiest for tertiary alcohols.
  • O—H bond breaking is easiest for methanol.

mcqs.q: Alcohols can act as both which pair?
mcqs.why: Alcohols can act both as electrophiles and as nucleophiles because both C-O and O-H bonds are polar and oxygen is electron-rich.

mcqs.q: Why is oxygen an electron-rich centre in alcohols?
options: It has two lone pairs of electrons
mcqs.why: Oxygen is an electron-rich centre because it has two lone pairs of electrons, in addition to its polar bonds.

mcqs.q: When a nucleophile attacks an alcohol, which bond breaks?
mcqs.why: When a nucleophile attacks the alcohol, the C-O bond breaks; electrophilic attack instead breaks the O-H bond.

mcqs.q: When an electrophile attacks an alcohol, which bond breaks?
mcqs.why: When an electrophile attacks the alcohol, the O-H bond breaks, which is the reverse mode to nucleophilic attack.

mcqs.q: The reactivity order for breaking the C-O bond is which?
mcqs.why: C-O bond breaking follows tertiary > secondary > primary > CH3OH, easiest for tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: The reactivity order for breaking the O-H bond is which?
mcqs.why: O-H bond breaking is the reverse order: CH3OH > primary > secondary > tertiary, easiest for methanol.

mcqs.q: Both C-O and O-H bonds in alcohols are polar because oxygen is what?
mcqs.why: Both bonds are polar as oxygen is an electronegative element, pulling electron density towards itself.

mcqs.q: C-O bond breaking is easiest for which alcohol?
mcqs.why: C-O breaking is easiest for tertiary alcohols in the order tertiary > secondary > primary > CH3OH.

mcqs.q: O-H bond breaking is easiest for which compound?
mcqs.why: O-H breaking is easiest for methanol, which heads the reverse order CH3OH > primary > secondary > tertiary.

mcqs.q: An alcohol acting as a nucleophile uses mainly which feature of oxygen?
mcqs.why: Oxygen's two lone pairs make it electron-rich, allowing alcohols to behave as nucleophiles in many reactions.

lessons.title: Reactions of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Reaction with Halogen Acids

Alcohols react with halogen acids to form alkyl halides:

R—OH + HX → R—X + H2O

Ethyl alcohol reacts with HCl in the presence of ZnCl2 catalyst to give ethyl chloride. HBr and HI react without a catalyst. The mixture of HCl and ZnCl2 is used in the Lucas test, which differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols. The reactivity order of the halogen acids is HI > HBr > HCl.

Reaction with Thionyl Chloride and Phosphorus Trihalides

Alcohols react with SOCl2 in the presence of pyridine to give alkyl chlorides:

R—OH + SOCl2 → R—Cl + SO2 + HCl

With phosphorus trihalides, three molecules of alcohol react:

3R—OH + PX3 → 3R—X + H3PO3

Key Reactions

ReagentProduct
HXAlkyl halide + H2O
SOCl2 / pyridineAlkyl chloride + SO2 + HCl
PX3Alkyl halide + H3PO3

Key Points

  • Halogen acids convert alcohols into alkyl halides.
  • HCl needs a ZnCl2 catalyst; HBr and HI do not.
  • The HCl + ZnCl2 mixture is the Lucas reagent, used to distinguish 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
  • Reactivity of halogen acids: HI > HBr > HCl.
  • SOCl2 and PX3 also replace the —OH group by halogen.

mcqs.q: Alcohols react with halogen acids to form which products?
mcqs.why: The general reaction is R-OH + HX -> R-X + H2O, converting an alcohol into an alkyl halide.

mcqs.q: Ethyl alcohol with HCl needs which catalyst to give ethyl chloride?
mcqs.why: Ethyl alcohol reacts with HCl in the presence of ZnCl2 catalyst to give ethyl chloride; HBr and HI need no catalyst.

mcqs.q: The mixture of HCl and ZnCl2 used to distinguish alcohol types is called what?
mcqs.why: The HCl + ZnCl2 mixture is used in the Lucas test, which differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

mcqs.q: What is the reactivity order of halogen acids with alcohols?
mcqs.why: The reactivity order of the halogen acids is HI > HBr > HCl, with HI the most reactive towards alcohols.

mcqs.q: Alcohols with SOCl2 in pyridine give which main organic product?
mcqs.why: R-OH + SOCl2 -> R-Cl + SO2 + HCl in the presence of pyridine, giving an alkyl chloride.

mcqs.q: With phosphorus trihalides, how many alcohol molecules react with one PX3?
mcqs.why: Three molecules react: 3R-OH + PX3 -> 3R-X + H3PO3, as stated for phosphorus trihalides.

mcqs.q: The phosphorus-containing product from 3R-OH + PX3 is which?
mcqs.why: The reaction 3R-OH + PX3 -> 3R-X + H3PO3 produces H3PO3 alongside three molecules of alkyl halide.

mcqs.q: Which halogen acids react with alcohols without a catalyst?
mcqs.why: HBr and HI react without a catalyst, whereas HCl requires the ZnCl2 catalyst to react with ethyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: SOCl2 reaction with an alcohol produces which gases/by-products besides R-Cl?
mcqs.why: R-OH + SOCl2 -> R-Cl + SO2 + HCl, so sulphur dioxide and hydrogen chloride are the by-products.

mcqs.q: The Lucas test differentiates which set of alcohols?
mcqs.why: The Lucas test with HCl and ZnCl2 differentiates primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols by their reactivity.

lessons.title: Dehydration of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
Dehydration is the removal of a water molecule from two adjacent carbon atoms of an alcohol. It is carried out with an acid catalyst such as concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4. The —OH group leaves from the alpha carbon and a hydrogen leaves from the beta carbon.

The product depends on the type of alcohol, the temperature and the concentration of the acid. The ease of dehydration follows the order of carbocation stability: tertiary > secondary > primary.

  • Primary alcohols are the most difficult to dehydrate and need high temperature and strong acid. Ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at 170–180°C gives ethylene (ethene). With excess ethanol at 140°C, diethyl ether is formed instead.
  • Secondary alcohols dehydrate at lower temperatures (100–140°C). 2-Butanol with 75% H2SO4 at 100°C gives 2-butene.
  • Tertiary alcohols dehydrate very easily, slightly above room temperature (25–80°C). 2-Methyl-2-propanol with 5% H2SO4 at 50°C gives 2-methylpropene.

Key Reactions

AlcoholConditionsProduct
Ethanol (1°)Conc. H2SO4, 170–180°CEthene
Ethanol (excess)Conc. H2SO4, 140°CDiethyl ether
2-Butanol (2°)75% H2SO4, 100°C2-Butene
2-Methyl-2-propanol (3°)5% H2SO4, 50°C2-Methylpropene

Key Points

  • Dehydration removes —OH from the alpha carbon and H from the beta carbon.
  • Acid catalysts used are concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4.
  • Ease of dehydration: tertiary > secondary > primary.
  • Ethanol gives ethene at 170–180°C but diethyl ether at 140°C.
  • Tertiary alcohols dehydrate under very mild conditions.

mcqs.q: Dehydration of an alcohol removes which molecule?
mcqs.why: Dehydration is the removal of a water molecule from two adjacent carbon atoms of an alcohol, using an acid catalyst.

mcqs.q: In dehydration, the -OH leaves from the alpha carbon and hydrogen leaves from where?
mcqs.why: The -OH group leaves from the alpha carbon and a hydrogen leaves from the beta carbon to form the alkene.

mcqs.q: Ease of dehydration follows the order of carbocation stability, which is what?
mcqs.why: Ease follows tertiary > secondary > primary, the order of carbocation stability; primary alcohols are hardest to dehydrate.

mcqs.q: Ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at 170-180°C gives which product?
mcqs.why: At 170-180°C with concentrated H2SO4, ethanol (a primary alcohol) gives ethylene, i.e. ethene.

mcqs.q: Excess ethanol with concentrated H2SO4 at 140°C gives which product instead of ethene?
mcqs.why: With excess ethanol at 140°C, diethyl ether is formed instead of ethene, showing temperature controls the product.

mcqs.q: 2-Butanol with 75% H2SO4 at 100°C gives which product?
mcqs.why: 2-Butanol, a secondary alcohol, with 75% H2SO4 at 100°C gives 2-butene as the dehydration product.

mcqs.q: 2-Methyl-2-propanol with 5% H2SO4 at 50°C gives which product?
mcqs.why: The tertiary alcohol 2-methyl-2-propanol dehydrates very easily at 50°C with 5% acid to give 2-methylpropene.

mcqs.q: Secondary alcohols dehydrate in which temperature range given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohols dehydrate at lower temperatures of 100-140°C, between primary and tertiary requirements.

mcqs.q: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate under which conditions?
mcqs.why: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate very easily, slightly above room temperature in the range 25-80°C.

mcqs.q: Which acid catalysts are used for dehydration of alcohols?
mcqs.why: Dehydration is carried out with an acid catalyst such as concentrated H2SO4 or H3PO4.

lessons.title: Preparation of Esters
lessons.notes_html:
Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 to form esters. This reaction is called esterification:

R—COOH + R—OH ⇌ R—COOR + H2O

For example, acetic acid reacts with ethyl alcohol to give ethyl acetate and water:

CH3COOH + C2H5OH ⇌ CH3COOC2H5 + H2O

The reaction is reversible. Concentrated H2SO4 removes the water formed, so almost all the reactants are converted into the ester.

Key Points

  • Esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form an ester.
  • Concentrated H2SO4 is used as catalyst and dehydrating agent.
  • The reaction is reversible.
  • Removing water shifts the reaction towards the ester.

mcqs.q: Esterification is the reaction of an alcohol with which compound?
mcqs.why: Esterification is the reaction of a carboxylic acid with an alcohol to form an ester and water.

mcqs.q: Esterification is carried out in the presence of which catalyst?
mcqs.why: Alcohols react with carboxylic acids in the presence of concentrated H2SO4 to form esters.

mcqs.q: The general esterification equation produces an ester plus what?
mcqs.why: R-COOH + R-OH reversibly gives R-COOR + H2O, so water is formed alongside the ester.

mcqs.q: Acetic acid reacting with ethyl alcohol gives which ester?
mcqs.why: CH3COOH + C2H5OH gives CH3COOC2H5, ethyl acetate, plus water in the example given.

mcqs.q: Esterification is described as which type of reaction?
mcqs.why: The reaction is reversible, shown by the equilibrium arrows in R-COOH + R-OH <-> R-COOR + H2O.

mcqs.q: Concentrated H2SO4 in esterification acts as catalyst and also does what?
mcqs.why: Concentrated H2SO4 removes the water formed, so almost all reactants are converted into the ester.

mcqs.q: Removing water in esterification shifts the reaction towards what?
mcqs.why: Removing water shifts the reversible reaction towards the ester, increasing the conversion to product.

mcqs.q: In CH3COOH + C2H5OH -> CH3COOC2H5 + H2O, the product CH3COOC2H5 is what?
mcqs.why: CH3COOC2H5 is ethyl acetate, the ester formed from acetic acid and ethyl alcohol with water as by-product.

mcqs.q: Which removal drives esterification nearly to completion?
mcqs.why: Because concentrated H2SO4 removes water, almost all the reactants are converted into the ester despite reversibility.

mcqs.q: The catalyst and dehydrating agent in esterification is which acid?
mcqs.why: Concentrated H2SO4 is used both as catalyst and as dehydrating agent in the esterification reaction.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
The addition of oxygen to a compound is called oxidation. Alcohols are oxidized by K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4. The product depends on the type of alcohol and the reaction conditions, so oxidation is used to differentiate primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols.

  • Methyl alcohol is oxidized first to formaldehyde and then to formic acid.
  • Primary alcohols are oxidized first to aldehydes and then to carboxylic acids, e.g. ethanol → acetaldehyde → acetic acid. The oxidation can be stopped at the aldehyde stage by removing the aldehyde from the oxidizing medium as it forms.
  • Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones. Ketones are not oxidized further easily, because that needs breaking of a C—C bond. Under drastic conditions they give carboxylic acids, e.g. acetone gives acetic acid, carbon dioxide and water.
  • Tertiary alcohols are not oxidized under acidic conditions, because the carbon bearing the —OH group is attached to three other carbons and cannot form a C=O double bond.

Cleavage of 1,2-Diols (Glycols)

Vicinal diols (glycols) are cleaved into two carbonyl compounds by periodic acid (HIO4) or lead tetraacetate. The products are aldehydes or ketones, depending on the glycol.

Ethylene glycol + HIO4 → 2HCHO (formaldehyde) + HIO3 + H2O

1,2-Propanediol + HIO4 → CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) + HCHO (formaldehyde) + HIO3 + H2O

Key Points

  • K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4 is the common oxidizing agent for alcohols.
  • Primary alcohols give aldehydes, then carboxylic acids.
  • Secondary alcohols give ketones.
  • Tertiary alcohols resist oxidation under acidic conditions.
  • Oxidation behaviour distinguishes 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols.
  • HIO4 or lead tetraacetate cleaves 1,2-diols into two carbonyl compounds.

mcqs.q: Oxidation is defined in the notes as what?
options: Addition of oxygen to a compound
mcqs.why: The addition of oxygen to a compound is called oxidation; alcohols are oxidized by K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4.

mcqs.q: The common oxidizing agent for alcohols is which?
mcqs.why: Alcohols are oxidized by K2Cr2O7 in aqueous H2SO4, and the product depends on the type of alcohol and conditions.

mcqs.q: Primary alcohols are oxidized first to aldehydes and then to what?
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols give aldehydes then carboxylic acids; ethanol goes to acetaldehyde and then to acetic acid.

mcqs.q: Oxidation can be stopped at the aldehyde stage by doing what?
options: Removing the aldehyde as it forms
mcqs.why: The oxidation can be stopped at the aldehyde stage by removing the aldehyde from the oxidizing medium as it forms.

mcqs.q: Secondary alcohols are oxidized to which products?
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohols are oxidized to ketones, which are not oxidized further easily because that needs C-C bond breaking.

mcqs.q: Under drastic conditions, acetone oxidation gives which set?
options: Acetic acid, carbon dioxide and water
mcqs.why: Under drastic conditions ketones give carboxylic acids; acetone gives acetic acid, carbon dioxide and water.

mcqs.q: Tertiary alcohols under acidic conditions are what?
mcqs.why: Tertiary alcohols are not oxidized under acidic conditions because the -OH carbon cannot form a C=O double bond.

mcqs.q: Methyl alcohol is oxidized first to formaldehyde and then to what?
mcqs.why: Methyl alcohol is oxidized first to formaldehyde and then to formic acid, following the primary alcohol pattern.

mcqs.q: Vicinal diols (glycols) are cleaved by which reagents?
mcqs.why: 1,2-Diols are cleaved into two carbonyl compounds by periodic acid (HIO4) or lead tetraacetate.

mcqs.q: Ethylene glycol with HIO4 gives which carbonyl product?
mcqs.why: Ethylene glycol + HIO4 -> 2HCHO + HIO3 + H2O, so two molecules of formaldehyde are formed by cleavage.

lessons.title: The Sulphur Analogous (Thiols, RSH)
lessons.notes_html:
Thiols are the sulphur analogues of alcohols. They are also called thioalcohols. They contain the mercapto group (—SH) instead of the hydroxyl group (—OH).

Thiols form strong complexes with mercuric oxide, i.e. they capture mercury:

2CH3CH2SH + HgO → (CH3CH2S)2Hg + H2O

Because of this mercury-capturing property, thiols are also called mercaptans.

Nomenclature of Thiols

  • Common system: name the alkyl group and add the word mercaptan, e.g. methyl mercaptan, ethyl mercaptan, phenyl mercaptan.
  • IUPAC system: name the alkane and add the suffix -thiol (alkanethiol), e.g. methanethiol, ethanethiol, 2-propanethiol, benzenethiol.
  • Select the longest chain containing the —SH group and number it from the end nearer to —SH. The —SH group has priority over alkyl groups and halogens.
  • If a higher-priority group is present, —SH is named as the prefix sulfanyl (or mercapto-). The —OH group has priority over the —SH group, e.g. 3-sulfanyl-2-pentanol.

Physical Properties of Thiols

  • Methanethiol is a gas; the higher members are colourless volatile liquids.
  • They have much lower boiling points than the corresponding alcohols because their intermolecular forces are weaker, e.g. methanethiol boils at 6°C while methanol boils at 65°C.
  • They are less soluble in water than alcohols of similar molecular mass.
  • Lower thiols have strong repulsive odours, like garlic and rotten eggs. Methanethiol and ethanethiol are used as odorants to detect leakage of natural gas.

Structure and Acidity of Thiols

The —SH group is bonded to an sp3 hybridized carbon, so the structure of thiols is similar to that of alcohols. The C—S—H bond angle in methanethiol is 100.3°. The S—H bond is less polar than the O—H bond because sulphur is less electronegative than oxygen.

Thiols are stronger acids than alcohols. The pKa of ethanethiol is 10.5, while the pKa of ethanol is 15.9 in dilute aqueous solution.

Key Points

  • Thiols (RSH) are the sulphur analogues of alcohols, with a —SH (mercapto) group.
  • They are called mercaptans because they capture mercury as complexes.
  • IUPAC names end in -thiol; common names end in mercaptan.
  • Thiols boil lower and dissolve less in water than alcohols.
  • Lower thiols have very unpleasant odours and are used as gas-leak odorants.
  • Thiols are stronger acids than alcohols (ethanethiol pKa 10.5, ethanol pKa 15.9).

mcqs.q: Thiols are the sulphur analogues of which compounds?
mcqs.why: Thiols are the sulphur analogues of alcohols, also called thioalcohols, containing -SH instead of -OH.

mcqs.q: The -SH group in thiols is called which group?
mcqs.why: Thiols contain the mercapto group (-SH) instead of the hydroxyl group (-OH) found in alcohols.

mcqs.q: Thiols are called mercaptans because they do what?
options: Capture mercury as complexes with mercuric oxide
mcqs.why: They capture mercury, forming strong complexes with mercuric oxide, e.g. 2CH3CH2SH + HgO -> (CH3CH2S)2Hg + H2O.

mcqs.q: In the IUPAC system, thiol names end with which suffix?
mcqs.why: IUPAC names add the suffix -thiol to the alkane (alkanethiol), e.g. methanethiol and ethanethiol.

mcqs.q: Methanethiol at room conditions is described as what, unlike higher thiols?
mcqs.why: Methanethiol is a gas; the higher members are colourless volatile liquids with strong repulsive odours.

mcqs.q: Methanethiol boils at 6°C while methanol boils at 65°C; the difference is how much?
mcqs.why: Working: 65 - 6 = 59°C. Methanethiol boils 59°C lower than methanol because its intermolecular forces are weaker.

mcqs.q: Lower thiols have odours described as like what?
mcqs.why: Lower thiols have strong repulsive odours like garlic and rotten eggs, and are used as gas-leak odorants.

mcqs.q: The C-S-H bond angle in methanethiol is given as what?
mcqs.why: The C-S-H bond angle in methanethiol is 100.3°, in a structure similar to alcohols with sp3 carbon.

mcqs.q: Thiols compared with alcohols are which kind of acids?
mcqs.why: Thiols are stronger acids than alcohols; ethanethiol pKa 10.5 is lower than ethanol pKa 15.9.

mcqs.q: The pKa difference between ethanol (15.9) and ethanethiol (10.5) is how much?
mcqs.why: Working: 15.9 - 10.5 = 5.4. Ethanethiol's pKa is 5.4 units lower, showing it is the stronger acid.

lessons.title: Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
The name phenol comes from phen, the old name of benzene, and ol, the suffix for a hydroxyl group.

Phenols are compounds in which one or more hydroxyl (—OH) groups are directly bonded to a carbon atom of the benzene ring. The simplest phenol is phenol itself (C6H5OH). Phenols are classified as monohydric or polyhydric according to the number of —OH groups.

Aromatic compounds in which the —OH group is not directly attached to the benzene ring are not phenols. They are aromatic alcohols, because they behave as derivatives of aliphatic alcohols, e.g. phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol) and 2-phenylethanol.

Key Points

  • In phenols, the —OH group is directly bonded to the benzene ring.
  • The simplest phenol is phenol, C6H5OH.
  • Phenols may be monohydric or polyhydric.
  • If —OH is on a side chain, the compound is an aromatic alcohol, not a phenol.

mcqs.q: In phenols, the -OH group is directly bonded to what?
options: A carbon of the benzene ring
mcqs.why: Phenols have one or more -OH groups directly bonded to a carbon atom of the benzene ring.

mcqs.q: The simplest phenol has which formula?
mcqs.why: The simplest phenol is phenol itself, C6H5OH, with -OH directly on the benzene ring.

mcqs.q: The name phenol comes from phen (old name of benzene) and which suffix?
mcqs.why: Phen comes from the old name of benzene and -ol is the suffix for a hydroxyl group, giving the name phenol.

mcqs.q: Phenols are classified as monohydric or polyhydric according to what?
mcqs.why: Phenols are classified as monohydric or polyhydric according to the number of -OH groups present.

mcqs.q: A compound with -OH on a side chain, not directly on the ring, is called what?
mcqs.why: Such compounds are not phenols; they are aromatic alcohols because they behave as derivatives of aliphatic alcohols.

mcqs.q: Phenylmethanol is also known by which common name?
mcqs.why: Phenylmethanol (benzyl alcohol) is an aromatic alcohol, since its -OH is not directly attached to the benzene ring.

mcqs.q: 2-Phenylethanol is classified as what?
mcqs.why: 2-Phenylethanol has -OH on the side chain, so it is an aromatic alcohol, not a phenol.

mcqs.q: Which condition must hold for a compound to be a phenol?
options: -OH directly attached to the benzene ring
mcqs.why: The defining condition is that the -OH group is directly attached to a carbon of the benzene ring.

mcqs.q: Aromatic alcohols behave as derivatives of which alcohols?
mcqs.why: Aromatic alcohols behave as derivatives of aliphatic alcohols, which is why they are separated from true phenols.

mcqs.q: How many -OH groups does a monohydric phenol contain?
mcqs.why: Monohydric phenols contain one -OH group; polyhydric phenols contain more than one -OH group on the ring.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
Phenol is the specific name for hydroxybenzene and is also used as the parent name. Substituted phenols are named as derivatives of phenol or as benzenols; common names are also used.

  • Give position 1 to the carbon bearing the —OH group, then number the substituents, e.g. 2-chlorophenol (o-chlorophenol), 3-ethylphenol (m-ethylphenol), 4-nitrophenol (p-nitrophenol).
  • Two —OH groups: 1,2-benzenediol (catechol), 1,3-benzenediol (resorcinol), 1,4-benzenediol (hydroquinone).
  • 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is commonly called picric acid.
  • Methylphenols are called cresols: 2-methylphenol (o-cresol), 3-methylphenol (m-cresol), 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).
  • Dimethylphenols are called xylenols, e.g. 2,6-xylenol, 3,5-xylenol.
  • If a functional group of higher priority is present, the compound is named as a hydroxy derivative, e.g. 3-hydroxybenzoic acid, 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde.

Isomerism in Phenols

Phenols show position isomerism when two or more substituents are present on the ring. Cresol has three position isomers: ortho, meta and para. Xylenol has six isomers.

Key Points

  • Phenol is the parent name; the —OH carbon is position 1.
  • Catechol, resorcinol and hydroquinone are the 1,2-, 1,3- and 1,4-benzenediols.
  • Methylphenols are cresols; dimethylphenols are xylenols.
  • 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is picric acid.
  • Phenols show position isomerism (cresol: 3 isomers; xylenol: 6 isomers).

mcqs.q: In naming substituted phenols, position 1 is given to which carbon?
options: The carbon with a methyl group
mcqs.why: Give position 1 to the carbon bearing the -OH group, then number the substituents around the ring.

mcqs.q: 2-Chlorophenol is also called by which prefix name?
mcqs.why: 2-Chlorophenol is o-chlorophenol; position 2 is ortho to the -OH group at position 1.

mcqs.q: 1,2-Benzenediol is commonly called what?
mcqs.why: 1,2-Benzenediol is catechol, while 1,3 is resorcinol and 1,4 is hydroquinone.

mcqs.q: 1,4-Benzenediol is commonly called what?
mcqs.why: 1,4-Benzenediol is hydroquinone; the 1,2 isomer is catechol and the 1,3 isomer is resorcinol.

mcqs.q: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is commonly called what?
mcqs.why: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol is commonly called picric acid, a strongly substituted phenol derivative.

mcqs.q: Methylphenols are commonly called what?
mcqs.why: Methylphenols are called cresols: 2-methylphenol is o-cresol, 3- is m-cresol and 4- is p-cresol.

mcqs.q: Dimethylphenols are commonly called what?
mcqs.why: Dimethylphenols are called xylenols, e.g. 2,6-xylenol and 3,5-xylenol, with six isomers possible.

mcqs.q: If a higher-priority functional group is present, a phenol is named as what?
mcqs.why: With a higher-priority group present, the compound is named as a hydroxy derivative, e.g. 3-hydroxybenzoic acid.

mcqs.q: Cresol has how many position isomers?
mcqs.why: Cresol has three position isomers: ortho, meta and para, due to position isomerism in phenols.

mcqs.q: Xylenol has how many isomers as given in the notes?
mcqs.why: Xylenol has six isomers, compared with three for cresol, because it has two methyl substituents on the ring.

lessons.title: Structure of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
In phenol, the —OH group is bonded to the aromatic ring. The oxygen atom has two bond pairs and two lone pairs of electrons, so phenol has a bent shape like water.

  • The C—O—H bond angle is 109°, slightly less than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.
  • The C—O bond length is 136 pm.
  • Phenol is a polar compound. Its dipole moment is 1.54 D.

Key Points

  • Phenol has a bent shape around oxygen, like water.
  • Its C—O—H angle is 109° and its C—O bond length is 136 pm.
  • Phenol is polar, with a dipole moment of 1.54 D.
  • The oxygen of phenol has two bond pairs and two lone pairs.

mcqs.q: Phenol has which shape around oxygen?
mcqs.why: The oxygen has two bond pairs and two lone pairs, so phenol has a bent shape like water around oxygen.

mcqs.q: The C-O-H bond angle in phenol is what?
mcqs.why: The C-O-H bond angle in phenol is 109°, slightly less than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°.

mcqs.q: By how much is phenol's C-O-H angle (109°) less than the tetrahedral angle (109.5°)?
mcqs.why: Working: 109.5 - 109 = 0.5°. Phenol's angle is 0.5° less than the tetrahedral angle.

mcqs.q: The C-O bond length in phenol is what?
mcqs.why: The C-O bond length in phenol is 136 pm, shorter than the 142 pm C-O length given for methanol.

mcqs.q: Phenol is a polar compound with dipole moment of what?
mcqs.why: Phenol is polar with a dipole moment of 1.54 D, as stated in its structure description.

mcqs.q: How many bond pairs and lone pairs does oxygen in phenol have?
mcqs.why: The oxygen atom in phenol has two bond pairs and two lone pairs of electrons, giving the bent shape.

mcqs.q: In phenol, the -OH group is bonded to which part of the molecule?
mcqs.why: In phenol the -OH group is bonded to the aromatic ring, which defines the phenol structure.

mcqs.q: Phenol's C-O-H angle is slightly less than which reference angle?
mcqs.why: At 109°, it is slightly less than the tetrahedral angle of 109.5°, by half a degree.

mcqs.q: Which property shows phenol is polar?
mcqs.why: Phenol is described as a polar compound and its dipole moment of 1.54 D quantifies that polarity.

mcqs.q: The oxygen in phenol resembles oxygen in which simple molecule in shape?
mcqs.why: Phenol has a bent shape like water because its oxygen also has two bond pairs and two lone pairs.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
• Pure phenols are generally colourless solids at room temperature. They turn reddish on exposure to air due to oxidation.
  • They have a characteristic phenolic odour.
  • They are generally insoluble in water, but phenol itself and dihydric and trihydric phenols are fairly soluble in water.
  • They have higher boiling points than aliphatic alcohols, because of strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding and high molecular masses.
  • Phenol itself is a colourless, crystalline, hygroscopic solid with a low melting point (43°C) and a medicinal odour.
  • Phenol is less soluble in water but more soluble in alcohol and chloroform. It becomes completely soluble in water above 68.5°C.
  • Phenol vapours are toxic, and phenol produces painful blisters on the skin. A 5% aqueous solution of phenol is called carbolic acid.

Key Points

  • Phenols are colourless solids with a phenolic odour; they turn reddish in air.
  • Hydrogen bonding gives phenols high boiling points.
  • Phenol melts at 43°C and is fully miscible with water above 68.5°C.
  • Phenol is toxic and blisters the skin; its 5% solution is carbolic acid.

mcqs.q: Pure phenols at room temperature are generally what?
mcqs.why: Pure phenols are generally colourless solids at room temperature and turn reddish on exposure to air due to oxidation.

mcqs.q: Phenols turn reddish in air due to what?
mcqs.why: They turn reddish on exposure to air due to oxidation, and they have a characteristic phenolic odour.

mcqs.q: Phenol itself melts at which temperature?
mcqs.why: Phenol is a colourless crystalline hygroscopic solid with a low melting point of 43°C and a medicinal odour.

mcqs.q: Phenol becomes completely soluble in water above which temperature?
mcqs.why: Phenol is less soluble in water at lower temperature but becomes completely soluble in water above 68.5°C.

mcqs.q: A 5% aqueous solution of phenol is called what?
mcqs.why: A 5% aqueous solution of phenol is called carbolic acid, as stated in the physical properties.

mcqs.q: Phenols have higher boiling points than aliphatic alcohols because of what?
options: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding and high molecular masses
mcqs.why: Strong intermolecular hydrogen bonding and high molecular masses give phenols higher boiling points than aliphatic alcohols.

mcqs.q: Phenol on the skin produces what effect?
mcqs.why: Phenol vapours are toxic and phenol produces painful blisters on the skin, so it must be handled carefully.

mcqs.q: Phenol is more soluble in which solvents than in water?
mcqs.why: Phenol is less soluble in water but more soluble in alcohol and chloroform, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which phenols are fairly soluble in water despite phenols generally being insoluble?
options: Phenol itself and dihydric and trihydric phenols
mcqs.why: Generally phenols are insoluble, but phenol itself and dihydric and trihydric phenols are fairly soluble in water.

mcqs.q: Phenol is described as a hygroscopic solid, meaning it does what?
mcqs.why: Phenol is a colourless, crystalline, hygroscopic solid, i.e. it absorbs moisture, with melting point 43°C.

lessons.title: Acidity of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
Phenol is more acidic than alcohols but less acidic than carboxylic acids:

Carboxylic acid > Phenol > Alcohol

The acidic behaviour of phenol is shown by the following facts:

  • It turns blue litmus red.
  • It reacts with sodium metal to give hydrogen gas: 2C6H5OH + 2Na → 2C6H5ONa + H2.
  • It produces H+ ions in water.
  • It reacts with a strong base to form a salt and water: C6H5OH + NaOH → C6H5ONa + H2O.
  • After losing H+, it forms a stable phenoxide (phenolate) ion.

The phenoxide ion is more stable than an alkoxide ion because its negative charge is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance. This resonance stabilization makes phenol lose its proton more easily than an alcohol.

Key Points

  • Acidity order: carboxylic acid > phenol > alcohol.
  • Phenol turns blue litmus red and reacts with Na and NaOH.
  • Phenol forms sodium phenoxide with sodium hydroxide.
  • The phenoxide ion is stabilized by resonance delocalization into the ring.
  • Resonance stabilization of phenoxide makes phenol more acidic than alcohols.

mcqs.q: What is the correct acidity order involving phenol?
mcqs.why: Acidity order is carboxylic acid > phenol > alcohol: phenol is more acidic than alcohols but less than carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: Phenol turns blue litmus to which colour?
mcqs.why: Phenol turns blue litmus red, showing its acidic behaviour in aqueous solution.

mcqs.q: Phenol reacts with sodium metal to give which gas?
mcqs.why: 2C6H5OH + 2Na -> 2C6H5ONa + H2, so hydrogen gas is evolved when phenol reacts with sodium.

mcqs.q: Phenol with NaOH forms which salt and water?
mcqs.why: C6H5OH + NaOH -> C6H5ONa + H2O, forming sodium phenoxide (phenolate) and water.

mcqs.q: After losing H+, phenol forms which ion?
mcqs.why: After losing H+, phenol forms a stable phenoxide (phenolate) ion whose charge is delocalized into the ring.

mcqs.q: The phenoxide ion is more stable than an alkoxide ion because of what?
options: Resonance delocalization into the benzene ring
mcqs.why: Its negative charge is delocalized into the benzene ring by resonance, making phenoxide more stable than alkoxide.

mcqs.q: Resonance stabilization of phenoxide makes phenol do what more easily than an alcohol?
mcqs.why: Resonance stabilization makes phenol lose its proton more easily than an alcohol, hence its greater acidity.

mcqs.q: In water, phenol shows acidity by producing which ions?
mcqs.why: Phenol produces H+ ions in water, consistent with turning blue litmus red and reacting with bases.

mcqs.q: The sodium product from phenol + sodium is named what in the equation?
mcqs.why: The equation 2C6H5OH + 2Na -> 2C6H5ONa + H2 names the salt product as sodium phenoxide.

mcqs.q: Phenol is less acidic than which class of compounds?
mcqs.why: Phenol is more acidic than alcohols but less acidic than carboxylic acids, placing it in the middle of the order.

lessons.title: Preparation of Phenol
lessons.notes_html:
From Benzene Sulphonic Acid

Benzene sulphonic acid reacts with NaOH at room temperature to give sodium benzene sulphonate. This is fused with NaOH at about 300°C to give sodium phenoxide, which gives phenol on hydrolysis with HCl. This is the oldest method of preparing phenol and is not used nowadays.

From Chlorobenzene (Dow's Method)

Chlorobenzene is heated with 10% NaOH at 350°C and 300 atm pressure to give sodium phenoxide, which gives phenol on acid hydrolysis. This method has limited laboratory application.

From Acidic Oxidation of Cumene

Cumene is oxidized by air to cumene hydroperoxide. Hydrolysis of cumene hydroperoxide with HCl gives phenol and acetone. Most of the phenol produced in the world today is made by this method.

From Hydrolysis of Diazonium Salts

Benzenediazonium chloride is warmed with water and then acidified. It gives phenol, with nitrogen gas released.

Key Points

  • Fusion of sodium benzene sulphonate with NaOH is the oldest method; it is no longer used.
  • Dow's method: chlorobenzene + NaOH at 350°C and 300 atm gives phenol.
  • The cumene method gives phenol and acetone, and is the main industrial method today.
  • Warming benzenediazonium chloride with water also gives phenol.
  • In every method, sodium phenoxide is acidified to get free phenol.

mcqs.q: The oldest method of preparing phenol uses which starting acid?
mcqs.why: Benzene sulphonic acid via sodium benzene sulphonate fused with NaOH is the oldest method and is not used nowadays.

mcqs.q: Fusion of sodium benzene sulphonate with NaOH is done at about which temperature?
mcqs.why: Sodium benzene sulphonate is fused with NaOH at about 300°C to give sodium phenoxide, then phenol on hydrolysis with HCl.

mcqs.q: In Dow's method, chlorobenzene is heated with 10% NaOH at which conditions?
mcqs.why: Dow's method heats chlorobenzene with 10% NaOH at 350°C and 300 atm to give sodium phenoxide, then phenol.

mcqs.q: The cumene method produces phenol along with which co-product?
mcqs.why: Cumene is oxidized to cumene hydroperoxide, whose hydrolysis with HCl gives phenol and acetone.

mcqs.q: Most phenol produced in the world today is made by which method?
mcqs.why: Most phenol today is made by acidic oxidation of cumene, via cumene hydroperoxide to phenol and acetone.

mcqs.q: Benzenediazonium chloride warmed with water gives phenol with release of which gas?
mcqs.why: Hydrolysis of diazonium salts: benzenediazonium chloride warmed with water gives phenol with nitrogen gas released.

mcqs.q: In the cumene method, cumene is first oxidized by air to what?
mcqs.why: Cumene is oxidized by air to cumene hydroperoxide, which is then hydrolyzed with HCl to phenol and acetone.

mcqs.q: Dow's method has which limitation noted in the notes?
options: It is the main industrial method
mcqs.why: Dow's method, despite giving phenol from chlorobenzene under harsh conditions, has limited laboratory application.

mcqs.q: In all phenol preparations via sodium phenoxide, free phenol is obtained by what?
mcqs.why: Sodium phenoxide formed in these methods gives free phenol on acid hydrolysis or acidification.

mcqs.q: Benzene sulphonic acid first reacts with NaOH at room temperature to give what?
mcqs.why: It reacts with NaOH at room temperature to give sodium benzene sulphonate, which is then fused with NaOH at 300°C.

lessons.title: Reactions of Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
The —OH group of phenol is electron donating. It increases the electron density at the ortho and para positions of the ring by donating its electron pair to the ring. So the benzene ring of phenol is more reactive towards electrophilic substitution than benzene itself, and phenols behave as nucleophiles in most reactions.

Phenols give two types of reactions: reactions due to the —OH group and reactions due to the benzene ring.

Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution

The —OH group is an ortho-para director.

  • Nitration: with dilute HNO3 at room temperature, phenol gives o-nitrophenol (30–40%) and p-nitrophenol (20%). With concentrated HNO3, it gives picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol): C6H5OH + 3HNO3 → C6H2(NO2)3OH + 3H2O.
  • Halogenation: with bromine water, phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol: C6H5OH + 3Br2 → C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr.

Reaction with Sodium Metal

On warming with sodium metal, phenol gives sodium phenoxide, a water-soluble salt, and hydrogen gas.

Oxidation

Phenol is oxidized to p-benzoquinone by stronger oxidizing agents such as silver oxide, lead tetraacetate, dichromate and atmospheric oxygen. Phenols are more easily oxidized than simple alcohols.

Key Points

  • The —OH group activates the ring and directs electrophiles to ortho and para positions.
  • Dilute HNO3 gives o- and p-nitrophenol; concentrated HNO3 gives picric acid.
  • Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol at once.
  • Phenol reacts with sodium to form sodium phenoxide and hydrogen.
  • Strong oxidizing agents convert phenol into p-benzoquinone.

mcqs.q: The -OH group of phenol is described as what towards the ring?
mcqs.why: The -OH group is electron donating; it increases electron density at ortho and para positions by donating its pair to the ring.

mcqs.q: Phenol's ring compared with benzene towards electrophilic substitution is what?
mcqs.why: The benzene ring of phenol is more reactive towards electrophilic substitution than benzene itself.

mcqs.q: The -OH group in phenol directs electrophiles to which positions?
mcqs.why: The -OH group is an ortho-para director, directing electrophilic substitution to ortho and para positions.

mcqs.q: Phenol with dilute HNO3 at room temperature gives which products?
mcqs.why: With dilute HNO3 at room temperature phenol gives o-nitrophenol (30-40%) and p-nitrophenol (20%).

mcqs.q: Phenol with concentrated HNO3 gives which product?
mcqs.why: With concentrated HNO3 phenol gives picric acid: C6H5OH + 3HNO3 -> C6H2(NO2)3OH + 3H2O.

mcqs.q: Phenol with bromine water gives which observation?
mcqs.why: Bromine water gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol at once: C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr.

mcqs.q: Phenol warmed with sodium metal gives which products?
mcqs.why: On warming with sodium, phenol gives sodium phenoxide, a water-soluble salt, and hydrogen gas.

mcqs.q: Strong oxidizing agents convert phenol into which product?
mcqs.why: Phenol is oxidized to p-benzoquinone by stronger oxidants such as silver oxide, lead tetraacetate, dichromate and air oxygen.

mcqs.q: Compared with simple alcohols, phenols are oxidized how?
mcqs.why: Phenols are more easily oxidized than simple alcohols, giving p-benzoquinone with strong oxidizing agents.

mcqs.q: How many Br2 molecules react with one phenol in the bromine water equation?
mcqs.why: Working from the equation C6H5OH + 3Br2 -> C6H2Br3OH + 3HBr: three Br2 molecules react per phenol molecule.

lessons.title: Difference between Alcohols and Phenols
lessons.notes_html:
AlcoholsPhenols
The —OH group is bonded to an alkyl groupThe —OH group is bonded to an aryl group
Hydroxyl derivatives of alkanesHydroxyl derivatives of benzene
General formula R—OHGeneral formula Ar—OH
Less acidicMore acidic
pKa values about 16–20pKa values about 10
Lower alcohols are colourless liquidsColourless crystalline solids
Characteristic sweet smellPhenolic smell
No action with bromine waterWhite precipitate with bromine water
Do not react with NaOH solutionReact with NaOH solution to form phenoxides

Antiseptics and Disinfectants

Antiseptics are mild antimicrobial chemicals applied to living tissue such as skin and wounds; they are safe for the body. Examples: surgical spirit (ethyl alcohol 60–70% or isopropyl alcohol at least 70%), iodine, dettol, boric acid and hydrogen peroxide.

Disinfectants are strong antimicrobial chemicals applied to non-living surfaces such as floors, doors and instruments; they can be harmful and corrosive. Examples: phenol, dettol, formalin and sodium hypochlorite.

Alcohols (ethyl and isopropyl) are widely used as antiseptics and disinfectants because they kill bacteria and viruses. Phenols are widely used as disinfectants in household products.

Key Points

  • In alcohols —OH is on an alkyl group; in phenols it is directly on the benzene ring.
  • Phenols (pKa about 10) are much more acidic than alcohols (pKa about 16–20).
  • Phenols react with NaOH and give a white precipitate with bromine water; alcohols do neither.
  • Antiseptics are mild and used on living tissue; disinfectants are strong and used on surfaces.
  • Alcohols and phenols are both used to kill bacteria and viruses.

mcqs.q: In alcohols the -OH is bonded to an alkyl group, while in phenols it is bonded to what?
mcqs.why: In phenols the -OH group is bonded to an aryl group (the benzene ring), unlike alcohols where it is on an alkyl group.

mcqs.q: General formulas are R-OH for alcohols and what for phenols?
mcqs.why: Alcohols have general formula R-OH and phenols have general formula Ar-OH, reflecting aryl attachment.

mcqs.q: pKa values given are about 16-20 for alcohols and about what for phenols?
mcqs.why: Phenols have pKa about 10, much lower than alcohols at about 16-20, showing phenols are much more acidic.

mcqs.q: With bromine water, alcohols show what, while phenols give a white precipitate?
mcqs.why: Alcohols have no action with bromine water, whereas phenols give a white precipitate of tribromophenol.

mcqs.q: With NaOH solution, alcohols do not react, while phenols do what?
mcqs.why: Phenols react with NaOH solution to form phenoxides; alcohols do not react with NaOH solution.

mcqs.q: Antiseptics are applied to which type of material?
options: Living tissue such as skin and wounds
mcqs.why: Antiseptics are mild antimicrobial chemicals applied to living tissue such as skin and wounds; they are safe for the body.

mcqs.q: Disinfectants are applied to which type of material?
options: Non-living surfaces such as floors and instruments
mcqs.why: Disinfectants are strong antimicrobial chemicals applied to non-living surfaces such as floors, doors and instruments.

mcqs.q: Surgical spirit, listed as an antiseptic, contains which alcohol content?
options: Ethyl alcohol 60-70% or isopropyl alcohol at least 70%
mcqs.why: Examples include surgical spirit (ethyl alcohol 60-70% or isopropyl alcohol at least 70%), iodine, dettol and boric acid.

mcqs.q: Which set are all listed as disinfectant examples?
options: Phenol, dettol, formalin and sodium hypochlorite
mcqs.why: Disinfectant examples given are phenol, dettol, formalin and sodium hypochlorite, used on non-living surfaces.

mcqs.q: Lower alcohols are colourless liquids, while phenols are described as what?
mcqs.why: The table contrasts lower alcohols as colourless liquids with phenols as colourless crystalline solids with phenolic smell.

lessons.title: Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers are compounds in which an oxygen atom is bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups. They may be considered as derivatives of water in which both hydrogen atoms are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups.

The two groups R and R' may be alkyl, aryl or vinyl groups. The general formula of ethers is R—O—R'. The bond angle at oxygen is somewhat greater than in water; in dimethyl ether it is 110°.

Types of Ethers

  • Symmetrical (simple) ethers: both groups on oxygen are the same, e.g. dimethyl ether and diphenyl ether.
  • Unsymmetrical (mixed) ethers: the two groups on oxygen are different, e.g. ethyl methyl ether and methyl phenyl ether.

Key Points

  • Ethers have the general formula R—O—R' and are derivatives of water.
  • Symmetrical ethers have two identical groups on oxygen.
  • Unsymmetrical (mixed) ethers have two different groups on oxygen.
  • The C—O—C bond angle in dimethyl ether is 110°.

mcqs.q: Ethers have an oxygen atom bonded to how many alkyl or aryl groups?
mcqs.why: Ethers are compounds in which an oxygen atom is bonded to two alkyl or aryl groups, with formula R-O-R'.

mcqs.q: Ethers are derivatives of water in which both hydrogens are replaced by what?
mcqs.why: Both hydrogen atoms of water are replaced by alkyl or aryl groups to give an ether, R-O-R'.

mcqs.q: The general formula of ethers is given as what?
mcqs.why: The general formula of ethers is R-O-R', where R and R' may be alkyl, aryl or vinyl groups.
