mcqs.q: The bond angle at oxygen in dimethyl ether is what?
mcqs.why: The bond angle at oxygen is somewhat greater than in water; in dimethyl ether it is 110°.

mcqs.q: Symmetrical (simple) ethers have which feature?
options: Both groups on oxygen are the same
mcqs.why: Symmetrical ethers have both groups the same, e.g. dimethyl ether and diphenyl ether.

mcqs.q: Unsymmetrical (mixed) ethers have which feature?
mcqs.why: Unsymmetrical ethers have two different groups, e.g. ethyl methyl ether and methyl phenyl ether.

mcqs.q: Dimethyl ether and diphenyl ether are examples of which ether type?
mcqs.why: Both have identical groups on oxygen, so they are symmetrical (simple) ethers as listed.

mcqs.q: Ethyl methyl ether is an example of which ether type?
mcqs.why: Ethyl methyl ether has different ethyl and methyl groups on oxygen, so it is an unsymmetrical (mixed) ether.

mcqs.q: The groups R and R' in ethers may be which types?
mcqs.why: The two groups R and R' may be alkyl, aryl or vinyl groups in the general ether structure.

mcqs.q: Methyl phenyl ether is classified as what?
mcqs.why: Methyl phenyl ether has different methyl and phenyl groups on oxygen, so it is an unsymmetrical ether.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Common System

The two groups attached to oxygen are named in alphabetical order, followed by the word ether. If both groups are the same, the prefix di- is used, e.g. dimethyl ether, ethyl methyl ether, diphenyl ether.

IUPAC System

In the IUPAC system, ethers are named as alkoxy derivatives of hydrocarbons:

  • The larger group is taken as the parent alkane.
  • The smaller group, together with oxygen, is named as an alkoxy group (methoxy, ethoxy, etc.).

Examples: CH3—O—CH3 is methoxymethane; CH3—O—CH2CH3 is methoxyethane; CH3—O—CH(CH3)2 is 2-methoxypropane; CH3CH2—O—CH(CH3)CH2CH3 is 2-ethoxybutane.

The common system is generally used, but the IUPAC system is used for compounds containing more than one ether linkage.

Key Points

  • Common name: groups in alphabetical order + ether; di- for identical groups.
  • IUPAC name: alkoxy group + parent alkane (larger group).
  • Dimethyl ether is methoxymethane in the IUPAC system.
  • The IUPAC system is used for compounds with more than one ether linkage.

mcqs.q: In the common system for ethers, groups are named in which order followed by 'ether'?
mcqs.why: The two groups attached to oxygen are named in alphabetical order, followed by the word ether.

mcqs.q: If both groups on oxygen are the same, which prefix is used in the common name?
mcqs.why: If both groups are the same the prefix di- is used, e.g. dimethyl ether and diphenyl ether in common naming.

mcqs.q: In IUPAC naming, ethers are named as which derivatives of hydrocarbons?
mcqs.why: In IUPAC, ethers are named as alkoxy derivatives: the smaller group plus oxygen is the alkoxy group.

mcqs.q: In IUPAC ether naming, the larger group is taken as what?
mcqs.why: The larger group is taken as the parent alkane and the smaller group with oxygen is named as an alkoxy group.

mcqs.q: CH3-O-CH3 in IUPAC is named what?
mcqs.why: CH3-O-CH3 is methoxymethane in IUPAC, though its common name is dimethyl ether.

mcqs.q: CH3-O-CH2CH3 in IUPAC is named what?
mcqs.why: CH3-O-CH2CH3 is methoxyethane: methoxy is the smaller group and ethane is the larger parent.

mcqs.q: The IUPAC system for ethers is mainly used when a compound contains what?
mcqs.why: The common system is generally used, but IUPAC is used for compounds containing more than one ether linkage.

mcqs.q: Alkoxy group names mentioned include which pair?
mcqs.why: Smaller groups with oxygen are named as alkoxy groups such as methoxy and ethoxy in IUPAC ether names.

mcqs.q: CH3-O-CH(CH3)2 is given as which IUPAC name?
mcqs.why: CH3-O-CH(CH3)2 is 2-methoxypropane, with the methoxy group at position 2 of propane.

mcqs.q: Which system is generally used for naming simple ethers?
mcqs.why: The common system is generally used for ethers; IUPAC is reserved for compounds with more than one ether linkage.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
• Lower ethers such as dimethyl ether and ethyl methyl ether are gases. Higher ethers are colourless, volatile liquids.
  • They have a pleasant odour.
  • They are highly inflammable.
  • They have low boiling points, because there is no hydrogen bonding between ether molecules.
  • They are slightly soluble in water, because they can form hydrogen bonds with water. Solubility decreases as the size of the alkyl groups increases.
  • They are readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene and chloroform.
  • They are lighter (less dense) than water.
  • Because of these properties, ethers are used as solvents.

Key Points

  • Lower ethers are gases; higher ethers are volatile, pleasant-smelling liquids.
  • Ethers are highly inflammable and have low boiling points.
  • They cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, but can hydrogen-bond with water.
  • They are less dense than water and slightly soluble in it.
  • Ethers are widely used as solvents.

mcqs.q: Lower ethers such as dimethyl ether are what at room conditions?
mcqs.why: Lower ethers such as dimethyl ether and ethyl methyl ether are gases; higher ethers are colourless volatile liquids.

mcqs.q: Higher ethers are described as what?
options: Colourless, volatile liquids with pleasant odour
mcqs.why: Higher ethers are colourless, volatile liquids; they have a pleasant odour and are highly inflammable.

mcqs.q: Ethers have low boiling points because of what?
options: Strong hydrogen bonding between ether molecules
No hydrogen bonding between ether molecules
mcqs.why: They have low boiling points because there is no hydrogen bonding between ether molecules themselves.

mcqs.q: Ethers are slightly soluble in water because they can do what?
mcqs.why: They are slightly soluble in water because they can form hydrogen bonds with water, unlike between themselves.

mcqs.q: As alkyl group size in ethers increases, water solubility does what?
mcqs.why: Solubility in water decreases as the size of the alkyl groups increases, similar to the trend in alcohols.

mcqs.q: Ethers are readily soluble in which solvents?
options: Organic solvents such as benzene and chloroform
mcqs.why: They are readily soluble in organic solvents such as benzene and chloroform, and are widely used as solvents.

mcqs.q: Compared with water, ethers are what in density?
mcqs.why: Ethers are lighter (less dense) than water, which is listed among their physical properties.

mcqs.q: Ethers are described as highly what, requiring care?
mcqs.why: Ethers are highly inflammable, volatile liquids or gases, which is why their solvent use needs care.

mcqs.q: Because of their properties, ethers are widely used as what?
mcqs.why: Because of these properties ethers are used as solvents, dissolving many organic substances.

mcqs.q: Ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond with each other mainly because they lack what?
mcqs.why: Ethers have no -OH group and no hydrogen on oxygen, so they cannot hydrogen-bond between their own molecules.

lessons.title: Preparation of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Williamson's Synthesis

An alcohol is first treated with sodium metal to form a sodium alkoxide. The alkoxide then reacts with an alkyl halide to form an ether:

R—ONa + R'—X → R—O—R' + NaX

This is the most important and widely used method for the preparation of ethers.

Reaction of Alkyl Halides with Dry Silver Oxide

Alkyl halides react with dry silver oxide on heating to form ethers:

2R—X + Ag2O → R—O—R + 2AgX

Key Points

  • Williamson's synthesis: sodium alkoxide + alkyl halide gives an ether.
  • Williamson's synthesis is the most important method for preparing ethers.
  • Dry silver oxide converts alkyl halides into ethers on heating.
  • In Williamson's synthesis, the alkoxide is made by reacting the alcohol with sodium metal.

mcqs.q: Williamson's synthesis first treats an alcohol with sodium to form what?
mcqs.why: An alcohol is first treated with sodium metal to form a sodium alkoxide, which then reacts with an alkyl halide.

mcqs.q: In Williamson's synthesis, the alkoxide reacts with which compound to form an ether?
mcqs.why: R-ONa + R'-X -> R-O-R' + NaX: the alkoxide reacts with an alkyl halide to form an ether.

mcqs.q: Williamson's synthesis is described as which kind of method?
options: The most important and widely used method for ethers
mcqs.why: It is the most important and widely used method for the preparation of ethers, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: The salt by-product in R-ONa + R'-X -> R-O-R' + NaX is what?
mcqs.why: The equation shows NaX as the inorganic by-product alongside the ether R-O-R' in Williamson's synthesis.

mcqs.q: Alkyl halides with dry silver oxide on heating form what?
mcqs.why: 2R-X + Ag2O -> R-O-R + 2AgX on heating, so dry silver oxide converts alkyl halides into ethers.

mcqs.q: How many R-X molecules react with Ag2O in the silver oxide method?
mcqs.why: The equation is 2R-X + Ag2O -> R-O-R + 2AgX, so two alkyl halide molecules react per Ag2O.

mcqs.q: The silver-containing by-product in the Ag2O method is what?
mcqs.why: Two molecules of AgX are formed alongside the ether in 2R-X + Ag2O -> R-O-R + 2AgX.

mcqs.q: In Williamson's synthesis, the alkoxide is made by reacting alcohol with what?
mcqs.why: The alkoxide is made by reacting the alcohol with sodium metal, as explicitly noted for Williamson's synthesis.

mcqs.q: Which reagent must be dry in the silver oxide preparation of ethers?
mcqs.why: Alkyl halides react with dry silver oxide on heating to form ethers; the oxide is specified as dry.

mcqs.q: Williamson's synthesis product R-O-R' can be which type of ether depending on R and R'?
mcqs.why: Since R and R' come from different reactants (alkoxide and halide), the product can be symmetrical or unsymmetrical ethers.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Ethers are stable compounds. They are less reactive than alcohols but more reactive than alkanes.

Ethers are less reactive because they have no active hydrogen bonded to oxygen, as alcohols have. They become reactive only when the oxygen is protonated in an acidic medium.

Ethers do not react with bases, dilute acids, metallic sodium, reducing agents or oxidizing agents in the cold state. However, they show some characteristic reactions with concentrated acids.

Key Points

  • Ethers are stable and much less reactive than alcohols.
  • They have no active (O—H) hydrogen.
  • They react only after protonation of oxygen in acidic medium.
  • They do not react with bases, dilute acids, sodium, or cold oxidizing and reducing agents.

mcqs.q: Ethers are described as which kind of compounds in reactivity?
mcqs.why: Ethers are stable compounds; they are less reactive than alcohols but more reactive than alkanes.

mcqs.q: Ethers are less reactive than alcohols but more reactive than what?
mcqs.why: The order given is alcohols more reactive than ethers, and ethers more reactive than alkanes.

mcqs.q: Ethers are less reactive because they have no what?
mcqs.why: They have no active hydrogen bonded to oxygen, as alcohols have in their -OH group, so they are less reactive.

mcqs.q: Ethers become reactive only when oxygen is what in acidic medium?
mcqs.why: They become reactive only when the oxygen is protonated in an acidic medium, enabling their acid reactions.

mcqs.q: Ethers do NOT react with which set in the cold state?
options: Bases, dilute acids, metallic sodium, reducing and oxidizing agents in the cold
mcqs.why: They do not react with bases, dilute acids, metallic sodium, reducing agents or oxidizing agents in the cold state.

mcqs.q: Ethers show characteristic reactions with which acids?
mcqs.why: However, they show some characteristic reactions with concentrated acids, such as forming oxonium salts and cleavage.

mcqs.q: Which statement about ethers and metallic sodium is correct?
options: They do not react with metallic sodium
mcqs.why: Unlike alcohols, ethers do not react with metallic sodium because they have no active O-H hydrogen.

mcqs.q: Protonation of ether oxygen occurs in which medium?
mcqs.why: Ethers become reactive only when oxygen is protonated in an acidic medium, as stated in the reactivity notes.

mcqs.q: Compared with alcohols, ethers are what in reactivity?
mcqs.why: Ethers are less reactive than alcohols, largely because alcohols have an active hydrogen on oxygen and ethers do not.

mcqs.q: In the cold state, ethers do not react with oxidizing agents; they react mainly after what?
mcqs.why: Cold oxidizing agents do not react; reactivity appears after protonation of oxygen in acidic medium.

lessons.title: Reactions of Ethers
lessons.notes_html:
Reaction with Cold Concentrated Acids

Ethers react with cold concentrated HCl or H2SO4 to produce oxonium salts:

(C2H5)2O + HCl → [(C2H5)2OH]+ Cl− (diethyl oxonium chloride)

(C2H5)2O + H2SO4 → [(C2H5)2OH]+ HSO4− (diethyl oxonium hydrogen sulphate)

Reaction with Hot Concentrated Acids

With hot concentrated HCl or HI, the ether is cleaved into an alcohol and an alkyl halide:

C2H5—O—C2H5 + HCl → C2H5OH + C2H5Cl

If excess acid is used, the alcohol formed reacts further with HX to give more alkyl halide.

Use of Ether as Anesthesia

Diethyl ether is a colourless, volatile and highly flammable liquid with a characteristic smell. It was one of the first chemicals used as an anesthetic in hospitals. An anesthetic causes loss of sensation or consciousness so that surgery can be done without pain. The three important early anesthetics were diethyl ether, chloroform and nitrous oxide. Diethyl ether is safer than chloroform and more effective than nitrous oxide, and it remained the standard general anesthetic until the 1960s. It is no longer used in advanced countries because it is extremely flammable and recovery from its anesthesia is prolonged; safer fluorinated hydrocarbons are used instead. It is still used in some developing countries because it is cheap.

Key Points

  • Cold concentrated acids convert ethers into oxonium salts.
  • Hot concentrated HCl or HI cleaves ethers into an alcohol and an alkyl halide.
  • With excess acid, the alcohol is also converted into alkyl halide.
  • Diethyl ether was the standard general anesthetic until the 1960s.
  • Ether is little used as an anesthetic now because it is highly flammable.

mcqs.q: Ethers with cold concentrated HCl or H2SO4 produce which salts?
mcqs.why: Cold concentrated acids produce oxonium salts, e.g. (C2H5)2O + HCl -> [(C2H5)2OH]+ Cl- .

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether with cold concentrated HCl gives which named salt?
mcqs.why: (C2H5)2O + HCl -> [(C2H5)2OH]+ Cl-, named diethyl oxonium chloride in the notes.

mcqs.q: With hot concentrated HCl or HI, an ether is cleaved into what?
options: An alcohol and an alkyl halide
mcqs.why: Hot concentrated HCl or HI cleaves the ether: C2H5-O-C2H5 + HCl -> C2H5OH + C2H5Cl, an alcohol plus alkyl halide.

mcqs.q: If excess hot acid is used on an ether, the alcohol formed does what?
options: Reacts further with HX to give more alkyl halide
mcqs.why: With excess acid, the alcohol formed reacts further with HX to give more alkyl halide, beyond the first cleavage.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether was used in hospitals as one of the first what?
mcqs.why: Diethyl ether was one of the first chemicals used as an anesthetic in hospitals, causing loss of sensation or consciousness.

mcqs.q: The three important early anesthetics listed are which?
mcqs.why: The three important early anesthetics were diethyl ether, chloroform and nitrous oxide, as listed in the notes.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether compared with chloroform and nitrous oxide was described as what?
options: Safer than chloroform and more effective than nitrous oxide
mcqs.why: Diethyl ether is safer than chloroform and more effective than nitrous oxide, and was the standard anesthetic until the 1960s.

mcqs.q: Diethyl ether remained the standard general anesthetic until which decade?
mcqs.why: It remained the standard general anesthetic until the 1960s, before being replaced in advanced countries.

mcqs.q: Ether is little used as an anesthetic now mainly because it is what?
options: Extremely flammable and recovery is prolonged
mcqs.why: It is no longer used in advanced countries because it is extremely flammable and recovery from its anesthesia is prolonged.

mcqs.q: In some developing countries diethyl ether is still used as anesthetic because it is what?
mcqs.why: It is still used in some developing countries because it is cheap, despite flammability and prolonged recovery.

lessons.title: Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones are carbonyl compounds: they contain the carbonyl group, C=O. They play an important role in chemistry, biology and biochemistry, and they are responsible for many flavours and odours.

  • Vanillin, an aldehyde, gives the vanilla flavour.
  • Benzaldehyde, an aldehyde, gives the almond flavour.
  • R-carvone, a ketone, gives the spearmint flavour.
  • The male and female sex hormones, testosterone and progesterone, also contain carbonyl groups.

In an aldehyde, one alkyl (or aryl) group and one hydrogen atom are bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group: general formula RCHO. Formaldehyde is the exception, because it has two hydrogen atoms bonded to the carbonyl carbon. In a ketone, two alkyl (or aryl) groups are bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group: general formula RCOR.

Key Points

  • Aldehydes and ketones are carbonyl compounds, containing the C=O group.
  • They give many natural flavours and odours, e.g. vanillin, benzaldehyde and R-carvone.
  • An aldehyde has one alkyl (or aryl) group and one H on the carbonyl carbon (RCHO).
  • Formaldehyde is the exception: it has two H atoms on the carbonyl carbon.
  • A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups on the carbonyl carbon (RCOR).

mcqs.q: What group do aldehydes and ketones both contain?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones are carbonyl compounds because they contain the carbonyl group, C=O, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Which aldehyde gives the vanilla flavour?
mcqs.why: The notes state that vanillin, an aldehyde, gives the vanilla flavour, while benzaldehyde gives the almond flavour.

mcqs.q: Benzaldehyde is responsible for which flavour?
mcqs.why: According to the notes, benzaldehyde, an aldehyde, gives the almond flavour found in almonds.

mcqs.q: R-carvone, which gives the spearmint flavour, is classified as what?
mcqs.why: The notes identify R-carvone as a ketone that gives the spearmint flavour, unlike vanillin and benzaldehyde which are aldehydes.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of an aldehyde?
mcqs.why: An aldehyde has one alkyl or aryl group and one hydrogen on the carbonyl carbon, giving the general formula RCHO.

mcqs.q: Why is formaldehyde an exception among aldehydes?
options: It has two hydrogen atoms on the carbonyl carbon
It has two alkyl groups on the carbonyl carbon
It has no hydrogen atoms at all
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is the exception because it has two hydrogen atoms bonded to the carbonyl carbon instead of one alkyl group and one hydrogen.

mcqs.q: What is the general formula of a ketone?
mcqs.why: In a ketone two alkyl or aryl groups are bonded to the carbonyl carbon, so the general formula is written as RCOR.

mcqs.q: Which pair of sex hormones is mentioned as containing carbonyl groups?
mcqs.why: The notes state that the male and female sex hormones testosterone and progesterone also contain carbonyl groups.

mcqs.q: In an aldehyde, what is bonded to the carbonyl carbon besides the carbonyl oxygen?
options: One hydroxyl group and one alkyl group
Two hydrogen atoms in every case
One alkyl or aryl group and one hydrogen atom
mcqs.why: The notes define an aldehyde by one alkyl or aryl group and one hydrogen atom bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group.

mcqs.q: How does a ketone differ from an aldehyde at the carbonyl carbon?
options: A ketone has one hydrogen and one alkyl group
A ketone has a hydroxyl group
A ketone has two alkyl or aryl groups
A ketone has no carbonyl group
mcqs.why: A ketone has two alkyl or aryl groups on the carbonyl carbon, whereas an aldehyde has only one such group plus a hydrogen.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Aldehydes
lessons.notes_html:
Both common and IUPAC names are used for aldehydes.

Common System

The common names of aldehydes are derived from the names of the corresponding carboxylic acids by replacing the ending -ic acid with the word -aldehyde. The position of substituents on the chain is shown by Greek letters α, β, γ, δ, etc. The α-carbon is the carbon directly bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group. Examples: formaldehyde (HCHO), acetaldehyde (CH3CHO), propionaldehyde (CH3CH2CHO), β-methylbutyraldehyde, γ-chloro-α,β-dimethylvaleraldehyde.

IUPAC System

The IUPAC names of aldehydes are derived from the names of the corresponding alkanes by replacing the ending -e with -al. Aldehydes are therefore named as alkanals: a three-carbon aldehyde is propanal and a four-carbon aldehyde is butanal. For higher aldehydes with substituents, find the longest chain containing the aldehyde group and number it so that the aldehyde group gets position one. There is no need to indicate the position of the aldehyde group, because it always lies at the end of the chain and is given position number one.

IUPAC examples: methanal, ethanal, propanal, 3-methylbutanal, 4-bromo-3-chloro-2-methylbutanal, 4-chloro-2,3-dimethylpentanal, 3,3-dimethylhexanal.

Key Points

  • Common names come from the corresponding acid: -ic acid is replaced by -aldehyde.
  • Substituent positions in common names use Greek letters α, β, γ, δ from the carbonyl carbon.
  • IUPAC names are alkanals: the alkane ending -e is replaced by -al.
  • The aldehyde carbon is always C-1, so its position is not written.
  • Examples: HCHO = methanal (formaldehyde); CH3CHO = ethanal (acetaldehyde).

mcqs.q: In the common system, aldehyde names are derived from the corresponding carboxylic acids by replacing which ending?
mcqs.why: Common names replace the ending -ic acid of the corresponding carboxylic acid with the word -aldehyde.

mcqs.q: In common aldehyde nomenclature, substituent positions are shown by what?
options: Greek letters alpha, beta, gamma, delta
mcqs.why: The position of substituents is shown by Greek letters alpha, beta, gamma, delta, etc., starting from the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: Which carbon is the alpha-carbon in an aldehyde?
options: The carbon farthest from the carbonyl group
The carbon directly bonded to the carbonyl carbon
The last carbon of the chain
mcqs.why: The alpha-carbon is defined as the carbon directly bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group in the common system.

mcqs.q: What is the common name of HCHO?
mcqs.why: HCHO is formaldehyde in the common system and methanal in the IUPAC system, as given in the notes examples.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CHO?
mcqs.why: CH3CHO is ethanal in the IUPAC system and acetaldehyde in the common system, a two-carbon aldehyde.

mcqs.q: How are IUPAC aldehyde names formed from alkanes?
mcqs.why: IUPAC names of aldehydes replace the alkane ending -e with -al, so they are named as alkanals.

mcqs.q: A three-carbon aldehyde has which IUPAC name?
mcqs.why: A three-carbon aldehyde is propanal and a four-carbon aldehyde is butanal, according to the IUPAC examples in the notes.

mcqs.q: Why is the position of the aldehyde group not written in IUPAC names?
options: Because it can be anywhere in the chain
Because it always lies at the end and is given position one
mcqs.why: There is no need to indicate the position because the aldehyde group always lies at the end of the chain and is given position number one.

mcqs.q: What is the IUPAC name for the four-carbon aldehyde?
mcqs.why: The notes state that a four-carbon aldehyde is butanal, formed from butane by replacing the ending -e with -al.

mcqs.q: In IUPAC naming of a substituted aldehyde, how is the longest chain numbered?
options: From the end farthest from the aldehyde group
So the aldehyde group gets position one
mcqs.why: For higher aldehydes, find the longest chain containing the aldehyde group and number it so the aldehyde group gets position one.

lessons.title: Nomenclature of Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Common System

The common names of ketones are obtained by naming the two alkyl (or aryl) groups bonded to the carbon of the carbonyl group, in alphabetical order, and adding the word ketone as a separate word. If the two groups are the same, the prefix di is used. The position of substituents on the chain is indicated by Greek letters (α, β, γ, δ, etc.), starting with the carbon next to the carbonyl group, and substituents are named in alphabetical order. Examples: dimethyl ketone, ethyl methyl ketone, ethyl isopropyl ketone, diphenyl ketone, methyl phenyl ketone.

Some ketones are known by their historical names: dimethyl ketone is always named acetone, diphenyl ketone is called benzophenone, and methyl phenyl ketone is known as acetophenone.

IUPAC System

The IUPAC names of ketones are derived from the names of the corresponding alkanes by replacing the ending -e with -one. Ketones are therefore named as alkanones: a four-carbon ketone is butanone and a five-carbon ketone is pentanone. For open-chain ketones, find the longest chain containing the carbonyl group and number it so that the carbonyl group is assigned the lowest possible number; the position of the carbonyl carbon is indicated before the stem name. If two or more ketonic groups are present, the suffixes dione, trione, tetraone are used. The positions of substituents are shown by the numbers of the carbons to which they are attached.

IUPAC examples: propanone, butan-2-one, 2-methylpentan-3-one, 2,4-dimethylpentan-3-one, 4-hydroxy-2-methylhexan-3-one, 6-chloro-4,5-dimethylheptan-3-one.

Key Points

  • Common ketone names: the two groups on the carbonyl carbon (alphabetical) + ketone.
  • Identical groups take the prefix di, e.g. dimethyl ketone.
  • Historical names: acetone, benzophenone and acetophenone.
  • IUPAC names are alkanones: the alkane ending -e is replaced by -one.
  • Number the longest chain so the carbonyl group gets the lowest possible number.
  • Two or more keto groups are shown by dione, trione, tetraone.

mcqs.q: How are common names of ketones obtained?
options: By naming the two groups on the carbonyl carbon alphabetically and adding ketone
From the parent acid by replacing -ic acid
mcqs.why: Common ketone names name the two alkyl or aryl groups on the carbonyl carbon in alphabetical order and add the word ketone.

mcqs.q: What prefix is used when the two groups on a ketone carbonyl are identical?
mcqs.why: If the two groups are the same, the prefix di is used, as in dimethyl ketone given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Dimethyl ketone is always known by which historical name?
mcqs.why: The notes state that dimethyl ketone is always named acetone, one of the historical names retained for ketones.

mcqs.q: Diphenyl ketone is called by which historical name?
mcqs.why: Diphenyl ketone is called benzophenone, while methyl phenyl ketone is known as acetophenone.

mcqs.q: Methyl phenyl ketone is known as what?
mcqs.why: The notes give methyl phenyl ketone the historical name acetophenone, distinct from acetone and benzophenone.

mcqs.q: How are IUPAC ketone names formed from alkanes?
mcqs.why: IUPAC names of ketones replace the alkane ending -e with -one, so ketones are named as alkanones.

mcqs.q: A five-carbon ketone belongs to which IUPAC family name pattern?
mcqs.why: A five-carbon ketone is pentanone and a four-carbon ketone is butanone, following the alkanone naming pattern.

mcqs.q: How is an open-chain ketone numbered in the IUPAC system?
options: So the carbonyl group gets the highest number
So the carbonyl group gets the lowest possible number
Always from the left regardless of position
mcqs.why: The longest chain containing the carbonyl group is numbered so the carbonyl group is assigned the lowest possible number.

mcqs.q: Which suffixes show two or more ketonic groups?
mcqs.why: If two or more ketonic groups are present, the suffixes dione, trione and tetraone are used in IUPAC names.

mcqs.q: In common ketone names, how are the two groups listed?
mcqs.why: The two alkyl or aryl groups bonded to the carbonyl carbon are named in alphabetical order before the word ketone.

lessons.title: Physical Properties of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
• The carbonyl group is polar, because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon. Due to this polarity, aldehydes and ketones show dipole-dipole interactions, which make their boiling points higher than those of the corresponding alkanes of comparable molecular masses.
  • They cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other, because they have no O-H bond. They are therefore less polar than alcohols and carboxylic acids, and have lower boiling points than alcohols and carboxylic acids.
  • Aldehydes and ketones having five or fewer carbon atoms are soluble in water, because they can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.
  • Those having more than five carbon atoms are insoluble in water, because the non-polar hydrocarbon portion is too large to dissolve in polar water.
  • Methanal and ethanal are gases; the other lower aldehydes and ketones are colourless liquids at room temperature. Higher aldehydes with more than twenty carbon atoms and ketones with more than thirty carbon atoms are solids at room temperature.
  • Lower aldehydes have pungent smells and higher aldehydes have pleasant smells; camphor, a ketone, has a sweet smell.
  • The density of aldehydes and ketones is less than that of water.

Formaldehyde: Sources, Health Risks and Recommendations

Formaldehyde is a colourless, flammable gas with a pungent, irritating odour. Its aqueous solution is called formalin. All organisms (such as bacteria, fish and humans) naturally produce formaldehyde as part of cell metabolism. It is commonly used as a preservative in medical laboratories and mortuaries, and as an industrial fungicide, germicide, fumigant and disinfectant. It is used in making chemical resins, rubber products, paper products and cosmetics, and is found in adhesives, glues, varnishes, paints, household products, plywood and fibreboard. It is also present in combustion products such as vehicle exhaust and tobacco smoke.

Health risks: short-term exposure irritates the eyes, nose and throat and can cause coughing and a sore throat; at high concentration it irritates the lungs, causing chest pain and shortness of breath. Long-term exposure makes all these symptoms worse and can cause allergic reactions of the skin (dermatitis), the eyes and the lungs (asthma). Repeated contact can cause numbness and hardening of the skin, and at high concentration formaldehyde can cause cancer in the nose, throat or lungs. Formalin is a skin irritant (smarting, drying, cracking and scaling), and formaldehyde can decrease fertility and increase the risk of spontaneous miscarriage in humans. Recommendation: students, teachers and workers who may be exposed should wear safety goggles, gloves, a face shield and an apron of appropriate materials before entering the workplace.

Key Points

  • The polar carbonyl group gives dipole-dipole interactions and higher boiling points than alkanes.
  • With no O-H bond, they cannot hydrogen-bond with each other, so they boil lower than alcohols and acids.
  • Members with five or fewer carbons dissolve in water; larger members do not.
  • Methanal and ethanal are gases; most others are liquids; the highest members are solids.
  • Formaldehyde is a pungent, irritating gas; its aqueous solution is formalin.
  • Formaldehyde is harmful on long exposure; protective equipment must be worn when handling it.

mcqs.q: Why is the carbonyl group polar?
options: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon
Carbon is more electronegative than oxygen
mcqs.why: The carbonyl group is polar because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, as explained in the physical properties notes.

mcqs.q: Why do aldehydes and ketones boil higher than comparable alkanes?
options: They form hydrogen bonds with each other
They show dipole-dipole interactions from the polar carbonyl
mcqs.why: Due to polarity they show dipole-dipole interactions, which make boiling points higher than those of corresponding alkanes of comparable mass.

mcqs.q: Why can aldehydes and ketones NOT hydrogen-bond with each other?
mcqs.why: They cannot form hydrogen bonds with each other because they have no O-H bond, unlike alcohols and carboxylic acids.

mcqs.q: Aldehydes and ketones with how many carbons are soluble in water?
mcqs.why: Members having five or fewer carbon atoms are soluble in water because they can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules.

mcqs.q: Why are aldehydes and ketones with more than five carbons insoluble in water?
options: The non-polar hydrocarbon portion is too large for polar water
mcqs.why: Larger members are insoluble because the non-polar hydrocarbon portion is too large to dissolve in polar water.

mcqs.q: Which aldehydes are gases at room temperature?
mcqs.why: The notes state that methanal and ethanal are gases, while other lower aldehydes and ketones are colourless liquids at room temperature.

mcqs.q: What is formalin?
options: A mixture of formaldehyde and methanol only
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde is a colourless flammable gas and its aqueous solution is called formalin, used as a preservative.

mcqs.q: Which ketone is noted for a sweet smell?
mcqs.why: Camphor, a ketone, has a sweet smell, while lower aldehydes have pungent smells and higher aldehydes have pleasant smells.

mcqs.q: How does the density of aldehydes and ketones compare with water?
mcqs.why: The notes state directly that the density of aldehydes and ketones is less than that of water.

mcqs.q: What long-term health effect can high-concentration formaldehyde cause, according to the notes?
options: Cancer in the nose, throat or lungs
mcqs.why: At high concentration formaldehyde can cause cancer in the nose, throat or lungs, besides irritation, dermatitis and asthma on long exposure.

lessons.title: Structure of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
The carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones is composed of one sigma bond and one pi bond. Both the carbon and the oxygen of the carbonyl group are sp2 hybridized. The fourth p-orbital of carbon remains unhybridized.

  • The three sp2 hybrid orbitals of carbon form three sigma bonds: one with oxygen and two with the other groups bonded to it.
  • The fourth, unhybridized p-orbital of carbon forms the pi bond with oxygen.
  • The three atoms or groups attached to the carbon of the carbonyl group lie in the same plane.
  • The bond angles between the bonded atoms or groups are around 120°, so the carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar.

Key Points

  • The C=O group has one sigma bond and one pi bond.
  • Both carbonyl carbon and oxygen are sp2 hybridized.
  • The unhybridized p-orbital of carbon forms the pi bond with oxygen.
  • The three groups on the carbonyl carbon lie in one plane, with angles of about 120°.

mcqs.q: The carbonyl group is composed of which bonds?
options: One sigma bond and one pi bond
mcqs.why: The carbonyl group of aldehydes and ketones is composed of one sigma bond and one pi bond, as stated in the structure notes.

mcqs.q: What is the hybridization of the carbonyl carbon and oxygen?
mcqs.why: Both the carbon and the oxygen of the carbonyl group are sp2 hybridized in aldehydes and ketones.

mcqs.q: Which orbital of carbon forms the pi bond with oxygen?
mcqs.why: The fourth p-orbital of carbon remains unhybridized and forms the pi bond with oxygen, while the sp2 orbitals form sigma bonds.

mcqs.q: How many sigma bonds do the three sp2 orbitals of carbonyl carbon form?
mcqs.why: The three sp2 hybrid orbitals form three sigma bonds: one with oxygen and two with the other groups bonded to carbon. Check: 1 + 2 = 3 sigma bonds.

mcqs.q: What is the approximate bond angle around the carbonyl carbon?
mcqs.why: The three groups lie in the same plane with bond angles around 120 degrees, so the carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar. Check: 3 x 120 = 360 degrees around the planar carbon.

mcqs.q: What geometry does the carbonyl carbon have?
mcqs.why: Because the three attached atoms or groups lie in one plane with angles of about 120 degrees, the carbonyl carbon is trigonal planar.

mcqs.q: Where do the three atoms or groups on the carbonyl carbon lie?
options: At the corners of a tetrahedron
mcqs.why: The notes state that the three atoms or groups attached to the carbonyl carbon lie in the same plane.

mcqs.q: In the carbonyl group, the sigma bond to oxygen is formed by which orbitals?
options: An sp2 hybrid orbital of carbon
An sp3 orbital of oxygen only
mcqs.why: Carbon uses its sp2 hybrid orbitals to form three sigma bonds, one of them with oxygen; the pi bond uses the unhybridized p-orbital.

mcqs.q: Why does carbon keep one p-orbital unhybridized in the carbonyl group?
options: To form the pi bond with oxygen
mcqs.why: The fourth p-orbital remains unhybridized so it can overlap with oxygen to form the pi bond of the C=O double bond.

mcqs.q: Which statement about carbonyl carbon bonding is correct?
options: It forms two sigma and two pi bonds
It forms three sigma bonds and shares in one pi bond
mcqs.why: Carbonyl carbon forms three sigma bonds from its sp2 orbitals and one pi bond from its unhybridized p-orbital with oxygen.

lessons.title: Ozonolysis of Alkenes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkenes react with ozone to form an explosive compound called an ozonide. On subsequent reductive cleavage with zinc dust and water, the ozonide produces aldehydes or ketones, or both, depending on the structure of the alkene.

Key Reactions

AlkeneProducts after O3, then Zn/H2O
R-CH=CH-R2 R-CHO (aldehydes)
R2C=CR22 R2C=O (ketones)

Each carbon of the double bond becomes a carbonyl carbon: a double-bond carbon carrying a hydrogen gives an aldehyde, and a double-bond carbon carrying two alkyl groups gives a ketone.

Key Points

  • Ozone adds to an alkene to form an ozonide, which is explosive.
  • Reductive cleavage with Zn/H2O breaks the double bond completely.
  • The products are aldehydes, ketones, or both, depending on the alkene's structure.

mcqs.q: What explosive compound forms when an alkene reacts with ozone?
mcqs.why: Alkenes react with ozone to form an explosive compound called an ozonide, which is then cleaved reductively.

mcqs.q: Which reagents carry out the reductive cleavage of an ozonide?
mcqs.why: On reductive cleavage with zinc dust and water, the ozonide produces aldehydes or ketones depending on the alkene structure.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis of R-CH=CH-R with O3 then Zn/H2O gives what?
mcqs.why: Each double-bond carbon carrying a hydrogen gives an aldehyde, so R-CH=CH-R gives 2 R-CHO. Check: 1 alkene molecule gives 2 aldehyde molecules, so moles double.

mcqs.q: Ozonolysis of R2C=CR2 gives which products?
mcqs.why: A double-bond carbon carrying two alkyl groups gives a ketone, so R2C=CR2 gives 2 R2C=O on ozonolysis with Zn/H2O.

mcqs.q: In ozonolysis, a double-bond carbon carrying a hydrogen becomes what?
mcqs.why: Each carbon of the double bond becomes a carbonyl carbon: one carrying a hydrogen gives an aldehyde, one with two alkyl groups gives a ketone.

mcqs.q: What happens to the carbon-carbon double bond during ozonolysis with Zn/H2O?
mcqs.why: Reductive cleavage with Zn/H2O breaks the double bond completely, converting each of its carbons into a carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: The products of ozonolysis depend on what?
mcqs.why: The ozonide produces aldehydes or ketones, or both, depending on the structure of the starting alkene.

mcqs.q: Why must ozonides be handled carefully?
mcqs.why: The notes describe the ozonide intermediate as an explosive compound formed when ozone adds to an alkene.

mcqs.q: A double-bond carbon carrying two alkyl groups gives which ozonolysis product type?
mcqs.why: A double-bond carbon carrying two alkyl groups gives a ketone, while one carrying a hydrogen gives an aldehyde.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly describes ozonolysis?
options: Alkene plus water to enol, then ketone
Alkene plus ozone to ozonide, then Zn/H2O to carbonyls
mcqs.why: Ozone first adds to form the ozonide, and reductive cleavage with zinc dust and water then gives aldehydes or ketones.

lessons.title: Hydration of Alkynes
lessons.notes_html:
Alkynes undergo hydration according to Markovnikov's rule in the presence of mercuric sulphate and sulphuric acid. The reaction forms an unstable enol, which on rearrangement gives aldehydes or ketones, or both, depending on the structure of the alkyne. Acetylene (ethyne) produces an aldehyde, while all other alkynes under the same conditions produce the corresponding ketones.

Key Reactions

AlkyneConditionsProduct
HC≡CH (acetylene)H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4CH3CHO (acetaldehyde), through an enol intermediate
HC≡C-CH3 (propyne)H2O, H2SO4, HgSO4CH3COCH3 (dimethyl ketone, acetone), through an enol intermediate

Key Points

  • Water adds to alkynes by Markovnikov's rule with HgSO4/H2SO4.
  • An unstable enol forms first and rearranges to the carbonyl compound.
  • Acetylene gives acetaldehyde; all other alkynes give ketones.

mcqs.q: Hydration of alkynes follows which rule?
mcqs.why: Alkynes undergo hydration according to Markovnikov's rule in the presence of mercuric sulphate and sulphuric acid.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst and acid are used for alkyne hydration?
mcqs.why: The hydration uses mercuric sulphate and sulphuric acid, forming an unstable enol that rearranges to the carbonyl compound.

mcqs.q: What unstable intermediate forms first in alkyne hydration?
mcqs.why: The reaction forms an unstable enol, which on rearrangement gives aldehydes or ketones depending on the alkyne.

mcqs.q: Hydration of acetylene (ethyne) gives which product?
mcqs.why: Acetylene produces an aldehyde, acetaldehyde CH3CHO, through an enol intermediate under HgSO4/H2SO4 hydration.

mcqs.q: Hydration of propyne gives which product?
mcqs.why: Propyne gives CH3COCH3, dimethyl ketone or acetone, because all alkynes other than acetylene give ketones on hydration.

mcqs.q: All alkynes except acetylene give what on hydration?
mcqs.why: Acetylene gives acetaldehyde, while all other alkynes under the same conditions produce the corresponding ketones.

mcqs.q: What happens to the enol formed in alkyne hydration?
options: It is reduced to an alkane
It rearranges to the carbonyl compound
mcqs.why: The unstable enol rearranges to give the aldehyde or ketone product, which is the stable carbonyl form.

mcqs.q: Which alkyne is the exception that gives an aldehyde on hydration?
mcqs.why: Only acetylene, ethyne, produces an aldehyde on hydration; every other alkyne produces a ketone under the same conditions.

mcqs.q: The product of ethyne hydration is formed through which intermediate?
mcqs.why: Ethyne hydration passes through an enol intermediate that rearranges to acetaldehyde, CH3CHO.

mcqs.q: Which set of conditions hydrates an alkyne to a carbonyl compound?
mcqs.why: Water adds to alkynes with H2SO4 and HgSO4 by Markovnikov's rule to give, after enol rearrangement, aldehydes or ketones.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Alcohols
lessons.notes_html:
The controlled oxidation of primary alcohols in the presence of an acidified solution of potassium dichromate or potassium permanganate produces aldehydes, whereas secondary alcohols result in the formation of ketones.

Key Reactions

AlcoholConditionsProduct
CH3CH2OH (ethyl alcohol, 1°)[O], K2Cr2O7/H2SO4CH3CHO (acetaldehyde) + H2O
CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 (sec-propyl alcohol, 2°)[O], K2Cr2O7/H2SO4CH3COCH3 (acetone) + H2O

Key Points

  • Controlled oxidation of a primary alcohol gives an aldehyde.
  • Oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
  • The oxidizing agents are acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4.

mcqs.q: Controlled oxidation of a primary alcohol gives what?
mcqs.why: Controlled oxidation of primary alcohols with acidified dichromate or permanganate produces aldehydes.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of a secondary alcohol gives what?
mcqs.why: Secondary alcohols result in the formation of ketones on oxidation with acidified K2Cr2O7 or KMnO4.

mcqs.q: Which oxidizing agents are used for oxidation of alcohols to carbonyls?
mcqs.why: The oxidizing agents are acidified potassium dichromate or potassium permanganate solutions, as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of ethyl alcohol CH3CH2OH gives which product?
mcqs.why: Ethyl alcohol, a primary alcohol, oxidizes to acetaldehyde CH3CHO plus H2O with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of sec-propyl alcohol CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 gives what?
mcqs.why: Sec-propyl alcohol is secondary, so oxidation gives the ketone acetone CH3COCH3 plus water.

mcqs.q: Why is the oxidation of primary alcohols described as controlled?
options: To stop at the aldehyde stage
mcqs.why: It is controlled oxidation because the primary alcohol is converted to the aldehyde product under the stated conditions.

mcqs.q: Ethyl alcohol is which type of alcohol in this reaction?
mcqs.why: CH3CH2OH is labelled ethyl alcohol, 1 degree, in the notes table, and primary alcohols give aldehydes.

mcqs.q: Sec-propyl alcohol is classified as what?
mcqs.why: CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 is labelled sec-propyl alcohol, 2 degree, and secondary alcohols give ketones on oxidation.

mcqs.q: Which product pair matches primary and secondary alcohol oxidation respectively?
mcqs.why: Primary alcohols give aldehydes and secondary alcohols give ketones, which is the central rule of this lesson.

mcqs.q: Acetone from sec-propyl alcohol is formed with loss of what else?
mcqs.why: The key reaction shows sec-propyl alcohol giving acetone plus H2O under oxidation with K2Cr2O7/H2SO4.

lessons.title: Friedel-Crafts Acylation of Aromatic Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
An aromatic compound (benzene) reacts with an acyl halide in the presence of a Lewis acid (AlCl3) to produce an aryl ketone.

Key Reactions

ReactantsConditionsProduct
Benzene + CH3COCl (acetyl chloride)AlCl3Methyl phenyl ketone (acetophenone) + HCl

Key Points

  • Benzene reacts with an acyl halide to give an aryl ketone.
  • AlCl3 is the Lewis acid catalyst.
  • Example: benzene + acetyl chloride → methyl phenyl ketone + HCl.

mcqs.q: In Friedel-Crafts acylation, benzene reacts with what?
mcqs.why: An aromatic compound such as benzene reacts with an acyl halide to produce an aryl ketone.

mcqs.q: Which catalyst is used in Friedel-Crafts acylation?
mcqs.why: The reaction is carried out in the presence of the Lewis acid AlCl3, which catalyzes the acylation of benzene.

mcqs.q: Benzene plus acetyl chloride with AlCl3 gives which ketone?
mcqs.why: Benzene plus CH3COCl gives methyl phenyl ketone, acetophenone, plus HCl, as shown in the key reaction.

mcqs.q: What by-product forms along with acetophenone in this reaction?
mcqs.why: The key reaction shows benzene plus acetyl chloride giving methyl phenyl ketone plus HCl as the by-product.

mcqs.q: The product of Friedel-Crafts acylation is best described as what?
mcqs.why: Friedel-Crafts acylation produces an aryl ketone because an acyl group is attached to the aromatic ring.

mcqs.q: Acetyl chloride has which formula in the notes reaction?
mcqs.why: The reactant is written CH3COCl, acetyl chloride, reacting with benzene in the presence of AlCl3.

mcqs.q: AlCl3 acts in this reaction as what?
mcqs.why: The notes identify AlCl3 as the Lewis acid catalyst for the Friedel-Crafts acylation of aromatic compounds.

mcqs.q: Which starting pair gives acetophenone?
mcqs.why: Acetophenone, methyl phenyl ketone, is made from benzene and acetyl chloride with AlCl3, releasing HCl.

mcqs.q: Friedel-Crafts acylation introduces which group onto benzene?
mcqs.why: An acyl halide supplies the acyl group that replaces a ring hydrogen, forming the aryl ketone product.

mcqs.q: What is the common name given for methyl phenyl ketone in the notes?
mcqs.why: Methyl phenyl ketone is known as acetophenone, the product of benzene plus acetyl chloride in this reaction.

lessons.title: Reactivity of Carbonyl Compounds
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones both contain a carbon-oxygen double bond. A ketone has an alkyl or aryl group on each side of the carbonyl, while an aldehyde has a hydrogen on one side and an alkyl or aryl group on the other side.

Oxygen of the carbonyl group is more electronegative than carbon. Therefore, the less tightly held pi electrons are strongly attracted by the oxygen atom. This makes the carbonyl group highly polar: a partial negative charge (δ-) develops on oxygen and a partial positive charge (δ+) develops on the carbon of the carbonyl group.

The positively charged carbon atom therefore acts as an electrophile, and the most characteristic reaction of aldehydes and ketones is nucleophilic addition to the carbon-oxygen double bond. During addition of a reagent to the carbonyl group, the negative part of the reagent adds to the carbon of the carbonyl group and the positive part adds to the oxygen of the carbonyl group.

Key Points

  • The C=O bond is highly polar: carbon is δ+ and oxygen is δ-.
  • The π electrons are pulled strongly towards the more electronegative oxygen.
  • The carbonyl carbon is an electrophile and is attacked by nucleophiles.
  • The characteristic reaction is nucleophilic addition to the C=O bond.
  • In addition, the negative part of the reagent joins the carbon and the positive part joins the oxygen.

mcqs.q: Why is the carbonyl group highly polar?
options: The pi electrons are strongly attracted by the more electronegative oxygen
Oxygen is less electronegative than carbon
mcqs.why: Oxygen is more electronegative, so the less tightly held pi electrons are strongly attracted to oxygen, making C=O highly polar.

mcqs.q: What partial charges develop on the carbonyl group?
mcqs.why: A partial negative charge delta-minus develops on oxygen and a partial positive charge delta-plus develops on carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: The positively charged carbonyl carbon acts as what?
mcqs.why: The positively charged carbon atom acts as an electrophile and is attacked in nucleophilic addition reactions.

mcqs.q: What is the most characteristic reaction of aldehydes and ketones?
mcqs.why: The most characteristic reaction is nucleophilic addition to the carbon-oxygen double bond, driven by the electrophilic carbon.

mcqs.q: During addition to C=O, the negative part of the reagent adds to what?
options: The carbon of the carbonyl group
The hydrogen of an aldehyde only
mcqs.why: The negative part of the reagent adds to the carbonyl carbon and the positive part adds to the carbonyl oxygen.

mcqs.q: During addition, the positive part of the reagent adds to what?
mcqs.why: In addition to the carbonyl group, the positive part of the reagent joins the oxygen while the negative part joins the carbon.

mcqs.q: How do aldehyde and ketone structures differ around the carbonyl?
options: Aldehyde has alkyl groups on both sides
Ketone has H on both sides
Both have H on both sides
Ketone has an alkyl or aryl group on each side; aldehyde has H on one side
mcqs.why: A ketone has an alkyl or aryl group on each side of the carbonyl, while an aldehyde has hydrogen on one side and a group on the other.

mcqs.q: Which electrons of C=O are pulled most strongly toward oxygen?
options: The less tightly held pi electrons
mcqs.why: The less tightly held pi electrons are strongly attracted by oxygen because oxygen is more electronegative than carbon.

mcqs.q: A nucleophile attacks which atom of the carbonyl group?
mcqs.why: Nucleophiles attack the carbonyl carbon because it carries a partial positive charge and acts as an electrophile.

mcqs.q: The polarity of C=O is caused by the electronegativity difference between which atoms?
mcqs.why: Oxygen of the carbonyl group is more electronegative than carbon, which creates the delta-plus carbon and delta-minus oxygen.

lessons.title: Nucleophilic Addition Reactions
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones react with nucleophiles to produce a wide variety of useful derivatives. They undergo addition of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nucleophiles. The carbon of the carbonyl group is highly electrophilic because of its partial positive charge, so the nucleophile adds to the electrophilic carbon. As the nucleophile adds, the hybridization of carbon changes from sp2 to sp3. These reactions can be catalyzed by an acid or by a base.

Base Catalyzed Nucleophilic Addition

These reactions occur in the presence of a strong nucleophile. The strong nucleophile is produced by the reaction of the base with the reagent: H-Nu + OH- → Nu- + H2O. The nucleophile uses its pair of electrons to make a bond to the carbonyl carbon, and the electrons of the π-bond are forced out onto the oxygen atom, producing an alkoxide anion. The alkoxide intermediate is then protonated on treatment with water, and the base is regenerated: alkoxide + H2O → addition product (an alcohol) + OH-.

Acid Catalyzed Nucleophilic Addition

These reactions occur in the presence of a weak nucleophile. A small amount of acid is used to initiate the reaction. The proton of the acid attacks the carbonyl oxygen atom to produce a protonated carbonyl group. Protonation increases the electrophilic character of the carbonyl carbon and makes it more reactive towards the nucleophile. The nucleophile then uses its pair of electrons to bond to the carbonyl carbon, the π-bond electrons are forced onto the oxygen, and the addition product (an alcohol) is formed.

Key Points

  • Nucleophilic addition is the most common reaction of aldehydes and ketones.
  • H, C, N and O nucleophiles all add to the carbonyl carbon.
  • On addition, the carbonyl carbon changes from sp2 to sp3.
  • Base catalysis works by producing a strong nucleophile; an alkoxide intermediate is protonated by water.
  • Acid catalysis works by protonating the carbonyl oxygen, making the carbon more electrophilic for a weak nucleophile.

mcqs.q: Which nucleophile types add to aldehydes and ketones?
options: Hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nucleophiles
mcqs.why: They undergo addition of hydrogen, carbon, nitrogen and oxygen nucleophiles to produce a wide variety of useful derivatives.

mcqs.q: Why does the nucleophile add to the carbonyl carbon?
options: The carbon is highly electrophilic from its partial positive charge
mcqs.why: The carbonyl carbon is highly electrophilic because of its partial positive charge, so the nucleophile adds to that carbon.

mcqs.q: How does the hybridization of carbonyl carbon change on addition?
mcqs.why: As the nucleophile adds, the hybridization of carbon changes from sp2 to sp3 in the addition product.

mcqs.q: In base-catalyzed addition, how is the strong nucleophile produced?
options: H-Nu plus OH- gives Nu- plus H2O
mcqs.why: The strong nucleophile is produced by H-Nu plus OH- giving Nu- plus H2O, the first step of base catalysis.

mcqs.q: In base catalysis, the nucleophile bond formation pushes pi electrons onto which atom?
mcqs.why: The pi-bond electrons are forced out onto oxygen, producing an alkoxide anion intermediate in base-catalyzed addition.

mcqs.q: How is the alkoxide intermediate converted to the final product in base catalysis?
options: It is protonated on treatment with water, regenerating the base
mcqs.why: The alkoxide is protonated with water to give the addition product alcohol and regenerate OH-, completing base catalysis.

mcqs.q: Acid-catalyzed addition is used in the presence of which nucleophile?
mcqs.why: Acid-catalyzed reactions occur in the presence of a weak nucleophile, with a small amount of acid to initiate reaction.

mcqs.q: In acid catalysis, what does the proton attack first?
options: The carbonyl oxygen, giving a protonated carbonyl
mcqs.why: The proton attacks the carbonyl oxygen to produce a protonated carbonyl group, increasing the carbon's electrophilic character.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of protonating the carbonyl oxygen?
options: It makes carbonyl carbon more electrophilic and reactive to the nucleophile
mcqs.why: Protonation increases the electrophilic character of the carbonyl carbon and makes it more reactive towards the nucleophile.

mcqs.q: Nucleophilic addition reactions can be catalyzed by what?
mcqs.why: These reactions can be catalyzed by an acid or by a base, with different mechanisms for strong and weak nucleophiles.

lessons.title: Relative Reactivity of Aldehydes and Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition reactions. An alkyl group is an electron-donating group, so it makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic. The carbonyl carbon of a ketone has two alkyl groups, so it is less reactive towards nucleophiles than an aldehyde, which has only one alkyl group. The order of reactivity is: formaldehyde > aldehydes > ketones.

Steric effects are also important in the transition state. An aldehyde has only one alkyl (or aryl) group, so its transition state is less crowded. A ketone has two alkyl (or aryl) groups, so its transition state is more crowded. Because of this greater steric crowding in the transition state, ketones are less reactive towards nucleophilic attack than aldehydes.

Key Points

  • Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition.
  • Reactivity order: formaldehyde > aldehydes > ketones.
  • Electronic reason: two electron-donating alkyl groups make the ketone carbonyl carbon less positive.
  • Steric reason: the ketone transition state is more crowded than the aldehyde transition state.

mcqs.q: Which are more reactive toward nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes are more reactive than ketones towards nucleophilic addition reactions, for both electronic and steric reasons.

mcqs.q: What is the order of reactivity toward nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: The order of reactivity is formaldehyde greater than aldehydes greater than ketones, as stated in the key points.

mcqs.q: Why does an alkyl group lower carbonyl reactivity?
options: It donates electrons, making carbonyl carbon less electrophilic
mcqs.why: An alkyl group is electron-donating, so it makes the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic and less reactive to nucleophiles.

mcqs.q: Why is a ketone carbonyl carbon less reactive than an aldehyde's?
options: It has two electron-donating alkyl groups
mcqs.why: A ketone carbonyl carbon has two alkyl groups donating electrons, so it is less reactive than an aldehyde with only one.

mcqs.q: What steric effect lowers ketone reactivity?
options: Its transition state is less crowded
Its transition state is more crowded
mcqs.why: A ketone has two alkyl or aryl groups, so its transition state is more crowded than an aldehyde's less crowded transition state.

mcqs.q: An aldehyde transition state is less crowded because it has what?
options: Only one alkyl or aryl group
mcqs.why: An aldehyde has only one alkyl or aryl group, so its transition state is less crowded and nucleophilic attack is easier.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde is the most reactive because it has what feature?
options: No alkyl group donating electrons to the carbonyl carbon
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde heads the reactivity order because it lacks electron-donating alkyl groups and crowding at the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: Both reasons for aldehyde being more reactive than ketone are what?
mcqs.why: The notes give an electronic reason, alkyl donation, and a steric reason, transition-state crowding, for the reactivity difference.

mcqs.q: If alkyl donation increases, carbonyl carbon becomes what?
mcqs.why: Electron donation from alkyl groups reduces the partial positive character, making the carbonyl carbon less electrophilic.

mcqs.q: Which compound is least reactive to nucleophilic addition?
mcqs.why: Ketones are least reactive in the order formaldehyde greater than aldehydes greater than ketones given in the notes.

lessons.title: Reduction to Hydrocarbon (Clemmensen Reduction)
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones undergo reduction in the presence of different reducing agents to produce hydrocarbons, alcohols or glycols. On reduction with zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl, aldehydes and ketones produce hydrocarbons: the carbonyl group is reduced completely to a CH2 group. This reduction is known as Clemmensen reduction.

Key Reactions

CompoundConditionsProduct
CH3CHO (acetaldehyde)Zn-Hg, conc. HClCH3CH3 (ethane) + H2O
CH3COCH3 (acetone)Zn-Hg, conc. HClCH3CH2CH3 (propane) + H2O

Key Points

  • Zn-Hg and conc. HCl reduce the carbonyl group completely to CH2.
  • Aldehydes and ketones are converted into hydrocarbons.
  • This is called Clemmensen reduction.
  • Example: acetaldehyde → ethane; acetone → propane.

mcqs.q: Clemmensen reduction uses which reagents?
mcqs.why: On reduction with zinc amalgam and concentrated HCl, aldehydes and ketones produce hydrocarbons; this is Clemmensen reduction.

mcqs.q: In Clemmensen reduction the carbonyl group is reduced completely to what?
mcqs.why: The carbonyl group is reduced completely to a CH2 group, converting aldehydes and ketones into hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Clemmensen reduction of acetaldehyde gives what?
mcqs.why: Acetaldehyde CH3CHO with Zn-Hg and conc. HCl gives ethane CH3CH3 plus H2O, as shown in the key reactions.

mcqs.q: Clemmensen reduction of acetone gives what?
mcqs.why: Acetone CH3COCH3 gives propane CH3CH2CH3 plus H2O under Clemmensen conditions with Zn-Hg and conc. HCl.

mcqs.q: Clemmensen reduction products are which class?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes and ketones are converted into hydrocarbons by Clemmensen reduction, unlike hydride reduction which gives alcohols.

mcqs.q: The zinc reagent in Clemmensen reduction is specifically what?
mcqs.why: The reagent is zinc amalgam, written Zn-Hg, used together with concentrated hydrochloric acid.

mcqs.q: Acetaldehyde to ethane keeps how many carbons?
mcqs.why: CH3CHO has two carbons and CH3CH3 also has two carbons; only the carbonyl oxygen is removed as water. Check: 2 carbons in reactant equals 2 carbons in product.

mcqs.q: Which reduction converts a ketone directly to an alkane?
mcqs.why: Clemmensen reduction with Zn-Hg and conc. HCl reduces the carbonyl completely to CH2, giving the hydrocarbon alkane.

mcqs.q: What acid is used in Clemmensen reduction?
mcqs.why: Clemmensen reduction uses concentrated HCl together with zinc amalgam to reduce aldehydes and ketones to hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Propane from acetone shows the carbonyl carbon became what?
options: A CH2 group in the chain
mcqs.why: In CH3CH2CH3 the former carbonyl carbon is now the middle CH2 group, showing complete reduction of C=O to CH2.

lessons.title: Reduction to Alcohols (Reduction with NaBH4)
lessons.notes_html:
Metal hydrides such as NaBH4 (sodium borohydride) or LiAlH4 (lithium aluminium hydride) are reducing agents. They reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Reduction with NaBH4 needs polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol.

Key Reactions

CompoundConditionsProduct
CH3CHO (acetaldehyde)NaBH4, H2OCH3CH2OH (ethyl alcohol, 1°)
CH3COCH3 (acetone)NaBH4, H2OCH3-CH(OH)-CH3 (isopropyl alcohol, 2°)

Key Points

  • NaBH4 and LiAlH4 are metal hydride reducing agents.
  • Aldehydes are reduced to primary alcohols.
  • Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols.
  • NaBH4 reduction is carried out in polar solvents such as water or ethanol.

mcqs.q: NaBH4 and LiAlH4 belong to which class of reducing agents?
mcqs.why: Metal hydrides such as NaBH4, sodium borohydride, and LiAlH4 are the reducing agents in this lesson.

mcqs.q: Reduction of aldehydes with NaBH4 gives what?
mcqs.why: Metal hydrides reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols, as shown by acetaldehyde giving ethyl alcohol.

mcqs.q: Reduction of ketones with NaBH4 gives what?
mcqs.why: Ketones are reduced to secondary alcohols; acetone gives isopropyl alcohol, a 2-degree alcohol.

mcqs.q: Which solvents does NaBH4 reduction need?
options: Polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol
mcqs.why: Reduction with NaBH4 needs polar solvents such as water and ethyl alcohol, according to the notes.

mcqs.q: NaBH4 reduction of acetaldehyde gives which alcohol?
mcqs.why: CH3CHO with NaBH4 and H2O gives CH3CH2OH, ethyl alcohol, labelled 1-degree in the key reactions.

mcqs.q: NaBH4 reduction of acetone gives which alcohol?
mcqs.why: Acetone with NaBH4 gives CH3-CH(OH)-CH3, isopropyl alcohol, labelled 2-degree in the notes.

mcqs.q: LiAlH4 is named in full as what?
mcqs.why: LiAlH4 is lithium aluminium hydride, listed with NaBH4 as a metal hydride reducing agent.

mcqs.q: How does hydride reduction differ from Clemmensen reduction?
options: Hydride gives alcohols; Clemmensen gives hydrocarbons
Hydride gives acids; Clemmensen gives alcohols
mcqs.why: NaBH4 reduces carbonyls to alcohols, while Clemmensen reduction with Zn-Hg/HCl reduces them completely to hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Isopropyl alcohol from acetone is classified as what?
mcqs.why: The product CH3-CH(OH)-CH3 is marked 2-degree, a secondary alcohol, because the ketone carbonyl carbon gains the OH.

mcqs.q: Sodium borohydride has which formula?
mcqs.why: Sodium borohydride is written NaBH4 and lithium aluminium hydride is written LiAlH4 in the notes.

lessons.title: Reduction with Carbon Nucleophiles
lessons.notes_html:
The carbon in HCN, in organometallic compounds such as RLi, in terminal alkynes and in Grignard's reagent acts as a nucleophile and adds to aldehydes and ketones to give various compounds (the book groups these addition reactions under reduction with carbon nucleophiles).

Addition of HCN: Cyanohydrin Formation

Hydrogen cyanide is a weak acid that adds to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins: RCHO + HCN → R-CH(OH)-CN. Examples: formaldehyde + HCN → formaldehyde cyanohydrin, HO-CH2-CN; acetaldehyde + HCN → acetaldehyde cyanohydrin, CH3-CH(OH)-CN; acetone + HCN → acetone cyanohydrin, (CH3)2C(OH)-CN.

Mechanism: the conjugate base of HCN, the cyanide ion, acts as a strong nucleophile. In step 1, the cyanide ion adds to the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion. In step 2, the alkoxide ion takes a proton from HCN to produce the cyanohydrin, and the cyanide ion is regenerated.

Addition of Grignard's Reagent (RMgX)

The reaction of an aldehyde or ketone with Grignard's reagent, followed by protonation in aqueous acid, forms a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol containing a new carbon-carbon bond: formaldehyde + CH3MgCl → ethyl alcohol (1°) after hydrolysis; acetaldehyde + CH3MgCl → isopropyl alcohol (2°); acetone + CH3MgCl → tert-butyl alcohol (3°).

Key Reactions

ReagentProduct type
HCNCyanohydrin, R-CH(OH)-CN
RMgX, then H2O/H+Alcohol with a new C-C bond (1°, 2° or 3°)

Key Points

  • Carbon nucleophiles include HCN, RLi, terminal alkynes and RMgX.
  • HCN adds to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins.
  • The cyanide ion is the real nucleophile; it adds first, then the alkoxide is protonated.
  • Grignard addition followed by hydrolysis gives alcohols and forms a new C-C bond.

mcqs.q: Addition of HCN to aldehydes and ketones forms what?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen cyanide adds to aldehydes and ketones to form cyanohydrins, R-CH(OH)-CN for an aldehyde.

mcqs.q: What is the general cyanohydrin formula from an aldehyde?
mcqs.why: The notes give RCHO plus HCN giving R-CH(OH)-CN, the cyanohydrin with both OH and CN on the same carbon.

mcqs.q: Which ion is the real nucleophile in cyanohydrin formation?
options: Cyanide ion, the conjugate base of HCN
mcqs.why: The conjugate base of HCN, the cyanide ion, acts as a strong nucleophile and adds first to the carbonyl carbon.

mcqs.q: In cyanohydrin formation step 2, the alkoxide ion does what?
options: Takes a proton from HCN, regenerating cyanide ion
mcqs.why: The alkoxide takes a proton from HCN to produce the cyanohydrin, and the cyanide ion is regenerated in step 2.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde cyanohydrin has which structure?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde plus HCN gives formaldehyde cyanohydrin, HO-CH2-CN, as listed in the examples.

mcqs.q: Acetone cyanohydrin has which structure?
mcqs.why: Acetone plus HCN gives (CH3)2C(OH)-CN, with two methyl groups on the carbon bearing OH and CN.

mcqs.q: Grignard addition to a carbonyl followed by hydrolysis gives what?
options: An alcohol with a new carbon-carbon bond
mcqs.why: Reaction with Grignard reagent then aqueous acid forms a primary, secondary or tertiary alcohol containing a new C-C bond.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde plus CH3MgCl then hydrolysis gives which alcohol?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde plus CH3MgCl gives ethyl alcohol, 1-degree, after hydrolysis, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: Acetaldehyde plus CH3MgCl then hydrolysis gives which alcohol?
mcqs.why: Acetaldehyde plus CH3MgCl gives isopropyl alcohol, 2-degree, after hydrolysis in the Grignard examples.

mcqs.q: Acetone plus CH3MgCl then hydrolysis gives which alcohol?
mcqs.why: Acetone plus CH3MgCl gives tert-butyl alcohol, 3-degree, showing ketones give tertiary alcohols with Grignard reagents.

lessons.title: Reduction with Nitrogen Nucleophiles
lessons.notes_html:
The nitrogen in ammonia and its derivatives acts as a nucleophile and reacts with aldehydes and ketones to give various compounds. In each case an addition product forms first, and then water is eliminated.

Addition of Ammonia

Ammonia adds to aldehydes to form imines: CH3CHO + NH3 → CH3-CH=NH + H2O. Mechanism: in step 1, ammonia adds to the aldehyde to form an unstable addition product; in step 2, a proton is transferred to give the carbinolamine-type intermediate; in step 3, water is eliminated to produce the imine.

Addition of Ammonia Derivatives

  • Alkyl amines: primary amines add to aldehydes and ketones to form an addition product, which undergoes elimination of water to produce imines: CH3CHO + R-NH2 → CH3-CH=N-R + H2O.
  • Hydroxylamine: hydroxylamine adds to aldehydes and ketones; elimination of water produces an oxime: (CH3)2C=O + NH2OH → (CH3)2C=N-OH (propanone oxime) + H2O.
  • Hydrazine: hydrazine adds to aldehydes and ketones; elimination of water produces a hydrazone: (CH3)2C=O + H2N-NH2 → (CH3)2C=N-NH2 (propanone hydrazone) + H2O.
  • Phenylhydrazine reacts in the same way to give phenylhydrazones.

Key Points

  • Ammonia and its derivatives attack through nitrogen.
  • Ammonia + aldehyde → imine + water.
  • Primary amines give imines; hydroxylamine gives oximes; hydrazine gives hydrazones.
  • All these reactions are addition followed by elimination of water.

mcqs.q: Ammonia adds to aldehydes to form what?
mcqs.why: Ammonia adds to aldehydes to form imines: CH3CHO plus NH3 gives CH3-CH=NH plus H2O.

mcqs.q: Reactions of nitrogen nucleophiles share which two stages?
options: Addition first, then elimination of water
mcqs.why: In each case an addition product forms first and then water is eliminated, for ammonia and all its derivatives.

mcqs.q: Primary amines reacting with aldehydes or ketones give what?
mcqs.why: Primary amines add and then lose water to produce imines: CH3CHO plus R-NH2 gives CH3-CH=N-R plus H2O.

mcqs.q: Hydroxylamine reacting with a carbonyl compound gives what?
mcqs.why: Hydroxylamine adds to aldehydes and ketones and elimination of water produces an oxime, such as propanone oxime.

mcqs.q: Hydrazine reacting with a carbonyl compound gives what?
mcqs.why: Hydrazine adds and water is eliminated to produce a hydrazone, for example propanone hydrazone (CH3)2C=N-NH2.

mcqs.q: Propanone oxime has which structure?
mcqs.why: Propanone plus NH2OH gives (CH3)2C=N-OH plus H2O, the oxime with an N-OH group.

mcqs.q: Phenylhydrazine gives which derivatives with carbonyls?
mcqs.why: Phenylhydrazine reacts in the same way as hydrazine to give phenylhydrazones with aldehydes and ketones.

mcqs.q: The intermediate after proton transfer in ammonia addition is described as what type?
mcqs.why: Step 2 transfers a proton to give the carbinolamine-type intermediate before water is eliminated to the imine in step 3.

mcqs.q: The imine from acetaldehyde and ammonia is written as what?
mcqs.why: CH3CHO plus NH3 gives CH3-CH=NH plus H2O, the imine product shown in the notes equation.

mcqs.q: Through which atom do ammonia derivatives attack the carbonyl?
mcqs.why: The nitrogen in ammonia and its derivatives acts as the nucleophile and attacks the carbonyl carbon.

lessons.title: Reduction with Oxygen Nucleophiles
lessons.notes_html:
The oxygen in water, alcohols, etc. acts as a nucleophile and reacts with aldehydes and ketones to give various products.

Addition of Water (Hydration)

Water adds to aldehydes or ketones to produce a germinal diol (gem-diol). The reaction is catalyzed by an acid or a base: R2C=O + H2O → R2C(OH)2. Examples: formaldehyde + water → formaldehyde hydrate, H2C(OH)2; acetaldehyde + water → acetaldehyde hydrate (1,1-ethanediol); acetone + water → acetone hydrate (2,2-propanediol). A 37% solution of formaldehyde in water is known as formalin and is used to preserve biological specimens.

Addition of Alcohols

Alcohols add to aldehydes (or ketones) in the presence of dry HCl to produce acetals. The reaction occurs in two steps. First, one molecule of alcohol adds to produce a hemiacetal, which is unstable. The hemiacetal then reacts with a second molecule of alcohol to produce the acetal: CH3CHO + CH3CH2OH → hemiacetal CH3-CH(OH)(OCH2CH3); hemiacetal + CH3CH2OH → acetal CH3-CH(OCH2CH3)2 (1,1-diethoxyethane) + H2O. On hydrolysis, the acetal converts back to the original aldehyde.

An acetal obtained from a ketone is often called a ketal. A ketone does not react with alcohols readily to form hemiketals or ketals because of steric hindrance. Acetals are common compounds: sucrose (table sugar) and cotton fabric are composed of acetals.

Key Points

  • Water adds to the carbonyl group to give a gem-diol (a hydrate).
  • Hydration is catalyzed by an acid or a base.
  • Formalin is a 37% aqueous solution of formaldehyde, used to preserve specimens.
  • Alcohols add in dry HCl: first a hemiacetal, then an acetal.
  • Acetals hydrolyse back to the original aldehyde; ketone acetals are called ketals.

mcqs.q: Addition of water to a carbonyl compound produces what?
mcqs.why: Water adds to aldehydes or ketones to produce a germinal diol, gem-diol: R2C=O plus H2O gives R2C(OH)2.

mcqs.q: Hydration of carbonyls is catalyzed by what?
mcqs.why: The hydration reaction R2C=O plus H2O to R2C(OH)2 is catalyzed by an acid or a base.

mcqs.q: Formaldehyde hydrate is written as what?
mcqs.why: Formaldehyde plus water gives formaldehyde hydrate, H2C(OH)2, with two OH groups on the single carbon.

mcqs.q: Acetone hydrate is named as what?
mcqs.why: Acetone plus water gives acetone hydrate, 2,2-propanediol, while acetaldehyde hydrate is 1,1-ethanediol.

mcqs.q: Formalin, used to preserve specimens, is what concentration of formaldehyde in water?
mcqs.why: A 37 percent solution of formaldehyde in water is known as formalin and is used to preserve biological specimens.

mcqs.q: Alcohols add to aldehydes in dry HCl to produce what finally?
mcqs.why: Alcohols add in dry HCl in two steps, first a hemiacetal then an acetal, as shown with acetaldehyde and ethanol.

mcqs.q: The first alcohol addition product, before the acetal, is called what?
mcqs.why: First one molecule of alcohol adds to produce a hemiacetal, which is unstable and reacts with a second alcohol molecule.

mcqs.q: On hydrolysis, an acetal converts back to what?
mcqs.why: On hydrolysis the acetal converts back to the original aldehyde, making acetal formation a reversible protection.

mcqs.q: An acetal obtained from a ketone is often called what?
mcqs.why: An acetal obtained from a ketone is often called a ketal, as distinguished in the notes from ordinary acetals.

mcqs.q: Why do ketones not readily form hemiketals or ketals with alcohols?
mcqs.why: A ketone does not react with alcohols readily to form hemiketals or ketals because of steric hindrance.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Aldehydes
lessons.notes_html:
Aldehydes and ketones show generally similar behaviour towards nucleophilic addition, but their behaviour towards oxidizing agents is quite different. Aldehydes are much more easily oxidized to carboxylic acids than ketones; ketones are oxidized to carboxylic acids only under drastic conditions.

Aldehydes can be oxidized by mild oxidizing agents such as silver oxide, Ag2O (Tollens' reagent), and cupric oxide, CuO (Fehling's solution or Benedict's solution). They can also be oxidized by strong oxidizing agents such as potassium permanganate or potassium dichromate in acidic medium: CH3CHO + [O] → CH3COOH (K2Cr2O7/H2SO4).

Composition of the Test Reagents

ReagentComposition
Tollens' reagentMixture of AgNO3 and NH4OH
Fehling's solutionMixture of CuSO4, NaOH and tartaric acid
Benedict's solutionMixture of CuSO4, NaOH and citric acid

Key Points

  • Aldehydes are easily oxidized to carboxylic acids with the same number of carbons.
  • Even mild oxidizers (Tollens', Fehling's, Benedict's) oxidize aldehydes.
  • Strong oxidizers KMnO4 and acidified K2Cr2O7 also oxidize aldehydes.
  • Example: acetaldehyde + [O] → acetic acid.
  • These mild-oxidizer tests distinguish aldehydes from ketones.

mcqs.q: Aldehydes are oxidized to which products?
options: Carboxylic acids with the same number of carbons
mcqs.why: Aldehydes are much more easily oxidized to carboxylic acids than ketones, keeping the same number of carbons.

mcqs.q: Which mild reagent is Tollens' reagent based on?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes can be oxidized by mild agents such as silver oxide Ag2O, Tollens' reagent, and cupric oxide in Fehling's or Benedict's solution.

mcqs.q: Oxidation of acetaldehyde with [O] using K2Cr2O7/H2SO4 gives what?
mcqs.why: The example reaction is CH3CHO plus [O] giving CH3COOH, acetic acid, with acidified dichromate.

mcqs.q: Tollens' reagent is a mixture of what?
mcqs.why: The composition table gives Tollens' reagent as a mixture of AgNO3 and NH4OH, distinct from Fehling's and Benedict's solutions.

mcqs.q: Fehling's solution contains which acid component?
mcqs.why: Fehling's solution is a mixture of CuSO4, NaOH and tartaric acid, while Benedict's uses citric acid instead.

mcqs.q: Benedict's solution contains which acid component?
mcqs.why: Benedict's solution is a mixture of CuSO4, NaOH and citric acid, differing from Fehling's solution in this component.

mcqs.q: Strong oxidizers that oxidize aldehydes include what?
mcqs.why: Aldehydes are also oxidized by strong agents such as potassium permanganate or potassium dichromate in acidic medium.

mcqs.q: Ketones are oxidized to acids only under what conditions?
mcqs.why: Ketones are oxidized to carboxylic acids only under drastic conditions, unlike aldehydes which react with mild oxidizers.

mcqs.q: The mild-oxidizer tests are useful because they do what?
mcqs.why: These mild-oxidizer tests distinguish aldehydes from ketones because only aldehydes are oxidized by them.

mcqs.q: Fehling's and Benedict's solutions are based on which oxide chemistry?
mcqs.why: The notes list cupric oxide CuO, Fehling's solution or Benedict's solution, as mild oxidizers for aldehydes.

lessons.title: Oxidation of Ketones
lessons.notes_html:
Ketones cannot be oxidized by mild oxidizing agents. They can be oxidized only by strong oxidizing agents such as potassium permanganate and potassium dichromate, at higher temperatures and at higher concentrations of acid or base. The oxidation of ketones produces a mixture of two carboxylic acids, because a carbon-carbon bond next to the carbonyl group breaks.

Key Reactions

KetoneConditionsProducts
CH3COCH3 (acetone) + 3[O]K2Cr2O7/H2SO4, strong conditionsCH3COOH (acetic acid) + HCOOH (formic acid)
