lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes are proteins that act as catalysts and increase the rate of chemical reactions in living organisms, such as respiration, photosynthesis and the formation of new proteins. Examples are lipase, zymase, glycosidase and isomerase. Enzymes are produced only by living cells and catalyse reactions inside and outside the cells. Without enzymes, life processes would be too slow and life would be practically impossible. Enzymes increase the rate of reaction by 10^4 to 10^20 times. They are highly specific: one enzyme catalyses only one type of reaction. For example, sucrase hydrolyses only sucrose, and glucokinase catalyses only glucose. An enzyme has two parts: the protein part, called the apo-enzyme, and the non-protein part, called the co-enzyme or co-factor.

Role of Enzymes as Biocatalysts

A natural substance that initiates or increases the rate of a reaction in a living body is called a biocatalyst. Enzymes play this role in metabolism, respiration and digestion. The body produces digestive enzymes, which digest food, and metabolic enzymes, which run all the biochemical reactions in the cells.

Amylase is made in two places. Salivary amylase, present in saliva, converts about 30% of the carbohydrates (starch and sugar) in food into simple sugars in the mouth; this is why bread tastes sweet when it is chewed for a long time. Pancreatic amylase, present in pancreatic juice from the pancreas, does the same work.

Lipase, present in pancreatic juice, breaks down dietary fats into fatty acids and glycerol. Fat digestion in the small intestine is helped by bile, which is made in the liver and breaks fat into small droplets on which lipase can act. Bile itself is not an enzyme.

Protease is the general term for pepsin, trypsin and chymotrypsin. Pepsin, present in the gastric juice of the stomach, breaks proteins into peptides. Trypsin and chymotrypsin are produced in the pancreas and released into the small intestine through the pancreatic duct; they complete the digestion of proteins into simple amino acids. Vitamins, minerals and water are not digested, because they are already small enough to be absorbed, and digestive enzymes cannot break down dietary fibre.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up reactions by 10^4 to 10^20 times and are highly specific.
  • An enzyme consists of a protein apo-enzyme and a non-protein co-enzyme or co-factor.
  • Amylase digests carbohydrates, lipase digests fats into fatty acids and glycerol, and proteases digest proteins.
  • Pepsin works in the stomach; trypsin and chymotrypsin from the pancreas work in the small intestine.
  • Bile helps fat digestion by making small fat droplets, but bile is not an enzyme.

lessons.notes_html:
Concentration

The rate of reaction increases with the enzyme concentration: for example, the rate of digestion increases as the concentration of pepsin increases. The rate is also directly proportional to the substrate concentration.

Temperature

Enzyme activity increases with temperature up to about 45°C. Above 45°C enzymes, being proteins, are denatured and become inactive, and at 100°C they are completely destroyed. At low temperature (0°C) activity is reduced but the enzyme is not destroyed. The optimum temperature for enzymes of the mammalian body is about 37°C to 40°C, and it differs for different enzymes.

Effect of pH

The pH at which an enzyme shows maximum activity is its optimum pH. The optimum pH of salivary amylase is 6.4 to 6.9, while that of pepsin of the stomach is 1.4. Pepsin is inactive in neutral and alkaline solutions. The optimum pH of enzymes is never found above 10.

Effect of Other Substances

Co-enzymes are the non-protein part of an enzyme; the protein part is the apo-enzyme, so Enzyme = Co-enzyme + Apo-enzyme. Vitamins are examples of co-enzymes, and certain enzymes cannot function without them. Activators are inorganic substances that increase enzyme activity, for example Mg2+ for phosphatase and Zn2+ for carbonic anhydrase. Inhibitors reduce or destroy enzyme activity; sulpha drugs, penicillin and streptomycin act as inhibitors and cure many infections.

Radiation

Enzymes are generally inactivated by ultraviolet light and by beta, gamma and X-rays.

Key Points

  • Reaction rate increases with both enzyme concentration and substrate concentration.
  • Activity rises with temperature up to about 45°C; above this enzymes denature, and at 100°C they are destroyed.
  • The optimum temperature for mammalian enzymes is about 37°C to 40°C.
  • Each enzyme has an optimum pH: salivary amylase 6.4-6.9 and pepsin 1.4.
  • Vitamins act as co-enzymes; Mg2+ and Zn2+ act as activators; sulpha drugs and penicillin act as inhibitors.
  • UV light and beta, gamma and X-rays inactivate enzymes.

lessons.notes_html:
Enzymes are among the most efficient catalysts known. They are used in the food, beverage, cosmetic, detergent, leather, agriculture and medicine industries, and in making biofuels and biopolymers.

Food Industry

Enzymes process carbohydrates, proteins and fats. Amylase, lactases and cellulases break complex sugars into simple sugars, and lipase breaks lipids into fatty acids and glycerol.

Beverage Industry

Enzymes increase the yield of juice and decrease energy consumption. Pectinase breaks down pectins in fruit juice and makes the juice less viscous. Cellulases and hemicellulases break the plant cell wall for efficient liquefaction of fruit pulp. Neutral proteases, alpha amylase, beta-glucanase and cellulases are used in alcoholic beverages such as beer, wine, brandy, whiskey and rum.

Detergent Industry

Proteases, lipases, amylases and cellulases are added to detergents. They break down and remove dirt and stains from cloth fibres.

Leather Industry

Enzymes are used in the soaking, dehairing and dyeing of leather. Proteases remove hair from hides, and pancreatic enzymes increase the softness of leather.

Paper Industry

Amylases, xylanases, cellulases, laccase, lipase and ligninases are used in the pulp and paper industry. They lower viscosity, help in coating paper, remove colour, smooth the fibres, enhance water drainage and increase softness.

Key Points

  • Enzymes are used in food, beverages, detergents, leather, paper, medicines, biofuels and biopolymers.
  • Pectinase clarifies fruit juice; cellulases and hemicellulases liquefy fruit pulp.
  • Proteases, lipases, amylases and cellulases in detergents remove dirt and stains.
  • Proteases dehair hides in the leather industry, and pancreatic enzymes soften leather.
  • Xylanases, laccase and ligninases are used in pulp and paper making.

lessons.notes_html:
Lipids are a naturally occurring heterogeneous group of organic compounds of animals and plants. They are soluble in organic solvents such as acetone, benzene and CCl4, but insoluble in water. Fats, oils and waxes are lipids. The word lipid comes from the Greek word Lipas, meaning fats. Fats and oils are the most important lipids in nature: lipids that are solid at ambient temperature are called fats, and those that are liquid are called oils.

Classification of Lipids

Simple lipids are esters of fatty acids with glycerol. The common fats and oils belong to this class.

Compound lipids have additional radicals along with fatty acids and alcohols. Examples are phospholipids and lipoproteins.

Derived lipids are obtained by the hydrolysis of simple or compound lipids and are also called associated lipids. Examples are sterols, vitamin D and terpenes. Steroids are lipids with high molecular mass tetracyclic compounds; cholesterol is an example.

The book also names edible lipids: the lipids which have fats, oils and waxes are called edible lipids.

Structure of Lipids (Fats and Oils)

Lipids do not have a single common structure. Fats and oils are triesters of glycerol with fatty acids, called triglycerides or glycerides. One glycerol molecule reacts with three fatty acid molecules to form a triglyceride and three water molecules. Common oils and fats are mixtures of saturated and unsaturated triglycerides. Solid or semi-solid triesters of long-chain saturated fatty acids are fats, while liquid triesters of long-chain unsaturated fatty acids are oils.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
Formation of a triglycerideGlycerol + 3 fatty acids → Triglyceride + 3H2O

Key Points

  • Lipids are soluble in organic solvents and insoluble in water; solid lipids are fats and liquid lipids are oils.
  • Simple lipids are esters of fatty acids with glycerol, such as fats and oils.
  • Compound lipids contain extra groups, for example phospholipids and lipoproteins.
  • Derived lipids come from hydrolysis of simple or compound lipids, for example sterols, vitamin D and terpenes.
  • Fats and oils are triglycerides: triesters of glycerol with three fatty acids.
  • Steroids are tetracyclic lipids; cholesterol is the common example.

lessons.notes_html:
Physical Properties

  • Pure fats and oils are colourless, odourless and tasteless.
  • They are liquids or non-crystalline solids at room temperature.
  • They are insoluble in water but readily soluble in organic solvents.
  • They form emulsions when shaken with water in the presence of a base such as NaOH.
  • They are poor conductors of heat and electricity, so they are excellent insulators for the animal body.

Chemical Properties

Hydrolysis: oils and fats give glycerol and fatty acids on hydrolysis with the enzyme lipase.

Saponification: the reaction of fats and oils with NaOH to give soap and glycerol is called saponification.

Hardening of oils: when hydrogen is passed through an unsaturated glyceride (an oil) in the presence of a nickel catalyst, a saturated glyceride (a fat) is obtained. This process is called hardening or hydrogenation. Glycerol trioleate (an oil) takes up 3H2 and forms glycerol tristearate (a fat). Hardened oils are used to make vegetable ghee and margarine, and also in soaps and candles.

Key Reactions

ReactionEquation
Hydrolysis (lipase)Triglyceride + 3H2O → Glycerol + 3 fatty acids
SaponificationTriglyceride + 3NaOH → Glycerol + 3 soap (R-COONa)
Hydrogenation (Ni)Glycerol trioleate (oil) + 3H2 → Glycerol tristearate (fat)

Key Points

  • Pure fats and oils are colourless, odourless and tasteless, and are insoluble in water.
  • Lipids form emulsions with water in the presence of a base and act as insulators in the body.
  • Hydrolysis with lipase gives glycerol and fatty acids.
  • Saponification with NaOH gives soap and glycerol.
  • Hydrogenation over nickel hardens oils into fats, used for vegetable ghee, margarine, soaps and candles.

lessons.notes_html:
• The main role of lipids is to provide energy for muscles and body processes. Fat gives 9 kcal per gram, while protein and carbohydrate give only 4 kcal per gram.
  • Lipids provide energy to digest and absorb food.
  • The essential lipids linoleic acid and alpha-linolenic acid cannot be synthesised in the body, so they must be taken in the diet. They are necessary for the regulation of blood pressure, blood clotting, liver function and immune and inflammatory responses, for the proper development and functioning of the brain and nervous system, and for healthy skin and hair.
  • Phospholipids, the second most common lipids, are structural components of cell membranes. The membranes act as barriers and prevent charged particles and large molecules from moving across them.
  • Cholesterol is the starting material for vitamin D and for bile acids, which aid the digestion and absorption of fats.
  • Cholesterol is also used in the synthesis of sex hormones.
  • Lipids are components of the nervous system.
  • Lipids act as carriers of the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K from the intestine to the bloodstream.

Hibernating Animals Accumulate Fat

Hibernation is a state of inactivity during winter in which body temperature, heart rate, breathing and metabolic rate all fall. The animal goes into a deep sleep and conserves energy, because food is stored in the body as fat. Fat is a rich and efficient energy source, giving 9 kcal per gram compared with 4 kcal per gram from carbohydrates and proteins. The hibernation period depends on the species, the time of year and the body condition of the animal, and may last for days, weeks or months.

Key Points

  • Fats give 9 kcal per gram, more than double the energy from carbohydrates or proteins (4 kcal per gram).
  • Essential fatty acids (linoleic and alpha-linolenic) must come from the diet.
  • Phospholipids form cell membranes, which act as selective barriers.
  • Cholesterol is the starting material for vitamin D, bile acids and sex hormones.
  • Lipids carry the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K.
  • Hibernating animals store food as fat because it is the most efficient energy store.

lessons.notes_html:
Nucleic acids are high molecular mass biopolymers of nucleotides. They are present in the nucleus of all eukaryotic living cells and in viruses, and they are the carriers of hereditary information. They were first isolated from the nuclei of pus cells (white blood corpuscles) in 1869 by Friedrich Miescher. They are called nucleic acids because they are present in the nucleus and are acidic in nature.

There are two main classes: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid). DNA is the master blueprint for life and is the genetic material in all free-living organisms and most viruses. RNA is the genetic material of certain viruses and is also present in all living cells, where it plays a role in making proteins. Both DNA and RNA are formed from a large number of nucleotides. Each nucleotide contains a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and phosphoric acid joined by ester linkage.

Nitrogenous Bases

The bases are purine and pyrimidine derivatives. Pyrimidines have a single six-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms at positions 1 and 3; their derivatives are cytosine, thymine and uracil. Purines have two rings, a pyrimidine ring and an imidazole ring (C3H4N2); their derivatives are adenine and guanine. DNA contains cytosine, thymine, adenine and guanine; in RNA thymine is absent and uracil takes its place.

Pentose Sugar and Phosphoric Acid

The sugar in DNA is D-2-deoxyribose and the sugar in RNA is D-ribose. The carbon atoms of the sugar are numbered with a prime symbol, for example 1', 3' and 5'. Phosphoric acid (H3PO4) forms the phosphodiester bonds between nucleotides.

ComponentDNARNA
PurinesAdenine, GuanineAdenine, Guanine
PyrimidinesCytosine, ThymineCytosine, Uracil
Pentose sugarD-2-deoxyriboseD-ribose
AcidPhosphoric acidPhosphoric acid

Key Points

  • Nucleic acids are biopolymers of nucleotides and carry hereditary information.
  • DNA is the genetic material of almost all organisms; RNA is the genetic material of some viruses and helps in protein making.
  • Each nucleotide has a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and phosphoric acid.
  • Purines are adenine and guanine; pyrimidines are cytosine, thymine and uracil.
  • DNA has deoxyribose and thymine; RNA has ribose and uracil instead of thymine.

lessons.notes_html:
DNA and RNA are polymers of nucleotides, so they are called polynucleotides. A nucleotide is made of three parts: a nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar and a phosphate group. The pentose sugar is the central component: the base is attached to carbon 1 of the sugar and the phosphate group is attached to carbon 5.

Nucleotides are linked to each other by phosphate ester bonds. The hydroxyl group of the phosphate on one nucleotide condenses with a hydroxyl group on the carbohydrate ring of another nucleotide, and in this way polynucleotides are built up. The phosphodiester bond joins the phosphate group at position 5 of one pentose sugar to the hydroxyl group at position 3 of the next sugar. DNA is a polydeoxyribonucleotide and RNA is a polyribonucleotide.

Storage of Genetic Information

Nucleic acids have two main functions: the storage of genetic information and the synthesis of proteins. DNA stores biological information in the sequences of its four bases: adenine, thymine, cytosine and guanine. A sequence of bases forms a gene. Genes are located on the chromosomal thread that runs along the entire length of a chromosome, and each gene occupies a specific position on the chromosome. Genes provide the instructions for making proteins, and proteins determine the structure and function of each cell. In this way, genes are responsible for inheritance.

Key Points

  • A nucleotide = base + pentose sugar + phosphate; the base is on carbon 1 and the phosphate on carbon 5 of the sugar.
  • Nucleotides join by phosphodiester bonds between the 5' phosphate of one sugar and the 3' hydroxyl of the next.
  • DNA is a polydeoxyribonucleotide; RNA is a polyribonucleotide.
  • DNA stores information in the sequence of its four bases.
  • Genes are base sequences on chromosomes that give instructions for making proteins and control inheritance.

Minerals are inorganic compounds that are essential in small amounts for good health and for the prevention of diseases. Major minerals are required in amounts of 100 mg or more per day; they include sodium, potassium, calcium and manganese, and the non-metals chlorine, sulphur and phosphorus. Trace minerals are required in only a few milligrams per day; they include iron, copper, zinc, selenium and iodine. The most important minerals are iron, calcium, phosphorus and zinc. Minerals are not synthesised in the body, so they must be obtained from the diet. Daily requirements differ slightly for children, youngsters, and during pregnancy and breastfeeding.

Key Points

mcqs.why: Phosphorus has a role in energy production as a component of ATP and is a component of nucleic acids DNA and RNA.

mcqs.why: Symptoms include frequent urination, fatigue, weight loss and excessive thirst and hunger, with too much sugar left in blood.

lessons.notes_html:
Iron

Iron is an essential mineral. It plays an important role in the production of red blood cells and helps the red blood cells to carry oxygen from the lungs to all parts of the body. It also plays an important role in the immune system and prevents us from feeling tired. Lack of iron in the red blood cells causes anaemia, whose symptoms are weakness, tiredness and shortness of breath.

Calcium

Calcium is essential for building strong bones and teeth in children and teens. It helps the muscles to contract and relax, and it is important in blood clotting, blood pressure regulation and the immune system. It also supports nerve transmission. Calcium deficiency may cause osteoporosis (brittle bones in adults), rickets (softening of bones in children), poor growth and mental depression.

Phosphorus

Phosphorus is important for healthy bones and teeth; more than 80% of the phosphorus in the human body is located in the bones as calcium phosphate. It has a role in energy production as a component of ATP, and it is a component of the nucleic acids DNA and RNA, which regulate protein synthesis. It is a constituent of plant cells and is essential for cell division and the development of new tissues, for the repair of body cells and tissues, for acid-base balance (regulating pH) in the body, and for the working of the muscular system, including the beating of the heart. Phosphorus deficiency is relatively uncommon, but it may cause rickets in children and osteomalacia (softening of bones) in adults, especially in pregnant women. An improper balance of phosphorus and calcium may cause osteoporosis. Symptoms of deficiency include poor formation of teeth, irregular breathing pattern, and joint stiffness and pain.

Zinc

Zinc is an essential element. It is important for normal growth, wound healing, the nervous system and especially the defensive (immune) system. It is needed for cell division, tissue growth and repair, and for the breakdown of carbohydrates. It enhances the action of insulin and is important for a proper sense of taste and smell. Lack of zinc may be associated with skin problems, slow healing of wounds, loss of appetite, weight loss and a decreased ability to taste food.

Hormones and Insulin

Hormones are chemical substances that act as chemical messengers in the body. They are secreted by specific organs and glands and travel in the bloodstream or other body fluids to their target organs. They control and regulate growth, development, reproduction, energy use and storage, and water and electrolyte balance. By chemical structure, hormones are of three groups: cholesterol-derived (steroid) hormones, secreted by the adrenal cortex, the gonads and the placenta; amino acid-derived hormones, made from tyrosine and tryptophan, such as epinephrine and norepinephrine from the medulla of the adrenal glands and thyroxine from the thyroid gland; and peptide (protein) hormones, such as insulin, glucagon, leptin, ADH and oxytocin.

Insulin is a protein hormone secreted by the pancreas. It lowers the glucose level in the bloodstream and promotes the storage of glucose in the liver, muscles and other tissues. It facilitates glucose transport, stimulates protein synthesis and enhances free fatty acid uptake and storage. Insulin is often described as a key that unlocks the cell to allow sugar to enter and be used for energy. In diabetes mellitus, insulin is either not produced by the pancreas (type 1 diabetes) or is produced in insufficient amounts (type 2 diabetes), so too much sugar is left in the blood. Symptoms include frequent urination, fatigue, weight loss, and excessive thirst and hunger. It can cause kidney failure, heart disease, stroke and loss of sight. Treatment includes changes in diet, oral medications and, in some cases, daily injections of insulin.

Key Points

  • Iron makes red blood cells and carries oxygen; its deficiency causes anaemia.
  • Calcium builds bones and teeth and is needed for clotting, muscles and nerves; its deficiency causes osteoporosis and rickets.
  • More than 80% of body phosphorus is in the bones as calcium phosphate; phosphorus is also part of ATP and nucleic acids.
  • Zinc is needed for growth, wound healing, immunity and the senses of taste and smell.
  • Hormones are chemical messengers of three types: steroid, amino acid-derived and peptide hormones.
  • Insulin deficiency causes diabetes mellitus, with high blood sugar and symptoms such as excessive thirst, hunger and frequent urination.

mcqs.why: Shelf life is defined in brackets as the period for which a product can be stored and remain fresh and suitable for use; food chemicals increase it.

mcqs.q: An industry is defined as:

mcqs.why: An industry is the branch of economic activity concerned with processing of raw materials and manufacture of goods in factories; those producing chemicals are chemical industries.

lessons.notes_html:
Industrial chemistry is the branch of chemistry which is concerned with using physical and chemical processes for the transformation of raw materials into useful and profitable products. These products are used both as consumer goods and as intermediates for the manufacture of other, more complex products, such as household appliances and automobiles. Industrial chemistry has raised the standard of living of people, and it brings prosperity to a nation by increasing exports and earning valuable foreign exchange.

An industry is the branch of economic activity that is concerned with the processing of raw materials and the manufacture of goods in factories. Industries that produce chemicals are called chemical industries. They convert raw materials such as oil, natural gas, air, water, metals and minerals into thousands (more than 70,000) of different products that we use in our day-to-day life. The chemical industry has touched all aspects of life, such as agriculture, environment, food, hygiene, decor and transportation. It provides:

  • Food chemicals such as preservatives, taste enhancers and flavours, which keep food edible and increase its shelf life (the period for which a product can be stored and remain fresh and suitable for use).
  • Fertilizers and pesticides to the farmers, which are essential for crop production.
  • Polymers and plastics, used in clothing, home decor, PVC piping, water tanks and many other things.
  • Medicines and drugs for saving the life of people and animals.
  • Toiletries such as soaps, detergents, shampoos, body wash, face wash, toothpaste, toothbrush and deodorant.

The chemical industry is a very important contributor to the wealth of a country. In Pakistan, the average growth in the chemical industry sector was recorded at about 10.01% during 2014-15 and 2015-16. The major chemical industries of the country include sulphuric acid (the king of chemicals), soda ash, caustic soda, paints, varnish, petrochemicals, polymer and plastic products, fertilizers, cement, limestone, gypsum and soaps. Most of these products are used inside the country, which saves valuable foreign exchange, and some amount is also exported, which earns foreign exchange.

Key Points

  • Industrial chemistry changes raw materials into useful and profitable products by physical and chemical processes.
  • Chemical industries convert oil, natural gas, air, water, metals and minerals into more than 70,000 products.
  • They provide food chemicals, fertilizers, pesticides, polymers, medicines and toiletries.
  • Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals.
  • Pakistan's chemical industry grew by about 10.01% during 2014-15 and 2015-16.
  • Chemical products save foreign exchange when used at home and earn it when exported.

lessons.title: Raw Materials Used in Chemical Industries

mcqs.q: The six important industrial gases separated from liquid air by fractional distillation are:
options: Nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, krypton and xenon
mcqs.why: Nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, krypton and xenon are separated from liquid air by fractional distillation; nitrogen is most abundant and oxygen second.

mcqs.q: Electrolysis of brine (aqueous NaCl) produces:
mcqs.why: Electrolysis of aqueous sodium chloride (brine) produces three useful products: hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide.

mcqs.q: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride produces:
mcqs.why: Electrolysis of molten sodium chloride produces two useful products: sodium and chlorine, unlike brine which also gives hydrogen and NaOH.

mcqs.q: How many useful products come from electrolysis of brine versus molten NaCl?
mcqs.why: Working: count brine products - hydrogen, chlorine, NaOH = 3; count molten NaCl products - sodium, chlorine = 2.

mcqs.q: Seawater is a source of:
options: Sodium chloride, magnesium, bromine and sodium hydroxide
mcqs.why: Seawater gives sodium chloride, magnesium, bromine and sodium hydroxide; NaCl is obtained by evaporating seawater.

mcqs.why: It is estimated we get 70% of all materials from the lithosphere, whereas before industrialization most materials came from the biosphere.

mcqs.q: The lithosphere provides, in addition to minerals and ores:
options: Coal, natural gas, crude petroleum and gemstones like diamond and amethyst
mcqs.why: The lithosphere gives coal, natural gas and crude petroleum for energy, and gemstones such as diamond and amethyst for jewellery.

mcqs.q: Products obtained from the biosphere include:
options: Oils, fats, waxes, resins, sugar, leather, cotton, wool and silk
mcqs.why: Biosphere products listed are oils, fats, waxes, resins, sugar, leather, cotton, wool, silk and other natural fibres.

mcqs.q: Minerals are defined as:
options: Natural compounds formed through geological processes
mcqs.why: The lithosphere provides minerals, which are natural compounds formed through geological processes; many elements are obtained from mineral ores.

mcqs.q: The most abundant gas in the atmosphere, according to the notes, is:
mcqs.why: Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere and oxygen is the second most abundant; the other industrial gases are in much smaller proportions.

lessons.notes_html:
All chemicals are derived from raw materials available in nature. The price of chemicals depends on the availability of their raw materials, so major chemical industries have developed around the most plentiful raw materials. The natural environment is the source of raw materials for the chemical industry.

Raw Materials from the Atmosphere

The atmosphere is a useful source of raw materials. The six important industrial gases, nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, krypton and xenon, are separated from liquid air by fractional distillation. Nitrogen is the most abundant gas in the atmosphere and oxygen is the second most abundant; the other gases are present in much smaller proportions.

Raw Materials from the Hydrosphere

Seawater is a useful source of raw materials. Sodium chloride, magnesium, bromine and sodium hydroxide are obtained from seawater. Sodium chloride is obtained by evaporating seawater. The electrolysis of an aqueous solution of sodium chloride (brine) produces three useful products: hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide. The electrolysis of molten sodium chloride produces two useful products: sodium and chlorine.

Raw Materials from the Lithosphere

The lithosphere provides minerals, which are natural compounds formed through geological processes. Many elements such as gold, silver, copper, aluminium and iron are obtained from the earth's crust in the form of mineral ores, and are used to make automobiles, airplanes, computer chips, windows and many other valuable things. In addition to minerals and ores, the lithosphere gives coal, natural gas and crude petroleum, which meet our energy needs. The lithosphere is also a source of valuable gemstones such as diamond and amethyst, which are used in jewellery and other adornments.

Raw Materials from the Biosphere

Before industrialization, the majority of our materials came from the biosphere. Now it is estimated that we get 70% of all materials from the lithosphere. Oils, fats, waxes, resins, sugar, leather, cotton, wool, silk and other natural fibres are products obtained from the biosphere.

Key Points

  • Raw materials come from the atmosphere, hydrosphere, lithosphere and biosphere.
  • Nitrogen, oxygen, argon, neon, krypton and xenon are separated from liquid air by fractional distillation.
  • Electrolysis of brine gives hydrogen, chlorine and sodium hydroxide; electrolysis of molten NaCl gives sodium and chlorine.
  • The lithosphere gives mineral ores, coal, natural gas, crude petroleum and gemstones.
  • About 70% of all materials now come from the lithosphere; the biosphere gives oils, fats, waxes, resins, sugar, leather and natural fibres.

lessons.title: Safety Considerations in Process Industries

mcqs.q: Why is a safety strategy required in process industries?
options: They process reactive chemicals, flammable liquids, vapours, gases and powders that can cause fires and explosions
mcqs.why: Chemical industries involve processing reactive chemicals, flammable liquids, vapours, gases and powders, so uncontrolled fires, explosions and reactions can create hazards.

mcqs.q: Before permitting workers to work, they should receive:
mcqs.why: Proper safety training should be given to all workers before permitting them to work, as the first safety consideration listed.

mcqs.q: Correct safety equipment includes:
options: Safety goggles, hard hats, gloves or a full-face mask
mcqs.why: The correct safety equipment should be worn, such as safety goggles, hard hats, gloves or a full-face mask, and checked that it is itself safe.

mcqs.q: Fire extinguishers should be:
options: Provided at all fire-hazardous locations and inspected, serviced and maintained
mcqs.why: Fire extinguishers and fire buckets should be provided at all fire-hazardous locations, and extinguishers should be inspected, serviced and maintained.

mcqs.q: Combustible waste should be:
options: Stored in metal containers and discarded daily
mcqs.why: Combustible materials are stored away from ignition sources, and combustible waste is stored in metal containers and discarded daily.

mcqs.q: Regular breaks for workers help them:
options: Stay fresh and more alert, reducing hazards
mcqs.why: Workers should take regular breaks, which help them stay fresh and more alert, as one of the safety considerations listed.

mcqs.q: A safety committee should be made to:
mcqs.why: A safety committee should be made to create safety consciousness, alongside government legislation to ensure industrial safety.

mcqs.q: Passageways and work areas should be kept clear to prevent:
options: Tripping or slipping, and spills should be cleaned; floors checked for holes, loose boards or nails
mcqs.why: Passageways kept clear and spills cleaned prevent tripping or slipping; workplaces are checked for holes, loose boards or projecting nails.

mcqs.q: Clear access must be kept to:
options: Equipment shutoffs, with work area and emergency exits kept clear
mcqs.why: Clear access to equipment shutoffs should be kept, equipment placed in proper storage after use, and work area and emergency exits kept clear.

mcqs.q: Regular inspection and maintenance of equipment:
options: Ensures it is safe to use and extends its lifetime
mcqs.why: Inspection and maintenance scheduled regularly ensures equipment is safe to use and its lifetime is extended, according to the notes.

lessons.notes_html:
Chemical industries involve the processing of reactive chemicals, flammable liquids, vapours, gases and powders. The safety record of the chemical industry is good, but uncontrolled fires, explosions and chemical reactions can result in hazardous situations. A safety strategy is therefore required, so that chemical manufacturing activities are carried out safely. Its objective is to establish and maintain safe manufacturing practices in a manner compatible with the plant design, the operating conditions, production demands, commercial requirements and economic factors.

The following safety considerations ensure the health and safety of workers and reduce the chances of damage to machinery and equipment:

  • Proper safety training should be given to all workers before permitting them to work.
  • The government has to make legislations in order to ensure industrial safety.
  • A safety committee should be made to create safety consciousness.
  • Communication in the workplace should be increased, so that employees communicate about potential problems effectively and reduce potential hazards.
  • Workers should take regular breaks, which help them stay fresh and more alert.
  • Tools and machines should be used properly and shortcuts avoided; tools and equipment should be regularly cleaned and inspected to ensure they are safe.
  • Clear access to equipment shutoffs should be kept, equipment should be placed in proper storage areas after use, and the work area and emergency exits should be kept clear.
  • The correct safety equipment should be worn, such as safety goggles, hard hats, gloves or a full-face mask, and it should be checked that the safety equipment is itself safe.
  • Extra care should be taken in the receipt, storage, handling and disposal of chemicals and other hazardous materials.
  • Fire extinguishers and fire buckets should be provided at all fire-hazardous locations, and the extinguishers should be inspected, serviced and maintained.
  • Inspection and maintenance of equipment should be scheduled regularly, so that the equipment is safe to use and its lifetime is extended.
  • Passageways should be kept clear and spills cleaned to prevent tripping or slipping; workplaces should be checked for holes, loose boards or nails projecting from the floor.
  • Combustible materials should be stored away from sources of ignition, and combustible waste should be stored in metal containers and discarded daily.

Industries that have an increased risk of workplace accidents must be extra attentive about potential hazards and implement key safety measures to keep their workers happy, healthy and productive.

Key Points

  • Process industries handle reactive chemicals and flammable liquids, vapours, gases and powders, so a safety strategy is essential.
  • All workers must receive proper safety training before starting work.
  • Workers must wear correct protective equipment such as goggles, hard hats, gloves and face masks.
  • Fire extinguishers must be provided at fire-hazardous places and regularly inspected and serviced.
  • Combustible materials must be stored away from ignition sources, and waste must be discarded daily in metal containers.
  • Regular inspection, clear passageways and good communication reduce accidents.

lessons.title: Dyes

mcqs.q: A dye must absorb strongly in the visible region, which is:
mcqs.why: High colour intensity depends on how strongly a dye absorbs radiation in the visible region, from 400 to 800 nm.

mcqs.q: The width of the visible range given (400 to 800 nm) is:
mcqs.why: Working: range width = 800 nm - 400 nm = 400 nm, using the visible region limits given in the notes.

mcqs.q: Chromophores are:
options: Unsaturated groups responsible for a compound looking coloured
mcqs.why: Chromophores are unsaturated groups; an organic compound looks coloured because of these groups, e.g. -NO, -NO2, -N=N-, C=C and C=O.

mcqs.q: Compounds that have chromophore groups are called:
mcqs.why: Compounds that have chromophore groups are called chromogens, as defined in the chemical composition of dyes section.

mcqs.q: Auxochromes are groups that:
options: Deepen or intensify colour in presence of a chromophore
mcqs.why: Auxochromes deepen or intensify colour in presence of a chromophore, e.g. -OH, -COOH, -SO3H, -NH2, -NHR and -NR2, and give no colour without a chromophore.

mcqs.q: Azobenzene is red coloured yet not a dye, while p-amino azobenzene is a yellow dye, because:
options: A chromogen without an auxochrome can never act as a dye
mcqs.why: The notes use this example to show a chromogen without an auxochrome can never act as a dye; p-amino azobenzene has the amino auxochrome.

mcqs.q: The first man-made organic aniline dye, mauveine, was discovered by:
mcqs.why: Synthetic dyes section states the first man-made organic aniline dye, mauveine, was discovered by William Henry Perkin in 1856.

mcqs.q: A mordant dye combines with dye and fibre, where the metal ion acts as:
options: A bridge between dye and fibre
mcqs.why: Mordants are salts of metals such as chromium, tin, copper, aluminium and iron; the metal ion acts as a bridge between dye and fibre.

mcqs.q: Natural dyes are described as:
options: Having unlimited shades and very durable
Cheaper and brighter than synthetic dyes
Having limited shades and not durable
mcqs.why: Natural dyes from plants, insects or minerals have limited shades and are not durable, unlike synthetic dyes which are cheaper, brighter and more colour-fast.

mcqs.q: Alizarin and indigo are examples of:
options: Natural dyes - alizarin red, indigo blue
mcqs.why: Prominent natural dye examples are alizarin (red dye) and indigo (blue dye) in the classification by source.

lessons.notes_html:
Dyes are organic compounds that are widely used for imparting colour to various substrates such as paper, leather, fur, hair, drugs, food, cosmetics, waxes, greases, plastics and textile materials. Dyes are normally water-soluble or water-dispersible organic compounds that are capable of being absorbed into the substrate. The dye molecules are usually chemically bonded to the surface and become a part of the material on which they are applied. A dye must have high colour intensity, which depends on how strongly it absorbs radiation in the visible region, from 400 to 800 nm. A dye should be resistant to the action of water, dilute acids and alkalies, because detergents and soaps are alkaline in nature.

Chemical Composition of Dyes

A dye is made up of two kinds of parts: chromophores and auxochromes. Chromophores are unsaturated groups; an organic compound looks coloured because of these groups. Important chromophores are the nitroso group (-NO), the nitro group (-NO2), the azo group (-N=N-), the ethylene group (C=C) and the carbonyl group (C=O). The intensity of colour increases with the number of chromophores or the degree of conjugation. Compounds that have chromophore groups are called chromogens. Auxochromes are groups that deepen or intensify the colour in the presence of a chromophore, so they are called colour-intensifying groups. Examples are the hydroxyl group (-OH), carboxyl group (-COOH), sulphonic acid group (-SO3H), amino group (-NH2), secondary amine group (-NHR) and tertiary amine group (-NR2). These groups impart no colour in the absence of a chromophore, and a chromogen without an auxochrome can never act as a dye: azobenzene is red coloured yet it is not a dye, while p-amino azobenzene is a yellow dye.

Classification of Dyes

Dyes are classified on the basis of their source, application, structure and the nature of their chromophores. On the basis of source there are two types. Natural dyes are derived from biological sources such as plants (roots, berries, bark, leaves, seeds, stem and flowers), insects (cochineal, lac and tyrian purple) or minerals (iron oxide and buff); fungi and lichens are other organic sources. Prominent examples are alizarin (red dye) and indigo (blue dye). Logwood is obtained from plants, tyrian purple from animals, and Prussian blue is an inorganic dye obtained from naturally occurring minerals. Natural dyes have limited shades and are not durable. Synthetic dyes are man-made dyes manufactured in the laboratory or industry, mostly from petroleum, sometimes in combination with mineral-derived components. The first man-made organic aniline dye, mauveine, was discovered by William Henry Perkin in 1856. Synthetic dyes are used everywhere, from clothes to paper and from food to wood, because they are cheaper to produce, brighter, more colour-fast and easy to apply to fabric. Examples are acid dyes, azo dyes, basic dyes and mordant dyes.

A mordant dye is a colourant that combines with the dye and the fibre. Mordants are commonly available in the form of salts of metals such as chromium, tin, copper, aluminium and iron; the metal ion acts as a bridge between the dye and the fibre. These dyes are economical and are generally used to produce dark shades such as dark blues, dark greens and blacks. They are most readily used for natural protein fibres, particularly wool, and sometimes for synthetic fibres, particularly nylon.

Key Points

  • Dyes are water-soluble organic compounds that bond chemically to the material and give it colour.
  • A dye has a chromophore (colour-producing group) and an auxochrome (colour-intensifying group).
  • Chromophores include -NO, -NO2, -N=N-, C=C and C=O; a compound with a chromophore is a chromogen.
  • Azobenzene is coloured but not a dye; p-amino azobenzene is a yellow dye.
  • Natural dyes (alizarin, indigo) have limited shades; synthetic dyes are cheaper, brighter and more colour-fast.
  • Mauveine, the first synthetic dye, was discovered by William Henry Perkin in 1856.

lessons.title: Pesticides

mcqs.q: Pesticides are chemicals used to:
options: Control pests, insects, weeds, fungus and so on
mcqs.why: Pesticides are chemicals used to control pests, insects, weeds, fungus and so on, generally on fruit, vegetable and horticulture crops.

mcqs.q: DDT was synthesized in which year and was effective against:
mcqs.why: Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) was synthesized in 1943 and found effective against many insects such as mosquitoes.

mcqs.why: Due to its hazardous nature, DDT is no longer used nowadays; safer similar chemicals such as aldrin, dieldrin and chlordane were synthesized.

mcqs.why: Targeted action means they control only the desired species and do not affect the good, helpful insects, as explained in the notes.

mcqs.q: Herbicides are used to control:
mcqs.why: Classification lists herbicides as chemicals used to control unwanted herbs (weeds) in the crops.

mcqs.why: Miticides are used to kill mites and ticks of the crops, distinct from nematicides for nematodes and rodenticides for rodents.

mcqs.why: Nematicides control harmful nematodes, the tiny hair-like worms that live in earth and feed on plant roots and juices from plant roots.

mcqs.why: A large quantity of crop is damaged by rodents such as rats, mice and raccoons; these are controlled by rodenticides.

mcqs.why: Repellents are chemicals that repel harmful pests, insects and other mammals, driving them away instead of killing them.

mcqs.why: Classification in the notes: insecticides control insects, fungicides control fungus, and herbicides control unwanted weeds.

lessons.notes_html:
Pesticides are chemicals used to control pests, insects, weeds, fungus and so on. They are generally used on fruit, vegetable and horticulture crops. Traditional pest control methods were in use for a long time, but with the increase in human population the demand for food increased many times, and a need was felt to control the diseases and insects that destroy a large part of vegetative crops. Newer chemical methods were therefore developed.

Dichlorodiphenyltrichloroethane (DDT) was synthesized in 1943 and was found to be effective against many insects such as mosquitoes. Due to its hazardous nature, DDT is no longer used nowadays. Other chemicals of a similar nature but safer were synthesized, such as aldrin, dieldrin, heptachlor, mirex and chlordane. These have a targeted action: they control only the desired species and do not affect the good, helpful insects.

Classification of Pesticides

Pesticides are classified on the basis of their action on the specific species that spread disease or affect the crops:

  • Insecticides: substances used to control insects.
  • Fungicides: substances used to control fungus.
  • Herbicides: chemicals used to control unwanted herbs (weeds) in the crops.
  • Miticides: used to kill mites and ticks of the crops.
  • Rodenticides: a large quantity of crop is damaged by rodents such as rats, mice and raccoons; birds and big mammals also affect the crops adversely. These are controlled by rodenticides.
  • Nematicides: chemicals that control harmful nematodes, the tiny hair-like worms that live in the earth and feed on plant roots and the juices from plant roots.
  • Repellents: chemicals that repel harmful pests, insects and other mammals.

Key Points

  • Pesticides are chemicals that control pests, insects, weeds and fungi, mainly on fruit, vegetable and horticulture crops.
  • DDT was effective against mosquitoes but is no longer used because of its hazardous nature.
  • Newer pesticides such as aldrin, dieldrin and chlordane have targeted action on specific species.
  • Insecticides kill insects, fungicides kill fungi and herbicides kill unwanted weeds.
  • Miticides kill mites and ticks, rodenticides control rodents, and nematicides control nematodes.
  • Repellents drive harmful pests and insects away instead of killing them.

mcqs.why: The chemicals derived from petroleum products and used for a variety of commercial purposes are called petrochemicals.

options: Natural gas liquids and oil refinery streams
mcqs.why: Petrochemicals are derived mainly from two feedstocks: natural gas liquids and oil refinery streams.

mcqs.q: Natural gas liquids (NGL) are mainly:
mcqs.why: NGL obtained from natural gas processing plants are mainly ethane, propane and butanes, cracked to ethylene, propylene, butylenes and butadiene.

mcqs.q: Oil refinery streams include:
options: Naphtha, kerosene oil and gas oil
mcqs.why: Oil refinery streams from fractional distillation of crude oil include naphtha, kerosene oil and gas oil, cracked to olefins and aromatics.

mcqs.q: The correct chain for petrochemical production is:
options: Feedstock -> Primary petrochemicals -> Secondary petrochemicals -> Final products
mcqs.why: The chain given is Feedstock to Primary petrochemicals to Secondary petrochemicals to Final products.

mcqs.why: Synthesis gas is carbon monoxide + hydrogen, used for ammonia and methyl alcohol; ammonia is further used to make urea fertilizer.

mcqs.why: Classification table lists olefins as ethylene, propylene, butadiene, while aromatics are benzene, toluene and xylenes.

options: Synthetic detergents, polyurethanes, plastics and synthetic fibres
mcqs.why: Aromatics uses listed are secondary products such as synthetic detergents, polyurethanes, plastics and synthetic fibres.

mcqs.q: Butadiene is mainly used for:
mcqs.why: The feedstock table lists butadiene uses as synthetic rubbers and polymer resins, while ethylene is for antifreeze, detergents, plastics and synthetic rubber.

mcqs.q: Secondary raw materials (intermediates) are produced by:
options: Chemical conversion of primary raw materials into more complicated derivatives like ethylene glycol and PVC
mcqs.why: Secondary raw materials are produced by chemical conversion of primary raw materials into derivative products, e.g. ethylene glycol, polyvinyl chloride and polyethylene resins.

lessons.notes_html:
The chemicals derived from petroleum products and used for a variety of commercial purposes are called petrochemicals. Petrochemicals can be converted into thousands of industrial and consumer products, including plastics, paints, rubber, pesticides, cosmetics, fertilizers, detergents, dyes, textiles and solvents.

Raw Materials for Petrochemicals

A raw material, also known as a feedstock or unprocessed material, is a basic material used to produce goods, finished products or energy, or intermediate materials which are themselves feedstock for future finished products. Petrochemicals are derived mainly from two feedstocks: natural gas liquids and oil refinery streams.

Natural gas liquids (NGL) are obtained from natural gas processing plants. They are mainly ethane, propane and butanes. They are cracked at high temperatures to yield the primary petrochemicals ethylene, propylene, butylenes and butadiene.

Oil refinery streams are obtained from the fractional distillation of crude oil. They include naphtha, kerosene oil and gas oil. They are cracked to produce higher ratios of propylene, butylenes and butadiene, plus the aromatic products benzene, toluene and xylenes, along with other co-products. Primary petrochemicals are reacted to form secondary petrochemicals and other chemical products, or polymerized to form synthetic resins, which are incorporated into a great variety of industrial and consumer products.

Primary raw materials are naturally occurring substances that have not been subjected to chemical changes after being recovered, for example olefins (ethylene, propylene, butadiene), aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes) and methanol. Secondary raw materials (intermediates) are produced by the chemical conversion of primary raw materials into more complicated derivative products, for example ethylene glycol, polyvinyl acetate, polyvinyl chloride, polyethylene resins and phenol-formaldehyde resins. Final products are obtained from secondary raw materials, for example detergents, dyes, cosmetics, solvents, polymers and fertilizers. The chain is: Feedstock → Primary petrochemicals → Secondary petrochemicals → Final products.

Classification of Petrochemical Feedstocks

GroupMain MembersUses
OlefinsEthylene, propylene, butadieneEthylene: antifreeze, detergents, plastics, synthetic rubber. Propylene: resins, fibres and many chemical products. Butadiene: synthetic rubbers and polymer resins.
AromaticsBenzene, toluene, xyleneSecondary products such as synthetic detergents, polyurethanes, plastics and synthetic fibres.
Synthesis gasCarbon monoxide + hydrogenAmmonia and methyl alcohol; ammonia is further used to make urea fertilizer.

Key Points

  • Petrochemicals are chemicals derived from petroleum, used for plastics, paints, rubber, fertilizers, detergents, dyes and solvents.
  • The two main feedstocks are natural gas liquids and oil refinery streams.
  • NGL (ethane, propane, butanes) are cracked to ethylene, propylene, butylenes and butadiene.
  • Refinery streams (naphtha, kerosene, gas oil) are cracked to olefins and the aromatics benzene, toluene and xylenes.
  • Feedstocks are classified as olefins, aromatics and synthesis gas (CO + H2).
  • Synthesis gas is used to make ammonia and methanol; ammonia is used for urea fertilizer.

lessons.title: Synthetic Polymers

mcqs.q: Polymerization is:
options: Process by which monomers are converted into polymers
mcqs.why: The process by which monomers are converted into polymers is called polymerization; polymers are high molecular mass compounds from many monomers.

mcqs.q: Condensation polymerization differs from addition polymerization because it involves:
options: Removal of water or alcohol, as in nylon
mcqs.why: Polymers form either by addition of many monomers, as in PVC, or by condensation with removal of water or alcohol, as in nylon.

mcqs.q: PVC is formed from vinyl chloride at which conditions?
options: 52 C and 9 atmosphere pressure with benzoyl peroxide catalyst
mcqs.why: PVC is formed by addition of vinyl chloride monomer units at 52 degrees C and 9 atmosphere pressure in presence of benzoyl peroxide catalyst.

mcqs.q: PVC is the most widely used plastic after:
mcqs.why: The notes state PVC is the most widely used plastic after polyethylene, and is used for pipes, tiles, bottles, cables and many other materials.

mcqs.q: Which is a natural polymer (biopolymer)?
options: Silk, rubber, cellulose, wool, starch, proteins and DNA
mcqs.why: Natural polymers derived from natural sources include silk, rubber, cellulose, wool, starch, proteins and DNA; polyethylene, PVC and nylon are synthetic.

mcqs.q: The monomer of PVC is:
mcqs.why: Key reaction shows n CH2=CHCl (vinyl chloride) -> -(CH2-CHCl)n- for PVC by addition polymerization.

mcqs.q: Which use of PVC is listed in the notes?
options: Pipes, floor tiles, bottles, electrical wiring, window frames, credit cards and rain coats
mcqs.why: PVC uses listed include pipes, floor coverings (tiles), bottles, electrical wiring and cables, window frames, blood storage bags, credit cards, synthetic leather, rain coats and shower curtains.

mcqs.q: Synthetic polymers are:
options: Man-made polymers prepared by a chemical reaction, often in a laboratory
mcqs.why: Synthetic polymers are man-made polymers prepared by a chemical reaction, often in a laboratory; examples are polyethylene, PVC, synthetic rubber and nylon.

mcqs.q: In the PVC reaction, n CH2=CHCl -> -(CH2-CHCl)n-, if n=1 the product unit contains how many carbon atoms?
mcqs.why: Working: CH2=CHCl has 2 carbon atoms (CH2 = 1 C, CH = 1 C), so one repeat unit -(CH2-CHCl)- also contains 2 carbon atoms.

mcqs.q: Polymers are also called:
mcqs.why: Polymers, also called macromolecules, are high molecular mass compounds formed from many smaller molecules (monomers).

lessons.notes_html:
Polymers, also called macromolecules, are high molecular mass compounds formed either by the addition of many smaller molecules (monomers), as in polyvinyl chloride (PVC), or by the condensation of many smaller molecules with the removal of water or alcohol, as in nylon. The process by which monomers are converted into polymers is called polymerization. Polymers are of two types: natural polymers and synthetic polymers.

Natural polymers, also known as biopolymers, are derived from natural sources. Examples are silk, rubber, cellulose, wool, starch, proteins and DNA. Synthetic polymers are man-made polymers prepared by a chemical reaction, often in a laboratory. Examples are polyethylene, PVC, synthetic rubber and nylon.

Formation and Uses of PVC

Polyvinyl chloride, commonly abbreviated as PVC, is formed by the addition of vinyl chloride monomer units at 52°C and 9 atmosphere pressure in the presence of benzoyl peroxide catalyst. PVC is the most widely used plastic after polyethylene. It is used in the manufacture of pipes, floor coverings (tiles), bottles, electrical wiring and cables, window frames, blood storage bags, stationery, seat coverings, packaging, credit cards, synthetic leather, rain coats, shower curtains and many other useful materials.

Key Reactions

PolymerFormation
PVC (addition polymerization)n CH2=CHCl (vinyl chloride) → -(CH2-CHCl)n- , with benzoyl peroxide at 52°C and 9 atm

Key Points

  • Polymers are high molecular mass compounds made from many monomer units; the process is polymerization.
  • Addition polymerization joins monomers directly (PVC); condensation polymerization removes water or alcohol (nylon).
  • Natural polymers include silk, rubber, cellulose, wool, starch, proteins and DNA.
  • Synthetic polymers include polyethylene, PVC, synthetic rubber and nylon.
  • PVC is made from vinyl chloride at 52°C and 9 atm with benzoyl peroxide catalyst.
  • PVC is used for pipes, tiles, bottles, cables, window frames, credit cards and rain coats.

lessons.title: Formation and Uses of Nylon

mcqs.q: Nylons are high molecular mass:
mcqs.why: Nylons are high molecular mass polyamides, of various types such as nylon 4,6, nylon 6, nylon 6,6 and nylon 6,12.

mcqs.q: Nylon 6,6 is prepared by condensation of:
options: Adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine at about 252 C
mcqs.why: Nylon 6,6 is prepared by condensation reaction of adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine at about 252 degrees C, with loss of water.

mcqs.q: Nylon 6,6 gets its name because:
options: Each monomer provides six carbon atoms
mcqs.why: Each monomer, adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine, provides six carbon atoms, which gives the name 6,6.

mcqs.q: Working from the formulas HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH and H2N-(CH2)6-NH2, total carbons in one pair of monomers is:
mcqs.why: Working: adipic acid carbons = 4 (CH2) + 2 (COOH) = 6; diamine carbons = 6 (CH2); total = 6 + 6 = 12 carbons per monomer pair.

mcqs.q: The nylon 6,6 reaction produces water in amount:
mcqs.why: Key reaction writes products as Nylon 6,6 + (2n-1)H2O at about 252 degrees C, showing condensation with loss of water.

mcqs.q: Nylon resists which conditions according to the notes?
options: High temperature (+85 C), fuel, lubricants and most chemicals, with high strength
mcqs.why: Nylon has high strength, medium stiffness and resistance to high temperature (+85 C), fuel, lubricants and most chemicals, and is believed as strong as steel.

mcqs.q: Which use of nylon is listed?
options: Carpets, textile fibres, brush bristles, ropes and tyre cord
mcqs.why: Uses listed include carpets, textile fibres, bristles of brushes, clothing, elastic hosiery, bearings, gears, food packaging, rope and tyre cord.

mcqs.q: Nylon is used as a substitute for metals in:
mcqs.why: Nylon is used as a substitute for metals in bearings and gears, as listed in the uses of nylon.

mcqs.q: Combining nylon with cotton gives:
options: More strength and durability of the product
mcqs.why: Nylon is used in combination with other materials, for example with cotton, for more strength and durability of the product.

mcqs.q: Nylon 6,6 formation is an example of:
mcqs.why: The key reaction labels nylon 6,6 as condensation polymerization, unlike PVC which is addition polymerization.

lessons.notes_html:
Nylons are high molecular mass polyamides. They are of various types, such as nylon 4,6, nylon 6, nylon 6,6, nylon 6,12 and nylon 12. Nylon 6,6 (read as nylon six, six) is the best-known example. It is prepared by the condensation reaction of adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine at about 252°C. Nylon 6,6 got its name from its monomers, adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine, each of which provides six carbon atoms.

Key Reactions

PolymerFormation
Nylon 6,6 (condensation polymerization)n HOOC-(CH2)4-COOH (adipic acid) + n H2N-(CH2)6-NH2 (hexamethylene diamine) → Nylon 6,6 + (2n-1)H2O, at about 252°C

Nylon has high strength, medium stiffness and resistance to high temperature (+85°C), fuel, lubricants and most chemicals. It is also used in combination with other materials, for example with cotton, for more strength and durability of the product, and it is believed to be as strong as steel metal.

Uses of Nylon

  • In the manufacture of carpets, textile fibres and bristles of brushes.
  • In dress socks, swimwear, activewear, shorts, track pants, windbreakers and bedspreads.
  • For making elastic hosiery.
  • As a substitute for metals in bearings and gears.
  • For food packaging.
  • For making rope.
  • In tyre cord.

Key Points

  • Nylons are polyamides; nylon 6,6 is the best-known type.
  • Nylon 6,6 is made by condensation of adipic acid and hexamethylene diamine at about 252°C, with loss of water.
  • Each monomer of nylon 6,6 provides six carbon atoms, which gives the name 6,6.
  • Nylon is strong and resists heat, fuel, lubricants and most chemicals.
  • Nylon is used for carpets, fibres, brush bristles, clothing, bearings, gears, ropes and tyre cord.

lessons.title: Cosmetics

mcqs.q: Cosmetics are defined as substances used to:
options: Enhance natural beauty and promote good health, applied to the body for cleaning, beautifying or altering appearance
mcqs.why: Cosmetics are substances used to enhance natural beauty and promote good health, applied to any part of the human body for cleaning, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering appearance.

mcqs.q: Colour cosmetics applied to the face are often called:
options: Make-up, e.g. lipsticks, eye liners, nail varnish and powder
mcqs.why: Colour cosmetics applied to the face to enhance appearance are often called make-up, for example lipsticks, eye liners, nail varnish and powder.

mcqs.q: The first known people who used cosmetics were:
mcqs.why: The first known people who used cosmetics to enhance their beauty were the Egyptians, as stated in the cosmetics lesson.

mcqs.q: Lipsticks are manufactured as:
options: Moulded sticks made from waxes, oils, pigments and emollients
mcqs.why: Lipsticks are manufactured as moulded sticks made from waxes, oils, pigments and emollients, with antioxidants, preservatives and fragrances as additives.

mcqs.q: In lipstick, the wax gives:
mcqs.why: Each ingredient has a role: wax gives the lipstick its shape and ease of application; oils give shine, pigments give colour and emollients soften lips.

mcqs.q: Oils in lipstick are added to:
options: Reflect light, provide shine and keep wax soft enough to spread easily
mcqs.why: Oils are added to reflect light and provide shine; they give ability to be easily applied, keeping the wax soft enough to spread easily.

mcqs.q: Emollients in lipstick, such as cocoa butter, shea butter, vitamin E and aloe vera:
options: Soften and smooth the surface of the lips
mcqs.why: Emollients soften and smooth the surface of the lips; important emollients listed are cocoa butter, shea butter, vitamin E and aloe vera.

mcqs.q: Antioxidants in lipstick prevent it from:
options: Becoming rancid, while preservatives extend its shelf life
mcqs.why: Antioxidants prevent the lipstick from becoming rancid, preservatives extend its shelf life, and fragrance gives a nice smell when applied.

mcqs.q: Waxes used in lipsticks include:
options: Beeswax, carnauba, candelilla wax and ozokerite
mcqs.why: The waxes used include beeswax, carnauba, candelilla wax and ozokerite; oils include castor oil, coconut oil, mineral oil, vegetable oil and petrolatum.

mcqs.q: Pigments in lipstick are responsible for:
options: Colour, improving the appearance of the lips
mcqs.why: Pigments are the colours: they give colour to the lipstick and improve the appearance of the lips, distinct from wax, oils and emollients.

lessons.notes_html:
Cosmetics are the substances used to enhance natural beauty and to promote good health. They may also be defined as any substance to be rubbed, poured, sprinkled or sprayed on, or introduced into or applied to any part of the human body, for cleaning, beautifying, promoting attractiveness or altering the appearance. Cosmetics make the skin feel soft, healthy and flawless. Colour cosmetics are designed to add colour to the skin and enhance the appearance of good health and youth; their pigments make the cheeks rosy, the lips ruby and the eyes smoky. Colour cosmetics applied to the face to enhance its appearance are often called make-up, for example lipsticks, eye liners, nail varnish and powder. Make-up also helps in protection from the harmful rays of the sun. The first known people who used cosmetics to enhance their beauty were the Egyptians. Cosmetics are available in the form of creams, lipsticks, shampoos, hair dyes, body wash, eye liners, eye shadows, perfumes, sunscreens, talcum powder, toothpastes, and nail varnish and remover.

Lipsticks

Lipstick is one of the inexpensive cosmetic products and is most widely used by women to give an attractive colour and appearance to the lips. Lipsticks are manufactured as moulded sticks. They are made from waxes, oils, pigments and emollients, with antioxidants, preservatives and fragrances as other important additives. The waxes used include beeswax, carnauba, candelilla wax and ozokerite. The oils used include castor oil, coconut oil, mineral oil, vegetable oil and petrolatum (petroleum jelly). Important emollients are cocoa butter, shea butter, vitamin E and aloe vera.

Each ingredient has a role. The wax gives the lipstick its shape and ease of application. Oils are added to reflect light and provide shine; they give the lipstick the ability to be easily applied, keeping the wax soft enough to spread easily. Pigments are the colours: they give colour to the lipstick and improve the appearance of the lips. Emollients soften and smooth the surface of the lips. Antioxidants prevent the lipstick from becoming rancid, preservatives extend its shelf life, and a little fragrance (perfume) is added by many manufacturers to give it a nice smell when it is being applied.

Key Points

  • Cosmetics are substances applied to the body for cleaning, beautifying or altering appearance.
  • Colour cosmetics applied to the face are called make-up; the Egyptians were the first known users of cosmetics.
  • Lipsticks are moulded sticks made of waxes, oils, pigments and emollients.
  • Wax gives shape, oils give shine and easy spreading, and pigments give colour.
  • Emollients soften the lips; antioxidants prevent rancidity and preservatives extend shelf life.

lessons.title: Nail Varnish and Nail Varnish Remover

mcqs.q: The correct name of nail varnish is:
options: Nail lacquer; varnish, polish, enamel, paint and lacquer are used interchangeably
mcqs.why: The correct name of nail varnish is nail lacquer; the terms nail varnish, nail polish, nail enamel, nail paint and nail lacquer are used interchangeably.

mcqs.q: The four major ingredients of nail varnish are:
options: Resins, plasticizers, organic solvents and colouring agents
mcqs.why: The four major ingredients in most brands are resins, plasticizers, organic solvents and colouring agents.

mcqs.q: Nitrocellulose in nail varnish is a:
options: Hard glossy resin acting as thickening and hardening agent
mcqs.why: Resins act as thickening and hardening agents; two types are hard glossy resins (for example nitrocellulose) and soft pliable resins.

mcqs.q: Plasticizers such as camphor and dibutyl phthalate make the polish:
options: More flexible after drying and increase its durability
mcqs.why: Plasticizers (camphor, dibutyl phthalate, adipates) make the polish more flexible after drying and increase its durability.

mcqs.q: The most common organic solvents in nail varnish are:
mcqs.why: Solvents dissolve ingredients and make polish spreadable; the most common are ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, and varnish must dry quickly.

mcqs.q: Nail varnish remover works by:
options: Softening dried polish and returning it to its liquid state
mcqs.why: Remover is a powerful solvent that works by softening the dried nail polish and returning it to its liquid state.

mcqs.q: Acetone-based removers have the disadvantage that they:
options: Can dry and make nails brittle, irritate nose, eyes, throat, lungs and skin, and remove acrylic nails
mcqs.why: Acetone works quickly but can irritate nose, eyes, throat, lungs and skin, make nails dry and brittle, and remove artificial acrylic or gel nails.

mcqs.q: Mild non-acetone removers preferred for strong, healthy nails use:
options: Ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, less harsh and toxic than acetone
mcqs.why: Most commonly used alternatives are ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, colourless volatile liquids less harsh and toxic than acetone.

mcqs.q: Sparkling particles sometimes in nail polish include:
options: Mica, bismuth, pearl essence (guanine) and aluminium powder
mcqs.why: Particles such as mica, bismuth, pearl essence (guanine) and aluminium powder give a shimmery look to the polish.

mcqs.q: Nail varnish is described as a flexible lacquer that:
options: Does not easily crack and flake with nail movement, and protects and beautifies nail plates
mcqs.why: Nail varnish is a flexible lacquer that does not easily crack and flake with nail movement; it protects and beautifies the nail plates.

lessons.notes_html:
Nail varnish is applied to the fingernails or toenails to colour them or make them shiny. It is used mainly by women, and it protects and beautifies the nail plates. The correct name of nail varnish is nail lacquer; the terms nail varnish, nail polish, nail enamel, nail paint and nail lacquer are used interchangeably. Nail varnish is sold in liquid form in small bottles and is applied by painting the nail with a tiny brush. It is a flexible lacquer that does not easily crack and flake with nail movement. People want brands that are easy to apply, dry quickly, look glossy and last a long time without chipping.

Ingredients of Nail Varnish

There is no single formula for nail varnish. The four major ingredients in most brands are resins, plasticizers, organic solvents and colouring agents.

  • Resins are types of polymers that act as thickening and hardening agents and serve as a colourless nail protector. Two types are used: hard glossy resins (for example nitrocellulose) and soft pliable resins (tosylamide/formaldehyde resin).
  • Plasticizers (for example camphor, dibutyl phthalate and adipates) make the polish more flexible after drying and increase its durability.
  • Solvents dissolve the ingredients and make the polish spreadable. The most common organic solvents are ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, and the varnish must dry quickly to increase the ease of application.
  • Colouring agents (pigments) create the colour of each polish; naturally occurring and synthetic pigments are mixed together to create varying shades.

Sometimes nail polish also contains particles such as mica, bismuth, pearl essence (guanine) and aluminium powder as sparkling and reflective particles, which give a shimmery look to the polish.

Nail Varnish Remover

Nail varnish (or nail polish) remover is a powerful solvent that can quickly remove polish from the nails, cuticles and surrounding skin. It works by softening the dried nail polish and returning it to its liquid state. Remover mainly consists of volatile organic solvents such as ethyl acetate or acetone, and may contain oils, scents and colouring. Acetone is one of the main components of nail polish remover; it is found naturally in the environment and is also produced in factories. It is a colourless, flammable liquid that evaporates easily. Removers that contain acetone work very quickly and effectively, but acetone can be harmful to nails and skin: it can irritate the nose, eyes, throat, lungs and skin, it can make nails dry and brittle, and it can also remove artificial nails made of acrylic or cured gel. Mild non-acetone removers are therefore preferred for strong, healthy nails. The most commonly used alternatives are ethyl acetate and butyl acetate, which are colourless, volatile liquids and are less harsh and toxic than acetone.

Key Points

  • Nail varnish (nail lacquer) colours and protects the nails; it is a flexible lacquer that does not crack easily.
  • Its four major ingredients are resins, plasticizers, organic solvents and colouring agents.
  • Nitrocellulose is a hard glossy resin; camphor and dibutyl phthalate are plasticizers.
  • Ethyl acetate and butyl acetate are the common solvents in nail varnish.
  • Acetone-based removers work fastest but dry and damage nails; ethyl acetate and butyl acetate removers are less harsh.

lessons.title: Hair Dyes

mcqs.q: The first safe commercial hair colour was created in 1909 by Eugene Schueller using:
mcqs.why: The first safe commercial hair colour was created in 1909 by French chemist Eugene Schueller, using the chemical paraphenylenediamine.

mcqs.q: Temporary hair dyes last for:
options: One or two washings, coating only the surface of hair
mcqs.why: Temporary dyes only coat the surface, cannot penetrate the hair shaft, contain no ammonia, and are easily removed with one or two washings.

mcqs.q: Semi-permanent hair dyes last for:
options: Five to ten washings, penetrating into the cuticle layer
mcqs.why: Semi-permanent dyes have smaller molecules, penetrate into the cuticle layer, are generally not formulated with ammonia, and last five to ten washings.

mcqs.q: A semi-permanent dye lasting 5-10 washings lasts how many times longer than a temporary dye removed in 1-2 washings (using maximum values)?
mcqs.why: Working: maximum semi-permanent = 10 washings; maximum temporary = 2 washings; ratio = 10 / 2 = 5 times longer.

mcqs.q: Permanent hair dyes contain ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, where ammonia:
options: Opens the cuticle, while hydrogen peroxide is the developer
mcqs.why: Permanent dyes contain ammonia and hydrogen peroxide: ammonia opens the cuticle and hydrogen peroxide is used as the developer.

mcqs.q: In permanent dyes, small monomer dye precursors penetrate all the way to:
mcqs.why: Dye precursors' small monomer molecules penetrate into the hair all the way to the cortex, giving permanent colour until new hair grows.

mcqs.q: Hair dyes generally contain:
options: Dyes, modifiers, antioxidants, alkalizers, soaps, ammonia, wetting agents, fragrance and other chemicals
mcqs.why: Most hair dyes contain dyes, modifiers, antioxidants, alkalizers, soaps, ammonia, wetting agents, fragrance and other chemicals in small amounts.

mcqs.q: Metal oxides often used as pigments in hair dyes are:
mcqs.why: Dye chemicals are usually amino compounds, and metal oxides such as titanium dioxide and iron oxide are often used as pigments.

mcqs.q: Ingredients in hair dyes suspected to be endocrine-disrupting chemicals are:
mcqs.why: Some ingredients such as resorcinol and parabens are suspected to be endocrine-disrupting chemicals, though chemicals remain at safe levels.

mcqs.q: Permanent hair dyes are usually packaged with:
options: Developer mixed in same bottle always
Developer in a separate bottle, most often based on hydrogen peroxide
Ammonia in a separate bottle only
mcqs.why: Permanent hair dyes are usually packaged with the developer in a separate bottle; the developer is most often based on hydrogen peroxide.

lessons.notes_html:
Hair dyes (also called hair colours) are chemicals that are used to change the hair colour; the preferred professional term is hair colour. The first safe commercial hair colour was created in 1909 by the French chemist Eugene Schueller, using the chemical paraphenylenediamine. This compound is present in colouring products along with ammonia and peroxide in varying proportions. Most hair dyes contain dyes, modifiers, antioxidants, alkalizers, soaps, ammonia, wetting agents, fragrance and a variety of other chemicals in small amounts, which impart special qualities to the hair, such as softening the texture, or give a desired action to the dye, such as making it more or less permanent. The dye chemicals are usually amino compounds, and metal oxides such as titanium dioxide and iron oxide are often used as pigments.

Types of Hair Dyes

Hair dyes are classified by the types of colour molecules used and the length of time they last. There are three main types.

Temporary hair dyes only coat the surface of the hair. They cannot penetrate into the hair shaft and are easily removed with one or two washings. They do not contain ammonia, so the hair shaft is not opened up during processing, and the natural colour of the hair is retained once the product washes out.

Semi-permanent hair dyes have smaller molecules than temporary dyes, so they can penetrate the surface of the hair into the cuticle layer. They are generally not formulated with ammonia, so they do not require any development. They last for five to ten washings, longer than temporary dyes.

Permanent hair dyes are the most common type of hair colouring. The change in hair colour is permanent, or lasts at least until new hair grows. They contain ammonia and hydrogen peroxide: the ammonia opens the cuticle and the hydrogen peroxide is used as the developer. The dyes used are actually dye precursors; their small monomer molecules penetrate into the hair all the way to the cortex. The shades of permanent hair dyes are often more natural-looking, but they can be more damaging to the hair, because the chemicals used are stronger and the mixture usually has to be left on for a longer period of time. Permanent hair dyes are usually packaged with the developer in a separate bottle; the developer is most often based on hydrogen peroxide.

Side Effects of Hair Dyes

The chemicals used in hair dyes remain at safe levels. However, some ingredients found in hair dye, such as resorcinol and parabens, are suspected to be endocrine-disrupting chemicals.

Key Points

  • Hair dyes change hair colour; the first safe commercial hair colour (1909) used paraphenylenediamine.
  • Hair dyes contain dyes, ammonia, peroxide, modifiers, antioxidants, alkalizers, soaps, wetting agents and fragrance.
  • Temporary dyes only coat the hair and wash out in one or two washings.
  • Semi-permanent dyes enter the cuticle and last five to ten washings.
  • Permanent dyes use ammonia to open the cuticle and hydrogen peroxide as developer, and colour the cortex until new hair grows.
  • Resorcinol and parabens in hair dyes are suspected endocrine-disrupting chemicals.

lessons.title: Adhesives

mcqs.q: An adhesive (glue) is a substance that:
options: Binds two surfaces together and resists their separation
mcqs.why: An adhesive, also known as glue, is applied to one or both surfaces of two objects and binds them together and resists their separation.

mcqs.q: Natural adhesives (bioadhesives) are:
options: Produced or extracted from natural resources such as plants or animals, e.g. starch, casein glue and natural gums
mcqs.why: Natural adhesives are produced or extracted from natural resources, examples starch, dextrin, casein glues, blood albumin glue, natural gums, bees wax and resin; they are inexpensive but low strength.

mcqs.q: Thermosetting adhesives are recommended for use at:
options: 93-260 C, for high load assemblies and severe service conditions
mcqs.why: Thermosetting adhesives are recommended for 93-260 degrees C, used for high load assemblies and severe conditions such as heat, cold and radiation.

mcqs.q: The width of the thermosetting temperature range 93-260 C is:
mcqs.why: Working: range width = 260 - 93 = 167 degrees C, using the recommended temperature range given for thermosetting adhesives.

mcqs.q: Thermoplastic adhesives differ because they:
options: Can soften or melt when heated without chemical change and harden on cooling
mcqs.why: Thermoplastic adhesives are fusible and soluble: they soften or melt when heated without chemical change and harden on cooling or by evaporation of solvent.
