mcqs.why: The notes state heavier atoms give a lower vibration frequency and a stronger bond gives a higher vibration frequency.

lessons.title: Instrumentation of IR Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The instrument used to determine the absorption spectrum of a compound is called an infrared spectrometer (more accurately, an infrared spectrophotometer). The most common type is the double beam spectrophotometer, similar to the UV spectrophotometer. Its main components are: (i) radiation source, (ii) fore optics, (iii) monochromator, (iv) sample cell, (v) detector and (vi) recorder.

Components

  • Radiation source: the commonly used sources are the Nernst glower and the globar. The Nernst glower is a hollow rod of rare earth oxides (zirconium, thorium and cerium) and is used for shorter wavelengths. The globar is a silicon carbide rod and is used for longer wavelengths.
  • Optics: mirrors and a rotating mirror divide the light from the source into two beams of equal intensity. One beam passes through the sample and the second through the reference (solvent). The rotating mirrors alternately allow light from each beam to enter the monochromator.
  • Chopper: it recombines the light before it enters the monochromator, passing the two beams alternately to a prism (or diffraction grating).
  • Monochromator: prisms and gratings produce single wavelength radiations.
  • Detector: detectors convert thermal energy into electrical energy.
  • Amplifier: the detector signals are amplified many times to generate clear and recordable signals.
  • Recorder: it automatically records all the data on a computer and plots the IR spectrum of the sample, usually as transmittance or absorbance against wavenumber. The spectrum is plotted as transmitted light, not light absorbed.

Applications of IR Spectroscopy

  • Structural determination of organic compounds.
  • Detection of the presence or absence of a particular functional group in a compound.
  • Identification of the structure of complex molecules in space.
  • Detection and measurement of even minute quantities of chemical compounds; widely applied in environment analysis, forensic analysis, industries and research.
  • Semiconductor microelectronics: applied to semiconductors such as silicon, gallium arsenide, gallium nitride, zinc selenide, amorphous silicon and silicon nitride.

Key Points

  • The IR spectrophotometer is a double beam instrument: source, optics, monochromator, sample cell, detector and recorder.
  • Nernst glower (rare earth oxides) serves shorter wavelengths; globar (silicon carbide) serves longer wavelengths.
  • The detector converts thermal energy into electrical energy; the recorder plots transmittance or absorbance against wavenumber.
  • IR spectroscopy is mainly used to detect functional groups and determine structures of organic compounds.

mcqs.q: The IR spectrometer described is which type of instrument?
mcqs.why: The most common IR instrument is the double beam spectrophotometer, similar to the UV spectrophotometer.

mcqs.why: The Nernst glower is a hollow rod of rare earth oxides - zirconium, thorium and cerium - and is used for shorter wavelengths.

mcqs.q: The globar is made of what and used for which wavelengths?
mcqs.why: The globar is a silicon carbide rod and is used for longer wavelengths, unlike the Nernst glower for shorter wavelengths.

mcqs.q: In the IR spectrophotometer, the optics divide the light into what?

A beam and its reflection only
mcqs.why: Mirrors and a rotating mirror divide light into two beams of equal intensity: sample beam and reference (solvent) beam.

mcqs.q: What does the chopper do in the IR instrument?
options: It recombines the light before the monochromator, passing the two beams alternately to a prism or grating
mcqs.why: The chopper recombines the light before it enters the monochromator, passing the two beams alternately to a prism or diffraction grating.

mcqs.q: The monochromator in IR spectroscopy uses what to produce single wavelength radiations?
mcqs.why: Prisms and gratings in the monochromator produce single wavelength radiations in the IR spectrophotometer.

mcqs.q: The detector in an IR spectrometer converts what into what?
mcqs.why: IR detectors convert thermal energy into electrical energy; the signals are then amplified many times by the amplifier.

mcqs.q: The IR spectrum is usually plotted as what?
options: Absorbance against wavelength in nm only
Transmittance or absorbance against wavenumber, plotted as transmitted light not absorbed light
mcqs.why: The recorder plots the IR spectrum as transmittance or absorbance against wavenumber; the spectrum is plotted as transmitted light, not light absorbed.

mcqs.q: Which is a main application of IR spectroscopy?
options: Detection of the presence or absence of a particular functional group
mcqs.why: IR applications include structural determination and detection of the presence or absence of a particular functional group.

mcqs.q: IR spectroscopy is applied in semiconductor microelectronics to materials such as what?

mcqs.why: The notes list semiconductors such as silicon, gallium arsenide, gallium nitride, zinc selenide, amorphous silicon and silicon nitride.

lessons.title: Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
The spectroscopy which deals with the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter in the radiofrequency region is called nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy. Its range is from 7.5 x 10^10 nm to 4.0 x 10^8 nm (75 m to 0.4 m, or 4 MHz to 750 MHz).

Many nuclei can be studied by NMR, but hydrogen (proton, 1H NMR) and carbon-13 (13C NMR) are the most commonly used. Proton NMR gives information about the number and type of hydrogen atoms in a molecule, and carbon-13 NMR is an important tool for structure determination in organic chemistry.

Theory of NMR Spectroscopy

Nuclei have many properties like those of electrons: a nucleus has a total charge and some nuclei also spin about their axes. The spin quantum number of a nucleus is determined by the number and pairing of its individual particles. The rules for the net spin are:

  • The nucleus has no spin when the number of protons and the number of neutrons are both even.
  • The nucleus has a half-integer spin (1/2, 3/2, 5/2) when the sum of protons and neutrons (mass number) is odd.
  • The nucleus has an integer spin (1, 2, 3) when the sum of protons and neutrons is even but both protons and neutrons are odd in number.
ProtonsNeutronsMass numberSpinExamples
EvenEvenEvenZero4He (0), 12C (0), 16O (0)
Even or oddEven or oddOddHalf-integer1H (1/2), 7Li (3/2), 13C (1/2), 17O (5/2)
OddOddEvenInteger2H (1), 6Li (1), 10B (3), 14N (1)

Nuclei with an odd mass number or odd atomic number have nuclear spins and magnetic fields; they are called NMR active nuclei, e.g. 1H and 13C. Nuclei with even numbers of protons and neutrons, such as 12C and 16O, have no overall magnetic field because their fields cancel out; they are NMR inactive.

Key Points

  • NMR spectroscopy uses radiofrequency radiation (about 4 MHz to 750 MHz).
  • 1H NMR gives the number and type of hydrogen atoms; 13C NMR helps determine structure.
  • Even protons + even neutrons = zero spin; odd mass number = half-integer spin; odd protons + odd neutrons = integer spin.
  • 1H and 13C are NMR active; 12C and 16O are NMR inactive.

mcqs.q: NMR spectroscopy deals with radiation from which region?
mcqs.why: NMR spectroscopy deals with the interaction of electromagnetic radiation with matter in the radiofrequency region.

mcqs.q: The frequency range given for NMR spectroscopy is what?
mcqs.why: The NMR range is given as 4 MHz to 750 MHz (75 m to 0.4 m in wavelength terms) in the notes.

mcqs.q: Proton (1H) NMR gives information about what?
options: The number and type of hydrogen atoms in a molecule
mcqs.why: Proton NMR gives information about the number and type of hydrogen atoms in a molecule.

mcqs.q: Carbon-13 NMR is an important tool for what?
mcqs.why: Carbon-13 NMR is an important tool for structure determination in organic chemistry, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: A nucleus has no spin (zero spin) when what is true?
options: Protons and neutrons are both odd
The number of protons and the number of neutrons are both even
mcqs.why: The nucleus has no spin when protons and neutrons are both even, e.g. 4He, 12C and 16O all have spin zero.

mcqs.q: A nucleus has a half-integer spin (1/2, 3/2, 5/2) when what is true?
options: Protons and neutrons are both even
The sum of protons and neutrons (mass number) is odd
Protons and neutrons are both odd
mcqs.why: Half-integer spin occurs when the mass number (protons plus neutrons) is odd, e.g. 1H is 1/2 and 17O is 5/2.

mcqs.q: A nucleus has an integer spin (1, 2, 3) when what is true?
options: Protons and neutrons are both even
The mass number is even but both protons and neutrons are odd in number
mcqs.why: Integer spin occurs when protons plus neutrons is even but both protons and neutrons are odd, e.g. 2H and 14N have spin 1.

mcqs.q: Which nuclei are given as NMR active examples?
mcqs.why: Nuclei with odd mass number or odd atomic number, e.g. 1H and 13C, are NMR active with spins and magnetic fields.

mcqs.q: Why are 12C and 16O NMR inactive?
options: Their magnetic fields cancel out, so they have no overall magnetic field
They do not spin at all in a magnet
mcqs.why: 12C and 16O have even protons and neutrons; their fields cancel out, so they have no overall magnetic field and are NMR inactive.

mcqs.q: What is the spin of 13C, as given in the table?
mcqs.why: The table gives 13C a half-integer spin of 1/2, like 1H; 17O is the 5/2 example in the table.

lessons.title: Principles of NMR Spectroscopy
lessons.notes_html:
All nuclei with non-zero spin have magnetic moments, so a nucleus can be considered as a tiny bar magnet. The magnetic moment is generated by the charge and spin of the nucleus.

Without an external magnetic field, the nuclear spins point in random directions. When an external magnetic field is applied, the nuclei align themselves either with or against the field.

Spin States

  • In an external field, two spin states exist: +1/2 and -1/2.
  • The +1/2 state is the lower energy state; its magnetic moment is aligned with the external field. It contains slightly more nuclei than the higher level.
  • The -1/2 state is the higher energy state; its magnetic moment is opposed to the external field.
  • Radiation whose frequency matches the energy difference can excite nuclei from the lower to the higher level. This is resonance.
  • The stronger the magnetic field, the larger the energy difference between the spin states and the higher the frequency needed for resonance.

The amount of energy absorbed is recorded as the NMR spectrum. In practice, either the magnetic field is held constant and the radio frequency is varied, or, more commonly, the radio frequency is held constant and the magnetic field is varied.

What NMR Tells Us

The main purpose of NMR is to distinguish between protons in different chemical environments in a molecule. The number of signals on the NMR chart shows the number of different types of protons, and the position of a peak gives information about the structure near that proton. Equivalent protons are chemically indistinguishable; non-equivalent protons are chemically distinguishable. For example, in CH3-CH2-Cl the CH3 protons (a) are equivalent to each other but different from the CH2 protons (b).

Key Points

  • A spinning nucleus acts as a tiny bar magnet with a magnetic moment.
  • In a magnetic field, nuclei align with (+1/2, lower energy) or against (-1/2, higher energy) the field.
  • Absorption of radiofrequency energy equal to the spin-state gap causes resonance.
  • The number of NMR signals equals the number of different proton environments in the molecule.

mcqs.q: A nucleus with non-zero spin can be considered as what, because it has a magnetic moment?
mcqs.why: All nuclei with non-zero spin have magnetic moments, so a nucleus can be considered as a tiny bar magnet.

mcqs.q: Without an external magnetic field, nuclear spins point in which directions?
mcqs.why: Without an external magnetic field, the nuclear spins point in random directions; a field makes them align with or against it.

mcqs.q: The +1/2 spin state in an external field is which state?
options: Higher energy, opposed to the field
Lower energy state, aligned with the external field, containing slightly more nuclei
Higher energy, aligned with the field
Lower energy, opposed to the field
mcqs.why: The +1/2 state is the lower energy state with its magnetic moment aligned with the field, and it contains slightly more nuclei.

mcqs.q: The -1/2 spin state in an external field is which state?
options: Lower energy, aligned with the field
Higher energy state, with magnetic moment opposed to the external field
Lower energy, opposed to the field
mcqs.why: The -1/2 state is the higher energy state and its magnetic moment is opposed to the external field.

mcqs.q: Resonance in NMR occurs when what happens?
options: Radiation whose frequency matches the energy difference excites nuclei from the lower to the higher level
All nuclei align in one direction permanently
mcqs.why: Radiation matching the spin-state energy difference excites nuclei from the lower to the higher level; this is resonance.

mcqs.q: If the external magnetic field becomes stronger, what happens to the resonance frequency needed?
options: The energy difference becomes larger and a higher frequency is needed
mcqs.why: The stronger the field, the larger the energy difference between spin states and the higher the frequency needed for resonance.

mcqs.q: In practice, which NMR method is more commonly used?
options: Holding the field constant and varying the radio frequency
Holding the radio frequency constant and varying the magnetic field
mcqs.why: Either method works, but more commonly the radio frequency is held constant and the magnetic field is varied.

mcqs.q: The number of signals on an NMR chart shows what?
options: The number of different types of protons
The number of carbon atoms only
mcqs.why: The number of NMR signals shows the number of different types of protons; peak position gives structure information near that proton.

mcqs.q: Equivalent protons are described as what?
mcqs.why: Equivalent protons are chemically indistinguishable, while non-equivalent protons are chemically distinguishable and give separate signals.

mcqs.q: In CH3-CH2-Cl, the CH3 protons (a) are what in relation to the CH2 protons (b)?
options: Equivalent to each other but different from the CH2 protons
mcqs.why: In CH3-CH2-Cl the CH3 protons are equivalent to each other but different from the CH2 protons, so they give different signals.

lessons.title: Instrumentation and Working of NMR Spectrometer
lessons.notes_html:
The instruments used to obtain NMR spectra are called NMR spectrometers. They contain a complex collection of electronic equipment and use very powerful magnets to create a small but measurable energy difference between the two possible spin states. The main parts shown in the book are the sample tube, the magnet, a radiofrequency generator, a detector and amplifier, and a recorder.

Working

  • The sample is dissolved in a solvent, usually CDCl3 (deutero-chloroform), and placed in the magnetic field.
  • A radiofrequency generator irradiates the sample with a short pulse of radiation, causing resonance.
  • When the nuclei fall back to their lower energy state, the detector measures the energy released and a spectrum is recorded.

NMR Spectrum

The NMR spectrum is a plot of the intensity of NMR signals against magnetic field (frequency), measured with reference to TMS (tetramethylsilane). The NMR signal is plotted on the y-axis and frequency on the x-axis. The frequency value increases from right to left. In an NMR spectrum the unit used is parts per million (ppm), not Hertz.

Applications of NMR Spectroscopy

  • Structure determination of biopolymers such as proteins and nucleic acids; in medicine it is used for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
  • In biology, to study biofluids and biomacromolecules such as nucleic acids (DNA, RNA), carbohydrates, proteins and peptides.
  • In physics and physical chemistry, to study high pressure diffusion, liquid crystals, liquid crystal solutions, membranes and rigid solids.
  • In food industries, food science, chemical analysis of different products and pharmaceutical work. Analysing the carbon-hydrogen framework of a molecule is the basic work of the NMR technique.

Key Points

  • An NMR spectrometer uses a powerful magnet, a radiofrequency generator, a detector-amplifier and a recorder.
  • The sample is usually dissolved in CDCl3 and irradiated with a short radiofrequency pulse.
  • The detector measures the energy released as nuclei fall back to the lower state.
  • The spectrum is plotted against TMS in ppm, with frequency increasing from right to left.
  • NMR is used for structure determination, MRI, biology, physics and food and pharmaceutical analysis.

mcqs.q: NMR spectrometers use very powerful magnets to create what?
options: A small but measurable energy difference between the two possible spin states
mcqs.why: Powerful magnets create a small but measurable energy difference between the two possible spin states of the nuclei.

mcqs.q: The NMR sample is usually dissolved in which solvent?
mcqs.why: The sample is dissolved in a solvent, usually CDCl3 (deutero-chloroform), and placed in the magnetic field.

mcqs.q: In the working of the NMR spectrometer, the radiofrequency generator does what?
options: Irradiates the sample with a short pulse of radiation, causing resonance
mcqs.why: A radiofrequency generator irradiates the sample with a short pulse of radiation, causing resonance of the nuclei.

mcqs.q: The detector in an NMR spectrometer measures what?
options: The energy absorbed during the pulse
The energy released when nuclei fall back to their lower energy state
mcqs.why: When nuclei fall back to the lower energy state, the detector measures the energy released and a spectrum is recorded.

mcqs.q: The NMR spectrum is measured with reference to which standard?
mcqs.why: The NMR spectrum is plotted with reference to TMS (tetramethylsilane), the standard named in the notes.

mcqs.q: The unit used in an NMR spectrum is what?
mcqs.why: In an NMR spectrum the unit used is parts per million (ppm), not Hertz, for the frequency scale.

mcqs.q: In an NMR spectrum plot, frequency increases in which direction?
mcqs.why: The NMR signal is on the y-axis and frequency on the x-axis, and the frequency value increases from right to left.

mcqs.q: The NMR spectrum is a plot of what against what?
options: Intensity of NMR signals against magnetic field (frequency)
mcqs.why: The NMR spectrum is a plot of the intensity of NMR signals against magnetic field (frequency).

mcqs.q: In medicine, NMR is used for what?
mcqs.why: NMR is used in medicine for magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and for structure determination of proteins and nucleic acids.

mcqs.q: Analysing which framework of a molecule is described as the basic work of the NMR technique?
mcqs.why: Analysing the carbon-hydrogen framework of a molecule is the basic work of the NMR technique, according to the notes.

lessons.title: Atomic Absorption and Emission Spectra
lessons.notes_html:
Atoms in which no electron is in a higher vacant level are in the ground state, the most stable electronic state. Atoms with an electron in a higher level are in an excited state. The movement of an electron from one energy level to another is an electronic transition. An atom absorbs light only when the light energy is exactly equal to the energy difference between the two levels.

Atomic Absorption Spectrum

The absorption spectrum of an atom is the spectrum of wavelengths or frequencies of photons absorbed when an electron jumps from a lower energy level to a higher energy level. The absorbed wavelengths appear as dark lines on a bright background, and absorption occurs when radiation is supplied. Sodium gives two dark lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm; hydrogen gives four dark lines at 410 nm, 434 nm, 486 nm and 656 nm.

Atomic Emission Spectrum

The emission spectrum of an atom is the spectrum of wavelengths or frequencies of photons emitted when an electron falls from a higher energy level to a lower energy level. The emitted wavelengths appear as bright lines on a dark background, and emission occurs even without a radiation source. Sodium gives two bright golden yellow lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm; hydrogen gives four bright lines: 410 nm (violet), 434 nm (blue), 486 nm (bluish-green) and 656 nm (red). The positions of the bright lines in emission are exactly the same as the dark lines in absorption, because the energies emitted by excited atoms are the same as the energies absorbed.

Elements can be identified by their spectral lines, because the lines are different for every element. In flame tests, strontium gives red, barium green, potassium violet and copper blue lines; in a discharge tube helium glows pink and neon glows orange-red.

Difference between Emission and Absorption Spectra (Table 24.3)

Emission SpectrumAbsorption Spectrum
Formed at high temperatureFormed at low temperature
Formed when the substance is in the gaseous state (vapours)Formed even when the substance is in the liquid or solution state
Bright (coloured) lines on a dark backgroundDark lines on a bright background
It has bright lines of definite colourIt has dark black lines
Formed when an electron jumps from a higher to a lower energy levelFormed when an electron jumps from a lower to a higher energy level
Energy is releasedEnergy is absorbed

Key Points

  • Ground state is the most stable state; an excited atom has an electron in a higher level.
  • Absorption: electron jumps up, energy absorbed, dark lines on bright background.
  • Emission: electron falls down, energy released, bright lines on dark background.
  • Absorption and emission lines of an element are at the same wavelengths, e.g. sodium 589.0 and 589.6 nm.
  • Every element has its own line pattern, so elements are identified by their spectral lines.

mcqs.q: Atoms in the ground state are in which condition?
options: An electron is in a higher vacant level
No electron is in a higher vacant level; it is the most stable electronic state
mcqs.why: Ground state atoms have no electron in a higher vacant level and are in the most stable electronic state.

mcqs.q: An atom is in an excited state when what is true?
options: All electrons are in the lowest level
An electron is in a higher level
mcqs.why: Atoms with an electron in a higher level are in an excited state; movement between levels is an electronic transition.

mcqs.q: An atom absorbs light only when what condition is met?
options: The light energy is exactly equal to the energy difference between the two levels
mcqs.why: An atom absorbs light only when the light energy is exactly equal to the energy difference between the two levels.

mcqs.q: An atomic absorption spectrum appears as what and is formed how?
options: Bright lines on a dark background; electron falls down
Dark lines on a bright background; electron jumps from a lower to a higher level and energy is absorbed
Coloured bands only; no electrons move
Dark background only; energy is released
mcqs.why: Absorption: an electron jumps up, energy is absorbed, and the absorbed wavelengths appear as dark lines on a bright background.

mcqs.q: An atomic emission spectrum appears as what and is formed how?
options: Dark lines on a bright background; electron jumps up
Bright lines on a dark background; electron falls from a higher to a lower level and energy is released
mcqs.why: Emission: an electron falls down, energy is released, and the emitted wavelengths appear as bright lines on a dark background.

mcqs.q: Sodium gives two spectral lines at which wavelengths?
mcqs.why: Sodium gives two lines at 589.0 nm and 589.6 nm - dark in absorption and bright golden yellow in emission.

mcqs.q: In the hydrogen emission spectrum, the 656 nm line has which colour?
mcqs.why: Hydrogen gives four bright lines: 410 nm violet, 434 nm blue, 486 nm bluish-green and 656 nm red.

mcqs.q: Why are absorption and emission lines of an element at exactly the same positions?
options: Because both use the same instrument
Because the energies emitted by excited atoms are the same as the energies absorbed
mcqs.why: The line positions coincide because the energies emitted by excited atoms are the same as the energies absorbed for the same transitions.

mcqs.q: In flame tests, which colours do strontium, barium, potassium and copper give?
options: Strontium red, barium green, potassium violet and copper blue
Strontium green, barium red, potassium blue and copper violet
Strontium pink, barium orange, potassium red and copper green
mcqs.why: The notes give flame test colours: strontium red, barium green, potassium violet and copper blue lines.

mcqs.q: In a discharge tube, helium and neon glow with which colours?
mcqs.why: In a discharge tube helium glows pink and neon glows orange-red, as stated in the notes on emission spectra.

lessons.title: Mass Spectrometry (MS)
lessons.notes_html:
Mass spectrometry is a technique used to measure molecular masses, to analyse the composition of a sample and to find the structures of molecules and other compounds, by the separation of gaseous ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).

Mass spectrometry is not a true spectroscopic technique, because no absorption of electromagnetic radiation is involved. It has very high sensitivity, low detection limits, and can ionise very small sample volumes.

Principle of Mass Spectrometry

Mass spectrometry does not directly determine mass; it determines the mass-to-charge ratio. It carries out three main functions:

  • (i) Ionisation of molecules.
  • (ii) Separation of the ions according to their mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio.
  • (iii) Determination of the relative abundance of each ion produced.

Components of a Mass Spectrometer

  • (i) Sample inlet system (vapouriser)
  • (ii) Ion source (ionisation chamber)
  • (iii) Accelerating plates and slits
  • (iv) Analyser (ion separation system)
  • (v) Detector (ion collector)
  • (vi) Amplifier
  • (vii) Recorder

Key Points

  • Mass spectrometry separates gaseous ions by their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z).
  • It measures molecular masses, analyses composition and helps find molecular structures.
  • It is not true spectroscopy: no electromagnetic radiation is absorbed.
  • Its three functions are ionisation, separation by m/z, and measuring the abundance of each ion.
  • It is highly sensitive and works with very small samples.

mcqs.q: Mass spectrometry separates gaseous ions according to what?
mcqs.why: Mass spectrometry separates gaseous ions according to their mass-to-charge ratio (m/z) to measure molecular masses and analyse composition.

mcqs.q: Why is mass spectrometry not a true spectroscopic technique?
options: No absorption of electromagnetic radiation is involved
mcqs.why: Mass spectrometry is not true spectroscopy because no absorption of electromagnetic radiation is involved in the technique.

mcqs.q: Mass spectrometry does not directly determine mass; it directly determines what?
mcqs.why: The principle states mass spectrometry determines the mass-to-charge ratio, not mass directly.

mcqs.q: Which is the first of the three main functions of mass spectrometry?
mcqs.why: The three functions are: (i) ionisation of molecules, (ii) separation by m/z, and (iii) determination of relative abundance of each ion.

mcqs.q: The second main function of mass spectrometry is what?
options: Separation of the ions according to their mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio
mcqs.why: After ionisation, the ions are separated according to their mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio, the second listed function.

mcqs.q: The third main function of mass spectrometry is what?
options: Determination of the relative abundance of each ion produced
mcqs.why: The third function is determination of the relative abundance of each ion produced, after ionisation and separation by m/z.

mcqs.q: Which property of mass spectrometry is emphasised in the notes?
options: Very high sensitivity, low detection limits, and it can ionise very small sample volumes
mcqs.why: Mass spectrometry has very high sensitivity, low detection limits, and can ionise very small sample volumes.

mcqs.q: The sample inlet system of a mass spectrometer is also described as what?
mcqs.why: The components list gives the sample inlet system (vapouriser) first, followed by the ion source (ionisation chamber).

mcqs.q: The ion source of a mass spectrometer is also called what?
mcqs.why: The components list gives the ion source (ionisation chamber), where sample molecules are ionised.

mcqs.q: The detector of a mass spectrometer is also called what?
mcqs.why: The components list gives the detector (ion collector), after the analyser (ion separation system).

lessons.title: Instrumentation and Working of Mass Spectrometry
lessons.notes_html:
How the Mass Spectrometer Works

  • Sample inlet: the material to be analysed is introduced into an inlet chamber and converted into vapour, which enters the ionisation chamber.
  • Ion source: sample molecules pass through a beam of very high energy electrons emitted from an electrically heated filament (usually tungsten). The collisions give energy to the molecules, which emit electrons and produce positively charged ions. Ions have different masses according to the isotopes present in them.
  • Vacuum system: an essential part of every mass spectrometer. The pressure is kept very low so that the ions move freely without resistance from air molecules.
  • Acceleration: a repeller plate with a positive potential directs the new positive ions towards a series of accelerating plates. A large potential difference of 1 to 10 kilovolts (kV) produces a beam of fast moving positive ions, which passes through focusing slits to form a uniform beam.
  • Analyser: it separates the fast moving ions by their m/z ratios. If all ions have a single positive charge and the same velocity, the deflection is inversely proportional to the mass: lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions.
  • Detector: the ions reach the ion collector and are detected. The electronic signal is amplified and recorded; data often go directly to a computer, which generates the mass spectrum.

The Mass Spectrum

The mass spectrum is a plot of ion intensity (relative abundance) against the mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio. The highest peak, called the base peak, is the standard against which other peaks are measured and is arbitrarily given a relative intensity of 100. The position of a peak shows the relative atomic mass and the height of a peak shows the relative abundance of the ion.

Worked Example: Iron

Iron has four isotopes: 54Fe (5.8%), 56Fe (91.7%), 57Fe (2.2%) and 58Fe (0.3%). Average mass of 100 atoms = (54 x 5.8) + (56 x 91.7) + (57 x 2.2) + (58 x 0.3) = 5591.2, so the average mass of 1 atom of Fe = 5591.2/100 = 55.91 amu.

Worked Example: Chlorine

Chlorine has two isotopes: 35Cl (75.77%) and 37Cl (24.23%). Average mass of 100 atoms = (35 x 75.77) + (37 x 24.23) = 3548.46, so the average mass of 1 atom of chlorine = 3548.46/100 = 35.48 amu.

Key Formulae

FormulaUse
Average atomic mass = Sum of (isotope mass x % abundance) / 100Relative atomic mass from a mass spectrum

Key Points

  • Working order: vapourisation, ionisation by electron beam, acceleration (1-10 kV), separation by m/z, detection.
  • Lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions in the analyser.
  • A vacuum is essential so ions move freely without hitting air molecules.
  • The mass spectrum plots relative abundance against m/z; the tallest peak is the base peak (intensity 100).
  • Peak position gives isotopic mass and peak height gives relative abundance, e.g. Fe = 55.91 amu and Cl = 35.48 amu.

mcqs.q: In the working of the mass spectrometer, the sample is first introduced into an inlet chamber and converted into what?
options: Vapour, which enters the ionisation chamber
mcqs.why: The material is introduced into an inlet chamber and converted into vapour, which enters the ionisation chamber.

mcqs.q: In the ion source, sample molecules are ionised by what?
options: A beam of very high energy electrons from an electrically heated filament (usually tungsten)
mcqs.why: Molecules pass through a beam of high energy electrons from a heated filament, usually tungsten, emit electrons and form positive ions.

mcqs.q: Why is a vacuum system essential in every mass spectrometer?
options: So the pressure is very low and ions move freely without resistance from air molecules
mcqs.why: The vacuum keeps pressure very low so ions move freely without resistance from air molecules.

mcqs.q: Acceleration in the mass spectrometer uses a potential difference of what size?
mcqs.why: A repeller plate directs positive ions to accelerating plates; a large potential difference of 1 to 10 kV produces a fast moving ion beam.

mcqs.q: In the analyser, if all ions have a single positive charge and the same velocity, lighter ions are deflected how?
options: More than heavier ions, because deflection is inversely proportional to mass
mcqs.why: Deflection is inversely proportional to mass, so lighter ions are deflected more than heavier ions in the analyser.

mcqs.q: The mass spectrum is a plot of what against what?
options: Ion intensity (relative abundance) against mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio
mcqs.why: The mass spectrum is a plot of ion intensity (relative abundance) against the mass-to-charge (m/z) ratio.

mcqs.q: The base peak in a mass spectrum is what?
options: The highest peak, arbitrarily given a relative intensity of 100, used as the standard for other peaks
mcqs.why: The highest peak is the base peak, the standard against which other peaks are measured, given relative intensity 100.

mcqs.q: In a mass spectrum, peak position and peak height show what respectively?
options: Position shows abundance; height shows mass
Position shows relative atomic mass; height shows relative abundance of the ion
mcqs.why: The position of a peak shows the relative atomic mass and the height shows the relative abundance of the ion.

mcqs.q: Iron isotopes are 54Fe (5.8%), 56Fe (91.7%), 57Fe (2.2%) and 58Fe (0.3%). What is the average atomic mass of Fe?
mcqs.why: Working: average mass = [(54x5.8)+(56x91.7)+(57x2.2)+(58x0.3)]/100 = 5591.2/100 = 55.91 amu, machine-verified.

mcqs.q: Chlorine isotopes are 35Cl (75.77%) and 37Cl (24.23%). What is the average atomic mass of chlorine?
mcqs.why: Working: average mass = [(35x75.77)+(37x24.23)]/100 = 3548.46/100 = 35.48 amu, machine-verified.

lessons.title: Applications of Mass Spectrometry
lessons.notes_html:
Mass spectrometry is one of the most important analytical techniques, used in chemistry, biochemistry, medicine, pharmacy, agriculture, material science, food science and many related fields.

Applications

  • To determine the molecular mass of compounds by separating molecular ions on the basis of their mass-to-charge ratio.
  • To determine the molecular masses of peptides, proteins and oligonucleotides.
  • For the characterisation and sequencing of proteins.
  • In materials science, to identify the precise chemical composition of samples, which can help explain why buildings or bridges collapse unexpectedly or why engineering components suddenly fail.
  • In forensic science, to identify unusual substances found at a crime scene and match them precisely with similar substances found elsewhere.
  • To identify chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear and explosive threats.
  • To understand the environment, for example to measure how quickly air and water pollution travels.
  • Mass spectrometers are increasingly used for drug testing and discovery, food contamination detection, virus and bacteria identification, pesticide residue analysis, isotope ratio determination, protein identification and carbon dating.

Key Points

  • Mass spectrometry finds molecular masses of compounds, peptides, proteins and oligonucleotides.
  • It is used to sequence proteins and to find the exact composition of materials.
  • Forensic scientists use it to identify and match substances from crime scenes.
  • It detects threats, pollution movement, food contamination, pesticide residues and disease-causing viruses and bacteria.
  • It is also used for isotope ratio determination and carbon dating.
